candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive a: This groups reviews that cite concrete program breadth and outcomes: square reviews repeatedly name AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, magnet and CTE pathways (EMT, cosmetology, aviation), high graduation/college‑matriculation rates, National Merit recognition and higher standardized scores, whereas circle reviews lack comparable program lists or outcome metrics (examples: dual‑enrollment credit claims, 98% graduation/97% college continuation, many AP/IB references vs. circle's no outcome data).
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, award‑win: This covers items naming many clubs/teams, state/national championships, award‑winning band/arts, active boosters, alumni ties and required fundraising/volunteer commitments; square reviews document measurable extracurricular achievements and strong booster/alumni engagement (marching band gold, back‑to‑back state champs, active PTSA/boosters, large alumni loyalty), while circle mentions only limited athletics or no comparable awards.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This groups allegations about pervasive peer violence, sexual harassment, racial/ethnic/anti‑LGBTQ harassment, drug dealing/vaping, suicides/protests and administrations failing to act or withholding evidence (examples: repeated fights, sexual assaults, Title IX complaint with 'no updates', police raids and suicides), which are largely absent or not as frequent in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document more pronounced: This groups concrete building and operational problems reported in square reviews—extreme heat/AC failures causing illness, nonfunctioning fire alarms, filthy/vandalized bathrooms, overcrowded classrooms, unresolved modernization needs and logistical breakdowns (device distribution, scheduling, transportation)—whereas circle reviews rarely report comparable facility or operational crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This clusters reports of authoritarian or politicized leadership, nepotism/favoritism, administrators who ignore bullying or reverse victim/attacker roles, staff gossip/privacy breaches, inconsistent counselor guidance or counselor cuts, and chaotic communication (examples: principal protecting child, teachers throwing things, counselors reduced from four to two, 'staff discuss students' private matters'), problems that circle reviews do not emphasize to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries document more pervasive s: These reviews report concrete, repeated safety failures (weekly fights, widespread bullying, drug and gang presence, knives/sexual misconduct, unsupervised dangerous incidents) and poor or inconsistent follow‑up (failed Title IX response, failure to notify parents), e.g. “There are fights all of the time…huge drug problem,” “students come to school high…bring knifes,” and administrators who “did absolutely NOTHING about the bullies.” This bucket groups items where square reviewers describe systemic physical‑safety and behavior problems and weak supervision/response that circle reviews do not.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more con: These reviews list tangible academic programs and credentials (many APs, IB evidence, dual‑enrollment/Kirkwood partnerships, Advanced Learning Center, new STEM buildings, block/mod scheduling, formal test‑prep) and measurable outcomes (rankings, scholarships), e.g. “lots of AP classes and concurrent enrollment,” “Partnership with Kirkwood allowing students to earn tuition free college credit,” and “new Science, Technology, Engineering and Math building.” This bucket captures cases where square reviews describe concrete programmatic college‑prep capacity that circle reviews lack.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more administrativ: These items describe leadership and district‑level problems—coverups, protected relatives/teachers, discipline favoritism for athletes, refusal to honor transfers for funding, dishonest/inconsistent communication, and board/superintendent nonresponse—e.g. “Rules don't apply to them or their relatives,” “denying parents transfer…because they need the money,” and “reaching out to the board members get you nowhere.” Grouped here are administrative actions and governance failures square reviewers attribute to the school/district more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight broader, higher: These reviews enumerate extensive, high‑quality extracurriculars and parent/community supports (large music/theater programs, national tours, state championships, 80+ clubs, booster fundraising, on‑site partnerships and boarding/international programs), e.g. “band is one of the best in the nation…traveled to China,” “over 80 clubs…AWESOME athletics,” and “parent involvement in the Booster Club has never been more robust.” This bucket groups concrete evidence of rich extracurricular and community engagement that square entries report more than circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: These reviews simultaneously report polarized instructional experiences—examples of very engaged, long‑tenured teachers, one‑on‑one academic help, strong special‑education supports and counseling, and formally organized remediation (math labs, tutoring/Bronco Nation)—alongside claims of many ineffective teachers, grade‑inflation/leniency, heavy homework, or outdated materials, e.g. “The principal helped me personally to help me pass,” “excellent guidance counselors,” but also “many teachers who need to be evaluated” and “we need new books in almost every class.” This bucket groups teacher‑level variability and the presence of individualized supports or remediation that square reviewers describe more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and more c: This bucket groups items where square reviews list specific program availability and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment/Running Start, CTE/BOCES, academies like AVID/Matador Scholar, specialized academies, and named college acceptances) while circle reviews lack comparable program depth or outcome evidence (examples: “AP courses, Running Start…college credits,” “new biotechnology lab…humanoid robotics,” and measurable college acceptances versus Circle’s absence of such offerings or outcomes).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete safety and climate reports concentrated in square: recurring physical fights, lockdowns, guns/drug incidents, cyber/verbal bullying, and claims of cameras or surveillance failures coupled with inadequate or inconsistent administrative responses (examples: “fights every day between classes,” “weekly lockdowns,” threats of shootings, “bullying…school does nothing,” and reports of suspension policies that remove students from learning).
candidate_defs.square entries show stronger facility, e: This bucket groups facility and scale issues found in square reviews—very large student populations, crowding, mandatory district busing, bond‑funded capital projects and simultaneous reports of both renovation and severe decay or cleanliness problems—contrasted with Circle’s portrayal of smaller scale or fewer facility crises (examples: “full size high school with 3000 students…so crowded,” “bond passed facilitating performing arts center,” and “old building…bathrooms/roof leaks”).
candidate_defs.square entries describe contested resour: This bucket includes concrete claims in square about where money goes and how access is funded—parent fundraising to keep arts afloat, fees for extracurricular participation, high‑cost turf/athletic projects amid textbook or staffing shortfalls, and explicit accusations that sports/facilities are prioritized over instruction (examples: “Invest more in students needs, less on 400,000 turf,” “parent fundraisers cover music,” and “pay to participate in extracurriculars”), which Circle reviews do not typically assert.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater operationa: This bucket groups operational and instructional service problems emphasized in square: teachers skipping instruction or giving work not taught, frequent absences/empty classrooms, crammed pacing, counselors who gatekeep advanced placement, reliance on paid tutoring or summer credit recovery, and IEP/504 coordination lapses or inconsistent special‑ed support (examples: “they just hand out a worksheet…empty classroom,” “you might have to know the guidance counselor to get into smart physics,” “parents paying for tutoring,” and “no IEP/504 coordinator”), patterns that Circle reviews do not portray to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety harms and failures absent from circle: daily fights, assaults, police escorting students, rampant bullying, drug/gang exposure, student suicide attempts and victim‑blaming by administrators (e.g., “There are fights every day… My child attempted suicide… They did nothing,” “Huntersville Police walk students out on a daily basis”). They also document ineffective or retaliatory responses to incidents, tying unsafe student behavior to an overall unsafe climate.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a wider, concret: Square reviews enumerate specific program offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/AVID/CTE, AFJROTC, award‑winning band/chorus/theatre, internships, STEM and culinary CTE, dual‑enrollment/college credit partnerships) and cite measurable successes (state band championships, 12 free college credit hours, National Merit counts), while circle reviews lack comparable named programs or competitive accomplishments.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square texts repeatedly report administrative problems and operational breakdowns—unreturned guidance/office calls, withheld transcripts/fees and aggressive collections, inaccurate grade/transcript errors, micromanagement/turnover, arbitrary or uneven discipline and favoritism (e.g., “Office doesn’t return calls… They will hold your transcripts if you don't pay… principals provide zero leadership… favoritism to athletes”). These are concrete governance/operations failures rather than mere tone.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, mai: Square reviewers raise tangible physical‑plant issues missing in circle: asbestos and mold claims, locked/insufficient bathrooms, extreme temperatures, leaking stairways, lack of A/C, overcrowded classrooms/portable trailers and limited parking, alongside both complaints about filthy conditions and accounts of recent capital upgrades (new buildings, renovated pools), indicating persistent facility and capacity instability.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater academic tra: Square reviews document pronounced within‑school stratification and instructional variability—honors/AP/IB students getting preferred teachers and resources while regular/ESL/special‑ed students are underserved, counselor scheduling barriers, refused AP placement, special‑education identification failures, and claims of grade inflation or low rigor in some tracks (e.g., “the smart kids get the good teachers… ESL students get the short end… guidance counselors refused to help with scheduling”). These are specific patterns of inequity and inconsistent instruction distinct from program availability.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: These reviews emphasize concrete school‑level academic offerings and evidence (AP/IB/honors counts, dual‑credit/CCP, AVID, specialized academies) and measurable outcomes (AP pass rates, Ivy/Selective acceptances, large scholarship awards) that Circle reviews do not. Examples: Square notes 'over 21 AP courses', an established IB program, College Credit Plus/dual enrollment, and students accepted to Johns Hopkins/Georgetown/ivy‑level scholarships, while Circle gives no program counts or concrete postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader extracur: These reviews list extensive non‑core programming—CTE shops, robotics, aviation, Academic Decathlon, performing arts, many clubs and electives—and concrete classroom/IT infrastructure (1:1 devices, Promethean boards, Apple/Adobe software) that Circle reviews rarely mention. Examples: Square names 'robotics, culinary, small animal care, #1 jazz/ band, a magnet arts program' and 'each classroom has a Promethean board; every student is given a netbook,' whereas Circle omits or limits such named programmatic and tech resources.
candidate_defs.square entries document a visible, commu: Square reviews both praise community support, large attendance, feeder systems and award‑winning teams and simultaneously report preferential leniency for athletes, hand‑picked/closed tryouts, and athletics dominating social status; Circle mentions sports but does not report favoritism or opaque selection. Examples: Square cites 'state football championship, great feeder system' alongside 'if you play a sport you don't get into trouble' and 'athletic director handpicked teams,' which Circle reviews do not assert.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent safe: These reviews catalogue concrete safety problems (fights, theft, sexual harassment, drug/gang activity, lack of supervision) and describe administration minimizing complaints, delayed punishment, or protecting favored students—patterns Circle reviews largely do not report. Examples: Square details 'students assaulted, stolen property, heroin epidemic, race wars, sexual harassment' plus statements like 'they try to down play parents when reporting bullying' and 'punishment is meted out days or weeks after the behavior,' while Circle contains little or no such incident-level reporting.
candidate_defs.square entries more often highlight oper: These reviews point to funding‑driven staff reductions and consequences (janitorial cuts, roaches, cafeteria problems), chronic overcrowding/trailers, long enrollment lines, limited transportation for after‑school activities, and either shortages or highly variable counselor/guidance services; Circle reviews rarely raise these combined operational/resource details. Examples: Square mentions 'cutting staff...closed one cafeteria...roaches in classrooms,' 'overpopulated schools...trailers,' '2 hours standing to get schedule,' limited bussing, and both 'guidance program is awful' and, in other reviews, concrete mental‑health and dropout‑prevention supports—operational facts Circle does not consistently report.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader formal a: These reviews repeatedly name formal tracks and partnerships—IB and magnet programs, many AP/Pre‑AP classes, dual‑credit/college partnerships, engineering/medical/CTE academies, plus strong music, marching band, theater, ROTC and athletics—while circle reviews rarely list comparable, school‑level programs (e.g., Square: “IB, PACE, AVID, AP, PLTW, Ski Academy, excellent band”; Circle: little or no IB/AP/magnet detail). Falling here means the school is described as having explicit, named program pathways and high extracurricular breadth and specialization relative to the other group.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: Many square reviews allege pervasive student‑safety issues—drugs and in‑school dealers, gang mentality, daily fights, sexual coercion for rides, unreported assaults, and suicidal/anxiety impacts—whereas circle reviews rarely document these systemic safety incidents. Content in this bucket centers on recurring student misconduct or unsafe peer climates that reviewers say materially harm wellbeing and require stronger safety response.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility and: Square reviewers frequently cite concrete physical problems—mice/cockroaches, closed bathrooms, severe overcrowding and 40+ class sizes, broken vocational equipment, outdated/insufficient computers and device rollouts—while circle reviews are more likely to mention planned new construction or incremental improvements rather than chronic neglect. Items in this bucket describe the school's built environment and material resource shortfalls (or crowding) as actually affecting daily operations and learning.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square contains many named incidents and systemic complaints about adult behavior—teacher/coach rudeness or sexual misconduct allegations, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, punitive/overzealous administrators (armed escorts, unfair sanctions), principal self‑promotion, lost transcripts, and ignored parental communications—while circle reviews more often describe caring teachers and fewer such governance failures. This bucket captures governance, adult professional conduct, biased discipline, and operational mismanagement problems distinct from classroom instruction.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater instructio: Square reviewers document instructional problems—frequent substitute‑covered classes, teachers teaching outside certification, misassignment, low differentiation for gifted/college‑bound or special‑needs students, missed graduation requirements—whereas circle reviews more often praise consistent, caring teachers and support. Content here is about the delivery of instruction and academic support (staffing, teacher quality, counseling/IEP follow‑through), not the mere presence of programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket groups reports about peer behavior and on-campus safety: square reviewers repeatedly describe fights in cafeterias, numerous bullying incidents, racial slurs and harassment, widespread drug/vaping use (even deaths), spectator misconduct, and sexualized/misconduct among students — complaints that circle reviews do not raise (circle emphasizes peer acceptance and brotherhood instead). Examples: “videos of fights in the cafeteria,” “I've never heard more racial slurs,” and “Drugs are a HUGE problem” are emblematic square items in this category.
candidate_defs.square entries document a broader set of: This bucket captures listings of formal academic and extracurricular pathways and their outcomes: many square reviews enumerate AP/IB/Cambridge programs, dual‑enrollment and college-credit wins, vocational/CTE tracks, strong arts and competitive teams, no‑cut policies, JROTC, and named extracurriculars, plus alumni/college placement evidence; circle entries generally lack that breadth of named programs or measurable outcomes. Examples: “dual enroll at KCC… Math and Science Center,” “17 AP classes… choir, band, theater,” and alumni succeeding at selective colleges.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects governance and personnel problems: square reviewers allege administration protects teachers, selectively enforces discipline, rehired or hired relatives, tolerated or mishandled sexual/unprofessional staff conduct, suppressed student political expression, and show signs of district-level corruption or lack of accountability — issues not claimed in circle. Examples: “administration 'always' backs the teacher,” “principal asked to resign pending police investigation,” “create[s] positions for friends and family,” and “told us not to make it political (walkout).”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, c: This bucket groups concrete evidence of staff responsiveness and instructional support: circle reviews frequently describe dependable, caring teachers, returning work, effective counseling or special-education support, and proactive teacher–parent communication, whereas square entries more often report teacher subject-knowledge gaps, poor feedback, inconsistent special-ed support, or unhelpful counselors. Examples: circle: “teachers that really care…returned emails,” “special needs aide provided”; square: “teachers didn’t know what they were teaching,” “counselors don’t reply to emails.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete oper: This bucket covers tangible infrastructure and operational limits: square reviewers cite overcrowded classes and trailers, full/limited AP sections, schedule/capacity forcing inappropriate placements, broken A/C and dirty facilities, locked bathrooms, slow security response and poor emergency drills, staffing cuts and shortages, and lack of COVID remediation, items circle seldom mentions. Examples: “overwhelmed by overcrowding… classes in trailers,” “only one or two of each AP class,” “A/C constantly broken,” and “pushed through the system without COVID remediation.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety/behavi: These reviews describe concrete student‑safety problems (frequent fights, drugs/vaping, weapons, lockdowns, gang activity) and explicit failures of anti‑bullying or safety follow‑through (victim punishment, inconsistent lockdown handling, bullying ignored) that circle reviews do not; examples include “lots of bullying and drugs,” “gun found in backpack,” “code red lock downs,” and “supports bullying, punishes victims.”
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: Many square reviews name specific, high‑level academic offerings and outcomes (AP/IB breadth, dual enrollment, PSEO, college credits, scholarships, alumni at selective universities and measurable test scores) whereas circle lacks comparable evidence; examples include “IB/DP prepares you for university,” “tons of AP classes,” “paid AP exams and 46 college credit hours,” and alumni at MIT/Stanford/Harvard.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater athletics: These entries repeatedly depict sports as prioritized (recruitment draw, state championships, athletics > arts/academics), coaches/admin protecting athletes from discipline, and counselor/teacher favoritism toward athletes—claims not present in circle; examples include “the district cares far more about its sports programs,” “if you are an athlete you get away with whatever,” and “counselors only support the students that are athletes.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete fa: Square reviews provide specific, actionable accounts of physical condition and operations—cleanliness, maintenance needs, overcrowding, bussing/out‑of‑district enrollment, cafeteria/food problems, tech access, grade/communication systems and front‑office registration/residency issues—whereas circle is less specific; illustrative lines include “unsanitary bathrooms,” “overcrowded (3100 kids),” “bussed in from other cities,” “no wifi for students,” and “they do not return phone calls.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff mistrea: Many square reviews allege active staff‑perpetrated mistreatment (demeaning remarks, swearing at students, shaming parents, coaches/administrators bullying, racial microaggressions and unequal discipline), in contrast to circle which frames staff problems more as indifference; supporting examples include “teacher telling a student they are worthless or cursing at them,” “staff... bullies,” “teachers shame you instead of partnering,” and reports of administrative/coaching misconduct.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket groups raw terms describing concrete student-safety harms and institutional failure to stop them — e.g., allegations of on-campus drug dealing, students bringing knives/brass knuckles, multiple suicides/overdoses, widespread vaping and substance use, violent assaults, and repeated reports that bullying (including racial/anti‑LGBTQ harassment) is tolerated or mishandled. Circle entries either omit these problems or explicitly minimize them, so items that document actual violent incidents, substance epidemics, suicides, or both high prevalence + poor institutional response belong here.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket captures concrete academic-program and support evidence in square reviews: multiple AP/IB/PSEO/dual‑enrollment offerings, accredited academies (STEM/NAF/CAPA), AP/ACT prep, named high‑quality instructors, tutoring programs, and stated outcomes (high test scores, scholarships, top university matriculation). Circle reviews generally lack this kind of concrete program catalog, outcome statistics, or teacher-run tutoring examples, so documents about formal advanced coursework, college pipelines, and hands‑on academic supports are placed here.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: This bucket includes concrete administrative and policy-related breakdowns: poor scheduling and course-pulling, misplaced or inconsistent course placement, ineffective guidance/counseling for course selection or college admission, late/untimely grade reporting, punitive pass/restroom/tardy policies that cause missed class time, canceled tutoring, and chronic communication failures (unreturned calls, broken portals). Circle reviews typically do not report this breadth of operational or guidance failures, so items documenting those logistics/policy breakdowns belong here.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit faci: This bucket groups concrete physical- and capacity-related evidence: claims that school buildings are unsafe/old or newly rebuilt, rodent infestations, filthy/locked/damaged bathrooms, severe overcrowding and wayfinding problems, major construction disruptions, perimeter fencing creating a 'prisonlike' feel, and consistent bussing/transportation mismanagement. Circle reviews largely omit these physical/infrastructure specifics, so terms focused on facilities, space, pests, renovations and transport fit here.
candidate_defs.square entries report more entrenched so: This bucket covers systemic social dynamics and inequity documented in square reviews: socioeconomic and racial segregation, pervasive cliquey/appearance-based exclusion, teacher/administrative favoritism (including sports-based nepotism), targeted exclusion of school‑choice or nonconforming students, and reports that race, religion, or sexual orientation invite harassment or discriminatory treatment. Circle entries emphasize a more inclusive, familylike mission and therefore items describing persistent social hierarchies, favoritism, or identity‑based exclusion are grouped here.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe richer, more div: These entries repeatedly list concrete program offerings and measurable outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑credit, CTE/vocational tracks, nursing/aviation/engineering pathways, extensive music/robotics/drama programs, sustained athletics championships and Ivy/conservatory matriculation) that Circle reviews do not; examples include named dual‑credit partnerships, magnet/academy lists, award‑winning robotics/band, and frequent college-placement citations.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews document frequent physical fights, drug/vape use, gang activity, quantified substance‑use claims, homophobia/racial harassment, teen suicides, and repeated allegations that incidents went unaddressed—concrete safety/crisis descriptions that Circle reviews lack.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more administrat: Square reviewers cite strict punitive attendance/documentation rules, forced transfers, heavy administrative red tape, frequent leadership turnover, accusations of favoritism/nepotism/grade manipulation, superintendent/board policy criticisms and even auditing/scandal claims—specific governance and policy problems not found in Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries contain more evidence of: These entries detail teacher apathy or excellence, verbal harassment, delayed grading, ineffective counselors/special‑education responses, uneven instruction and homework/rigor disparities, and high staff turnover or low morale—concrete classroom/staff behaviors and communication patterns that distinguish Square from Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more acute facilit: Square reviews provide specific facility and resourcing facts—overcrowded halls, trailers, asbestos or renovation projects, 1:1 tablet/iPad programs (sometimes malfunctioning), cafeteria crowding, and explicit out‑of‑pocket fundraising or activity fees and community scholarships—that Circle reviews do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket groups notes that square reviews enumerate concrete advanced-course and college-prep offerings (AP classes, IB diploma, engineering honors, dual enrollment, magnet/academy programs, CNA/EMT or career pathways) and cite measurable postsecondary outcomes (high college continuation rates, scholarships, National Merit, Ivy acceptances) while circle reviews give only generic claims about education; examples: square mentions 'IB Diploma,' 'AP to freshmen,' 'dual enrollment with UI/MCC,' and '95% go to college.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more organized, di: This captures square reviewers' specific listings of many clubs, arts/performing‑arts programs, competitive sports, travel/opportunity programs, and concrete facility spending (new field, gym floor, $12M athletic facility), contrasted with circle reviews that mention few or discontinued activities; examples: 'almost 30 after‑school clubs,' 'outstanding music and theater programs,' and 'new football field & gym floor' appear in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete spec: Square reviews frequently name special‑education staff, IEP work, counseling outreach (including pandemic check‑ins), transition programs, bilingual/military liaison supports and explicit accommodations, whereas circle reviews contain little or no evidence of these supports; examples: 'autism support teacher,' 'counselor inquired as to his mental health during COVID‑19,' 'good special education teams to work on IEP,' and Spanish‑language parent praise.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups concrete incident reporting in square reviews — recurring fights, bathroom vaping closures, drug availability, violent bullying and even law‑enforcement presence — whereas circle reviews rarely offer comparable incident detail; examples: 'bathrooms closed due to vaping,' 'fights every day,' 'easy access to drugs,' and 'cops in the parking lot' are documented in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational,: Square reviewers provide repeated, specific claims about administrators and district governance — refusal to return calls, leadership turnover, alleged corruption, union/board conflict, arbitrary or inconsistent enforcement, gradebook errors/grade inflation, and favoritism — while circle offers far fewer such governance‑level complaints; examples: 'superintendent raised salary and corruption investigated,' 'counselors don't return your calls,' 'many teachers are not qualified,' and 'parents pressure teachers to inflate grades.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: These reviews name and quantify formal college-prep offerings and results (AP/IB/dual-enrollment/honors, AP credit hours, National Merit, named college placements) — e.g., “30+ hours of credit from AP courses,” “has excelled to become an IB school,” “students accepted to Ivy League schools” — details that are largely absent from circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries document more numerous, h: Square reviews enumerate large, award-winning extracurricular infrastructures and competitive pipelines (championship athletics, nationally‑recognized band/choir, robotics, internships, JROTC, CTE certifications and leadership awards) and list specific programs and successes (state championships, National History Day, Rotary/Hoosier awards), whereas circle reviews rarely provide comparable program breadth or high‑level competitive outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic stud: These entries contain multiple concrete incidents and harms (racial slurs and assaults filmed on social media, sexual harassment, repeated threats that forced online enrollment, drug/violence reports) plus allegations of poor follow‑up or concealment by staff/administration — e.g., “horrifying story of bullying, racism and the lack of urgency,” “so now I’m basically forced to enroll my children into online schooling to insure their safety.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Reviews document district/school policy and governance failures (budget cuts and alleged misuse of funds, enrollment-for-funding claims, administration dominated by coaches, pressured grade inflation, suppression of dual‑credit programs, frequent principal turnover and hiring controversies) — concrete operational decisions and favoritism/selection problems not present in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: These texts specify physical and logistical facts about the school: overcrowded enrollment and buses, dilapidated vs thoughtfully‑renovated buildings, block scheduling and in‑day tutoring (smart lunch), 1:1 laptop programs, fab labs, poor entrance design and cafeteria quality (e.g., “student population is out of control, over 2500 students,” “we recently installed a distance learning lab,” “food stinks”), which circle entries typically do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe concrete, recurring safety problems—weekly fights, gang activity, on-campus drug use/vaping, sexual harassment/assault, thefts and threats—and many accounts that reporting was ignored or handled poorly (e.g., 'gang activity, constant fights, a huge presence of drugs', 'they do nothing about bullying unless the child has been hit'). Circle entries do not document comparable frequencies or severities of violence, drugs, or systematic failure to protect students.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader advanced: Many square reviews list extensive honors/AP/IB curricula, dual-enrollment/A+ opportunities, AP test funding (VASS), and concrete outcomes (high SAT/ACT scores, high college-admit rates, US News rankings), e.g. 'JF offers the most AP classes... VASS grant', '95% get into the college of their choice', whereas circle reviews lack comparable claims of AP breadth, dual-credit programs, or strong outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a wider, better-: Square reviews repeatedly praise substantial arts and competitive programs (standout band, choir, robotics, speech & debate, wrestling, long-running athletic dominance) and organized parent fundraisers/PTSA (FoSOTA), for example 'an amazing band program', 'robotics received regional recognition', and 'an engaged PTSA,' while circle reviews mention athletics but do not report the same breadth, competitive success, or structured booster support.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews include allegations of cover‑ups, retaliation, strict zero‑tolerance/harsh filtering policies, leadership turnover and experiments (firing calls, 'caught them red-handed and I was let go', 'zero tolerance... very strict', removal of planning periods), and claims of favoritism/'good old boys' dynamics—distinct governance and personnel complaints that circle reviews do not raise with comparable frequency.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive ins: Circle reviews emphasize that teachers 'don't even teach' or are uniformly 'terrible', and describe dysfunctional instructional practices that undermine preparation (e.g., middle-school instruction that discouraged SHSAT prep), limited hands‑on or shop competency, and poor leadership contact with parents—patterns of classroom-level instructional breakdown and lack of preparatory structure that are more prominent in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pervasive saf: Reviews grouped here describe frequent, concrete safety problems (daily fights, gang violence, weapons on campus, repeated lockdowns), normalized racist/slur usage, widespread bullying left unaddressed, and active drug/alcohol use with inconsistent security responses (examples: “fights on a daily basis,” “students who have weapons on campus,” “bullying is HORRIBLE and the administration did nothing,” “drug dogs often find contraband”), whereas Circle reviews do not document this level of ongoing physical-threat incidents or enforcement failure.
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader and stro: These reviews enumerate concrete programs and outcomes—IB programs, high AP counts, AP/dual‑credit and early‑college pathways, vocational certificates (welding, CNA), JROTC, Running Start, MBIT, and reported college admissions/scholarship metrics (examples: “IB Diploma Program…they were more than prepared for college,” “graduated with almost 60 college credits,” “early college program…associates degree”), while Circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth, credentialing, or concrete postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more teacher unpro: This bucket covers concrete staff behaviors and classroom practices: teachers verbally abusing students, routinely failing to teach or enforce classroom management, accepting late work for full credit, or inflating grades so students pass without mastery (examples: “Teacher called me dumb,” “teachers rarely teach,” “passed my older child with 'A's rather than actually requiring her to learn anything,” “assignments accepted for full credit at any point”), whereas Circle reviews generally emphasize consistently helpful or rigorous teachers and do not document these pervasive instructional failures.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: Reviews in this group describe concrete governance issues—lost enrollment/registration paperwork, unanswered calls/emails, alleged nepotism or leaders protecting friends, contested budget priorities or manipulations of statistics, and punitive/opaque policy choices (examples: “No Response to calls/emails,” “hostile work environment…save his spouse, friends,” “question the financial integrity of this school,” “lost the school they were transferring in from paperwork”), while Circle reviews present fewer or no such district‑level misconduct or systemic transparency accusations.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more failures, inc: This bucket groups concrete accounts of denied accommodations, unenforced 504s/IEPs, discriminatory tracking that blocks IEP students from AP/honors, overloaded or unresponsive counselors, alongside occasional reports of excellent special‑ed/counselor support (examples: “accommodations I had from my 504 were not enforced,” “they will not allow IEP students to take AP,” “the counselors each have 300 kids…won't even listen,” and also “the special education team was awesome”), whereas Circle reviews lack comparable, consistent evidence of special‑education procedural failures or varied counseling access.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket groups reports of on‑campus physical harm and safety threats: fights, bullying escalating to assaults, hallway drug deals and overdoses, vaping, gun/bomb threats, and recurring police/ security presence or absence (e.g., 'drug deals are made in the hallways', 'so many deaths of drug overdoses and drunk driving', 'there are A LOT of fights', 'police cars outside every single day'). These items describe concrete student behavior and safety conditions inside and around the school rather than perceptions of tone or satisfaction.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: This bucket captures concrete program availability and measurable outcomes reported by reviewers: explicit lists of AP/IB/Honors classes, dual‑enrollment and Governor's‑school links, CTE/academy pathways, STEM partnerships, and named college matriculations or SAT/test achievements (e.g., 'lots of AP classes including AP Calculus', 'Dual Enrollment at Greenfield Community College', 'students accepted to UNC‑CH/NC State and Ivy/Stanford/MIT'). These are factual program/outcome claims about course pathways and college/career results, distinct from everyday teaching quality or climate.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups operational and governance failures tied to adults: slow/absent communication (weeks to respond, outdated portals), punitive discipline and victim‑blaming (suspending attacked students), mishandled credits/transcripts/enrollment and remote‑learning barriers, rapid principal/staff turnover, and allegations of teacher misconduct or financial malfeasance (e.g., 'they didn’t calculate credits correctly…we are still fighting them', 'most of the good teachers have left due to the horrible administration', 'one teacher was fired for sleeping with a student', 'teachers absconded funds'). These items concern how staff and leaders run the school and manage policies/records rather than program listings or student supports.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and bett: This bucket groups concrete non‑academic offerings and campus assets: named extracurriculars (award‑winning bands, theater, robotics, culinary restaurant, JROTC), athletic championships and new athletic facilities (new pool, stadium, ropes course), after‑school programs and community fundraising (Project Rise, parental $4M support), and facility amenities (labs, workout rooms) mentioned as distinct features (e.g., 'marching band won state and supernationals', 'They even have a restaurant…', 'new stadium and Olympic sized pool'). These items are programmatic/facility resources that materially expand student opportunity.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures or i: This bucket aggregates concrete service‑delivery failures for vulnerable students: IEP/504 non‑implementation, ineffective aides/TA training, severely understaffed or unhelpful counseling departments, and special‑education students slipping through the cracks (e.g., 'They do not do what they say they will do in class for IEP or 504', 'The counseling department is severely understaffed', 'special ed students are treated like dogs when they’re having a breakdown'). These are specific operational shortcomings in individualized supports distinct from overall academic program breadth or general administrative responsiveness.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger formal ad: This bucket captures statements that Square reviews name concrete, high‑level academic offerings and results (AP/Pre‑AP, IB, many AP classes, dual‑enrollment/DE calculus, honors, academies/pathways) and cite measurable college outcomes (top college placements, scholarships, Ivy/HYPSM acceptances), whereas Circle reviews contain little or no comparable programmatic detail or demonstrable postsecondary outcomes (examples: Square mentions IB, DE Calculus 2/3, dozens of APs and students getting into top colleges; Circle contains no sustained AP/IB/dual‑credit evidence).
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, better‑: This groups reports that Square schools list extensive, high‑quality extracurriculars and specialized facilities—award‑winning band, nationally ranked sports, marching band, competitive music/theatre, JROTC, woodshop, 3D printers, pools, turf fields, vocational shops and magnet programs—while Circle reviews mention athletics only generically and lack comparable program breadth or named specialized labs (examples: Square details marching band, CIF wins, engineering/STEM programs, teacher‑run radio/culinary/auto shops; Circle merely notes athletics without program-level depth).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers concrete claims of acute safety and behavior problems in Square reviews—suicide, sexual harassment, shooting threats, bomb threats/evacuations, widespread drug/vaping use, gang activity, repeated fights—and reviewers’ accounts that these incidents are tolerated or poorly addressed; Circle reviews do not report comparable severe incidents (examples: Square mentions ‘student took their own life,’ ‘shooting threats,’ ‘dogs sent monthly for drugs,’ gangs and police on campus; Circle lacks these reports).
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This groups reports of school/district operational failures and governance issues in Square reviews—no returned calls/emails, scheduling/registration/billing errors, credit withdrawals without consent, mid‑year reshuffles, failure to follow IEPs, appeals to advocates/attorneys, and allegations of nepotism or protection of athletes/staff families—while Circle reviews do not document the same extent of mismanagement or systemic favoritism (examples: Square: ‘bill before acceptance,’ ‘screwed up my child’s schedule,’ ‘children of coaches get away with anything,’ ‘CC: state education agency’).
candidate_defs.square entries report weaker or inconsis: This bucket captures Square reviewers’ repeated claims that students with disabilities, those needing remediation, or with mental‑health needs receive inadequate or inconsistent support—IEP/504 non‑enforcement, students denied diplomas/certificates instead, lacking counseling and mental‑health care, no in‑school remediation, parents forced to involve advocates/attorneys—whereas Circle reviews do not raise systemic special‑education or counseling failures (examples: Square: ‘They do not follow IEPs,’ ‘had to file a formal complaint,’ ‘care for students with mental health isn’t really there,’ ‘NO extra services during school for kids who struggle’).
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: These reviews repeatedly list concrete program capacity (IB/AP/Calc BC/dual-credit, college-readiness counselors, ROP/CTE and named academies like Engineering, Performing Arts, Health/Business) and measurable outcomes (college placements, rising test scores), whereas circle entries lack comparable program inventories or outcomes; examples include ‘first high school in Indiana to offer IB,’ ‘22 AP and 8 dual-credit classes,’ ‘engineering program links with SDSU,’ and multiple alumni accepted to top universities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive, hi: Square reviews enumerate high‑level extracurricular achievements and infrastructure—state/national band, WGI world champs colorguard, renowned choir/theatre, large sport facilities, PAC performing arts center and marching-band traditions—while circle reviews do not present comparable program breadth or awards; illustrative lines are ‘band is amazing,’ ‘Drumline best in 4 states,’ ‘excellent theatre program,’ and ‘huge college‑level sport and band facilities.’
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent an: Many square reviews recount concrete safety events (multiple fights, on‑campus drug/alcohol use, a locker fire, sexual misconduct allegations, alleged police brutality) and report failures or minimization in handling (nurses not calling ambulance, inadequate harassment responses, claims of suicidality tied to bullying), whereas circle reviews do not present comparable high‑severity incident patterns; examples include ‘a boy caught a girl's locker on fire,’ ‘young man severely beaten in a classroom with a teacher present,’ ‘drug culture was rampant,’ and ‘highest number of students that commit suicide due to bullying.’
candidate_defs.square entries allege more administrativ: Square reviewers frequently describe systemic governance problems—favoritism to athletes/insiders, nepotism, inconsistent enforcement (victim punished, athlete exemptions), bullying/authoritarian administrative tactics, retaliatory responses to complaints, and poor parent engagement—distinct from circle’s lack of these claims; supporting quotes include ‘There’s a LOT of favoritism,’ ‘administration relies on bullying tactics,’ ‘they punish the victim,’ ‘parent involvement is not wanted,’ and ‘principal nepotism.’
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic facil: Square reviews contain concrete, recurring operational complaints—no/old computers or restrictive Chromebook policies, pest/mold/bedbug problems, heavy traffic/unsafe drop‑off, parking shortages, prison‑like bell systems, denied lunch for low accounts, blocked bathroom access, chaotic registration and scheduling (block schedule tradeoffs, missed logins)—while circle reviews rarely raise comparable facility/logistics failures; examples include ‘The school has no computers,’ ‘you can’t go one day without smelling mold or seeing a roach,’ ‘only one road to the drop off area—HEAVY TRAFFIC,’ ‘closed most of the bathrooms because students were vaping,’ and ‘registration was unorganized and chaotic.’
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive adv: These reviews name concrete program offerings and results (AP, IB, honors, dual‑enrollment/Early College, academies, national merit finalists, state A ratings, college credit & top‑university placements) and describe formal curricular structures (area‑of‑interest pathways, ability tracking). Circle entries rarely mention AP/IB/honors or quantified outcomes and instead give only generic college‑prep claims, so this bucket captures program availability, rigor, and measurable postsecondary success emphasized in square but absent in circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more severe studen: Square reviews contain many incident‑level claims—'bullying is OBSCENE,' 'fights after fights,' widespread drug/alcohol problems, students bringing guns, and police called to campus—while Circle reviews describe a safer, welcoming environment or only mild social issues. This bucket groups concrete safety incidents, pervasive peer misconduct, and failures to remediate them into a single school‑climate/safety theme.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more staff and l: Square reviewers repeatedly accuse the school of systemic personnel problems (one of the lowest teacher‑retention rates; many good teachers concentrated in AP; layoffs; pay raises for friends; administrators encouraging falsified absences; public humiliation by staff; biased discipline), and document both toxic and outstanding individual staff to show high variability. Circle reviews, by contrast, rarely allege the same breadth of ethical/HR failures, so this bucket captures personnel/leadership practices and misconduct.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviews give many operational specifics—'mall like design' and hallway congestion, poor cleaning, closed bathrooms, traffic near Lilly Rd, missing textbooks, active construction or new facilities, district millage/funding debates and alleged budget mismanagement—while Circle mostly omits such location/operational detail. This bucket groups tangible building, scheduling, maintenance, and resource‑management facts.
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader and high: Square reviews enumerate no‑cut sports, successful teams (especially soccer/competitive athletics), award‑winning band and arts results, film and vocational programs, FLEX lunch for clubs, and examples of out‑of‑area families drawn to programs; they also frequently describe athletics/music as central to status (athlete favoritism). Circle may mention athletics or a single program but does not present the same breadth, competitive accomplishments, or program‑centered social ordering that characterize square.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more severe studen: These reviews detail frequent and serious student misbehavior (weekly fights, drug use/selling, locker thefts, pervasive bullying, dangerous age‑mixing of younger and older students) and describe teachers/administration failing to intervene effectively (threats ignored, parents transferring children). Examples: reports of "fights almost every week," "heavy drug use by students," "been threatened with scissors and there was barely anything done about it," and parents fearing a child might be "shot."
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader, higher‑: These reviews enumerate concrete programs, competitive successes, and visible recognition—large numbers of clubs, trophy cases/announcements, state‑champion band and performing arts, JNROTC/Aerospace, strong vocational/trade programs and shared teams—whereas Circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth or award records. Examples: "24 state championships" for band, "outstanding JNROTC program," "around 200 clubs and sports," and "Blue Ribbon Performing Arts program."
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This cluster captures concrete governance and personnel failures: slow or no replies to parents, counselors/staff who ignore or dismiss concerns, favoritism toward athletes/children of staff, tenure‑protected poor teachers, staff misconduct (verbal abuse, physical hitting, racist comments), and selective or arbitrary punishments. Illustrative lines: "The Vice Principal disregards parents/students concerns," "teachers are given permission to verbally abuse parents," "they're afraid to punish certain people... the bully was a student athlete," and principal office staff being "horrible" or legally evasive (hiding nurse records).
candidate_defs.Square entries report worse physical fac: Reviews cite concrete facility and logistic problems—old computers/Windows 98, mold/ceiling cracks, trailers everywhere, bus seat shortages, broken shop equipment, poor food quality and dirty buildings—that impede instruction and student experience. Examples include "old macs and windows 98," "library closed due to mold growth," "teachers are outnumbered 30 to 1," and "The food is worse than anything I ever experienced."
candidate_defs.Square entries provide more concrete aca: These reviews are rich in specific academic-pathway information (AP/IB/AVID/dual‑enrollment, honors entrance exams, diploma tracks, measurable college acceptances and scholarships) while simultaneously describing mixed instructional quality: pockets of excellent college prep and vocational success alongside reports of poor AP rigor, guidance scheduling errors, IEP noncompliance, grade‑inflation/failing on state tests, and debilitating homework pressure. Examples: "The AVID program... graduate your student as a sophomore in college!", "lots of AP classes... top students accepted to Ivy leagues," alongside "no advance placement," counselors who 'screwed up my schedule,' IEPs not followed, and students reporting "7 hours of homework" or being "not nearly as prepared for standardized tests."
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger/more exte: This bucket captures concrete program and outcome differences — square reviews repeatedly name IB, STEM/magnet academies, many AP/dual‑credit/PSEO options, college‑credit pathways and explicit alumni/valuation metrics (valedictorians, SAT/AP success, multiple college acceptances), whereas circle reviews rarely cite such programs or measurable postsecondary outcomes; examples include 'full IB diploma', 'well over 10 AP classes', 'numerous upper level, PSEO and college‑credit classes', and alumni college placements from square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain many concrete safety and misconduct reports — ongoing bullying, bloody fights, drug/vape culture, sexual assault allegations, and teacher/staff sexual or physical misconduct — often paired with claims that staff or administrators failed to act (e.g., 'sexually assaulted... told I was lying', 'students involved in bloody fights', 'significant drug problem', 'staff were inappropriate with the girls'), while circle reviews do not document this breadth/severity of safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket groups concrete governance and process failures reported in square — misfiled IEPs, dishonest or defensive principals, secretive/nepotistic board behavior, changed grades, refusal to remove automated calls, underreporting incidents, and prioritizing test/image over student wellbeing (e.g., 'principal lied', 'found another student’s information on my daughter’s IEP', 'school board meets secretly', 'care more about being #1 than welfare') — issues that are far more prevalent in square than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and richer: Square reviews enumerate many tangible extracurricular and career programs (unique Cirque or magnet programs, thriving band/marching programs, many clubs, vocational pathways like Auto/Cosmetology/Engineering, and recurring scholarship athletes) while simultaneously calling out pay‑to‑play, sports‑first budget priorities, or athletics crowding out academics (e.g., 'only public Cirque program', 'many scholarship athletes', 'most of the money goes to sports', 'sports regularly takes precedence over academics'); circle reviews rarely list this program breadth or the same funding/priority tensions.
candidate_defs.square entries show wider variability in: Square reviews contain numerous concrete, often conflicting teacher-level reports: teachers who 'go out of their way' with after‑school tutoring and doctoral‑level instructors alongside claims of lazy, unresponsive, abusive, or absent teachers and paras (e.g., 'teachers provide lunchtime and after school tutoring', 'many faculty had doctorates', versus 'teachers refuse to respond', 'had a math teacher grab my head and scream'), indicating far greater within‑school variance in teacher competence and responsiveness than the more uniformly described faculty in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, better‑: This bucket captures cases where reviewers describe a wide menu of clubs, state‑level athletic championships, strong band/choir/theatre programs, and booster/parent funding that enable competitive extracurricular success (e.g., 'plethora of clubs and sports', 'state competitive band', 'recent championships', 'booster clubs fund sports') contrasted with circle entries that make no comparable claims or describe limited extracurricular options.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Includes concrete accounts of fights, gun/bomb threats, drug use, police calls, ankle monitors, viral fight videos, tolerated bullying and claims of privacy invasions or online‑monitoring (e.g., '2–4 fights a week', 'Ar‑15 incident', 'they have begun watching students actions online', 'lots of bullying tolerated by faculty'), whereas circle entries generally lack such severe safety/monitoring incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger advance: Encompasses explicit program and outcome evidence—many AP/IB/Honors offerings, Early College/dual‑enrollment, documented AP/IB rigor, formal outcome stats and elite college admits (e.g., 'IB/AP classes', 'students accepted to Harvard/Cornell', 'Chromebook + dual enrollment'), while circle entries rarely cite comparable systematic advanced programs or school‑level college‑prep metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete sc: Covers references to district/school‑level policy and program decisions and named leaders—de‑tracking/ranking changes, PBIS, 1:1 technology rollouts, freshman‑lunch policy shifts, busing reforms, and credited principals or failed BOE interventions (e.g., 'stopped reporting class standings', 'PBIS', 'taken away freshman lunch', named principals), whereas circle entries mostly report teacher‑ or incident‑level issues without comparable systemwide policy descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize facility/resour: Groups reviews that discuss capital/facility quality, material shortages, funding priorities, booster money, preferential resourcing for program tracks or wealthy students, and socioeconomic mixing effects (e.g., 'state‑of‑the‑art gym and track', 'bathrooms beyond filthy', 'IB kids enjoying A/C', 'parents move into district for school'), while circle entries do not frequently surface detailed facility, funding, or resource‑equity narratives.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially mo: These reviews repeatedly list concrete program availability and outcomes at square schools (AP/IB offerings, 18+ AP classes, Project Lead the Way engineering/biomed, dual‑enrollment and Running Start, summer college‑credit programs, specialized magnet/STEAM academies) plus explicit college results (high GPAs, acceptances to Yale/Northwestern/Syracuse, students graduating with associate degrees), whereas circle reviews rarely name AP/IB/dual‑credit programs or college matriculation evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report a much broader and: Square reviews enumerate dozens of clubs, robust arts and music programs (award‑winning band, LISA/auditorium performances), many niche electives, and documented athletic success (state championships, strong varsity programs, college athletics placements), while circle reviews mostly reference limited extracurriculars or only a small sports culture and lack comparable named programs or competitive achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent an: Square reviewers supply explicit incidents—fights in bathrooms and cafeterias, vaping/drug culture, multiple drug arrests and fatal ODs, bomb threats, sexual misconduct allegations, weapons/gang activity, and unsafe dismissal/security lapses—often noting slow or absent administrative response; circle reviews contain far fewer or no comparable reports of violence, drug fatalities, gang or weapons issues.
candidate_defs.square entries show more discussion of a: Square reviews repeatedly call out lost paperwork, outdated event calendars, long delays fixing grades/attendance in PowerSchool, denied parent communications, procedural errors that harmed student grades, and named principal turnover or contested board actions (both praise and blame), whereas circle reviews rarely document this level of concrete operational or governance detail.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater polarity: Many square reviews describe both strong personal supports (dedicated tutors, before/after school help, counselors aiding FAFSA/college apps, Saturday tutoring) and opposite experiences (teachers refusing to teach, chronic teacher apathy, IEP/co‑teacher failures, poor counseling), indicating inconsistent instructional quality and mixed special‑education/counseling performance that circle reviews do not describe as extensively.
candidate_defs.square entries report pervasive student: These reviews recount frequent physical fights, lockdowns, thefts, arrests, drug use, teen pregnancy, and sustained clique-based or identity-based bullying—often paired with teacher inaction or administrators who punish victims or fail to intervene (e.g., “constant fights,” “many arrests were made,” “bullying... life put at risk,” and “teachers don’t do anything when students get bullied”). Circle reviews contain little or no evidence of recurring violence or systemic mishandling of safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher‑: Many square reviews list concrete program infrastructure and results—AP/IB rosters, 18+ AP courses, SUPA/Syracuse partnerships, dual‑enrollment credits, AVID/IB status, and named elite college acceptances or scholarship outcomes (e.g., '42 college credits,' 'full IB candidates,' 'admitted to MIT/Harvard/Berkeley'). Circle reviews lack comparable, specific advanced‑course partnerships or quantified postsecondary metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries describe large, well‑reso: Square reviews repeatedly cite program scale and achievements—very large marching bands, award‑winning music and debate teams, strong robotics/Career Center offerings, and active club leadership pipelines (e.g., 'biggest marching band in the region,' 'Wind Symphony,' 'FIRST Robotics,' 'Career Center is the best'), whereas circle reviews do not report this level of extracurricular scale or competitive success.
candidate_defs.square entries report pronounced adminis: Numerous square critiques name district budgeting/tax complaints, favoritism toward wealthy families or athletes, arbitrary dress‑code/phone enforcement, rageful meetings, or slow/lying office responses (e.g., 'they gave an enormous wage increase... My taxes increased,' 'players can get away with anything,' 'administration... flat out lie to your face,' and 'ignores reports of fights'). Circle reviews raise some administrative concerns but do not show the same mixture of politicized favoritism, fiscal mismanagement, and punitive arbitrary enforcement.
candidate_defs.square entries evidence sharp instructio: Square reviewers describe three-tiered curricula where AP/pre‑AP students get high‑quality instruction and college prep while standard‑level classes suffer from inexperienced or disengaged teachers, coaching‑priority hires, inconsistent grading, and burnout (e.g., 'tremendous difference between honors/AP teachers and the normal crowd,' 'stop hiring coaches and using them as teachers,' 'some phenomenal teachers—and some that should be kicked out'). Circle reviews do not document this organized, schoolwide stratification to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries report more on-campus saf: These reviews describe concrete, recurring safety problems at the school — fights, physical assaults, sexual misconduct, guns/lockdowns, pervasive drug/vaping use and overdoses, repeated contraband searches, and unsafe event practices — plus administration that fails to stop or remediate them (e.g., student attacked in bathroom and school ‘did nothing,’ ‘1–2 fights a week,’ ‘kids constantly doing drugs,’ multiple lockdowns after guns).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, formal a: Many square reviews name structured programs and credentials (IB Diploma, AVID, large AP/dual‑enrollment offerings, honors/double‑honors, specialized magnet/University programs) and cite concrete outcomes (National Merit semifinalists, scholarships, alumni college placement, AP/college credits, high test scores), while circle reviews lack these formal program details.
candidate_defs.square entries report more persistent st: Square reviewers give multiple concrete examples of poor communication, rudeness or manipulation by front‑office staff and administrators, nepotism/pay‑to‑play/favoritism toward athletes or staff‑children, biased or arbitrary discipline (dress‑code/racial targeting), and occasional abusive behavior (threatening or stalking allegations, transcript mishandling), contrasts circle’s absence of these systemic staff misconduct or favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report clearer facility/s: Square reviews repeatedly note tangible capital outcomes (brand‑new buildings, rebuilt facilities, air conditioning) or, conversely, serious degradation (pests, filth, broken library), chronic overcrowding/large class sizes, and contested budget choices (new stadium/football funding vs. underfunded arts and paper shortages), whereas circle lacks comparable, concrete facility or contested‑funding descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit spec: Square reviewers both describe institutional roles (hosting district special‑education/ELS services, College/Resource Centers) and document failures of special‑needs support (IEP noncompliance, being told families must pay for tutoring/large‑print books, inaccessible campuses for handicapped students), a mixed but distinct pattern not present in circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive adv: These reviews name concrete curricular offerings and outcomes (AP/Pre‑AP/IB, large AP counts, dual‑enrollment/PSEO/Running Start, academy/magnet tracks, college credits earned, high ACT/SAT results and alumni college placements) that square reviewers cite as evidence of college preparation, whereas circle reviews rarely list such structured advanced offerings or strong postsecondary metrics.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent seri: Square reviews contain recurring accounts of physical assaults, sexual assaults, frequent fights, widespread drug use, homophobic/racist harassment and claims that administration failed to protect victims; circle reviews do not present comparable reports of violent incidents or sustained administrative non‑response.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more inconsisten: Square reviewers cite both harsh enforcement (excessive ISS/suspensions, humiliating punishments, strict tardy and dress‑code removals, long phone confiscations) and permissive supervision (students leaving campus, on‑campus smoking, truancy not addressed), documenting inconsistent application of rules and discipline that circle reviews do not portray.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly allege governance problems — favoritism and political decision‑making, misuse or misallocation of funds, retire/rehire scandals, ignored petitions, dishonest or unresponsive staff, botched records/transfers and other procedural failures — a pattern of leadership and board failures not reflected in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader and high: Square reviewers enumerate many high‑profile extracurricular assets — superior music/band programs, distinguished arts facilities, extensive clubs, no‑cut sports, strong athletic wins and visible parental volunteerism/fundraising — and sometimes note athletics being prioritized over academics; circle reviews generally lack the same breadth or prominence of extracurricular/parent‑support claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report far stronger and b: These reviews describe concrete, named programs and assets at square schools — abundant AP/IB/STEM/CIS magnets, vocational/technical center partnerships, ROTC, nationally ranked band/choir, large athletics/stadium investments, and alumni college/award outcomes — while circle reviews rarely list comparable advanced courses, magnet programs, or high-profile extracurricular infrastructure (examples: “many choices of AP and Honors…IB program…140+ member marching band…Fred Eberly Technical Center” vs circle’s lack of such program detail).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: Square reviews repeatedly document bullying, daily/regular fights, drug/paraphernalia problems, vandalism/arson, weapons, police/Taser incidents and both excessive suspension or lax enforcement; circle entries largely lack these claims and often state bullying/fighting is not tolerated (examples: “fight school…police walking around…drugs and paraphernalia…fights happen approximately every 2 days” vs circle’s “Bullying is not tolerated,” no fights reported).
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers give multiple concrete examples of dysfunctional office practice, ignored parent emails, altered/dysfunctional procedures, mismanaged funds or facilities, front-office rudeness, and questionable hiring/firing choices, whereas circle reviews rarely allege systemic administrative incompetence (examples: “office never informed her…principal does not return parent emails…parents throw money at funding (poorly managed)…lost yearbook photo”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more inadequate or: Many square reviews allege failure to follow IEPs, ADA noncompliance, poor services for students with learning differences or English learners, and instances of racial, LGBTQ, or economic exclusion or teacher discrimination; circle reviews do not contain comparable systemic special‑needs or discrimination allegations (examples: “they are not doing the IEP guidelines…If your child has a special need forget about ADA rights…horrendous job protecting my child from racialized bullying”).
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit more polarized an: Square reviews contain both claims of weak instruction, inconsistent grading, poor AP preparation and graduates feeling unprepared for college, alongside other reports of rigorous AP/IB success and strong alumni placements — creating a highly variable picture — while circle reviews are comparatively consistent in reporting steady instruction or uniformly positive/negative classroom experiences (examples: “teachers don’t prepare students for AP…felt underprepared in college” vs “many choices of AP…students to MIT/Harvard”; circle lacks this polarization).
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: These reviews name specific offerings and results (AP/IB/Pre‑AP, dual‑credit/early college pathways, university partnerships), cite rigorous coursework and heavy homework, and provide measurable outcomes (A ratings, scholarship totals, college matriculations) — e.g., mentions of IB/AP presence, university engineering credit pathways, 'full scholarship to Columbia', and top AP-school rankings — whereas circle reviews rarely list programs, metrics, or concrete college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more detailed clas: Square reviews give concrete in‑class examples (lack of lesson objectives, low‑level questioning, excessive movie‑watching, tests over untaught material), allege verbal abuse or dishonesty by teachers, and show stark heterogeneity (some 'phenomenal' teachers alongside many poor instructors), while circle reviews do not supply the same level of classroom‑instruction detail.
candidate_defs.square entries describe worse student sa: Square documents frequent fights, drug/vaping use (even on buses), police presence, racial/LGBTQ harassment, ganglike behavior and incidents where victims were criminalized or ignored, often coupled with claims that staff/administration failed to protect students (e.g., police called on victims); circle reviews lack these sustained reports of violence, drugs, policing, or systemic discriminatory incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight broader and hig: Square reviews enumerate many clubs, strong band/arts, competitive athletics, after‑school programs, ASB activity, volunteer mentoring, and community traditions or turnout (e.g., nationally ranked band, top state sports, FFA, many clubs), while circle reviews rarely provide this catalog of organized extracurricular breadth or program‑level achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries surface more district/boa: Square reviewers complain about district or board misprioritization (spending millions on stadiums/turf instead of infrastructure), alleged corruption or unresponsive superintendents, staffing/turnover at leadership level, and operational breakdowns (bussing gaps, gradebook/reporting failures, phone/web unreliability, overcrowding and facility maintenance), whereas circle entries do not present this consistent set of governance and system‑level failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report richer advanced-ac: These reviews describe concrete, school-run academic pathways and outcomes (AP breadth, IB/AICE, Early College/dual-enrollment, vocational certs, high AP/ACT averages, scholarship and matriculation data) that square reviewers name explicitly while circle reviewers generally do not (examples: “Early College, Dual Credit and AP classes…almost entire class scored 5’s,” “IB programme…no AP,” “welding tech (can get cert.)”). Falling in this bucket means the review emphasizes program availability and quantified student outcomes (credits, scores, admissions) as a distinguishing fact about the school.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive bul: Square reviews repeatedly document hostile student climates, racialized harassment, frequent fights/violence, staff-perpetrated harassment or sexual-misconduct allegations, and administrators who fail to act (examples: “MAJOR bullying issues…teacher's as the bully,” “There have been at least two suicides due to bullying,” “a lot of pedo teachers,” and “administration…took ZERO responsibility”). Content in this bucket centers on concrete safety/harm incidents and the school’s inadequate or biased response procedures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Square reviewers give tangible, operational facility and campus reports—aging or rundown buildings, freezing classrooms, filthy restrooms, overcrowded cafeterias/halls, bomb-threats/security searches, chronic maintenance failures and also named new construction projects (examples: “desperately in need of renovation…ceiling tile fell off,” “impossible to find a seat at lunch,” and “brand new track/new Performing Arts Center”). Membership in this bucket means the review centers on physical plant, space/capacity, sanitation, safety-incident, or concrete construction/renovation activity as a key school characteristic.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater staff unpr: These items document personnel- and governance-level problems: frequent teacher/admin turnover or absenteeism, inability to hold poor staff accountable (union protections), grade‑tampering or athletic-protection by administrators, rude office staff, and parents’ distrust of leadership (examples: “teachers are chronically absent…principal told me to pass him anyways,” “leadership is inept…refusing to acknowledge the real issues,” and “many teachers and administrators have left”). Reviews in this bucket focus on staffing practices, discipline/enforcement legitimacy, and administrative capacity.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pr: Square reviewers enumerate expansive extracurricular offerings, competitive arts/sports achievements, vocational certifications, internships and high‑visibility travel while also alleging booster/athletics favoritism and unequal resource allocation (examples: “countless clubs…Fine Arts Academy…marching band invited to China,” “welding certs…athletic boosters buy uniforms,” and “all the money raised ALWAYS goes to football”). Reviews here emphasize the presence, scale, and resourcing/prioritization of co-curricular programs as a defining school feature.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents (frequent fights, bus bullying, drug overdoses, gang activity, bomb/shooting threats) and allege inconsistent or absent administrative/security responses (no follow-through on bullying, biased guards, ineffective deans, delayed parent notification, K9 searches/strong security measures). Example evidence: “There are quite a few fights a week,” “Bullying on the busses is seldom followed up,” “riddled with drugs…students drop unconscious,” and claims of gang violence and hiring of outside security, none of which Circle reviews report.
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger advanced: These entries catalog formal program breadth (AP/IB/Pre‑AP, dual enrollment, Engineering/STEAM/ROTC academies, vocational pathways) and cite measurable outcomes (AP pass rates, rising test scores, alumni placements at top colleges, college credit earned in high school). Examples include: “many AP offerings…started their Freshman year in college with 16 credit hours,” “IB program…college credit,” and long lists of alumni universities—features Circle reviewers do not enumerate.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: Reviews repeatedly allege concrete operational breakdowns—scheduling errors, paperwork mishandling, inaccessible or unresponsive counselors/administrators, manipulated graduation practices, biased enforcement, and failures in special‑education identification/504 supports—creating service and governance gaps. Illustrative lines: “took a week to get my son’s schedule changed…form was never processed,” “administration pays lip service to bullying,” “counselors did not see her grades,” and “They will do anything to make their graduation rate look good.”
candidate_defs.Square entries report more variable inst: These reviews document uneven classroom delivery (poorly taught or excellent AP classes side‑by‑side), permissive grading/social promotion or grade‑inflation practices, and inconsistent homework policies or extreme workload/pressure.
