Representative evidence: “Most AP courses are not taught appropriately…others have no control,” “received a D‑ with averaged scores <50 yet passed,” “homework 2+ hours nightly or unpredictable 0–8 hours,” and “cell phones are commonplace in class instead of learning.”
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive ext: These reviews emphasize concrete extracurricular breadth and achievements (marching band trips to Carnegie Hall, travel to Rome, strong arts and vocational programs, robust sports and feeder programs) while also noting facility/resource contrasts (new buildings or athletic spending vs lacking textbooks, overcrowding, cafeteria quality) and active parent involvement or polarization (PTO volunteers, parental pressure, threats to leave or demand closure). Examples: “choir traveled to Carnegie Hall,” “spent on new K‑2 building but teachers lack books,” “join the PTSA…PTO asks for volunteers,” and parents threatening media action—topics not raised by Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent, sev: This bucket covers concrete safety and climate problems described much more in Square: multiple fights a day, bathroom arson, gang affiliation, drug offers, sexual-assault mishandling, racial hate incidents/blackface, students returning with bruises, and administrators who ignore or punish victims — whereas Circle reviews largely omit these specific, ongoing safety events or describe a safer, improving climate.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more concrete, n: Square reviews repeatedly list program breadth (IB, AP, JROTC, dual enrollment, extensive language offerings), cite AP credits/college acceptances and test-score percentages (e.g., 90% reading, Ivy placements, full‑ride scholarships), and note explicit college-prep pipelines — while Circle contains few or no comparable, concrete program inventories or measurable outcome claims.
candidate_defs.Square entries show greater polarization: Square reviewers document both extremes—teachers who create extra review sessions and teachers who are apathetic, frequently absent, or poorly qualified (long‑term subs, tenure-protected complacency, unprofessional conduct)—whereas Circle reviews present a more uniformly caring/consistent faculty without the same degree of wide variance.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures complaints about principals and office staff who ignore parents, threaten students, favor relatives or insiders (hiring/raises, athletic selections), dodge communications, apply discipline unevenly or protect reputation over student wellbeing — problems that Square documents repeatedly while Circle offers little or contrasting evidence of such governance dysfunction.
candidate_defs.Square entries provide more detailed acc: Square reviews include specific infrastructure and operational details—heating/AC problems, new vs dated buildings, overcrowded classes and lunch logistics, short passing times, 1:1 laptop programs, metal detectors, funding choices favoring stadiums/athletics or neglecting arts—that Circle reviews rarely enumerate or contrast as concretely.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and broad: These texts repeatedly cite concrete curricular offerings (AP/IB/Cambridge, many AP courses, dual‑enrollment, CU/college credit, career academies) and named post‑secondary outcomes (Ivy/elite admits, scholarship counts, West Point appointments, test pass rates), whereas circle entries rarely supply comparable program lists or measurable outcomes; examples include Cambridge diploma counts, ‘over 30 hours of college credit’ and explicit AP/IB course rosters in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews contain numerous concrete safety and behavior incidents (frequent fights, widespread drinking/drug use, suicidality linked to school stress) plus harsh or public punitive practices (ISS without restroom access, in‑line lunch punishments, expulsions), whereas circle reviews do not describe this scale or severity; illustrative items include 'fights near everyday', 'students drinking on a day‑to‑day basis', and students 'made to stand an hour' in ISS.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more detailed fac: Square texts frequently describe concrete infrastructure and operational issues or upgrades — overcrowding and quantified enrollment pressures, sanitation problems (cockroaches, mold), cafeteria/food complaints, locked bathrooms, AND explicit capital projects/new science buildings/solar panels — while circle rarely provides this level of facility detail; examples include '4,200 students…terribly overcrowded', 'cockroaches everywhere', and 'brand new science building'.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit admi: Square reviews more often allege administration-level problems such as grade tampering, nepotism/'good ol' boy' cultures, fiscal misallocation, ignoring IEP/504 requirements (OCR complaints), and unresponsive or harmful counselor actions, whereas circle reviews lack comparable systemic governance accusations; representative claims include 'VP changing the teachers grades', 'they won't follow our IEPs', and 'budget miscalculations…cut mode'.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger or more: Square texts repeatedly document high-profile, award‑winning extracurriculars (marching band, theater Emmys, state championship teams, dominant football programs), plus frequent notes that resources/favoritism flow to athletes (funding concentrated on football, athletes treated preferentially), whereas circle mentions fewer program accolades or athlete‑centric resource concentration; examples include 'football program is…highest grossing', 'very large marching band program', and 'funding for everything except football is underfunded'.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe and fr: This bucket captures reports of acute safety and criminalized student behavior in square reviews — e.g., guns/lockdowns/school‑shooting scares, repeated fights and physical assaults ("beat with a metal marching band baton"), bomb threats, on‑campus drug/alcohol use and sexual activity in bathrooms, and widespread intimidation/harassment. These are concrete, recurring safety incidents and substance problems described in multiple square reviews that circle reviews do not document.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This groups allegations about leadership and district-level dysfunction in square reviews — e.g., "good‑ol‑boys club," cronyism and athletic nepotism, chronic principal/superintendent turnover, hiring unqualified leaders, front‑office rudeness, and officials who ignore or minimize complaints (parents calling state, reports met with lip‑service). These are system‑level governance and accountability problems distinct from classroom behavior or program offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive, co: This bucket covers concrete program availability and documented outcomes emphasized in square reviews — e.g., many AP/IB/CAS/dual‑enrollment options, CTE and hands‑on labs (welding, aquaculture, auto tech), JR/NS ROTC, award‑winning band/theater, state athletic championships, high test scores and college placements (Ivy acceptances, National Merit, AP metrics). It describes what the school provides and measurable student achievements rather than how classrooms are run.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive cla: This captures square reviewers' reports about everyday learning conditions: huge class sizes and overcrowding ("classes are huge", "warehouse school"), chronic classroom disruption and disrespect impeding instruction, reliance on substitutes/unlicensed teachers, high student failure rates/promotion irregularities, and observable poor teaching practices — distinct from acute safety incidents or governance problems because it focuses on instruction, supervision, and operational conditions that degrade learning.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more small‑town/: This bucket groups attributes more commonly reported in circle reviews: small‑community oversight and spirit, teachers who are easy to reach and "keep up with new learning," proactive pastoral/counselor intervention and individualized accommodations, and explicit parental endorsements/recommendations. These are concrete supportive practices and community conditions (communication, counseling, coordinated instruction) that circle reviewers emphasize relative to square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports of concrete student-safety incidents and supervision breakdowns that appear repeatedly in Square but not in Circle — e.g., bullying and fights, pervasive drug and vaping use, gang-related assaults, threats of shootings, students leaving campus during lunch, SRO/security shortages, vandalism, and cases where staff failed to investigate or intervene. Items like “people doing drugs in the bathroom,” “bullying goes unchecked,” ‘‘teacher beaten by students,’’ and ‘‘SROs are at a bare minimum’’ illustrate the kind of operational safety problems that group Square documents far more often than Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete fac: Square reviews repeatedly name specific physical-plant and resourcing facts — renovations and new amenities (new pool, remodeled buildings), severe overcrowding and portables (e.g., nearly 1,000 per grade; 102 portables), pest/cleanliness problems, outdated or vandalized technology, one-to-one laptop rollouts, construction-caused operational disruptions, and transportation barriers — whereas Circle rarely supplies comparable facility or capacity detail. Examples include ‘‘walk through a construction site,’’ ‘‘rats and cockroaches,’’ ‘‘too many students per class/portables,’’ ‘‘first-class facilities and cutting-edge tech,’’ and ‘‘graduation moved because of construction.''
candidate_defs.square entries document more and broader: Square reviews list concrete programmatic pathways (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, career academies, JROTC/NJROTC, marine/magnet/STEM pipelines, veterinary certifications, marching band and fine-arts achievements) and measurable outcomes (scholarships, college acceptances, API/SAT score claims) far more often than Circle. Representative evidence: ‘‘IB program with high participation,’’ ‘‘AP and dual-enrollment leading to college credits and scholarship recipients,’’ ‘‘career academy and FVMA CVA certification,’’ and long-term alumni college/career trajectories.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket covers Square’s recurrent claims of uneven teacher quality, unstable course placement and pacing, grading/academic-standards problems (promotion without mastery, punitive zeroing, forced AP enrollment), heavy substitute use, and variable homework/rigor — contrasted with Circle’s uniformly consistent-teacher narratives. Illustrative items include ‘‘some great teachers but many bad ones,’’ ‘‘students passed despite failing,’’ ‘‘math program is very poor/quality varies widely,’’ ‘‘too much homework/0 period causing late nights,’’ and ‘‘placement/pacing misalignments in language sequence.''
candidate_defs.square entries allege more explicit admi: Square reviews frequently accuse leadership of politicized discipline, favoritism (athletes or connected parents), retaliatory treatment of complaining parents, prioritizing athletics/image over instruction, resource misallocation (admin devices vs. teacher pay), rigged student elections, and refusal to remedy wrongdoing — charges that Circle does not make with the same frequency or specificity. Examples include ‘‘parents who post frustrations get called into the superintendent’s office,’’ ‘‘administration values sports over teachers,’’ ‘‘administrators show blatant favoritism,’’ ‘‘docked teacher pay while buying iPads for admin,’’ and ‘‘refuse to retract allegations even when caught.''
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize concrete curric: These entries enumerate specific programs, courses, and achievements (many AP/IB/dual‑enrollment offerings, magnets, vocational/CTE tracks, 30+ clubs, strong band/music programs, state/national competition wins, and named college acceptances) rather than making only generic claims; examples include repeated mentions of wide AP catalogs, law/health magnets, robust music/band departments, DECA/ROTC/robotics, and documented Ivy/Selective college placements that Circle reviews do not supply.
candidate_defs.square entries contain far more detailed: Reviewers in Square give operational specifics about buildings and services — new state‑of‑the‑art construction, recent capital improvements, short lunch lines, or conversely chronic failures like no AC/water, leaks, roach/rat infestations, contaminated bathrooms, and prison‑like security doors — whereas Circle provides little or only general facility commentary.
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent an: Square reviews report concrete safety failures and severe student conduct problems (daily fights, direct threats forcing withdrawals, sexual harassment claims, rampant drug use, SRO misconduct) alongside punitive enforcement (suspensions for self‑defense, Saturday School, heavy uniform/detention policies), while Circle rarely describes comparable violent incidents or such disciplinary extremes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adul: These include named, high‑performing teachers and visible principal involvement as well as explicit allegations of nepotistic hiring, favoritism (toward athletes/connected families), administrative unresponsiveness, leadership churn, politicized district behavior, and staff retaliation; Square reviews therefore supply detailed personnel narratives that Circle lacks (e.g., named praised teachers vs claims that the superintendent never returns calls or that promotions follow family ties).
candidate_defs.square entries give more specific eviden: Square reviewers provide procedural and outcome details — IEP/504 noncompliance, denied accommodations, inadequate life‑skills classrooms, guidance counseling failures around scholarships/college, dyslexia support availability or gaps, and examples of one‑on‑one remediation — documenting concrete support‑service practices and breakdowns that Circle reviews do not similarly detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more advanced acad: This bucket captures claims that square schools list concrete, formal academic offerings and quantified college success—AP/IB/Honors, dual‑enrollment, specialized academies, National Merit and scholarship totals, and Ivy/private placements—while circle entries do not. Example evidence: square reviewers name IB certification, many AP classes, dual‑enrollment agreements, “8 National Merit Scholarship winners,” “$16 MILLION” in scholarships and specific Ivy admits; circle reviews lack comparable program names or measured outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive ext: This groups descriptions where square reviewers enumerate broad, organized extracurricular life (band, theater, mock trial, science teams, no‑cut sports), award‑winning arts/athletics facilities, booster/Foundation funding, and state championships—claims largely absent from circle. Examples: square lists dozens of clubs and teams, calls out a top performing‑arts center and championship teams, cites Booster Club/Niwot Foundation support; circle typically mentions few or failing extracurricular supports.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket covers reports that square schools experience recurring physical fights, on‑campus drug use/odors, racial or targeted harassment, and administrative inaction/favoritism (victims isolated, bullies retained, no reporting systems), whereas circle reviews do not describe this combination of pervasive safety/climate incidents. Illustrative items: many square comments about daily fights, smelling pot in halls, racial slurs, students put on homebound while bullies stay, and administrators who 'turn a blind eye' or protect athletes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete admi: This bucket groups operational failures described by square reviewers—lost records delaying grade placement or nearly preventing graduation, months‑long transcript transfers, ignored parent emails, failing or nonexistent IEP/504 follow‑through, and ineffective college counseling—problems circle reviewers do not raise. Examples: reports of missing freshman data causing held back students, parents told to keep an attorney over special‑ed denials, counselors who are 'hard to get a hold of,' and scheduling errors that jeopardized graduation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more detailed and: This bucket captures that square reviews provide many specific classroom‑level claims—teachers who offer retakes/after‑hours help and strong mentoring alongside accounts of lazy, unqualified, or ideologically driven teachers (e.g., refusing to teach evolution), inconsistent classroom management, punitive grading, and grade‑posting problems—while circle seldom gives this level of granular, mixed teacher practice detail. Examples: square notes teachers who 'stay after class' and offer rewrites, but also alleges teachers allowing cheating, giving zeros for medical absences, shouting in class, or refusing evolution instruction.
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups reviews where square schools list concrete rigorous offerings (AP, IB, dual‑enrollment, Early College, AP Capstone), college‑credit/dual enrollment, and measurable outcomes (ACT/SAT averages, scholarship totals, Ivy/competitive college placement) that circle reviews do not. Examples: many square reviews cite multiple AP/IB/ROP classes, students starting college with credits, Early College AA programs, above‑average ACT/SAT scores, and full academic scholarships—claims absent from circle entries.
candidate_defs.Square entries report broader, higher‑qu: This bucket captures reviews that describe abundant clubs, award‑winning performing arts (band, choir, theatre), competitive teams, large participation, and recent athletic/music facility investments at square schools—features circle reviews rarely mention. Illustrative evidence includes square mentions of near‑Broadway musicals, 1,100‑seat theaters, award‑winning marching bands, plentiful niche clubs, and new stadiums/uniforms versus circle’s lack of comparable organized arts/athletics detail.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent seve: This bucket groups accounts of tangible safety problems (frequent fights, stabbings, assaults, drug deals, vandalism, bathroom lockdowns) and the contrasting presence of heavy security/policing or invasive surveillance/discipline (random searches, cameras everywhere, ID‑based restroom permissions) reported for square schools but not circle. Examples: square reviews recount multiple fights, gun lockdowns, students selling drugs in hallways as well as reports of cameras, school police searches, and punitive bathroom/technology controls that circle reviews do not describe.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete stud: This bucket captures square reviews that list tangible supports and infrastructure—tutoring, mentoring, accessible principals, special‑education departments, 1:1 Chromebooks, renovated buildings, and structured mastery/retest policies—that circle reviews generally omit. Evidence includes square mentions of lunch/after‑school tutoring, mentoring programs, excellent special education services, state‑of‑the‑art campuses and one‑to‑one device programs.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers reviews blaming administration or guidance for failures: unreturned counselor calls, transcript/scheduling errors that harmed college admission, cover‑ups, board resistance, mis‑spent funds, forced residency transfers, and high turnover—patterns emphasized in square entries but largely absent in circle. Illustrative cases: square reports counselors who refused calls, lost transcripts causing application rejections, principals accused of covering complaints, budget misallocation claims, and repeated dean/advisor turnover.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports of frequent physical violence, bullying, drug use, gang activity, weapons, suicide/assault incidents and reviewers’ claims that discipline or investigations are inconsistent or do not adequately protect victims (examples: “fights in the bathrooms every week,” “guns being brought to school,” “so many bullies…never gets punished,” “HUGE issue with gangs…administration turns a blind eye,” multiple suicide attempts, and claims that vice principals/principals didn’t act). It also includes health-safety protocol failures (mask/COVID enforcement inconsistencies) and law-enforcement involvement described as a response to recurring threats, distinguishing schools where reviewers describe active safety crises and weak/erratic remediation from circle entries which lack such pervasive safety allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: This bucket groups items about physical infrastructure, custodial/health conditions, overcrowding, specific campus amenities and logistics — both complaints (exposed wires, mold, falling-apart textbooks/lockers, disgusting restrooms, insect infestations, extreme overcrowding, parking-lot free-for-all) and named investments/amenities (recent renovations, new auditorium, fitness center, cafe, late bus). It captures the presence of explicit facility/resource evidence (renovation dates, pools, labs, specialized equipment) and operational logistics that reviewers cite, which appear far more concretely in square entries than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and more-spec: This bucket captures named curricular/programmatic breadth (IB/Pre‑IB, AP/honors lists, academies, BioMed 4‑year programs, ROTC, Career‑Tech labs, dual-enrollment/college destinations) and concrete outcome metrics (scholarship totals, Ivy admissions, National Merit counts), including reviewers’ claims about AP pass rates or unequal access. It describes schools where reviewers enumerate program names, pathways, and post‑secondary results—distinct from general claims about instructional quality and appearing far more often in square entries than circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket covers reviewer evidence of uneven teacher competence and responsiveness, protected/incompetent staff, favoritism (toward athletes or specialty students), discriminatory grading/discipline, administrative blacklisting/punitive public shaming, and special‑education legal noncompliance or segregation (examples: ‘incompetent teachers are protected,’ ‘grading me harder because of my sexuality,’ ‘doesn't follow the law when it comes to special needs,’ and ‘building a school far away to house kids with disabilities’). It groups personnel and governance failures distinct from program availability or facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries document a broader, more: This bucket captures detailed accounts of many clubs, performing-arts strengths, extensive sports/JROTC/robotics/academic teams, community performances, and participation policies (low‑barrier team access, dozens of clubs, state-level awards), plus community/parent volunteer support—facts reviewers cite as concrete offerings (e.g., ‘fabulous theatre arts dept,’ ‘dozens of clubs,’ ‘Academic Decathlon wins,’ ‘television production equipment’). It separates program breadth/participation and community partnerships from curricular/academic-program specifics and from staff conduct.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups texts that describe concrete governance failures — frequent principal/superintendent turnover, indicted or absent leaders, school‑board capture, nepotistic hires, contested spending decisions, and persistent unresponsiveness to parents (e.g., “superintendent put on leave…business manager indicted on stealing 400k,” “The school board does whatever the superintendent decides,” “nepotism issues,” and repeated unanswered parent emails). Falling here means reviewers point to structural leadership and governance problems (hiring, budgeting, oversight, recordkeeping) as central, not just isolated poor teaching.
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety incide: This bucket captures reports of concrete safety failures and disciplinary breakdowns — frequent fights/assaults, gang presence, weapons/lockdowns, sexual assault complaints, widespread bullying and vaping, staff or security misconduct, plus administrators who 'look the other way' or ineffective punishments (e.g., “multiple lockdowns…kid bringing a gun,” “Bullying is prevalent and no one does anything,” “security guards follow students into bathrooms,” and accounts of ignored assaults). Texts here focus on student safety, violent incidents, and failure of the school’s discipline/safety systems.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and mor: This bucket groups entries that list concrete programmatic academic strengths — AP/IB/honors growth, transcripted dual‑credit and concurrent enrollment partnerships (RIT, University of Rochester, OSU, community colleges), magnet tracks, and explicit college placement or scholarship evidence (e.g., “transcripted college work…many graduate with over a semester,” “AP programs growing,” “full academic scholarship,” and structured Science & Technology magnet). Inclusion means the review emphasizes available rigorous courses, dual credit pipelines, and measurable postsecondary outcomes as defining school features.
candidate_defs.square entries report more physical‑plan: This bucket covers concrete, recurring facility and resource complaints — aging or failing buildings, pest infestations, mold/expired food, extreme heat/cold, collapsed ceilings, outdated textbooks, parents paying for supplies, and overcrowded classrooms (e.g., “cockroaches in the cafeteria,” “ceilings falling,” “most textbooks are very dated,” and “we are on a paper shortage due to budget cuts”). Reviews in this group emphasize material infrastructure and supply failures that impair daily teaching and safety.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray a smaller, cohesi: This bucket groups reviews that describe a small‑school, tight‑knit, and reliably supportive environment — stable, visible leaders and exemplary teachers/counselors, strong mentoring/role models, low reported safety crises, and community/alumni boosterism (e.g., “The greatest school on earth!”, “small town, small school…able to connect better with your teachers,” and “teachers were as good as any in the state,” plus named counselors praised). Falling here means the text presents an overall well‑functioning, welcoming school climate and dependable student supports rather than governance, safety, or infrastructure crises.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more acute student: This bucket groups reviews describing pervasive unsafe student behavior and inadequate remediation — e.g., daily fights, widespread drug/alcohol use, documented violent assaults, and bullying — together with claims that punishments are weak or incidents are ignored (examples: “fights literally every single day,” “about 60% of the students... done drugs,” and a recorded assault the administration would not share). It captures both the prevalence/severity of student misconduct and reviewers’ reports that the school’s discipline and incident-response practices fail to protect students.
candidate_defs.Square entries report broader and more c: This bucket contains claims about the existence, recent expansion, and measurable success of curricular and co‑curricular programs — explicit AP/IB/dual‑credit participation and AP pass rates, robust CTE/technical classes, award‑winning bands and state‑level sports, and high college matriculation/college‑credit totals (examples: “AP and dual enrollment... 18 college credit hours,” “Cisco Engineering, Project Lead the Way,” and “marching band... national recognition”). It groups concrete program availability, competitive extracurricular accomplishments, and quantifiable post‑graduation outcomes as a single programmatic-capacity theme.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more instructional: This bucket covers criticisms of day‑to‑day instruction and staffing: claims that many teachers can't or won't teach, substitutes are unqualified or inattentive, certification gaps exist, and teacher/coach turnover is high (examples: “teachers who couldn't teach a dog to fetch,” “many teachers aren't even certified,” and “a lot of teacher/coach turnover”). It isolates classroom delivery and personnel stability as distinct from program availability or administrative policies.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects descriptions of leadership misconduct and policy-level failures — secretive handling of curriculum or discipline, alleged fake social‑media profiles to monitor students, sexism/nepotism, administrators ignoring or retaliating against complainants, and dismantling of traditions/programs (examples: “principal that makes false profiles,” “male chauvinist... ‘Boys Club’,” and administrators ‘refused to share’ D&I materials). It captures governance, trust, and equity problems distinct from operational breakdowns or classroom teaching.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more facility, cap: This bucket groups tangible infrastructure and day‑to‑day operations complaints: chronic overcrowding and students becoming invisible, pest/mold problems or poor maintenance, long class/schedule issues, broken or aging technology, and requests for basic supplies (examples: “really SMALL And Crowded,” “rats, cockroaches, mold,” “old netbooks... printers barely work,” and “they do not have books and often ask for ink and paper”). It distinguishes physical capacity and operational execution issues from programmatic offerings, staff quality, or governance failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer facilities,: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete building and infrastructure decay (asbestos, collapsing portables, leaking roofs, roaches/mice, sewage odors, broken HVAC, overcrowded lunches and fire‑marshalled violations) and ongoing maintenance neglect; examples include 'asbestos in the classroom tiles,' 'cockroaches... literally jump on me,' 'portables... caved in,' and 'severe over crowding during lunch,' contrasted with Circle which does not raise comparable facility/health failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete ad: This groups reviews that list specific curricular options, higher‑level coursework, and career pathways (AP/IB/AP scores, honors/accelerated tracks, engineering/IT/health academies, ROP/ vocational pathways, internships and strong college outcomes); representative lines include 'many opportunities for advanced coursework,' '24 AP and Honors courses,' 'Information Technology Systems program,' and 'shadowing in health academy led to PA school,' while Circle rarely names such concrete programmatic offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student misco: Contains accounts of pervasive student safety problems and peer misconduct—fighting, gang activity, on‑campus drug/alcohol use, weapons, sexual/physical assaults, and sustained bullying with weak response—evidenced by phrases like 'students showing up drunk and high on a daily basis,' 'multiple cases of drug and alcohol incidents,' 'survival of the fittest,' 'loaded handgun and drugs,' and 'bullying is not addressed,' contrasts where Circle omits or downplays comparable safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries depict more administrativ: This bucket groups descriptions of leadership problems and policy failures—high principal/teacher turnover, inconsistent or dishonest leadership, cover‑ups/favoritism, budget/prioritization choices (athletics over instruction), punitive or coercive discipline, scheduling and reporting errors, and poor parent communication—e.g. '3 principals in four years,' 'administration sweeps things under the rug,' 'uses funds for sports rather than special needs,' and 'refuses to listen to parent concerns,' a pattern Circle's reviews do not exhibit at the same scale.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broader extracu: Groups reviews that highlight a wide variety and strength of out‑of‑class opportunities and local backing—numerous clubs, award‑winning music/choir/band, competitive athletics and stadium investment, boosters/alumni support, and strong parent involvement—illustrated by 'one of the most competitive choral programs,' 'best band program,' 'hundreds of clubs,' 'large stadium with turf,' and 'strong parent support,' features Circle's reviews largely do not enumerate.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms describing concrete safety incidents and climate: square reviews repeatedly recount bullying (including clique‑targeting, teacher‑bullying of students), frequent fights, weapons/violent assaults, pervasive vaping/drug use and in‑school sales, teen pregnancy, and claims that staff/SROs ‘look away’ or fail to stop/appropriately respond — whereas circle reviews contain little or no parallel evidence of ongoing violent/drug problems and emphasize friendlier, safer student interactions (e.g., “no riff raff,” expulsions for fighting).
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially mo: This bucket captures concrete programmatic strengths in square reviews: many named AP/IB/STEM/magnet academies, JROTC, dual‑enrollment and college partnerships, career‑pathway certifications, robust arts/music/athletics programs, scholarships and selective‑college placements (e.g., Ivy, West Point, Texas A&M), and off‑site technical course partnerships — while circle reviews rarely list such formalized offerings or documented alumni outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater extremes and: This bucket groups observations that square reviews oscillate between strong praise for ‘amazing’ teachers, mentorship and after‑school tutoring and harsh accusations of teacher gossip, bullying, incompetence, burnout, and denied accommodations for students with disabilities or 504/IEP failures; circle reviews tend to present a narrower, more uniformly described teacher experience and do not contain the same breadth of contradictory teacher‑level evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups tangible, operational complaints found in many square reviews — overcrowded classes, broken intercoms, restroom/cafeteria/passing‑time logistics, traffic/transportation problems, running out of supplies, and requests for security upgrades — whereas circle reviews rarely document this range of persistent facility/operations failures and sometimes instead note newer or well‑maintained facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries document more punitive or: This bucket covers reviewer claims about formal policies and leadership: square reviews cite strict monetary penalties (ID fines, summer‑school fees), inflexible scheduling that threatens graduation, athletic favoritism/priority over academics, exclusionary practices to boost metrics, incompetent or unresponsive superintendents/boards, and parental fundraising/advocacy dynamics — circle reviews lack these repeated governance/policy‑level accusations or portray administration as more proactive on discipline/safety.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive saf: These reviews describe routine fights, gang/drug activity, bomb threats, overdoses, pervasive bullying, punitive or inconsistent punishments (excessive suspensions, ISS, isolation) and frequent claims that staff/administration fail to protect victims — e.g., “fights EVERY day,” “5 freshman overdosed,” daily bullying with teachers who “wouldn’t do anything,” and suspension-as-default policies — none of which are present in Circle’s accounts.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader/stronger: Many Square reviews name extensive AP/honors offerings, dual enrollment, CTE/credential programs (CNA, Running Start), internships, academy tracks and concrete alumni/college metrics (perfect SATs, Ivy admits, students entering college with 30+ credits), e.g. “wide array of AP classes,” “dual enrollment credit is guaranteed,” and named elite admit/scholarship outcomes — programmatic and outcome detail largely absent from Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent admi: Square reviews repeatedly cite lost credits, front-office incompetence, slow/unreliable communication, contested principals, alleged district cover‑ups or metric manipulation, graduation/credit barriers and budget mismanagement — examples include a missing VOE that derailed a DMV appointment, claims of district “covering up” incidents, and counselors refusing to accept accelerated credits, whereas Circle contains far fewer such operational failure allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more variable and: Square reviewers document teachers gossiping, playing favorites (often toward athletes), giving arbitrary grades, discussing inappropriate political/sexual content, or doing minimal instruction, and explicitly contrast caring AP/honors teachers with neglectful regular-track teachers (e.g., “Points are freely given to help failing kids,” “teachers gossip... play favorites,” and “Honors/AP teachers are the only ones who really care”), criticisms that Circle does not make at the same scale.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize more concrete e: Square reviews list many named clubs, strong music/band and athletics programs, specialized magnets/STEM/charter tracks (Tesla Engineering, Envirothon dominance), plus detailed facility notes (moldy lunches, dilapidated wings, new windows, planned pools, overcrowding and traffic bottlenecks) and recurring claims that resources are often channeled to athletics at the expense of other programs — programmatic and facility specifics that Circle rarely details.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly name concrete advanced programs and outcomes—AP/IB/ AICE courses, dual‑enrollment and college‑credit, scholarship totals and high external rankings—while circle reviews rarely list such programs; examples include ‘I took 9 AP classes,’ ‘International Baccalaureate (IB) program,’ dual‑enrollment credits, and $1.7M+ in scholarships versus Circle’s lack of named advanced-course offerings and middling test comments.
candidate_defs.square entries report more numerous, hig: Many square reviews enumerate broad arts and club portfolios, state‑level band/orchestra achievements, championship athletic histories, and facility investments (stadiums, pools, music boosters), whereas circle reviews contain little comparable program breadth or high‑level athletic/arts recognition; examples: ‘11 state championships,’ ‘state‑of‑the‑art swimming pool,’ ‘best band program in the state’ vs Circle’s few or problematic team mentions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain multiple concrete accounts of fights, bullying, students intoxicated at school, police in halls, gang shirts at drop‑off, and building health hazards (mold, sewage leaks, vermin), while circle reviews do not document the same breadth or severity of safety and sanitation incidents; examples include ‘constant fights,’ ‘students come to school intoxicated,’ and ‘sewage pipes burst leaking into the hallways.’
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize administrative/: Circle reviews disproportionately focus on institutional/mission failures and punitive rules—claims that the school ‘does not foster a CATHOLIC education,’ accusations of principals lying or leaking private matters, and objections to strict tardy or suspension policies that drive dropouts—issues that are raised far more as central complaints in Circle than in Square.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater teacher/: Square reviews frequently describe a ‘revolving door’ of teachers, extended substitute coverage, loss of experienced staff, and favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families or insiders, while circle reviews present more uniformly described teaching staff; examples: ‘my son has had over 14 teachers,’ ‘many underqualified teachers,’ and ‘if your child is one of the favorites from a wealthy family you will not have any issues.’
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete curricular offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑credit, honors tracks, Cambridge/IB diplomas, STEM/magnet academies, dual‑enrollment credit totals and elite college acceptances) and emphasize programmatic rigor and college matriculation (examples: named IB/AP classes, graduates accepted to Ivy/MIT/Caltech, students with 20+ college credits). A review that emphasizes course availability, diploma requirements, quantitative transfer credits, or named college placements would fall in this bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews document repeated safety incidents and student misconduct plus problematic discipline or inadequate responses (daily fights, drug availability, 2021 riot, recurring shelter‑in‑place events, high local suicide concerns) and often allege that staff/administration fail to intervene effectively or punish victims. Content describing chronic bullying, frequent physical fights, on‑campus drug use, gang activity, suicide history, or systematic failure to enforce safety belongs here.
candidate_defs.square entries describe richer, better‑d: These reviews list concrete non‑curricular offerings and supporting infrastructure (award‑winning TV/production programs, marching band ensembles, MCJROTC, numerous clubs, internship pathways, booster support, new turf/athletic upgrades) and name staff or facilities tied to those programs. Reviews that emphasize extensive clubs/arts/sports, program awards, internships or visible booster/facility investments should be grouped under this bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff/adminis: These items allege personnel- and governance‑level failures (named staff misconduct or threats, racial/wealth/athlete favoritism, covering up safety/code violations, suppressing complaints, opaque budgeting or misuse of funds, calls for state takeover). Any review alleging deliberate administrative concealment, targeted favoritism by staff or board, explicit discriminatory treatment, or fiscal/governance malfeasance is assigned here.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational,: These reviews document concrete, day‑to‑day infrastructure and resourcing constraints — overcrowded buses/cafeterias, class‑change/scheduling problems, HVAC or plumbing failures, cockroach/cleanliness or toilet‑paper shortages, parking permit issues, failed levies and budget shortfalls — or conversely specific recent renovations; any text centered on building condition, space/staffing ratios, scheduling logistics, or district funding dynamics fits this bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries document richer specializ: This bucket groups raw terms that report concrete program availability and breadth: square entries list IB and AP programs, academies (Academy of Media & Entertainment, Science & Health academies), JR ROTC, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit options, robust CTE electives (forensic science, welding, video production), extensive arts/competition teams, international trips, and scholarship/endowment programs—while circle entries offer little or no comparable evidence of these structured, named programs or formal college‑credit pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater teacher/st: This bucket captures complaints about personnel and instruction: square entries repeatedly note high teacher attrition, long‑term or online substitutes, inconsistent use of LMS, sweeping claims of poor teaching or apathetic instructors, classroom‑management failures, and favoritism (teachers/cluster favorites affecting opportunities), whereas circle entries generally describe mostly competent, engaged teachers and do not report the same scale of staffing instability.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms documenting safety and wellbeing incidents: square entries contain numerous reports of pervasive bullying, gang‑related fights, drug and tobacco use on campus, sexual harassment by SROs, arson/hazardous incidents, students self‑harming/PTSD, and parents transferring children for safety—claims that are largely absent or far less severe in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pronounced: This bucket covers concrete facility and capacity evidence: square entries cite overcrowded classrooms and halls, toxic mold and health impacts, broken/restroom/cleanliness issues, transportation/parking/traffic pains, AND simultaneously report large capital investments or state‑of‑the‑art rebuilds, new buildings, or upgraded athletic/theater facilities—while circle entries rarely enumerate either the same facility crises or the same breadth of capital/program amenities.
candidate_defs.square entries show more inconsistent or: This bucket groups terms about governance and policy: square entries contain both praise for highly visible, proactive principals and descriptions of strong parental engagement, and contrasting reports of inequitable discipline, favoritism toward influential families, exclusionary PTOs, unresponsive or rude counselors/administrators, broken registration/records processes, demands for outside audits, and contested discipline policies—whereas circle entries present a more consistent picture of supportive staff/administration and do not report the same mix of high‑impact governance controversies.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: These reviews describe concrete, recurring safety problems (fights “like 3 times a day,” hallway fights, bomb scares), pervasive bullying and harassment, drug exposure, self-harm concerns, and repeated claims that leadership ‘brushes aside’ incidents or fails to enforce discipline — examples include “Bullies are allowed free reign,” “Drugs are a big problem here,” and video of bullying with no action; circle reviews contain little or no comparable evidence and often emphasize an accepting, safer student community.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more numerous, n: Square reviews enumerate specific offerings and outcomes (AP/IB, honors, dual‑enrollment, Project Lead The Way, CNA/Vocational tracks, award‑winning DECA/FBLA/robotics, state athletic championships, alumni scholarships) — e.g., “numerous AP courses,” “dual enrollment…Ohio Northern University,” and “boys swimming won state” — whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable program inventories or concrete college/competition outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Many square reviews accuse leaders of being unresponsive or hostile, protecting insiders/athletes, covering up incidents, or prioritizing bonuses/PR over students (e.g., “cover up scandals,” “favor star athletes,” “school kicks out kids with bad grades to protect image”), while circle reviews lack this broad pattern of systemic cover‑ups and favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviewers repeatedly document physical and logistical failures — outdated buildings, sewage/odor, broken restrooms, 20‑minute lunches with long lines, lack of bus drivers, overcrowded campuses and traffic issues, and routine construction/renovation impacts — examples include “sewer treatment plant…school smells,” “20 minutes for lunch,” and “no bus drivers,” whereas circle reviews rarely report this cluster of operational/facility breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: Square reviews contain many concrete claims about mixed teacher quality and subject‑specific weaknesses, chronic counseling understaffing or mixed college‑counseling help, and uneven special‑education IEP implementation (both failures and some praised exceptions) — e.g., “science and math are mostly a joke,” “3 counselors for ~3000 students,” and “if you have an IEP…this was the first school I have not had to fight” — while circle reviews do not show the same depth of documented instructional/support variability.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: These texts describe concrete threats and harms inside the building — fights, gang presence, drugs/alcohol, lockdowns, threats of guns/knives, sexual-misconduct allegations, on-campus assaults and property theft — plus parents saying staff under‑respond or conceal incidents; examples include repeated daily fights, lockdowns, reports that the school ignored hate crimes, and accounts of assault and mishandled sexual‑misconduct cases. Falling into this bucket means a school’s reviews name tangible safety/crime events and describe insufficient or slow administrative remediation.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and stro: These reviews list programmatic offerings and measurable postsecondary results — IB and AP courses, PLTW/STEM, specialized magnet/academy tracks, dual‑enrollment and college credit, CTE/vocational pathways and certificates, and concrete scholarship and college‑placement stories (selective admissions, alumni degrees). A review fits here when it documents specific advanced courses, structured pathways (magnet/IB/AP/dual enrollment/CTE) or quantified college/certificate outcomes tied to those programs.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Many entries name procedural and leadership breakdowns — lost/destroyed transcripts, counselor turnover and poor college counseling, misallocated funds, front‑office rudeness, selective enforcement/favoritism (especially toward athletes), punitive dress and discipline practices, and claims that administration hides problems or refuses parental cooperation. A school belongs here when reviewers cite concrete administrative errors, biased or punitive leadership behaviors, or systemic operational failures that affect student records, discipline, or access to services.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pr: These reviews enumerate many organized nonacademic programs and achievements — award‑winning music and performing‑arts, competitive marching band, drama/speech teams, ROTC, culinary and many clubs, active boosters/parent fundraising, and visible school spirit/mascot pride. A text falls in this bucket when it documents named, diverse extracurricular/arts programs, competitive accomplishments, and sustained parent/community infrastructure that expands student participation opportunities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistently: Circle texts repeatedly praise teacher caring, encouraging classrooms, responsive counselors/administrators, and an overall positive, welcoming atmosphere (e.g., “I love it here,” “Teachers are encouraging and helpful,” progressive administrative engagement), with few or no reports of the severe safety/administrative failures found in square. A review matches this bucket when it emphasizes reliable adult support, effective counselor/administrator responses, and a generally safe, inclusive day‑to‑day environment rather than program inventories or major operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: Reviews grouped here describe frequent, escalating harm and unsafe campus climates — e.g., 'fights on campus weekly/daily,' students hospitalized, 'a few suicides in recent years due to awful bullying,' gang targeting of students, drug sales/vaping/sexual activity in bathrooms — and repeatedly cite staff/coach non‑intervention; comparable, severe safety incidents are absent from circle reviews, which rarely report hospitalizing assaults or suicides.
candidate_defs.square entries report more formal advanc: These reviews enumerate concrete program offerings and outcomes — multiple APs, IB programs, honors, dual‑enrollment, reported 100% graduation or high US News/SAT rankings and alumni getting into top colleges — whereas circle reviews offer few named advanced programs and more often complain about lack of honors/AP and weak college preparation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: This cluster contains complaints about large class sizes and overcrowding (e.g., 'core classes are 30+', 'nearly 2,000 pupils'), aging or poorly designed buildings and construction that interferes with learning, operational failures during athletic upgrades (kitchen staff driving food while turf/stands are funded), high lunch/parking/extra fees, and claims that money is prioritized for athletics/facilities over instructional programs — issues that circle reviews do not raise to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Reviews in this group allege systemic leadership problems — hiring family/friends, administration 'withholds and quells information,' favoritism to athletes/wealthy students, arbitrary discipline (e.g., 'drawing names out of a hat'), superintendent resignations and calls for fiscal transparency — while circle reviews lack comparable allegations of district‑level corruption or pervasive administrative cover‑ups.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures of s: These texts document concrete service shortfalls — 'they will fight you on special education,' counselors 'too busy to be effective,' students with IEPs poorly treated or mainstreamed without support, ignored self‑harm/mental‑health crises, and families forced to hire tutors or advocate aggressively for schedule/special‑services fixes — problems that circle reviews do not describe at the same scale or intensity.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete safety crises (daily/’rampant’ bullying, suicide attempts, fights/arrests, gang presence, students punched/assaulted, vaping-triggered fire alarms, drugs that sent students to hospital) and administrators/staff who fail to stop or who blame victims (e.g., “bullied to the point of attempting suicide,” “9 fights in one day,” “police have been called,” “they did nothing… my daughter took pills”). Circle entries lack or minimize these severe, unresolved safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a much broader,: This bucket groups concrete program breadth and achievement claims: many named, high‑level activities and wins (speech & debate #1 nationally, state athletic championships, nationally recognized theater/music, “over 80 activities,” professional performance/mentorship opportunities) and alumni/professional outcomes tied to extracurriculars, whereas circle entries omit or report far narrower/no such high‑achievement extracurricular programming.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger explicit: These reviews list concrete academic pathways and results—AP/honors availability, college counselors and SAT prep, national rankings, high Ivy/Selective‑college admits and strong college matriculation rates, or clear statements that honors/AP students are well served—while circle entries generally lack comparable AP/honors depth, national recognition, or named college‑outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries show more evidence of tea: This bucket captures classroom‑level practices described concretely: teachers staying after school, phone calls home, targeted ADHD/IEP accommodations, after‑hours tutoring, hands‑on instruction and permissive/structured retake policies (e.g., “teachers help me through struggles with my ADHD,” “teachers bend over backwards,” “I have never waited more than 24 hours for an email response”), whereas circle reviews do not provide the same range of explicit teacher outreach examples.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers leadership, office, and system-level facts: weak or disrespectful boards/principals, victim‑blaming or blanket suspension policies, favoritism tied to donors/athletics, broken commitments/poor parent communication, selective auditioned admissions or forced transfers, overcrowding/room‑capacity constraints, transportation failures and campus logistics, and program cuts—concrete operational governance problems circle entries do not describe (circle instead often reports responsive administration or lacks these structural complaints).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger/more exte: These reviews describe concrete curricular offerings and outcomes (multiple AP/Honors classes, IB and magnet programs, named academies, university partnerships, AP-to‑college credit and scholarship totals, heavy homework and credit incentives) and frequently link them to college matriculation and test success (e.g., AP classes leading to college credit, Ivy placements, $1.2M in scholarships). Circle entries lack comparable program detail or measurable college‑prep evidence and instead give only generic statements about teaching or limited STEM options, so this bucket groups items about program availability, rigor, and documented postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete safe: Many square reviews list specific safety events and behaviors (recurrent fights, lockdowns, gun/knife incidents, stabbings, drug/alcohol use on campus, bus accidents) and describe failures or inconsistency in enforcement (police involvement with poor follow‑up, staff ignoring substance use, video evidence unreviewed). Circle entries rarely supply incident‑level safety detail and generally do not report this scale or specificity of violence/substance problems, so this bucket captures documented safety/discipline incidents and enforcement failures.
candidate_defs.square entries document more facility, c: Square reviews repeatedly cite physical‑plant deterioration and health hazards (mold, filthy bathrooms, falling‑apart buildings), overcrowding and modular trailers, parking/transport logistics, and disputed resource choices (money funneled to athletics, rising fees/tuition, per‑student participation costs). Circle entries do not present this same mix of chronic facility decay, capacity strain, or explicit funding/fee disputes, so this bucket groups infrastructure, space, and contested resource‑allocation issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater classroom‑: Multiple square reviews name after‑school help, free tutoring programs, teachers who stay late, task blocks for differentiation, strong guidance/counseling coordination, and concrete special‑education supports or failures (e.g., successful 504/IEP advocacy vs. mismanagement). Because circle reviews seldom describe these organized, teacher‑level academic or counseling supports, this bucket groups claims about tangible in‑classroom/helping practices and structured student support services.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Square reviews frequently allege nepotistic hiring, coach/athlete favoritism, political/board influence, gaslighting or administrative stonewalling, punitive attendance/discipline rules, and parents threatened with child‑services involvement or legal action. Circle reviews generally do not report this mix of governance problems, so this bucket captures leadership/policy failures, favoritism, and problematic parent‑administration relations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute student: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents and frequency (daily fights, bomb/gun threats, visible drug use, sexual harassment, high gang activity), staff-condoned violence, and parental withdrawals over safety—claims that Circle reviews largely do not raise (e.g., 'multiple k-9 unit drug searches', 'a boy was bullied... escalated into physical violence', 'I withdrew my two teenagers because of behavior').
candidate_defs.square entries report more and broader a: Square reviewers frequently list concrete program breadth (many AP/IB classes, Cambridge/AVID, dual‑enrollment with community colleges, CVCC/Career Center pathways, award‑winning arts, championship athletics) and tangible outcomes (top-college acceptances, scholarships, awards), whereas Circle reviews typically omit or downplay these program- and outcome-level offerings (e.g., 'AP classes allowed me to start college as a sophomore', 'full orchestra... award winning Arts Department', contrasting with Circle's silence or limited magnet-only mentions).
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic fail: Multiple Square reviews document IEP noncompliance, improperly placed special‑education cohorts, denied services that block graduation, chronically unavailable/ineffective counselors, and poor college counseling or remedial steering (e.g., 'IEPs are supposed to be honored and it is clear that they are not', 'The counselors are no help... very ill prepared for college'), problems not reported in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers describe leadership problems and actionable governance failures—intimidating principals/VPs, administrators who lie or avoid mandatory reporting, retention-for-revenue practices, nepotism/favoritism toward donors or athletes, and district fiscal mispriorities (asking parents to fund services, overpaid superintendents)—while Circle reviews rarely make such district- or admin-misconduct claims (e.g., 'The administration is worthless... intimidate and bully the teachers', 'quota for return super seniors', 'they want the PARENT to fund something taxes used to pay for').
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: Square reviews repeatedly document a wide spread—from highly committed, proactive teachers to tenure‑protected ineffective or unprofessional staff (affairs, online mockery, absenteeism), high turnover or layoffs stretching staff, and mixed outreach practices—whereas Circle reviews present a more consistent staffing picture (e.g., 'many teachers have advanced degrees' vs 'some of the teachers are good, most are mediocre'; 'teachers will go out of their way' contrasted with 'most teachers don't care').
candidate_defs.square entries document far broader / mo: These reviews name specific curricular and co‑curricular offerings (IB/AP/honors, dual enrollment, vocational/CTE tracks, many clubs, award‑winning band/drama, extensive sports, one‑to‑one laptops, theater and new gyms) that Circle reviews do not; examples include detailed AP/IB lists, culinary/automotive/welding programs, Cybersecurity teams, and newly built HS facilities and gyms.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent safe: Many Square reviews recount bullying 'rampant', vaping/juuling and drug use, fights, stabbings/shootings, lockdowns, and restorative practices that reviewers call ineffective—claims and specific incidents largely absent from Circle texts.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more problematic: Square reviewers repeatedly allege administrative mismanagement—favoritism toward athletes or wealthy/connected families, nepotism, legal/financial controversies, residency exceptions for athletes, and claims that budgets prioritize athletics or publicity over academics—whereas Circle rarely raises these governance or politicized‑resource issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize more consistent: Circle reviews frequently highlight approachable teachers, engaged staff, welcoming employees, and character/community supports (e.g., 'door is always open', strong teacher communication and inclusion), while Square reviews more often document uneven teacher quality, unresponsive counselors, or variable staff responsiveness.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete, me: Square reviews cite ranked test results, IB diplomas, AP/college credits, selective university acceptances, GPA before/after transfers and families moving or open‑enrolling to attend or leave the school—specific outcome metrics and relocation decisions that Circle entries generally do not supply.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups raw items that describe ongoing, severe safety and behavioral problems—daily fights, stabbings, gang activity, drug/vape use and smells, multiple suicides, police on campus frequently—and reviewers saying staff/administration ignore or inadequately respond (e.g., 'fights everyday', 'The police are at this school almost everyday', 'Death threats heard everyday and teachers do nothing about it').
candidate_defs.square entries document a substantially: Includes specific program breadth and outcome claims—many AP/IB/STEM offerings, IB workload descriptions, 20+ APs, named honors programs, specialized offerings (aviation hangar), award‑winning JROTC/band/theatre, state championships and Ivy/elite college matriculations—that Circle reviews do not enumerate (e.g., 'There are over 20 APs', 'full hanger built on campus for the aviation program', 'winning the Superindentant's Cup 7 years in a row!', 'students going to Harvard, Duke, MIT').
candidate_defs.square entries allege more entrenched ad: Covers complaints that administration shields underperforming staff, hires/reacts for political/social reasons, enacts arbitrary rules or punitive policies (e.g., blanket punishments, bathroom closures, schedule changes removing APs), and resists accountability—examples include tenure protection claims, 'Nepotism galore', 'admin protects their supporters', and 'the principal single‑handedly revised the daily schedule, making AP Biology impossible to teach.'
candidate_defs.square entries report greater instructio: This groups evidence that the school concentrates quality on a select cohort (AP/Honors teachers praised) while average/struggling students face crowded classes, minimal remediation, failing special‑education services, or unhelpful counselors (e.g., 'AP courses definitely have the best teachers... mediocre at best for anyone other than the top 30', 'Special education system here is terrible', 'The guidance department... was practically useless in our college search', 'They push honors/AP on students who are not prepared').
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete, nam: Clusters reviews that reference specific facility/capital differences—major recent remodels and up‑to‑date tech, specialized on‑site facilities (aviation hanger, top‑notch athletic/music facilities) versus Circle's note that 'You won’t see a lot of $ donating big ticket items' (e.g., '192 million dollar remodel', 'most modern high school... technologically up-to-date', 'full hanger built on campus for the aviation program').
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and bro: These reviews emphasize concrete course- and outcome-level offerings (AP/IB/Honors, PLTW Biomed/Engineering, dual‑enrollment, AP Capstone, many college‑credit options) and measurable outcomes (high AP counts, scholarships, Ivy/UF placements) that circle reviews do not; examples include repeated claims of 19+ college‑level classes, district‑paid AP exams, and formal college partnerships versus Circle's lack of such program detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more abundant, wel: Square reviewers list extensive extracurricular breadth and campus amenities (marching band fees, theater/music buildings, top athletic complexes, ROTC, many clubs, 1:1 laptops, partnerships with community colleges and Jane Goodall Institute) and booster/fundraising activity that Circle reviews rarely mention, signaling a materially broader activities ecosystem in Square schools.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These entries document concrete safety failures—physical assaults, fights, pervasive bullying and cyberbullying, drug use/vaping, lockdowns—and describe insufficient counselor/administrative protection or retaliation against reporters (e.g., assaulted students ignored, counselors minimizing abuse), whereas Circle reviews lack this pattern of chronic unsafe behavior or failed protection.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly cite leadership failures, cronyism, high‑level turnover, scheduling and counselor miscues, unresponsive or rude front‑office staff, mislabeled transcripts/credit disputes, and unreliable homework/grade tracking systems, contrasting with Circle's fewer operational complaints and more organized administrative descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more punitive, exc: These reviews describe formal and informal practices—encouraging at‑risk students to drop out, strict dress‑code and ISS over minor infractions, police‑led enforcement, placement of disruptive students into special ed, and racial/socioeconomic bias—that produce exclusionary outcomes and inequity not evidenced in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute student: This bucket groups raw terms describing concrete safety incidents and pervasive peer misconduct: e.g., reviewers saying “bullying goes on in every nook & cranny,” “fights almost every day,” “kids see drug deals in the hallway,” “lock‑down almost every day,” and special‑needs students bullied and pushed to transfer. These items are about student behavior and school safety failures (incidents, drug searches, police presence, unreported fights) rather than staff policy or facilities, and they occur far more often in square entries than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries document more and clearer: This bucket collects concrete program‑level evidence found mainly in square entries: dual enrollment and 5.0 GPA weighting, robust AP/IB course lists, Project Lead The Way/pre‑engineering, health‑care academies with CNA/EMT certifications, performing‑arts magnets and national trips, and named measurable outcomes (Ivy acceptances, scholarship totals, college credits earned). These items describe actual programs, course pathways, certification opportunities and student outcome metrics (not general impressions of teaching), which square reviewers report much more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer staff and a: This bucket groups concrete complaints about adults’ behavior and policies in the building: examples include “administrators aren’t productive,” “did not respond to emails,” “yelling and scare tactics when disciplining,” athletic favoritism and protection for athletes, micromanagement of teachers, and principals who degrade staff. These are operational and behavioral claims about staff/leadership conduct, communication and discipline enforcement (distinct from student safety incidents or program availability) and are much more prominent in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater overcrowdi: This bucket contains concrete facility and resource problems described by square reviewers: explicit enrollment figures (2,500–3,500 students), legal‑limit cafeteria crowding, broken AC/cold classrooms, older buildings, threatened bus cuts, fees blocking graduation, and understaffed arts programs. These are physical, space, staffing and finance constraints (distinct from program lists or staff behavior) and appear far more often in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a stable, small: This bucket captures circle reviewers’ recurring concrete claims about stable leadership, family‑like small‑school atmosphere, responsive teachers and administrators, PTA/parent involvement, and retention/recommendation (e.g., “we raised two daughters… not disappointed,” “well run… amazing, supportive school board and administration,” and “teachers go above and beyond”). These are concrete community/administration‑stability and engagement features (not mere tone) that distinguish circle entries relative to square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent an: These reviews repeatedly name physical assaults, daily fights, pervasive drug use, racial/anti‑LGBTQ harassment, theft and vandalism—and show administration/staff failing to stop or only giving token 'stern talkings' (e.g., 'fights every day', 'DRUGS.ARE.EVERYWHERE.HERE', Nazi graffiti, student assaulted; 'This school does NOTHING about bullying'). Circle entries contain few or no parallel reports of widespread violence or systemic failure to respond.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially ri: Many Square reviews enumerate program offerings and hard outcomes—IB and honors academies, dozens of AP/ECE credits and concrete AP/IB scores, CNA/ServSafe/Culinary/Auto‑Body/Work‑Based Learning tracks, remediation camps and measurable scholarships—(e.g., 'my son came in with 16 credits', 'IB diploma', 'offers more than a dozen AP courses'), while Circle mostly praises general preparation without comparable program lists or quantified outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviewers frequently reference tangible infrastructure and resource facts—new high schools and multimillion-dollar renovations, athletic field upgrades, but also roach/rodent problems, moldy food, disintegrating buildings, overcrowded halls, lack of A/C and bathroom hygiene—(e.g., 'newly renovated' vs 'bathrooms are unusable', '80 million in renovations' and 'no AC'), whereas Circle seldom gives this level of facility or capital‑project specificity.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: Square reviews present repeated operational and governance failures: unanswered emails, counselors with 200+ students, favoritism in recognition and placements, administrative cover‑ups, high principal/teacher churn and explicit accusations of unethical 'good ol' boy' behavior (e.g., 'FIVE emails... no response', 'counselors prefer advanced/wealthy students', 'principals DONT CARE'). Circle reviews more often describe accessible counselors and involved leadership and lack the same systemic governance complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries document more uneven inst: Square reviews repeatedly say strong teachers are concentrated in honors while average classes are neglected, describe teachers lecturing nonstop, substituting apps for teaching, lost/misgraded paperwork, widespread cheating, teachers on phones or throwing objects, and inconsistent accountability (e.g., 'Excellent teachers in honors; average classes are awful', 'teachers on their phones', 'cheating is a large issue'). Circle entries generally report more consistent, caring instruction and lack these pervasive classroom‑practice failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures repeated accounts in the square texts of ongoing peer harassment, racial slurs, teacher/staff‑perpetrated bullying, physical fights/arrests and extreme responses (pepper spray, suicides) alongside administrators who fail to remediate — e.g., “fights at least once a week,” “The N word is used a lot… I hear it daily,” “teachers do nothing to stop the bullying,” and reporting that administration ‘turns a blind eye’ or only says ‘ignore it.’ Circle entries do not present sustained, systemic safety/harassment incidents or evidence of major admin non‑response.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more num: This bucket groups concrete program/offering evidence in square reviews: multiple AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, named college‑prep tracks (SAS, Distinguished Scholars), National Merit mentions, and alumni college placements (Duke, MIT, USC) — e.g., “only IB school… higher proportion earning IB diplomas,” “offer almost every AP there is,” and “15 college credits transferred so far.” Circle reviews lack these program inventories and measurable outcome claims.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit more polarized, u: This bucket covers the pattern of sharply mixed reports in the square set — co‑occurring glowing endorsements and severe condemnations about the same school — and explicit statements about inconsistent teacher competence and student outcomes (some students ‘thriving’ while others ‘failing 3 classes’), e.g., “now an ‘A’ school” vs “horrible experience,” and “some good teachers … but most do not.” Circle entries are comparatively uniform and do not show that same degree of internal polarization.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize larger, more de: This bucket aggregates square reviewers' concrete lists of broad extracurriculars, strong athletics, booster support, capital projects and named facilities together with critiques that athletics are prioritized (large athletic scholarships, dean focused on football, athletes ‘get away with anything’), e.g., “great variety of extracurricular activities,” “new $14 million science and arts wing,” and “thousands of dollars… top athletic scholarships while top art scholarship was only $200.” Circle reviews do not document comparable extracurricular breadth, facility investment, or athletics‑first favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups operational governance failures described in square reviews: counselors blowing scholarship deadlines, a public grade‑changing trial, lost assignments/late grades, phone/system breakdowns, extreme understaffing and extended substitute coverage, and parents unable to reach administrators — e.g., “counselor has blown deadlines for students to receive scholarships,” “very public grade changing trial for 3 years,” and “phone system is horrendous.” Circle entries do not present the same prevalence of these concrete administrative and operational failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: These reviews repeatedly name concrete program breadth ("many AP classes," "dual enrollment," "Health Academy," "engineering academy," "AVID/IB/CAS classes") and measurable results ("earned college credit," "accepted to top universities," "highest SAT average"), while Circle reviews rarely list comparable academies, AP/dual‑credit pathways, or documented college-credit outcomes. A school falls in this bucket when reviewers point to formal advanced-course pipelines, credentialing programs, or clear postsecondary placement evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain many explicit safety claims — "beaten by bullies every day," "daily fights," "gang problem," "drugs, sex and alcohol are rampant," "outsiders breach security," "no anti‑bullying system in place" — whereas Circle entries do not report pervasive fighting, gang activity, or campus security breaches. Include a school in this bucket when reviewers describe ongoing physical assaults, pervasive bullying/harassment, substance use, sexual‑safety concerns, or unlocked/insufficient campus security.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, broade: Square reviews frequently enumerate and celebrate many named extracurriculars ("award‑winning band—24 state championships," "orchestra, jazz band, choir, robotics, film program," strong athletics and house/mascot pride) and note active alumni/parent pride, while Circle reviews more often report discontinued arts programs or limited extracurricular breadth. This bucket captures schools where reviewers emphasize a wide roster of competitive arts/club/athletic programs and community/legacy engagement.
