candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent,: Square reviewers document erratic enforcement and targeted privilege or punishment — "teams are already established before tryouts," "the dean allows his wrestling team to get away with murder," "suspend for tardies," "retaliation if you complain," "favoring NJHS/kids with money or white kids" — whereas Circle reviews do not present the same pattern of systemic favoritism or punitive retaliation. Use this bucket when reviews allege unequal discipline, athlete/wealth/race‑based favoritism, punitive policies, or administration that defends or retaliates rather than fairly enforcing rules.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic fundi: Square reviews repeatedly cite long‑term budget shortfalls and program cuts, misdirected purchases ("wastes money on flat screens instead of basics"), overcrowded classes and lunchrooms, and deteriorating or unsanitary facilities ("outdated textbooks," "school is in shambles," "mice in the halls"), while Circle reviews more often describe maintained facilities or program rollouts. This bucket covers concrete statements about fiscal distress, misallocation, inadequate materials, overcrowding, or physical plant decay.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: These entries document concrete safety events (guns/lockdowns, bomb threats, daily fights, assaults, on‑site drug use, sexual activity in bathrooms) and often say school security/staff failed to contain or properly respond (e.g., lockdowns, gun scares, students selling drugs near portables, assaulted students ignored), whereas circle reviews do not describe comparable acute safety/crime incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more abundant ad: These entries list formal accelerated programs and measurable outcomes—AP course breadth, IB diploma, dual‑credit/Early College programs, specialized academies (STEM, MERIT, CTE), high AP/ACT/SAT scores and Ivy/top‑college matriculations—whereas circle reviews lack comparable program inventories, AP/IB evidence, or concrete college-placement examples.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broader, higher: These reviews report extensive extracurricular breadth and high‑end facilities (large marching bands, arts tours, JROTC, championship athletics, $60M stadiums, boarding/campus logistics) and also debate capital priorities (spending on stadiums vs. asbestos/AC) and note both recent renovations and separate sanitation/maintenance problems (leaks, roaches, mice), topics largely absent from circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These entries recount systemic operational failures—unreturned counselor emails, counselors overloaded (300 students), poor parent–teacher communication tools, chronically absent teachers, inconsistent grade/attendance posting, scheduling/overcrowding problems, busing and dismissal lapses, and pandemic‑policy conflicts—whereas circle reviews do not present these pervasive administrative or logistical failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inequitable p: These reviews allege biased attention and enforcement (athletes/honors/students with connections favored, nepotism/'townie' advantage), racially or gender‑skewed discipline and dress‑code enforcement, blacklisting of returning students, and concrete special‑education failures or cuts (IEP noncompliance, denied aides), complaints that do not appear in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms where reviewers describe ongoing fights, physical assaults, pervasive bullying, drug/alcohol problems, prostitution/convicted‑felon students, and parents fearing for children’s safety (e.g., 'fights everyday', 'afraid for his safety... wondering if my child is going to make it home alive', 'drugs at school', 'quarterly fights', 'I was bullied non stop...'). These items focus on student conduct and campus/community safety incidents and their direct effects on student wellbeing and are distinct from administrative response or program availability.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures procedural and responsiveness failures: record‑keeping errors, wrong parent calls, omitted yearbook entries, strict punitive absence coding, absent/unavailable counselors, administrative victim‑blaming, wrongful searches/suspensions, and routine non‑response to parents (e.g., 'called the wrong parent', 'The office has marked my student absent multiple times', 'No communication between the school and the parents. None.'). These are concrete management/operations problems distinct from student behavior, program offerings, or curricular quality.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket groups descriptions of concrete academic program availability and outcomes: detailed IB workloads and diplomas, many AP courses, dual‑enrollment college credits, PLTW/Biomed/Robotics/STEM academies, career technical certificates, and lists of elite college placements (e.g., '50 math problems everyday... 150 hours of community service', 'graduated with enough college credits to start with 3 semesters', 'one graduated from Harvard', 'PLTW Biomed, First Robotics, AP Capstone'). These entries are about the presence, scope, and measurable results of advanced curricular offerings and differ from how well classes are taught or administrative conduct.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and broader e: This bucket groups concrete mentions of extracurricular breadth, strong arts and band programs, nationally ranked teams, large facility projects, new buildings/stadiums, experiential/outdoor amenities and costly class trips (e.g., 'excellent fine arts and solid athletic teams', 'brand new stadium', 'flight simulator', 'Class trips to New York City, Disney World, Peru'), as well as explicit investments (solar panels, new science/math buildings). These claims concern programmatic/activity infrastructure and capital/facilities choices, not classroom instruction or equity/favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic favo: This bucket groups allegations of unequal treatment and institutional bias: athletic and district-employee favoritism, nepotism/insider advantage, tracked two‑tier programs (IB vs regular), grade‑inflation/curving to protect certain students, and concrete failures to accommodate or protect students with disabilities and minority students (e.g., 'All the athletes get so much special treatment', 'Education is for only those that work in the district', 'special ed kids get bullied... punishes kids for having symptoms of autism', 'tenure protects ineffective teachers'). These items center on inequitable policies/practices and differential protection/penalties across student groups and are separable from general discipline, administrative responsiveness, curricular breadth, or extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures reviewer claims about school leadership, district/office governance, and policy enforcement (e.g., unanswered phones/slow emails, punitive rule changes, nepotism toward prominent families or staff kids, reported principal incompetence or sudden policy redesigns). Examples: 'How does this school not have a live person answering phones... response time to emails/calls... takes a week,' 'excessive nepotism… Sports programs are all about who you know,' and 'the principal didn’t know how to be in charge so he took away all senior privileges.' It focuses on administrative behaviors and governance decisions (communication, transparency, hiring/discipline policy, enforcement posture) rather than classroom teaching, physical safety incidents, program inventory, or special‑education casework.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket groups reports of on‑site violence, daily fights, gang presence, drug/alcohol incidents, thefts, arson/ bathroom fires, visitor/security lapses, and failures to keep students safe. Examples: 'fights breaking out almost daily,' 'Someone set fire to the bathrooms 3 days this week,' 'Gang mentality,' and 'drug users in every bathroom.' It is narrowly about the prevalence/severity of unsafe student behavior and concrete security failures (and not about how administrators respond to those incidents, which is placed in the administrative bucket).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and broad: This bucket covers availability and scale of curricular pathways, advanced coursework, dual‑enrollment/college credit, vocational shops, performing-arts and music strength, extracurricular breadth, and facility/technology investments or renovations. Examples: 'IB Curriculum is phenomenal… a ton of work,' 'over thirty AP classes… students go to Ivy League and UC schools,' 'auto tech class… two lifts,' '192 million dollar remodel,' and 'introduced Chromebooks into our school system.' It captures what the school concretely provides (courses, programs, capital/tech) and their measured outcomes rather than classroom pedagogy or special‑education casework.
candidate_defs.square entries report more special‑educa: This bucket groups reviewer evidence about IEP compliance, special‑education program quality, denial or misuse of accommodations, low‑incidence supports, and counseling/mental‑health programming (including both reports of systemic neglect and instances of active counselor involvement or college counseling). Examples: 'Have an IEP? Good luck getting the school to follow it,' 'the special education program... after school program (best buddies)... low incidence classroom,' and 'We have a counselor specifically for college and he is a big help.' It focuses on formal student‑support services (IEPs, special ed staffing, counselors, mental‑health programming), distinct from administration governance or general classroom teaching.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: This bucket captures teacher‑level evidence: inconsistent pedagogy, unfair grading, teachers prioritizing coaching over academics, teacher bullying or rudeness, instructional time misuse, and also examples of teachers offering extra help and strong individual instructors. Examples: 'ALL of my academic teachers are also COACHES… priority is on coaching rather than academics,' 'AP teachers are incredibly rude and harsh… yelled at the first day,' 'many teachers offer extra hours… to help tutor students,' and 'teachers not current on latest strategies.' It separates classroom practice and professional conduct from program availability, administrative policy, or special‑education/counseling services.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups raw terms where Square documents recurrent physical fights, frequent threats, clique‑targeted and racist bullying, metal detectors/locker searches, and families withdrawing or homeschooling for safety (e.g., “fights like 3 times a day,” “pervasive bullying and racist comments,” “enroll my children into online schooling to insure their safety”), while Circle generally describes a safer, caring environment. It captures both the high frequency/severity of incidents and complaints that the school fails to remediate them (e.g., “They don't take care of handle bullying very well,” “plagued with the worst follow-thru of an anti-bullying campaign”).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, named ad: This bucket covers Square’s repeated concrete program and outcome claims—AP, IB, honors, concurrent enrollment, engineering courses, Presidential Scholars, specific college matriculations and test-score records (e.g., “AP program…IB is the most prominent,” “3 SHS seniors were selected to be Presidential Scholars,” “One of them graduated from BU”), whereas Circle rarely lists named advanced programs or specific college placements. It captures availability of specialized curricula, recognized extracurricular/competition achievements, and explicit college/certification outcomes that Square reviewers cite.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket groups raw terms describing governance and policy failures in Square—secretive boards, ‘good ol’ boy’ nepotism, administration focused on revenue/image, inconsistent enforcement, threats/overly punitive practices, and unethical behavior (e.g., “the administration is only in it for the cash,” “hired an unethical man… keep the good ole boys in control,” “strict set of rules where there is no second chance”). Circle’s comments lack this pattern of opaque/nepotistic governance or reputation‑first punitive leadership. It captures structural, policy, and governance flaws distinct from classroom practice or facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: This bucket captures Square’s frequent, specific complaints about overcrowding/portables, outdated or unsafe infrastructure, blocked educational internet access, cafeteria and food problems, parking/traffic and scheduling/logistics issues (e.g., “3500+ students…primarily portables,” “They have blocked every single thing…File manager is blocked,” “The lunch is a mess,” “not a functioning fire alarm”), whereas Circle rarely raises these facility/operational deficits. It groups physical capacity, technology/filtering, food/services, and day‑to‑day logistics problems as a distinct operational dimension.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent/: This bucket groups Square evidence of wide teacher quality variation, teacher burnout/high turnover, poor instructional practices, and unreliable student supports (counseling, college office, special‑education compliance) — for example: “Some teachers are incredible…some are awful,” “8 algebra teachers since the beginning of the year… mostly subs,” “college office was AWFUL,” and “IEP accommodations were inconsistently provided.” Circle entries tend to portray more consistently caring/engaged teachers and intact support pathways. This bucket isolates classroom instruction and direct student‑support systems from governance or facility issues.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: These reviews list specific, named academic and programmatic offerings (AP/IB/honors, magnet academies, dual‑enrollment, CTE shops like automotive/woodshop/culinary, robotics, music/theater, clubs) and device/tech programs (netbooks, iPads, 1:1 laptops) that circle reviews do not; examples include long lists of AP/CTE courses, named academies and performing‑arts awards, state‑recognized band, and concrete device loan programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more on‑campus vio: Many square reviews document specific safety incidents, ongoing fights, drug sales, gang activity, thefts, sexual assaults, students leaving campus undetected, and failures to review video or supervise hotspots — a pattern circle reviews rarely present (circle tends to omit or downplay these concrete safety incidents).
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Square reviews repeatedly cite operational failures (mismanaged schedules, wrong books, chaotic onboarding), administrators who ignore/defend problem students or show favoritism to athletes, hardline punitive attendance/tardy regimes, and poor responsiveness to parents (no callbacks, inaccessible leaders), whereas circle reviews seldom name these systemic administrative and discipline practices.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: Square entries contain both praise for devoted, responsive teachers and many reports of poor instruction (teachers who don't teach, frequent substitutes, absenteeism), unprofessional staff conduct (swearing, public insults, racist behavior), and contradictory postsecondary outcomes (both high AP/college success and graduates unprepared), indicating wider instructional inconsistency and outcome divergence than circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize a stronger athl: Square reviews frequently portray sports as central to school identity (football‑centered culture, multi‑decade rival wins, booster disputes), allege preferential treatment of athletes in discipline and funding, and tie athletics to scholarship pathways — themes that circle reviews do not foreground to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: This bucket captures claims that Square schools offer named advanced programs (IB, many AP classes, Advanced Placement Academy, block/dual‑enrollment, SAT prep) and cite measurable postsecondary results (Ivy/Stanford/MIT placements, high college‑matriculation percentages, alumni success stories) that Circle reviews do not provide — e.g., “one of two schools in the county that offer IB,” “AP courses are intensely rigorous,” and multiple named Ivy/college matriculation anecdotes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seri: This bucket groups accounts of repeated peer aggression, physical assaults, gang activity, hall fights and threats paired with staff inaction, inconsistent sanctions, or insufficient security — e.g., “girls started bullying her… it’s non stop,” “students being rowdy and throwing desks… teachers standing by,” reports of students hospitalized, and claims that security or administrators ‘turn a blind eye.’
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize athletics promi: This bucket covers claims that athletics are central to school priorities (high spending, top facilities, award‑winning teams, strong wrestling/football programs), plus allegations that athletes receive preferential treatment or that athletic finances are mismanaged — e.g., “Best athletics in the valley…fantastic facilities,” “if you aren’t a jock… you’re nothing,” and accusations about misallocated concession/athletics revenue.
candidate_defs.square entries report administrative and: This bucket collects concrete governance and personnel failures: unresponsive or punitive office staff, counselor/guidance breakdowns, transcript/credit mistakes, nepotism, cover‑ups, frequent principal/teacher turnover, and opaque or appearance‑first leadership — e.g., “they screwed up my daughter’s transcript… almost didn’t let her graduate,” “the Deans have favorites,” and “guidance here was a joke.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more facilities, c: This bucket captures physical‑plant and resource complaints like overcrowded classrooms (40–50 students), failing HVAC, pest infestations, moldy lunches, crumbling buildings, underfunded programs and outdated technology, as well as explicit space/renovation needs — e.g., “crowded classrooms… no heat or air,” “the lunches are absolutely terrible,” and “the school is dirty… rats, cockroaches, and bedbugs.”
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: This bucket captures mentions of explicit course offerings, programs, and outcomes: AP/IB/Honors, dual‑enrollment and academy programs, STEM and CTE lists, named internships/scholarships, and numeric college‑matriculation rates (e.g., “many AP classes,” “IB program,” “dual enrollment,” “98% of students go to college,” scholarship and alumni success stories). These items are program‑level, verifiable facts about what the school offers and how students fare, not general praise of teaching quality, and are far more frequently present in square reviews than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups concrete accounts of student misbehavior and safety incidents: recurring fights and daily violence, pervasive bullying and identity‑targeted harassment, widespread drug use/dealing, multiple suicides or mental‑health crises, teen pregnancy, bus‑based incidents, and claims that such behavior is normalized (e.g., “a fight happening every day,” “Drugs run rampant,” “Full of bullies and pretentious people,” “they have had multiple suicides”). Many square reviews also tie adult inaction into the safety climate (teachers/security do nothing), whereas circle reviews rarely describe these severe, chronic safety problems.
candidate_defs.square entries evidence more administrat: This bucket covers governance and disciplinary practices: alleged administrative malpractice (lying, suspending victims, invasive misconduct like breathalyzing/photographing students), politicized team selection and pay‑to‑play demands, nepotistic hiring/ favoritism, opaque or punitive discipline policies, and parents being shut down or ignored (e.g., “you might as well bring your lawyer,” “Nepotism runs rampant,” “You pay to play… donate an extra 5k,” “administrators are anti parent”). These are institutional/leadership-level behaviors and policies that square reviewers report much more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: This bucket groups concrete extracurricular facts: long club lists, strong music/theater programs, championship athletics, named coaches, partnerships (college, competitions), and also contested resource priorities or pay‑to‑play practices (e.g., “many extra curriculars,” “Grammy nominated teacher,” “won CIFs… Nationals,” alongside “You pay to play… donate 5k,” and alleged athlete favoritism). Square reviews more often report both the breadth/achievements and the politics/funding tradeoffs of extracurricular life than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more instructional: This bucket captures teacher and building operational issues: inconsistent/underqualified teachers, unresponsiveness or reliance on paid tutoring, poor classroom management, large class sizes and chaotic class changes, overcrowded hallways, outdated or leaking facilities, supply shortages and cleanliness problems (e.g., “teachers are not qualified,” “parents paying for tutoring,” “35+ people in classes,” “halls were so crowded,” “roof leaked… no pencils or paper,” “bathrooms are a MESS”). These concrete instructional and infrastructure constraints appear far more often in square reviews than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced/: These reviews describe concrete programmatic breadth (AP/honors, dual‑enrollment, Engineering/STEM/Visual & Performing Arts academies, magnet tracks, Work‑Based Learning, vocational centers, study‑abroad and scholarship pipelines) and downstream outcomes (college acceptances, credits earned, graduates attending selective universities) that square reviewers cite but circle reviewers largely do not (examples: 'Engineering Academy', 'Work‑Based Learning program', 'AP and dual‑enrollment', '16 college credit hours', 'graduated with honors and scholarships').
candidate_defs.square entries report more varied but st: Square reviews disproportionately note teacher-level academic practices and supports — both positive (teachers who 'take a personal interest', one‑on‑one tutoring/mentoring, sustained AP teacher relationships, good command of content) and distinct instructional patterns (high homework loads, rigorous honors/AP expectations, or teaching‑to‑the‑test), whereas circle reviews rarely document these concrete classroom supports or sustained rigor (examples: 'teachers truly take an interest', 'extra help after school', '3+ hours of homework nightly', 'teaching to the exam').
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers more often describe non‑instructional, operational breakdowns and policy obstacles — unclear/inconsistent communication, misfiled IEPs, parent‑required meeting policies, tuition/enrollment rejections, leadership turnover, scheduling/placement mistakes, mandated busing problems, overcrowded halls/desks, and facility/HVAC/cafeteria problems or renovations — while circle reviews mention few of these concrete failures (examples: 'found numerous mistakes on my children’s paperwork', 'still no school buses for the high school kids', 'turnover of principals', 'renovation but overcrowded').
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe safety: Square reviews disproportionately document high‑severity safety problems and weak remedial action — stabbings/shootings, sexual harassment, repeated fights, regular bullying and ignored threats, drug searches, and complaints that administration fails to act or applies punitive/automatic punishments inconsistently — claims that are largely absent or far less severe in circle reviews (examples: 'Kids have been stabbed', 'sexually harassed every single day', 'Bullying happens at least four times a day and the administration does absolutely nothing').
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced st: Square reviewers frequently describe a bifurcated social and academic structure — two distinct tracks (honors/AP vs everything else), visible cliques and exclusion, preferential treatment for athletes/high achievers, and socioeconomic/racial exclusionary cultures — whereas circle reviews do not emphasize this kind of organized favoritism or tracked social hierarchy (examples: 'two “tracks” ... two different schools', 'if you are good at sports or school then the teachers care', 'they are all so clique invested').
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger/specific: These reviews repeatedly name concrete offerings and outcomes—AP/IB/AVID classes, multivariable/linear algebra, selective STEM and Dual‑Language magnets, dual‑enrollment and college credits, large scholarship/National Merit totals, and alumni college/ career success (e.g. “48 AP credits,” “$16 MILLION,” National Merit winners, graduates at Princeton/Harvard”)—claims that Circle reviews do not supply or quantify, so Square entries emphasize program breadth, vocational/CTE pathways, and documented college/career results more than Circle entries.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: Many Square reviews document recurring safety problems (daily fights, sexual harassment/assault, gang targeting, student overdoses/deaths, bomb threats), on‑campus searches/metal detectors, routine K‑9 locker searches and vaping/drug use, and reviewers saying staff/admin failed to stop or under‑enforced incidents—claims far more numerous and specific than in Circle entries, which rarely describe this level or frequency of safety/criminal incidents.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers frequently accuse leaders of prioritizing reputation or athletics over students, show explicit favoritism/nepotism (legacy families, PTO favoritism), document unresponsive front offices/boards, threats of lawsuits, attempted leadership coups, and high principal/assistant‑principal turnover (even numerical claims), painting governance and leadership as active drivers of problems far more than Circle entries do.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more consistent te: Circle reviews repeatedly praise helpful, engaged teachers and counselors, individualized follow‑through (e.g. grief accommodations, pandemic check‑ins), a welcoming school climate, and active parent/community involvement, whereas Square entries more often report inconsistent or indifferent staff/counselor responsiveness and mixed parent‑school communication experiences.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete oper: Square reviews supply many specific operational complaints and contested policies—severe overcrowding/parking shortages, leaking roofs/mold, recent facility upgrades in other cases, contentious block schedules and 90‑minute periods, late buses and third‑lunch line problems, online courses replacing hands‑on instruction, and established online credit‑recovery/dual‑enrollment practices—practical, reproducible operational details that Circle entries seldom describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more specialized a: This bucket groups items where reviewers list concrete programs and pathways available at the school (e.g., IB diploma, AICE, many AP/honors options, dual enrollment with community college and Running Start, STEM academies, CTE/vocational tracks, extensive band/arts and named clubs like Model UN, TSA, JROTC). Square entries repeatedly enumerate these course/program offerings and college-credit options while Circle entries lack comparable named program breadth or dual‑credit pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports of acute safety problems and hostile student behavior documented in reviews (examples: repeated fights, weapons on campus, bomb threats, shelter‑in‑place events, gummy bears laced with substances, pervasive drug use, sexual harassment, homophobic and racially‑targeted assaults and hate‑crime reports). Square entries raise these concrete safety incidents and resulting harms far more often than Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced ca: This groups mentions of visible capital work (brand‑new school buildings, Olympic‑sized pools, remodeled campuses, modern security cameras) together with complaints about spending priorities and fiscal governance (money funneled to athletics/technology while textbooks/substitutes lack funding, failed levies, complaints about mismanaged tax dollars or district debt). Square reviewers often pair concrete facility upgrades with arguments that resources were misallocated, a pattern Circle entries do not mirror.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: This bucket covers administrative/operational breakdowns and governance problems described in reviews — long delays or missing report cards and truancy notices, unreturned special‑education communications, rude front‑office behavior, high principal/board turnover, nepotistic hiring, and inconsistent or biased enforcement of discipline/Title IX. Square entries contain many concrete examples of those administrative failures and alleged unfairness, whereas Circle entries tend not to report them.
candidate_defs.square entries report more variable and: This bucket groups classroom‑level staffing and instructional evidence: instances of highly supportive, award‑winning teachers and formal teacher collaboration alongside reports of chronic teacher vacancies, unqualified substitutes, teachers 'showing up for a paycheck,' uneven departmental quality, tenure/hiring abuses, and complaints about rigor or virtual‑learning failures. Square entries present both ends of this staffing/quality spectrum in concrete examples, a variability less evident in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student-: This bucket captures concrete harmful incidents and campus-safety lapses where Square reviewers describe frequent/severe bullying, fights, gang activity, drug use/vaping/overdoses, sexual assaults, and failures of on-site security (e.g., ‘people doing drugs in the bathroom’, ‘fondled by a teacher’s son’, ‘fend for themselves against the gang violence’, ‘smell marijuana…’, calls for metal detectors), while Circle contains little or no comparable evidence of pervasive safety incidents or systemic physical violence.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: This covers reports that leadership and district governance protect staff, ignore complaints, engage in cover‑ups, scapegoat students, or apply biased discipline (e.g., ‘administration always backs the teacher’, ‘deans are biased because one is a coach’, ‘reaching out to the board gets you nowhere’, ‘principle is firing teachers, blaming them’), in contrast to Circle reviews which report more accessible or supportive administrators and no board-level cover‑up allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and mor: This groups concrete program offerings and outcome claims—AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, college counselors, organized college trips, documented Ivy/Scholar placements, and quantifiable test/college results (e.g., ‘full IB diploma’, ‘more AP classes than typical’, ‘graduates with 20+ college credits’, ‘perfect SAT scores’), whereas Circle reviews seldom list such formal advanced-program structures or measurable college-placement evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more uneven instru: This bucket includes classroom-level delivery and support: inconsistent teacher competence and differentiation, high turnover and morale problems, punitive or inflexible grading/homework practices, counseling/tutoring availability, and special-education noncompliance or shifting costs to families (examples: ‘teachers don’t differentiate’, ‘many teachers inadequate’, ‘IEPs are not honored’, ‘counselors are no help’), while Circle generally lacks these patterns of systemic instructional/support breakdowns.

candidate_defs.square entries document broader, more va: Square schools are described with named magnet programs, award‑winning performing arts centers, strong athletics and technical/trade offerings (and also notes about funding tradeoffs or underfunded areas), while circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth (examples: 'PAC performing arts center', 'BioHealth Magnet', 'Technical center is great' vs. circle's limited elective/arts mentions).
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete acc: Reviewers of square schools cite explicit supports (dyslexia programs, AIS/remedial classes, tutors, accessible counselors, individualized medical accommodations) alongside concrete failures (IEP noncompliance, understaffed counselors, poor college guidance), whereas circle reviews rarely describe these structured supports or detailed special‑education problems (examples: 'any time of the school day...dyslexia program', 'they are not doing the IEP guidelines', 'overworked, understaffed counseling department').
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket covers concrete reports of routine fights, physical assaults, gang activity, on-campus injuries, property vandalism, pest infestations, nonfunctional emergency systems, and staff-involved harassment — plus reviewers’ claims that staff/administration ignored or inadequately responded (e.g., “kids get jumped and beat up,” “There are fights EVERY day,” ceiling tile struck a student, nonworking intercom, allegations that administrators made sexualized comments or threatened community members). candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews repeatedly describe severe safety problems—physical assaults, frequent fights, sexual harassment, vaping/drug use, bathroom smoking, threats to teachers, and security-staff misconduct (e.g., invasive searches)—and criticize weak or inconsistent school responses; examples include a student punched and suspended, a reported 'vaping epidemic,' 'violence is everywhere you look,' and security guards who 'bully' students, none of which Circle reviews document to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries document substantially st: Many Square reviews list concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes—AP/IB/dual-enrollment, early-college/College Academy pathways, named gifted programs (CAS), career-technical partnerships (LCTC), high AP pass rates and students admitted to elite colleges—along with external recognitions and transcripted college credit, whereas Circle seldom names comparable advanced-course infrastructure or measurable college-placement metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers cite leadership failures (calls to replace principals/superintendents), opaque or unethical administrative practices (lost files, advice to falsify attendance, closed offices), arbitrary or uneven discipline, and general bureaucracy that obstructs resolution, illustrated by comments like 'The principal is a bully,' 'bureaucracy is an absolute nightmare,' and 'administration turns a blind eye,' contrasts that Circle reviews do not make.

candidate_defs.square entries describe a wider, deeper,: Includes descriptions of many clubs, arts and vocational programs, award‑winning band/ROTC/teams, sustained championship athletics, and explicit program partnerships that Square reviewers list but Circle reviewers do not (examples: 'more than 100 clubs,' 'award winning magnet programs,' 'top track and cross country team for 28 years,' 'broadcasting and culinary programs' vs Circle's sparse extracurricular mentions).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups concrete reports of on‑campus threats and harms—recurrent fights, thefts, in‑school drug/alcohol use, sexual assaults, homophobic/racial harassment, and even suicides/attempts—that Square reviewers recount at scale while Circle reviews do not document comparable safety crises (examples: 'Drugs are a big problem here,' 'I've seen more fights than on Jerry Springer,' multiple suicides and suicide attempts, racial harassment at sporting events).
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Captures complaints about leadership and systems: scheduling and grade errors, administrators who ignore or retaliate against parents/students, grade‑changing, secrecy/corruption accusations, inconsistent discipline and bureaucracy—Square supplies many named incidents and district‑level controversies, whereas Circle contains little or only mixed administrative criticism (examples: 'screwed up my child’s schedule,' 'refused to release nurse records,' 'the blame game is a tradition among the administration').
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures (and: This bucket covers concrete denials or poor delivery of IEP/504 services, lack of special‑education coordination, ineffective or nonexistent counseling, mental‑health neglect (and ties to student departures/self‑harm), plus tracked/segregated access to honors; these operational support failures are repeatedly described in Square but are absent or less pronounced in Circle (examples: 'no IEP/504 coordinator,' 'counseling nonexistent,' 'they give Certificates of Completion instead of diplomas,' 'great for honors/AP kids but terrible for those with learning challenges').
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: These reviews emphasize concrete curricular and extracurricular resources at square schools — AP/IB/GT tracks, magnet/JROTC/STEM/career academies, dual‑enrollment (UCONN ECE), expansive arts/robotics/athletics teams, and named college matriculations — claims that Circle reviews do not list (examples: “AP English… almost every AP there is,” “IB Diploma Program… particularly strong,” “UCONN ECE,” “over 20 APs,” and students admitted to Ivy/MIT/Penn).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: Many square reviews recount concrete safety problems and inadequate responses — regular hallway fights, assaults and marks on students, widespread drug/alcohol use and in‑school dealers, overwhelmed resource officers and drug‑detection dog searches, plus staff complacency about bullying — contrasted with Circle’s lack of comparable safety incident reporting (examples: “Fights almost everyday,” “drugs run rampant,” “Bullying is common and unpunished,” and “resource officers overwhelmed”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Square reviewers frequently cite tangible infrastructure and operational issues — dilapidated/aging buildings and collapsing portables, pest infestations, flooded/unusable fields, chronic overcrowding and long bus delays, poor cafeteria/phone systems, and disputes over capital spending priorities — often blaming uneven funding or misallocated capital (examples: “portables...caved in from the cockroaches,” “afternoon bus is always 30–45 minutes late,” “facilities are delapidated,” and complaints that money was spent on an ag department or locker rooms instead of books/security).
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Reviews of square schools document management and personnel practices that harm students and families — controlling/unqualified principals, nepotism and coach favoritism, chaotic scheduling/communication, incorrect guidance counseling, inconsistent IEP/504 implementation or scholarship/advising failures, punitive or misapplied discipline, and front‑office rudeness — issues Circle reviews do not similarly raise (examples: “Nepotism galore,” “counselors gave wrong information 3 times,” “They do not do what they say they will do in class for IEP or 504,” and “principal is too controlling”).

candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: These reviews name and document real curricular depth and college supports (many AP classes, IB/Aerospace/NJROTC tracks, virtual/dual‑credit options, dedicated college counselors, FAFSA/free SAT programs) and cite measurable alumni/college outcomes (Ivy/UT/Cornell acceptances, national merit, scholarships), whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable course catalogs or concrete admission/scholarship evidence. candidate_defs.square entries describe broader academic: This groups specific, concrete program offerings and outcomes—AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment/transcripted credit, vocational pathways (CNA/EMT/CAD/auto/cosmetology), specialized academies and clubs, large arts and music programs, and named college matriculations—frequently documented in square but absent or far less detailed in circle (examples: “many APs,” “dual enrollment,” “Center for Communication and Technology,” “band is one of the best in the state,” and “students going to Princeton/Yale/etc.”).

candidate_defs.square entries report more acute safety: These texts document concrete safety incidents and pervasive student misbehavior—daily fights, drug/alcohol use, bomb threats, sexual assaults, on‑campus childcare implying teen pregnancy, and repeated ineffective anti‑bullying responses (e.g., students removed for bullying, administrators sharing confidential reports). candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: This bucket collects square reports about physical resources and budgets—overcrowding/space problems and split‑campus layouts, aging vs new buildings, cleanliness/pest problems, technology availability or failures (one‑to‑one laptops vs rotten netbooks), meal/service breakdowns (denied food, out‑of‑date items), material shortages, mandatory fees/fundraising pressure, and explicit per‑pupil funding shortfalls (e.g., “books are not supplied,” “roaches in classrooms,” “community pays $54 per student/year”). candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews recount concrete safety incidents and pervasive disciplinary problems—fights/riots, lockdowns, vaping/drugs, sexual harassment—and add charges that staff punish victims or fail to report/address incidents; circle reviews generally contain little or only isolated behavioral complaints (examples: 'riots and fights in the cafeteria,' 'guns on campus/lockdowns,' 'sexual harassment…victim suspended' vs. Circle's lack of comparable incidents).
candidate_defs.square entries describe more punitive, i: Square reviews frequently call out rigid/nitpicky discipline, monetary fines, administrative favoritism toward athletes/programs, alleged manipulation/grade/graduation statistics, poor BOE or principal integrity, and failures to implement IEPs or counseling supports—problems that circle reviews do not commonly report (examples: 'charged $1 each day for no ID,' 'kids graduate despite failing,' 'IEP has been useless,' 'administration lacks integrity').
candidate_defs.square entries report a broader, more vi: Square school reviews list many named clubs, competitive arts and athletics, capital improvements and external STEM/industry partnerships alongside concrete resource issues (overcrowded cafeterias, outdated textbooks, locked bathrooms, funding skewed to athletics/technology), while circle reviews tend to omit that same level of program/facility detail (examples: 'new stadium and Olympic sized pool,' 'over 80 activities,' 'Robotics team/awards' and also 'no gym…overcrowded' and 'parents supply toilet paper').

candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent safe: Multiple square reviews describe recurring fights/lockdowns, visible drug and vaping use in bathrooms, bullying (including alleged suicides related to bullying), lax supervision (students leaving campus, buses causing disruption), and intrusive security responses (metal detectors, searches), whereas Circle reviews lack these concrete safety/substance incidents.
