Example evidence: square contains 'numerous fights every year,' 'students smoke pot in the classroom,' 'she was bullied daily,' 'bomb threat and a soft lockdown,' and complaints that bullying is 'swept under the rug' or that security 'high five' fighters; circle reviews contain little or no comparable reporting of these safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket groups reviews alleging weak or dishonest leadership, cronyism, favoritism for athletes/children of staff, uneven discipline enforcement, misuse/misallocation of funds, tenure‑protected poor teachers, school-board unresponsiveness, and politicized hiring/layoffs. Example evidence: square reviewers accuse principals/superintendents of 'refusing to acknowledge real issues,' 'preference given to children of town favorites,' 'misspending of appropriated funds,' firing good teachers while keeping poor ones, and 'school board does not listen to the community.'
candidate_defs.square entries show pronounced polarizat: This bucket captures reviews that present sharply divergent firsthand accounts within the same school — simultaneous high praise and severe criticism — and evidence of wide variation across teachers/departments (some outstanding teachers/programs vs many poor ones). Example evidence: square includes 'fantastic in every way' alongside 'avoid at all costs,' multiple conflicting reports about principal visibility, and subject-level contrasts like excellent AP/STEM tracks coexisting with failing math/science departments; circle reviews are more internally consistent and rarely present such polarized internal contradictions.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more granular fac: This bucket covers concrete, day-to-day operational and physical-plant issues described in square reviews — major remodels/renovations, overcrowded passing periods, short lunch windows, cafeteria quality/line logistics, parking/athletics fees, restroom restrictions, uniform controversies, night-school/alternative scheduling — which circle reviews rarely mention. Example evidence: square mentions 'major remodel... state of the art facility,' '4,200 students... overcrowded,' 'parking fees at a public school,' detailed lunch-line systems and 10‑minute lunches, restroom sign-in/I.D. policies, and construction disruptions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute and fre: This bucket groups items describing concrete safety incidents and ineffective protective responses — e.g., reports of "fights every day between classes," gang affiliation, student drug/alcohol availability, guns/weapons, a 2021 riot, frequent lockdowns, and cases where parents say the school/administration did nothing when a child's life was threatened. These raw terms emphasize on-campus violence, substance issues, pervasive bullying, and direct failures to secure student safety that are largely absent from circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher-: This bucket captures concrete program availability and outcomes — e.g., named IB and STEM academies, many AP/Pre-AP classes, dual-enrollment/college-credit programs, Medical/Engineering/Creative Arts magnets, JROTC championships, internship/research experiences, and alumni college-credit/GPA/scholarship totals — plus program awards and national competition placements that square reviewers cite but circle reviewers typically do not. It emphasizes tangible offerings and measurable postsecondary results rather than subjective teaching quality.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: This bucket groups reports about leadership and operational dysfunction — e.g., "3 principals in 4 years," named administrators accused of unprofessionalism, alleged nepotistic pay raises, union‑protected underperforming teachers, scheduling errors and website shutdowns, dismissed parent safety complaints, and calls for greater school-board oversight. These are organizational/governance problems distinct from classroom instruction or program availability and are reported far more in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater polarization: This bucket collects the mixed instructional evidence — e.g., first‑person stories of teachers who "bond" and provide remediation that improves grades alongside many accusations of unqualified instructors, poor math teachers, high substitute usage, and teacher bullying. The defining feature is high within‑school variance (some teachers exceptional, others ineffective), whereas circle reviews present more consistent, uniformly positive teacher performance.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray a more consistent: This bucket captures traits emphasized by circle reviews — e.g., repeated statements of a "supportive community," "friendly students," steady administration and staff who are available and caring, consistent positive outcomes across siblings, and active parental/community involvement — a uniformly positive, stable social climate and staff responsiveness that contrasts with the fragmentation, safety incidents, or governance problems reported in many square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reviews that describe recurring physical fights, sexual harassment, shootings/guns, pervasive drug dealing/use, daily police escorts, coordinated threats, and systemic bullying (including racialized or staff‑tolerated bullying). Examples: 'fights almost every day,' 'massive amounts of drug use... admin turns a blind eye,' 'student took their own life,' and teachers laughing as an autistic girl was bullied — contrasts with Circle, which contains little or no evidence of frequent fights, guns, or pervasive drug cultures.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader and more: This bucket groups concrete program‑and‑outcome evidence: named AP/dual‑enrollment/CCP courses, magnet/science/arts centers, vocational shops, extensive club lists, championship records, scholarships and alumni college acceptances. Examples: '17 different AP courses,' 'College Credit Plus & CVCC partnerships,' 'state champions in music/athletics,' 'endowment-backed scholarships' — while Circle reviews generally list few specialized programs and no comparable systemic outcome data.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers reviews alleging withholding transcripts/records, counselors who ignore students, administrators who bully or hide incidents, inconsistent/arbitrary rule enforcement, and favoritism toward athletes/influential families. Examples: 'counselor denied graduation/was unhelpful,' 'administration bullies kids that don't conform,' 'rules only apply to some,' and 'they will hold your transcripts if you don't pay' — contrasted with Circle, which contains fewer claims of pervasive admin misconduct and more examples of supportive teachers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute facilit: This bucket groups concrete infrastructure and day‑to‑day operational failures: disgusting bathrooms, mice/rats, parts of campus without air conditioning, terrible Wi‑Fi and app blocking, overcrowded grade cohorts, missing lockers, no auditorium/intercom, and inadequate after‑school transportation. Examples: 'bathroom looks absolutely disgusting,' 'THE WIFI IS TERRIBLE,' 'nearly 1,000 per grade,' and 'no locker until two weeks into school' — Circle reviews do not report comparable, repeated facility or logistics failures.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: This bucket captures contradictory but specific claims about instruction and supports: reports of extreme homework and mental‑health harm alongside high AP/college success for other students; both praised and failed IEP/counseling outcomes; program‑level staff quality splits and inconsistent grading practices. Examples: 'school will destroy your mental health' vs. 'rigorous programs enhanced my life,' 'IEP follow‑through improved' vs. 'special education is awful — hire an attorney,' and 'few exceptional teachers while many don't care' — whereas Circle tends toward a more internally consistent portrayal of academic experience.
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader formal a: This bucket groups reviews that report concrete program breadth (IB, many AP/honors, dual‑enrollment, required financial literacy, STEM/medical apprentice pathways) plus high‑profile extracurricular achievements (Carnegie Hall invitations, state championships, national awards) and explicit college/test outcomes (high SAT/ACT scores, many students into top‑tier colleges, full‑ride scholarships). Example evidence: multiple square reviews cite a full IB diploma program, 40+ clubs, AP credits that skipped college semesters, and named college matriculations—claims absent or far weaker in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reviews describing on‑campus fights, vaping/drug incidents (including fire‑alarm disruptions), alcohol at games, suicides/protests tied to bullying, police presence/ankle monitors, locker searches, surveillance software/IDs/audio on buses, and punitive suspensions or expulsions. Example evidence: square reviewers recount 2–4 fights a week, students suspended after social‑media photos with police interviews, repeated drug/alarm incidents, and surveillance spyware—situations circle reviews do not document.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pronounced st: This bucket covers reviewer claims about teacher/administrator misconduct (yelling, insults, humiliation), favoritism, staff entitlement, forced departures of good teachers, poor front‑office responsiveness, and inconsistent enforcement of rules. Example evidence: square reviews name teachers calling students 'stupid' or joining bullying, assert 'good teachers forced out,' complain 'office doesn't return calls' and describe arbitrary rule enforcement—patterns that circle reviews rarely allege.
candidate_defs.Square entries document clearer gaps or: This bucket groups reports of inadequate special‑education accommodations, need for parental advocacy to secure services, overloaded/uneven counselors, absence of peer‑support groups, mental‑health stigma, and mixed evidence of both strong and failing support staff. Example evidence: square reviewers describe parents 'fighting tooth and nail' for IEPs, denial of graduation accommodations for a traumatic‑brain‑injury student, counselors described as both 'overloaded' and 'wonderful' depending on program, in contrast with circle which rarely mentions special‑ed or counseling detail.
candidate_defs.Square entries highlight facility, capac: This bucket includes concrete claims about overcrowding/high student‑to‑teacher ratios and class sizes, facility condition (mold, roaches, asbestos, broken escalators), renovation activity or new buildings, and contentious budget priorities (athletics spending vs academics, alleged misallocation). Example evidence: square reviews cite class sizes of 38–41, mold and rodent problems, $4.2M spent on a football field while academics suffer, and both reports of complete facility renovations and of desperate maintenance needs—topics circle reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews repeatedly name concrete offerings and results (IB program, many AP/honors classes, AP pass‑rates, college credits earned, students admitted to top universities) that square reviewers cite as evidence of rigorous curriculum and post‑secondary readiness (examples: “There are 15 AP classes…over 30% enrolled,” “full IB Programme,” “students got into top 20 colleges,” “start college with several college credits”), while circle reviews lack comparable program lists, AP/IB outcomes, or measurable college-placement claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews describe weapons, mass fights, sexual assault, pervasive bullying, vaping/drug problems and administrators/staff who ignored or minimized complaints (e.g., “a student had a bullet… fights inside of class rooms,” “I was sexually assaulted… told I was lying,” “HUGE drug problem,” “administration insists it does not exist”), whereas circle reviews do not document the same breadth and severity of safety incidents or systemic nonresponse.
candidate_defs.square entries document a broader, bette: Square reviewers enumerate rich co‑curricular offerings, named award‑winning bands, theatre, JROTC, thriving sports, Booster Club fundraisers and capital investments (examples: “musical theater and choir programs are outstanding,” “Parents provided over $4 million… Washington Township Schools Foundation,” “superb athletic facilities”), while circle reviews rarely cite comparable program breadth, awards, or large‑scale parent fundraising.
candidate_defs.square entries depict greater intramural: Square reviews contain many juxtaposed claims about staff—teachers who 'volunteer before and after school' and 'go out of their way to help' alongside accusations of incompetence, favoritism, unprofessionalism, sexism, political proselytizing, or 'there for a paycheck' behavior (examples: “teachers volunteer time… ” vs. “replace those teachers… there for a pay check,” “teachers gossip…snap,” “atrocious math teacher”), producing a wide performance spread that circle reviews do not show to the same extent.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more visible adm: Square reviewers frequently cite concrete administrative policies or failures—visitor‑policy revisions, block/schedule changes, metal detectors, district buyouts, careless budgeting cutting programs, inconsistent communication systems, lost paperwork and scheduling/credit errors (examples: “Four classes… eighty minutes,” “the school policy failed to protect my children… rules later changed,” “district paid many teachers to take early retirement,” “constantly schedule and cancel events”), whereas circle reviews rarely document this level of operational policy detail or explicit administrative policy change.
candidate_defs.square entries show substantially strong: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize concrete curricular offerings and outcomes—AP, IB, honors, dual‑enrollment, Cambridge/AVID tracks, and measurable results (high AP/IB participation, scholarship totals, students admitted to MIT/NYU/etc., SAT/ACT rankings). Examples: multiple Square lines list “IB program (EXCEPTIONAL)”, “23 dual credit courses and 18 AP courses”, “helped me skip a semester at NYU”, and large scholarship/college‑matriculation claims; Circle contains no comparable AP/IB/dual‑credit/program outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete safety/behavior incidents and climate: repeated fights, stabbings, arson, drug culture and overdoses, gang activity, sexual‑assault mishandling, lockdowns, and pervasive bullying described as unresolved. Illustrative Square claims include “a student was stabbed in the hallway,” “huge drug problem,” “bullying is a severe issue,” and “We had so many deaths of drug overdoses,” while Circle’s texts lack such severe, recurring safety incident reports.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: This groups reviews alleging governance and policy failures—administration unresponsiveness to formal complaints, protecting bad teachers, nepotism, board corruption/censorship, budget mismanagement or prioritizing athletics over academics, and opaque/unfair policies. Representative Square evidence: “We tried to file report but administration did nothing,” “nepotism is rampant,” “budget is a joke…needs a good outside audit,” and “administration sticks behind bad teachers,” contrasts with Circle’s absence of such governance/fiscal accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a broader, highe: This bucket contains concrete programmatic breadth and physical‑plant claims—many clubs and teams, strong band/music accolades, vocational/H‑Hall programs, well‑maintained or newly rebuilt facilities, and upgraded athletic fields. Examples: Square lists “over 200 clubs…over 20 sports,” “band invited to Normandy,” “football field better than some college stadiums,” and “brand new facilities,” whereas Circle rarely enumerates comparable extracurricular breadth or facility investments.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: This bucket covers on‑the‑ground instructional and support features—wide swings from caring/innovative teachers and active social‑worker/counseling interventions to punitive or neglectful teacher behavior, inconsistent SPED/ELL services, uneven guidance counseling, and extreme homework/scheduling complaints. Square examples include “Teachers go out of their way…,” “Great support system of social workers and psychologists,” but also “Teachers yell at students,” “most teachers could care less,” “AP teachers throw too much work at you,” and contradictory SPED reports; Circle generally lacks this same mix of strong/weak classroom‑and‑support service detail.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more student safet: This bucket groups raw terms that describe concrete safety problems (frequent fights, bullying and cyberbullying, gang activity, theft, on-campus drug/alcohol use, vaping, locker‑room harassment) and concrete security responses (security cameras, K9 searches) — e.g., “every other week a fight is breaking out,” “verbal harassment and cyber bullying are huge issues,” “Drugs run wild… PPD to pick up confiscated drugs,” and “there were camera's inside the school.” These items focus on student-to-student or student-safety events and the school’s security hardware/interventions, not on leadership or instructional quality.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more administrat: This bucket captures reviews that single out principals/administrators/office staff for absence, non‑response, punitive or arbitrary discipline, hiding information, transcript or scheduling mishandling, and confused or fragmented leadership — e.g., “the principal never responded… the office forgot to send out my transcript,” “administration withholds information from parents,” “zero tolerance… punish hardworking students,” and “three principals for the ninth graders… no communication between administrators.” These items are about administrative behavior, enforcement choices, and record/policy management rather than classroom teaching or program offerings.
candidate_defs.Square entries provide more concrete, va: This bucket groups raw terms describing teacher practice and student support: availability/extra‑help and exceptional teachers alongside claims of inadequately trained staff, high turnover, and failing special‑education or counseling services — e.g., “teachers would leave at 7:00 if I needed help,” “guidance is beyond useless,” “not enough resources or properly trained teachers,” and “If your child is in special education you must stay on top of the IEP.” These items are centered on classroom instruction, counseling/guidance, special‑ed delivery, and teacher accessibility.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more extensive c: This bucket covers explicit programmatic offerings and partnerships — advanced-course breadth, dual‑enrollment, career/technical institutes, strong arts/music programs, and community/university links — e.g., “Dual College program with Bunker Hill Community College,” “Many AP/dual credit courses,” “Fine and Performing Arts Magnet,” and “UCD Math Circle / Seed learning center partnership.” These items describe what programs the school provides (or suddenly lacks), distinct from how well they are delivered or discipline issues.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more facility, cap: This bucket groups concrete operational and physical constraints: chronic overcrowding and crowded hallways, poor or upgraded facilities, traffic and entrance bottlenecks, fees and coercive payment policies, technology maintenance failures, and scheduling/prerequisite errors that delay graduation — e.g., “classes are overcrowded… no seat some days,” “it takes at least 30 minutes to get my child to school,” “they charge for summer school” and “class placement mistakes… you cannot graduate with your class.” These items concern school infrastructure, capacity, and operational policy rather than instructional content, extracurricular breadth, or disciplinary conduct.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket covers reports of violence, gangs, frequent fights, pervasive bullying, police involvement, and concrete safety crises at school combined with ineffective or punitive school responses (e.g., calling police on victims, lawsuits, students withdrawing). Examples: “riddled with violence,” “principal called the police on the VICTIM of bullying,” “gangs move everything inside the school,” “bullying runs rampant…the school does nothing,” and parents removing children for safety reasons.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: This bucket groups accounts that list concrete programmatic offerings (AP, IB, dual‑enrollment, specialized academies/CTE, STEM accelerators) and quantifiable postsecondary results (high SAT/ACT, Ivy placements, scholarship totals, >90% college attendance). Examples: “tons of AP classes, IB program,” “Academy of Justice / Environmental Innovation,” “graduates go to Princeton…many full academic scholarships,” and “dual enrollment / Early College” placements.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical cap: This bucket captures concrete facility and capacity deficits: extreme class sizes, trailers and insufficient rooms, building disrepair, pest/mold/unsanitary conditions, and HVAC/comfort problems. Examples: “about 40 kids in every class,” “roaches, mold, dead rat,” “trailers because our school is too small,” and “no AC/heating problems,” which are described more often in square than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket collects reports of dysfunctional governance and office-level practices—board-level money priorities, ‘good‑old‑boys’ favoritism, lost transcripts/credits, arbitrary fees, silencing of complaints, inconsistent discipline, and broken communication systems. Examples: “the school board…only care about money,” “they refused to send transcripts…my application was rejected,” “favoritism runs rampant,” and “communication is terrible…you are on your own.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent te: This bucket covers descriptions of hands‑on, approachable teachers and counselors, visible/practical administrative outreach, and strong parent/community ties that reviewers attribute to student support and wellbeing. Examples: “The principal is always in the halls…calling parents,” “The guidance counselors are fantastic,” “teachers are caring and inspiring,” and “parents are really involved / staff live in our town,” which appear more often in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers reports that schools suffer ongoing physical threats, daily fights, lockdowns/weapons incidents, rampant drug/vaping access, persistent bullying (sometimes leading to legal action or therapy), and that staff/administration routinely fail to investigate or protect victims; examples include 'we get threats every single week,' 'multiple lockdowns...kid bringing a gun,' 'drugs are a HUGE problem,' and parents obtaining protective orders — contrasts with circle’s lack of these systemic safety claims.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader advanced: This groups concrete programmatic and outcome evidence (AP/IB availability, early-access AP, Running Start/dual enrollment, ROP/CTE pathways, CNA/EMT certifications, numeric ACT/AP gains, and named Ivy/Johns Hopkins acceptances) where square reviewers cite exact classes, test scores, and college placements—e.g. 'AP courses and Running Start,' 'API jumped...to over 800,' 'accepted to Johns Hopkins'—facts largely absent or unquantified in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive,: This bucket captures descriptions of many and varied clubs, national/international performance tours, trophy‑winning arts programs, major athletic facilities and stadiums, and on-campus career experiences—examples: band invited to Macy’s and China, theater awards and Carnegie Hall performances, 'multi-purpose stadium with lights,' and 'Student Store' work experiences—whereas circle seldom lists comparable program breadth or high‑profile achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries report more problematic l: Includes allegations that administrators prioritize image over safety, hide incidents, enforce arbitrary or punitive policies, favor athletes/wealthy families, mishandle budgets or unpaid contractors, and maintain unwelcoming front offices — e.g. 'principal more concerned about the public view,' 'they keep things quiet,' 'coaches picked favorites,' and 'constant fundraisers/guilt campaigns' — contrasting with circle’s fewer or different administrative criticisms.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater polarizat: Covers repeated, role-specific contradictions and spread—from reports of long‑tenured, highly committed teachers who mentor and run tutoring/retake systems to claims of many unprepared, inattentive, or frequently absent/turnover-prone teachers and union-protected poor performers; representative lines include 'excellent teachers... alongside administration that cares about bottom line,' 'teachers willing to stay after school,' and 'revolving door of new people who can’t make it.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seri: These reviews document concrete safety failures at square schools — fights, arson, gang activity, arrests, lockdowns, random canine locker searches, widespread drug/alcohol use, racialized harassment, sexualized conduct, and student self‑harm/trauma — whereas circle reviews routinely lack such incident detail and often describe a safe, comfortable environment; examples include 'too many fights,' 'big drug problem,' 'two fires set by students,' and 'horrendous job protecting my child from constant racialized bullying.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: Square reviewers repeatedly list concrete programmatic assets — numerous AP/IB/honors classes, PSEO/dual‑credit and Governor’s‑school links, distinct academies and vocational partnerships, award‑winning music/theater, extensive clubs and travel athletics, and cited alumni college placements — while circle reviews rarely name comparable programs or measurable outcomes (e.g., 'graduated with 18 college credits', 'AP and PSEO helped me get an associates by graduation', 'award‑winning music department').
candidate_defs.square entries report greater teacher cr: Many square reviews cite higher teacher qualifications, regular tutoring/after‑school help, lunch/one‑on‑one instruction, and counselor availability that produce college readiness for some students, whereas circle reviews more often describe lack of support or remedial instruction; representative evidence includes 'teachers have advanced training', 'free tutoring M–TH', 'teachers will teach you during lunch 1 on 1' contrasted with circle's absence of these supports.
candidate_defs.square entries document more systemic fa: Square reviews contain repeated allegations of biased discipline and favoritism — racialized punishment, athletic/affluent/student‑status favoritism, principal protecting relatives, 'Good Ol' Boy' nepotism, and union‑shielded staff — while circle reviews do not present this cluster of systemic inequity; examples: 'majority of the children ... reprimanded are black', 'principal's son can literally walk out of the classroom', and 'they cater to affluent students who give money.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: Square reviewers frequently cite concrete infrastructure and logistics failures — 30–40+ portables, overcrowded classrooms and buses, filthy bathrooms, broken shop equipment, unreliable Wi‑Fi, meal complaints, bus schedule breakdowns, and opaque/poor phone or attendance systems — whereas circle reviews rarely raise these operational faults; representative lines include '40+ portables', 'wifi is extremely unreliable', 'the phone system is horrendous', and 'the cafeteria is small and unkempt.'
candidate_defs.Square entries describe stronger, more n: These reviews repeatedly name concrete programmatic offerings (IB, mandatory Cambridge, many AP courses, CTE pathways including associate-degree options, robust band/choir/theatre, and dozens of clubs) and measurable outcomes (AP/IB/college credit, national awards), while circle reviews seldom enumerate comparable program depth or institutional arts/CTE strength (examples: 'IB and AP rigor', 'Associates Degree in cyber technology', 'performing arts school … top notch').
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews cite daily/weekly fights, pervasive drug/vaping use in bathrooms and halls, repeated racial harassment toward minorities, sexualized behavior in corridors, and accounts of students returning home injured — often paired with administrators who 'did nothing' or advised families to leave; circle reviews rarely document these specific, repeated safety incidents.
candidate_defs.Square entries show more inconsistent, b: Square reviewers describe selective enforcement (e.g., cell-phones enforced but dress codes ignored), favoritism toward athletes or donors, hand‑picked teams, unequal punishments tied to parent influence, and punitive attendance rules that disproportionately harm families — a pattern of unequal enforcement and nepotism not reflected in circle entries.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more operational: This cluster covers repeated complaints about inaccessible or rude office staff, missed/incorrect schedules, broken registration/device distribution processes, robotic misdirected calls, counselors who don’t respond or give poor college advising, and delayed grade/credit processing — concrete procedural breakdowns and counseling gaps that circle reviews more often describe as responsive or absent altogether.
candidate_defs.Square entries exhibit greater within-sc: Square reviews commonly report polarized teacher performance (both highly dedicated teachers and many ineffective ones), high turnover, inconsistent differentiation (IEP dismissal vs. some success stories), uneven feedback/grading practices, and both strong individualized tutoring coordination and cases where special‑needs students were neglected — a pronounced variability in instruction and special‑education supports that is less evident in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger/more ex: This bucket captures concrete program offerings and documented results (availability of IB/AP/dual‑enrollment/vocational/STEM/ROTC academies, broad arts/music ensembles, many clubs and sports, and measurable outcomes like rankings, scholarship totals, and selective college matriculation). Examples: numerous Square claims of IB accreditation, 'tons of AP classes', dual‑credit courses, vocational shop/auto and engineering certifications, award‑winning band travel, US News rankings and $26M in scholarships versus Circle’s lack of comparable programmatic detail or outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent STUD: This bucket groups claims about on‑campus danger and exclusionary social climate—repeated fights, daily violence/lockdowns, drug/tobacco use, pervasive bullying, racial/LGBTQ harassment, unequal punishments, and at least one staff sexual‑misconduct allegation. Examples: Square reports 'two fights a day', stabbings, 'half of the baseball and football team are smoking pot', racial slurs and LGBTQ harassment, and 'One teacher was fired for sleeping with a student', while Circle contains few or no such safety/harassment reports.
candidate_defs.square entries document more ADMINISTRAT: This bucket covers leadership behavior and district‑level governance problems—hostile or evasive principals, rude front office, manipulation of metrics/image, billing errors, chronic unresponsiveness to parents, high leadership turnover, labor disputes, and complaints about fiscal priorities (overpaid superintendents, asking parents to fund things). Examples: Square notes 'Administration is hostile', 'principal lied to save money', 'teachers and admins take weeks to reply', recurring labor problems and accusations that 'all the income goes to football', while Circle’s reviews contain far fewer of these governance and communication failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more INSTRUCTIONAL: This bucket groups concrete classroom‑level evidence about how teaching and assessment operate—uneven teacher effectiveness, pervasive lecturing or busywork, harmful grading policy changes, flawed online/assignment design that masks poor mastery, chronic substitute use/teacher absenteeism, and mixed evidence of strong after‑school help. Examples: Square criticisms include 'lecture every lesson', 'busy‑work grades only', 'new grading policy is harmful', and teachers seen only rarely, contrasted with Square’s separate reports of teachers who stay after school and 'drive' students—while Circle provides little parallel documentation of detailed classroom assessment design or teacher availability.
candidate_defs.square entries report more FACILITIES, C: This bucket covers physical and operational conditions—overcrowding and modular classrooms, dilapidated or odor‑filled buildings, broken equipment, parking fees/shortage, cafeteria/menu complaints, and also explicit facility investments or construction projects. Examples: Square repeatedly cites 'overcrowded', '8 modular buildings', 'not renovated in 40 years', missing ceiling tiles, $50 parking passes, and plans for a new high school or upgraded bleachers/gyms; Circle rarely reports comparable facility detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute student: This bucket groups reviews that describe frequent physical fights, gang presence, on‑campus drug sales/vaping, police/Taser incidents, suicides and widespread bullying — plus claims that staff/administration do not effectively stop or prevent these harms (e.g., 'fights every day,' 'gang members walking the halls,' 'drug dealing on campus,' 'bullying is prevalent and no one does anything'). These items all indicate a school safety/climate problem rather than routine misbehavior and are distinct from administrative rudeness or facility complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive for: This bucket captures concrete program/policy offerings and outcomes: many AP/IB courses, full IB diplomas, named dual‑enrollment partnerships (UCONN, community colleges), vocational certifications/CNAs, and higher college matriculation or credits earned (e.g., '18 AP and numerous PreAP,' '60 college credits from AP,' 'dual enrolling at Western; UCONN classes offered'). These are program‑level resources and measurable postsecondary outcomes — separate from how well day‑to‑day instruction is delivered.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and better‑re: This bucket groups descriptions of robust after‑school life and parent booster involvement — award‑winning marching band, elite choral/ theatre programs, successful sports teams, many clubs and flexible participation ('band AND chess AND soccer') and active PTO/boosters — and also notes critiques that administration prioritizes sports over academics in some reviews. These are concrete program offerings and fundraising/parent engagement patterns distinct from classroom instruction or facility condition.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects complaints about leadership and policy enforcement: administrators protecting certain students/coaches, arbitrary enforcement (drawing names from a hat, selective dress‑code), withdrawing credits without consent, administrative rudeness to parents, coverups, and repeated leadership/staff turnover (e.g., 'administration supports inept teachers,' 'withdrawn from class with no credit,' 'principals are rude'). These signal governance and fairness problems distinct from safety incidents or program availability.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced fa: This bucket groups concrete physical and operational resource complaints: overcrowded lunchrooms and buses, windowless classrooms and failing code, cockroaches/pest infestation, broken chairs, old textbooks/desks, locked bathrooms and heavy bag/security checks, plus apparent misprioritized purchases (smart boards/iPads versus building repairs). These are infrastructure, scheduling and resource‑allocation issues distinct from curricular offerings, extracurriculars, staff behavior, or safety/climate.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures concrete accounts of on-campus danger and misconduct plus failures in handling them — e.g., “fights every single day,” “drug usage rate is at least 70%,” students ‘afraid to use the restrooms,’ mishandled sexual-assault and bomb-threat incidents, rampant vaping, and repeated complaints that staff/administration do little or make things worse. Circle reviews rarely describe such daily, severe safety incidents or systemic enforcement failures, so items in this bucket are distinguished by operational safety/discipline breakdowns and unresolved student conduct problems.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frontline adm: This groups reports of concrete administrative and governance failures — e.g., ‘The staff in the registration desks are extremely rude,’ ‘two deans and three advisors in 1.5 years,’ ‘almost cost my child his diploma by not giving him English 12,’ named staff misconduct, patronage (band director helping secure jobs), and inconsistent/biased discipline policies. Circle entries do not show this same pattern of pervasive scheduling errors, rudeness to parents, politicized hires, or documented leadership turnover, so these reviews map to problems in how the school is run and communicates with families.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete, ext: This bucket groups specific curricular assets and documented outcomes: e.g., IB/Cambridge programs, dozens of APs, dual-credit/early-college pathways yielding transferable credits, high SAT scores and alumni who matriculate to selective universities or earn scholarships. Circle reviews generally lack evidence of such named advanced pathways, measurable test/college outcomes, or organized selective academic academies, so items here indicate stronger, explicit college‑prep and advanced-course infrastructure.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more and more-vari: This bucket covers programmatic extracurricular detail and tensions: examples include ‘Drama & Band programs are excellent,’ abundant clubs and JROTC, specialized arts/STEM academies, but also complaints like ‘most money goes to sports,’ $1000+ activity costs, selective/audition admission to arts/sports, and coaches being protected despite problems. candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive ext: This bucket groups reviews that describe many clubs, top-ranked band/choir/theatre, championship athletics, and explicit resource or recognition tradeoffs favoring sports over arts/science (examples: “hundreds of clubs,” “band program is the best,” “11 state championships,” and complaints that “the whole budget” goes to athletics while arts get little funding). Belonging here means the school is portrayed as having broad extracurricular offerings and/or an athletics-dominant institutional priority that shapes budgeting and student recognition, a pattern not emphasized in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: This bucket includes reviews detailing operational and governance problems: unresponsive principals/registrars/guidance offices, mishandled disciplinary hearings, exclusionary practices to improve metrics, denial of graduation or last‑minute credit errors, board/superintendent protectionism, and legal-threat complaints (examples: “Guidance office and Principal unresponsive,” “they dropped her down to needing 22 credits… prevented from graduating,” “one hand washes the other” school‑board behavior). Items here point to systemic administrative failures or punitive policies that block student opportunities, which circle entries rarely assert.
candidate_defs.square entries report more variable and: This bucket groups evidence about in-class delivery and student support: widely varying teacher quality (teachers who ‘play videos’ or ‘don’t teach’), teacher bullying/public humiliation, inconsistent grading/group‑grading abuses, counselors who favor athletes or are ineffective, poor IEP/504 accommodation, and uneven access to extra help (examples: “some teachers are awesome… some just suck,” “Teachers bully students,” “The guidance counselors are not helpful at all,” and “not the place for students with special needs”). Reviews in this bucket emphasize failures or inconsistency at the teacher/counselor/classroom level distinct from district or facility issues described elsewhere.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures raw terms describing repeated physical fights, gang activity, drug use/overdoses, severe bullying, assaults, and reviewers’ claims that administrators fail to intervene or protect victims (e.g., “constant fights, huge presence of drugs,” “They let people assault children and suspend the victim,” “5 freshman overdosed together”). Circle entries by contrast contain little/no evidence of these kinds of pervasive safety incidents and instead emphasize trusting or effective student safety.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, more co: This bucket groups claims about explicit program offerings and outcomes — a rich AP/IB/STEM/CTE catalog, PLTW/engineering/SolidWorks, dual enrollment, a long list of clubs and award-winning music/athletics, and cited college rankings or alumni success (e.g., “AP...Calculus AB/BC… robotics team won First Place,” “PLTW teachers are amazing,” “ranked the 3rd best high school,” alumni attend Marquette). Circle entries rarely enumerate such programmatic detail or measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries allege greater administra: This bucket captures governance-level problems and district/policy breakdowns — accusations of nepotism and administrative pay impropriety, board hostility toward staff, billing before enrollment, coverups, opaque budgeting and misallocation (e.g., “Suffering from an intense level of nepotism… superintendent gave raises to wife and principals,” “We received a bill before my child was even officially accepted,” “sweeps things under the rug”). Circle entries do not present comparable district-level misgovernance claims and are more often neutral or praise leadership.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater unevenness a: This bucket groups reviewer evidence that some teachers/counselors are exceptional while many are ineffective, plus variable special‑education supports and inconsistent mental-health awareness (e.g., “we've had some really good teachers, we've had some horrible teachers,” “If your child has an IEP, know it will be a major struggle,” “some teachers understood anxiety and others didn't”). Circle entries tend to report more uniform, consistently caring/competent staff and fewer claims of systemic instructional variability.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete ope: This bucket covers tangible campus and operational features — crowding and requests to expand, recent renovations or old/deteriorated buildings, hygiene/food complaints, schedule formats and access periods, active parent portals, bus/busing cuts and pandemic remote-learning breakdowns (e.g., “overcrowded… should expand campus,” “bathrooms are a wreck… smell like vape,” “the Parent Portal… grades every Friday,” “Distant learning was a total joke”). Circle entries rarely include this level of concrete facility/operational detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews describe concrete leadership problems (grade‑tampering pressure, administrators bullying or retaliating, monetization/self‑promotion, hiring/board nepotism, image‑over‑resolution policies, and calls to replace principals) — e.g., “principal came to me and told me to pass him anyways,” “new football coach gets $100,000 in salary… invented for the football coach,” and threats to parents who complain — contrasts with Circle’s far fewer or milder administrative criticisms.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews recount recurrent fights, drug/vaping/gang activity, victim‑blaming, racialized assaults, and ineffective discipline or protection (students leaving for safety), e.g. “fights at LEAST once a week,” “full of drugs and lowlifes,” and ‘the principal yelled at my daughter for not being kinder to the perpetrator,’ while Circle contains fewer or isolated safety incidents and more accounts of teacher/administrative protection.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader but more: Many Square reviews list abundant specialized programs, high AP/IB/STEM/arts/athletics achievements and scholarship evidence for top students (e.g., IB diploma, AP exam stats, college acceptances), but the same texts also document pronounced stratification and low expectations for non‑tracked students (‘strong AP program but other 4/5 of the school provides a very low education’, ‘social promotion’), whereas Circle rarely shows this stark program/outcome polarization.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviewers repeatedly cite overcrowding, major maintenance and hygiene failures, heat/AC outages, insect infestations, technology/budget shortfalls, lost‑and‑found/front‑office unresponsiveness, and transportation gaps (e.g., “made students go to school when it was 112 degrees,” “The lunch room always runs out of food,” “no bus service to the high school”), while Circle seldom reports these kinds of facility/capacity failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more polarized and: Square reviews often contain two co‑occurring but distinct instructional claims — concrete examples of highly accessible teachers, long‑term special‑education support, credit‑recovery pathways and counselors who saved graduations (e.g., sustained IEP support, homework centers), alongside repeated allegations of teachers not teaching, phone distraction, uneven AP teaching, and staffing shortages/turnover — whereas Circle’s accounts are more consistently one-sided and do not show this same internal instructional variability.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete curricular breadth and outcomes at Square (AP/IB offerings, multiple honors levels, dual‑enrollment, magnet/SAS programs, rising test scores and external rankings, and documented college placements/credit accumulation) that Circle reviews do not (examples: 'seven AP courses', 'IB Diploma Programme', 'test scores continue to climb', 'students admitted to UCLA/Harvard', '30+ hours of AP credit').
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews repeatedly cite on‑campus violence and safety incidents—daily/recurring fights, gang presence, lockdowns, pervasive drug use, racial slurs and bullying, and visible police/SRO activity—while Circle reviews typically lack or downplay such chronic safety claims (examples: 'lock‑down almost every day', 'The school is filled with pot heads', 'every day there is at least one fight', 'police cars outside every single day').
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: Square reviewers give numerous concrete operational and governance complaints (unreturned emails and missed investigations, erased credits, failure to follow truancy/504 rules, coercive threats, alleged data manipulation, board rubber‑stamping, scheduling/placement glitches), indicating systemic accountability and process breakdowns that Circle rarely reports (examples: 'teachers DO NOT RESPOND to emails', 'They erased all his credits', 'principal said he'd make sure I was put in juvenile hall', 'complete disregard of students in the 504 programs').
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical inf: Square accounts cite tangible facility and resource deficits—aging buildings and lack of basic infrastructure (no A/C, outdated equipment), pest/cleanliness problems, congested hallways and overcrowding, no lockers or adequate dining space, and maintenance shortfalls—whereas Circle seldom documents comparable physical deterioration (examples: 'cockroaches and mice', 'very old and in need of repair including no air conditioning', 'hallways are always packed', 'few places to sit; no lockers').
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, better‑: Square reviews list many concrete, well‑resourced out‑of‑class opportunities—state‑level arts/band/theatre, championship sports and scholarship athletes, extensive clubs and robotics/CTE certifications, booster/alumni networks and capital projects—that Circle reviews typically do not (examples: 'top notch band and theatre', 'many scholarship athletes year after year', 'welding tech (can get cert.)', 'huge network of famous alumni', 'outdoor amphitheater that seats a whole school').
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups descriptions of routine, serious student conduct and safety problems and the school’s failure/inconsistency in addressing them (daily hallway fights, routine vaping/drug sales, regular bullying and homophobic/racist harassment, even law-enforcement interventions). Examples: reports of "fights daily in the hallways," "half the school vapes," students selling drugs on campus, and repeated claims that complaints are ignored or only get a 'stern talking to.'
candidate_defs.square entries document broader and more: This bucket captures concrete program availability and outcome evidence: named AP/IB/dual-enrollment/CTE pathways, specialized academies, and explicit outcome metrics (scholarships, Ivy/elite acceptances, API/test scores). Examples: listings of IB/AP/DECA/robotics/PLTW programs, dual enrollment and vocational centers, and claims of multiple scholarship and top-college acceptances.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers governance and process failures: frequent principal/counselor turnover, alleged grade tampering, concealment of problems, retaliatory responses when parents complain, bureaucratic hurdles to services (IEPs), and calls for district restructuring. Examples: reports of 'grade changes by VPs,' 'admin hides problems,' 'when you file a complaint they make claims against you,' long IEP delays and costly documentation, and '3 principals in four years.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe more instruction: This bucket collects classroom-level teaching and learning evidence: uneven teacher quality (snide comments, mocking, apathetic teachers), busywork/test-prep focus, poor classroom management, large teacher caseloads and poor parent communication, and allegations that classes do not meet standards. Examples: 'most homework is just busy work,' teachers 'mocked' students with ADHD, 'teachers having 180 kids' relying on online portals, and claims instruction 'not teaching state standards' or AP classes that 'did not prepare me for college.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: This bucket groups physical- and resource-related facts: overcrowded classes and undersized hallways, mixed reports of new additions alongside aging infrastructure, transportation/busing and parking complaints, and contested funding choices (too much to sports, parent-paid supplies). Examples: 'packed into classes like sardines,' 'halls and stairwells are SO undersized,' paid parking without cameras, buses that don’t run and families walking in extreme weather, and parents funding uniforms/umpires while science labs go unfunded.
candidate_defs.square entries describe richer advanced/: These reviews report concrete program offerings (AP, IB, honors, dual‑enrollment/concurrent credit, internships, vocational tracks/CNA, early college) and cite college placements, scholarships, and selective‑college matriculation as evidence; Circle reviews lack those named programs and outcomes. Examples: multiple Square comments listing IB/AP/dual‑enrollment, internships and documented graduates to Ivy/UC schools versus Circle’s absence of named advanced pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries report more on‑campus vio: Square reviews include frequent concrete safety incidents (large fights, on‑campus drug deals, weapons entering campus, arrests, police patrols) and describe weak or punitive responses (victims suspended, bullying swept under the rug), whereas Circle contains little to no comparable evidence of pervasive violence or failed safety mitigation. Representative items: police walking hallways, multiple 20‑student fights, rampant drug/gang claims, and ineffective anti‑bullying handling in Square.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviewers frequently allege nepotism and favoritism (athlete protection, family/political preference), cover‑ups and retaliation, board/superintendent capture, rigid or over‑punitive discipline (blanket suspensions, random searches), and disputed spending priorities—claims that Circle reviews generally do not make. Illustrative examples include claims of athletic favoritism in discipline, administrators “turning a blind eye,” misallocated bond/operating funds, and reported retaliation against complaining parents in Square.
candidate_defs.square entries provide far more concrete: Square reviews routinely name bond‑funded renovations, new buildings, 1:1 laptop programs or failing tech, explicit tutoring/schedule times, crowded classrooms, and specific operational failures (food quality, water, bus routing), whereas Circle rarely supplies these granular facility or operational facts. Examples: Square noting bond‑funded performing arts renovations, Mac grants/1:1 laptops, before‑school/Saturday tutoring times, and complaints about bathrooms or lunch service.
candidate_defs.square entries report more granular clas: These reviews give detailed evidence about how instruction and supports are delivered—examples include teacher‑led cheating, large variation in teacher quality, high turnover, inadequate college counseling, IEP follow‑through failures, either too‑light or excessively heavy homework loads, and tutoring/remediation operational details—topics Circle reviews raise far less or not at all. Representative Square items: allegations of teachers giving test answers, counselors who don’t help with college/scholarships, teachers leaving, and specific reports of ineffective or exceptional teachers and tutoring schedules.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete prog: These reviews describe specific, named offerings and documented results (AP/IB/dual enrollment, honors, career‑tech, LISA/theater, large JROTC units, internships) and cite measurable outcomes (national merit finalists, 30+ college credits, college matriculation); circle entries rarely list comparable programs or outcome evidence, instead offering general statements about opportunities without program names or outcome data.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews repeatedly recount fights, gang problems, drug use (even heroin), sexual misconduct in class, bomb threats, suicides linked to bullying, unlocked access and calls for metal detectors, and other actionable safety failures; circle reviews do not report these kinds of recurrent or extreme safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers cite superintendent/board capture, fiscal mismanagement and tax hikes, cover‑ups, politicized hiring (nepotism), principal self‑promotion, and frequent leadership turnover or mass teacher departures—concrete governance and transparency failures not described in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more instructional: Square reviews document teachers who don’t teach (videos or online work instead), poor gradekeeping, multiple confusing digital platforms, daily substitutes/high absenteeism, unreturned parent emails, and chaotic/ineffective tutoring or after‑school supports—specific operational and instructional shortfalls that circle reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.square entries report more entrenched fa: Square accounts include gatekeeping of AP/honors to protect averages, athlete/popular‑student immunity from discipline, counselor favoritism, racial/economic segregation in honors tracks, and biased dress‑code or discipline enforcement—concrete patterns of unequal access and preferential treatment absent from circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more (and more: This bucket captures concrete program availability described by reviewers — presence of IB/magnet tracks, JROTC, AFJROTC, health/law/engineering academies, strong band/theatre/arts, wide CTE/vocational offerings, many clubs, dual‑enrollment/college partnerships and explicit lists of AP/honors/STEM offerings (examples: “International Baccalaureate World School… Palmetto Center for the Arts… AFJROTC… broadcasting program… automotive classes… Early College Program”). Items that belong here report the school materially offers or markets those distinct programs and specialized electives, not judgments about how well they are taught.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete clai: This bucket groups statements about how academically rigorous or effective the instruction and credentialing are (AP/IB rigor and workloads, grade‑inflation or inconsistent grading, students arriving underprepared or accelerated into college credit, lists of college destinations, and claims about who has access to honors tracks), e.g. “plenty of honors/AP courses…10 to Northeastern… IB program is extremely rigorous… grades have statistically dropped… teachers lower standards to inflate AP grades.” These are about curriculum strength, measurable outcomes, workload and equitable access — distinct from mere availability of programs or from staff conduct issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket includes reports of student‑on‑student violence and safety hazards (recurrent fighting, gangs, drugs, sex in bathrooms, vaping, school‑shooting scares), pervasive peer bullying, xenophobic or homophobic exclusion, and accounts of ongoing harassment that staff fail to stop (examples: “Lots of drugs and sex in the bathrooms…I was bullied constantly…name calling…school shooting scares…vape in the bathrooms”). These items describe campus climate and student behavior/safety outcomes rather than staffing, programming, or facility condition.
candidate_defs.square entries report more personnel pro: This bucket covers adult behavior and personnel practices: coach and teacher bullying, staff rudeness, nepotistic hiring or alumni‑favoring employment, favoritism toward athletes or popular students, explicit sexist/anti‑Semitic remarks by named staff, punitive security or policing, and administrators/counselors who ignore parents (examples: “coaches run school by bullying students…if you're an alumni you'll be guaranteed a spot…Mr. Lawless said she looked 'whorish'…Counselor ignoring us for months”). These are complaints about adult conduct, hiring and discipline cultures and responsiveness, distinct from program availability, instructional quality, or physical resources.
candidate_defs.square entries report more detailed phys: This bucket captures concrete, physical resource descriptions: modernized buildings, air conditioning, Smartboards and campus Wi‑Fi, new turf and athletic complexes, overcrowded classrooms or extreme enrollment, cafeteria/lunch crowding or unpaid lunches, leaking roofs or outdated gyms, and district capital vs classroom supply tradeoffs (examples: “brand new facilities…Smartboards in every classroom…3100 kids here/classes are overflowing…they did not have any pencils or paper…building a NEW k‑2 building while teachers lack books”). These are infrastructure/resource facts, not administrative policy failures or instructional evaluations.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more on-campus saf: This bucket captures concrete reports of fights, stabbings/threats, daily police involvement, guns, wide drug/alcohol/vaping/chewing-tobacco use, racially-motivated fights, sexual-misconduct claims, and systemic bullying that reviewers attribute to weak enforcement (e.g., 'fights almost every week', 'police walk students out on a daily basis', 'drug use at school and at football games', 'They call people of color racial slurs'). Circle entries lack these kinds of safety/crime specifics or portray a comparatively calm social environment, so items that document tangible safety incidents and enforcement failures fall here.
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader advanced: This bucket groups concrete curricular offerings and outcomes: AP course breadth, dual-enrollment/college-credit accrual, named magnet/academy programs (Math/Science, Technology, Law, Fire Science), free college trips, Ivy placements, and explicit college-credit totals or early graduations (e.g., 'entered UNC with 25 credit hours', 'left FHC with 33 college credits'). Circle entries rarely list this level of program detail or measurable matriculation evidence, so all specific program availability and documented college-prep outcomes belong here.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more problems and: This bucket covers personnel- and governance-level facts: difficulty recruiting teachers, high turnover, coaches/teachers accused of abuse or favoritism, secretive/nepotistic board hiring, administrators who ignore complaints or threaten students, paid private tutoring conflicts, and uneven assignment of strong teachers to honors/AP sections (e.g., 'teachers play favorites... especially the vice principal', 'The school board meets secretly', 'many of the good teachers are assigned to AP sections'). Circle entries generally describe responsive, caring staff and stable leadership or do not raise governance malpractice, so concrete allegations about staff misconduct, biased governance, or dysfunctional administrative communication are grouped here.
candidate_defs.Square entries provide more concrete evi: This bucket captures detailed, actionable accounts of support systems: proactive college counseling and individualized schedule fixes ('counselors stepped in... raised GPA'), formal inclusion programs and buddy clubs for special-needs students ('special needs football buddy', 'Bulldog Buddies'), reports of ADA noncompliance or denied accommodations, as well as criticisms of poor mental-health counseling ('counselors are terrible'). Because circle entries rarely mention counseling, special-education, or targeted student-support practices, any review offering concrete counseling/SE/case-management evidence is placed here.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more concrete fa: This bucket groups tangible, physical and resource matters: high-quality performing-arts centers, Olympic pools, many orchestras/bands, extensive clubs and sports, or conversely dilapidated buildings, pest infestations, overcrowded classrooms, parking/busing logistics, fundraising demands and pay-to-participate fees (e.g., 'best performing arts center', 'brand new Olympic sized pool' vs. 'bathrooms are nasty', 'they are ALWAYS asking for money', 'parking lot an absolute free-for-all'). Circle entries do not contain comparable facility/program breadth or these detailed resource complaints, so concrete descriptions of facilities, extracurricular scale, and funding/participation barriers belong here.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete safety/crime/behavior problems (gang activity, on‑site drug use, repeated fights, sexualized mischief, students carrying weapons, multiple suicides) and failing or complicit responses (staff condoning violence, daily bullying not disciplined, SROs or police present). Examples: “Gang activity… many serious assaults… multiple suicides… a lot of students are on drugs,” and “Bullying is a large problem… they wouldn’t care,” all appear in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket captures specific leadership and policy breakdowns: unresponsive/rude administrators, lost credits or near loss of accreditation, retaliation against reporters, ignoring Education Code, prioritizing image/ratings, arbitrary or punitive discipline, and gaming special‑education placements. Examples: “The administration is worthless… school almost lost their accreditation,” “administration share names of bullying reporters,” and “they place disruptive students in Special Education classes,” all reported in square and not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more formal adva: This groups concrete evidence about school academic offerings and results — IB/AP/STEM academies, dual‑enrollment/college credit, AP/IB/ACT/SAT success, selective admissions — and the intense pressures accompanying them (high workload, student stress). Examples: “Wall to Wall IB… majority take at least one IB course,” “almost the entire class scored 5s… exempted Calc 1,” and warnings like “Pressure to perform is huge… check suicides,” are frequent in square but absent or far less detailed in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, more deta: This bucket contains reports of extensive extracurricular life, arts and athletics accomplishments, active booster/PTA fundraising, and families moving into the district for programs — concrete programmatic and community supports rather than generic praise. Examples: “marching band, orchestra and theater programs are top‑notch,” “VIP Boosters… dedicated parent volunteers,” and families who “move into our district or apply and appeal decisions to transfer,” appear in square but not circle.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more detailed fac: This groups reviews that cite concrete physical/operational conditions and logistics: toxic mold or pest infestations, unsanitary bathrooms and food safety complaints, bussing/transportation reliability or long parent commutes, scheduling conflicts/limited course capacity, missing textbooks or heavy online‑course reliance, and capital‑plan notes. Examples: “tested positive for toxic mold… son had seizure‑like symptoms,” “bussing is reliable” and “no books… majority of the courses are online,” are concrete, operational items reported in square far more than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and bett: This bucket groups raw items where square reviews name concrete programmatic offerings and pathways (AP, IB, AVID, dual‑enrollment, named academies, CTE/MBIT, law/STEAM/magnet tracks, CNA pilots) and measurable college outcomes, while circle reviews lack or downplay such breadth; examples: multiple square mentions of IB/AP/dual credit, Business/Performing Arts/Law academies, pilot CNA/MBIT, and graduates accepted to selective colleges.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This bucket captures descriptions of violence, fights, stabbings/threats, pervasive drug use and dealers, bomb threats, heavy police/dog presence, camera/surveillance practices, and both over‑zealous and inconsistent punitive security policies in square reviews versus no or fewer such incidents in circle; examples: accounts of drugs 'running rampant,' repeated fights, a student threatened with stabbing, plus hiring of sheriffs and 'tardy sweeps.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe worse physical f: This groups operational/resource complaints in square reviews—dilapidated buildings (asbestos, leaks, roaches), construction odors, crowded classes/long cafeteria lines, short lunches, parking/traffic hazards, outdated textbooks and broken online processes—contrasted with circle’s lack of comparable facility/operational failings; examples: 'roaches in classrooms,' '20 minutes for lunch including lines,' and 'crumbling books / outdated materials.'
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize a larger, more: This bucket covers square reports of extensive extracurricular breadth, award‑winning music/drama/band, strong sports culture and championships, community turnout and active PTSO/SIC involvement, plus named competitive successes—while circle reviews omit or downplay comparable programmatic depth; examples: state‑level music awards, marching band/Drumline wins, many named clubs, and parent‑led facility/bond campaigns in square.
candidate_defs.square entries document more pronounced: This captures square evidence of administrative misconduct, favoritism, unresponsiveness, coverups, high turnover and morale problems alongside highly variable teacher behavior (from exemplary AP/IB teachers to disengaged, abusive, or uncaring instructors) and uneven enforcement of discipline; examples: named staff criticism, 'administration bully students,' mass teacher exodus, and reports that AP teachers are excellent while regular classes are 'out of control.'
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more con: This bucket groups items where reviewers describe named AP/IB/honors/magnet/dual‑credit tracks, measurable college matriculation, National Merit/award counts, and formal college pathways (e.g., AP/IB classes, dual enrollment, high college acceptance rates). Examples: many square notes of AP/IB offerings, honors seminars, dual‑credit/STEM programs and alumni college placements contrast with Circle's lack of sustained AP/IB evidence or only occasional/limited college‑prep mentions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, spe: This bucket captures concrete accounts of bullying, drug use, arrests, assaults, targeted discrimination (race/LGBTQ/military families), safety procedural lapses, and reviewers saying anti‑bullying or supervision follow‑through is ineffective. Examples: square reports pervasive bullying, drug culture, student arrests, failure to dismiss or secure students after incidents, and statements like 'bullying is a huge problem' or 'no follow through at dismissal,' whereas Circle contains few or no such systematic safety incident reports.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more detailed fac: This bucket groups concrete facility/capacity descriptions — overcrowded classes, trailers, parking shortages, HVAC/water problems, building renovations or 'disgusting' interiors, and security gates or nonfunctional intercoms — reported by reviewers. Examples: square reviewers reference trailers and 35+ class sizes, lack of working bubblers/AC, recent renovations or state‑of‑the‑art centers, parking/bus shortages, and malfunctioning intercoms; Circle reviews rarely provide such granular operational detail.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete al: This bucket captures reports about administrators or staff abusing authority, protecting underperforming teachers via tenure, refusing appropriate accommodations, lying or punitive handling of parents/students, front‑office rudeness, and explicit staff misconduct claims. Examples: square items include allegations of principals denying diplomas, administrators lying or telling teachers to avoid consequences, tenure‑protected poor teachers, rude registrars, and even sexual misconduct claims, while Circle rarely levels such governance/protectionism accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete inst: This bucket groups reviewer claims about teaching quality variability, heavy homework/AP workloads, grade‑curving/passing without remediation, missing grade records, counselor shortages/misplacement, and special‑education IEP/IDEA noncompliance or dedicated autism staff. Examples: square includes statements about teachers offering extra help, teachers who 'simply read from a book,' daily multi‑hour homework loads, grade posting errors, understaffed counseling, and explicit special‑education failures, whereas Circle provides few comparable, concrete operational descriptions of these academic‑management and classroom practice issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report more robust advanc: These reviews repeatedly name concrete academic offerings and outcomes in square schools (e.g., 15–18 AP courses, numerous dual‑credit/UC or RIT partnerships, college centers, 88–90% college matriculation, national merit finalists and scholarship wins), while circle reviews rarely cite AP counts, dual‑enrollment, or concrete college matriculation statistics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews document repeated bullying, physical assaults, vaping/drug use, gang targeting, bomb threats and at least one alleged teacher sexual misconduct incident, including accounts that staff often fail to stop or fully remediate those incidents; circle reviews contain far fewer such incident-level safety claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers commonly describe unreturned calls, lost or mishandled transcripts/records, rude or arrogant principals, mishandled discipline hearings, inconsistent rule application and top‑down lack of accountability, whereas circle reviews more often describe timely phone responses or do not report comparable systemic procedural failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pr: Square entries frequently list strong band/choir state honors, many sports, formal magnet/extracurricular programs and no‑cut options, but they also document politicized team selection, coaching favoritism, fundraising requirements to participate, and unequal budget support for arts vs. football; circle reviews rarely offer the same mix of high‑profile achievements plus politicized access complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: Square reviews cite widespread substitute‑covered classes, teachers often absent or relying on passive methods (videos/self‑teaching), overcrowded classes, punitive grading or lost accommodations, and high turnover/low morale; circle reviews more often credit teachers with consistent support and do not report the same scale of instructional instability.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger specializ: These reviews enumerate concrete program offerings and outcomes that square schools provide but circle reviews do not (e.g., Cambridge, IB, AVID, STEM academies, many AP/dual‑credit classes, CTE certifications, STEM/robotics teams) and cite measurable college results (National Merit winners, scholarship totals, elite college matriculation). Examples: 'one of the only high schools in WA to offer the Cambridge International program', 'offers many dual credit courses…graduating college a year early', and quantified scholarship/AP outcomes noted in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain explicit accounts of physical safety failures and serious incidents—ongoing bullying and sexual harassment, daily or frequent fights, gang activity, in‑school drug/alcohol use, lockdowns and assaults—that circle entries do not describe. Illustrative raw evidence: 'There is severe sexual harassment…', 'on average two fights a day', 'Extremely high gang activity', and 'exposed to drugs on a daily basis.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Square reviewers repeatedly document tangible infrastructure and capacity constraints—very large enrollment and enormous class sizes, multi‑shift lunchtimes, overflowing/unsanitary bathrooms, roof leaks and pests, broken shop/equipment and vending/food complaints—that circle reviews largely omit. Examples include 'a school of 3000+ students', 'Classes are approx. 38–41', 'bathrooms could be compared to hell…cockroaches everywhere', and broken machine‑shop equipment and poor cafeteria food.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: Square reviews give concrete governance examples—unreturned parent requests and rude office staff, punitive whole‑school discipline, politicized hiring and favoritism, counselors who mishandle transcripts/scheduling or drop the ball, and budget‑driven program cuts—whereas circle lacks comparable policy/process failure claims. Representative items: 'I have made requests to meet…never received a response', 'the building decides to punish their entire student body', 'the new counselor didn't even know how to submit transcripts', and 'jobs are cut…what higher academic courses they once offered, will no longer be.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more variable staf: Square reviews frequently describe staffing churn and uneven instruction (high turnover, coordinators leaving, teachers sleeping or failing to grade) alongside pronounced social stratification and parent/community power dynamics (affluent parent influence, tuition/fundraising pressure, athlete preferential treatment, cliques/exclusion) that produce polarized experiences. Examples: 'turnover rate of 47%', 'teachers fall asleep at their desk', 'it’s of athletes on drugs but since they win it’s ok', 'Majority of parents are professionals…book suspensions', and repeated statements about cliques and 'if you don't come from a rich family…you don’t really matter.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, formal: These reviews repeatedly enumerate concrete program offerings and formal pathways at square schools—AP/Pre‑AP and PSEO courses, dual‑credit & magnet centers, vocational trades (automotive, welding, culinary), strong music/theater programs, JROTC, FBLA and many clubs/athletics—whereas circle reviews lack comparable inventories or say AP/advanced offerings are absent. Examples: multiple square notes of AP/dual credit, magnet programs, trades lists, and nationally ranked speech/debate or performing‑arts programs versus circle statements like “no AP classes only dual credit” or limited athletics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews document recurring physical fights, weapon incidents, on‑campus drug use and overdoses, pervasive bullying/harassment (including racist and anti‑LGBTQ+ attacks), K‑9 searches and visible substance problems—claims absent or far less frequent in circle. Examples include reports of stabbings, students bringing knives, multiple overdoses, daily fights, locker searches, and reports that victims’ complaints went unpunished.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Reviewers of square schools provide concrete examples of arbitrary discipline (random dress‑code enforcement, ISS/segregated programs), leadership favoritism toward athletes or PTA‑connected families, alleged cover‑ups or image‑management, and nepotistic hires; circle entries generally lack this pattern or focus on different operational issues. Illustrative items: assistant principals ‘drawing names out of a hat’ for dress code, administration protecting popular athletes, accusations that administration prioritizes public image over safety, and claims of district nepotism.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: Numerous square reviews report understaffed or unresponsive counseling departments, missed or removed IEP supports, special‑education identification failures, procedural IEP violations, and inconsistent college/career guidance—specific service breakdowns less visible in circle.
