Examples include counselors described as unresponsive or narrow (only tracking credits), students removed from IEP supports without permission, and parents forced to pay for supports the school won’t provide.
candidate_defs.square entries report more salient facil: Square reviews contain both descriptions of significant recent capital investments (new stadiums, rebuilt campuses) and frequent operational/resource problems—budget shortfalls or questionable spending, overcrowding from consolidation, traffic bottlenecks, facility disrepair, restrictive fees and restroom/health hazards—that circle reviews rarely raise. Examples: $52.4M facility builds and new stadiums noted alongside complaints of near‑bankruptcy budgeting, crowded commons/single intersection drop‑offs, peeling CTE wings, closed bathrooms and hefty parent fees.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: These reviews repeatedly allege fights, lockdowns, rampant bullying, on-campus drug use (including on buses), medical emergencies from drugs, and administrators/staff who ignore or mishandle threats (e.g., lockdowns, bomb-threat mismanagement, expelled students returning to campus); Circle reviews lack comparable reports of drugs/violence and more often describe manageable behavior or single isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader formal a: Many square reviews name concrete curricular assets (AP/IB/dual‑credit catalogs, vocational labs and nationally recognized welding/machining credentials, pre‑apprenticeships, JROTC, specialized magnets) and cite measurable outcomes (high proficiency percentages, scholarships, notable college placements), while Circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth, credentials, or numeric outcome data.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer administrat: Square reviewers cite unresponsive or rude front office and central‑office staff, alleged cover‑ups, selective punishment and nepotism (favoring wealthy/athlete families), heavy-handed suspensions/expulsions, and BOE inaction; Circle reviews more often describe accessible, supportive staff and do not make the same pattern of systemic administrative cover‑ups or authoritarian discipline.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater variabili: Square content frequently documents wide swings from excellent to ‘rarely teach’—inconsistent grading practices, teaching-to-the-test or worksheet reliance, teacher apathy/unprofessionalism (swearing, bullying), and failures in FAPE/special‑ed accommodations—whereas Circle reviews more consistently report supportive teachers and fewer systemic instructional neglect claims.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize large-scale fac: Square reviews describe top‑notch athletic complexes, large music/theater programs, amphitheaters, recent renovations, and heavy funding for sports (often at the expense of arts or classroom resources), alongside overcrowding, parking and cafeteria problems—Circle reviews do not report the same mix of high-capacity athletics/amenities plus the attendant crowding and resource-allocation tensions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket captures reviews describing concrete safety problems inside/around the school — repeated fights, daily brawls, assaults requiring hospitalization, routine bullying (including special-needs targets), widespread drug/vaping use and overdoses, and K9 searches or ambulance calls (e.g., “fights every day,” “DRUGS.ARE.EVERYWHERE,” “MY FRIEND...NOW SHE IS IN THE HOSPITAL,” and special-needs bullying accounts). Circle entries either lack these claims or emphasize safety and kindness instead, so inclusion means the review reports frequent, severe student-safety incidents or resident substance problems.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This groups items where reviewers report administration-level problems and formal policies: long delays or missing report cards/truancy notices, refusal to comply with accommodations, administrators hiding problems, favoritism (honor-society/athlete preference), strict movement/dresscode/ bathroom rules, invasive searches and heavy security hardware, budget misuse or district corruption, and systematic operational breakdowns (e.g., “8 MONTHS to notify us,” “principal flat out refused to comply,” K9 searches, and claims about misallocated capital spending). Circle entries typically describe better communication or fail to allege this mix of governance/operational malpractice, so membership indicates systemic administrative or policy-level dysfunction or deliberately opaque choices.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive for: This bucket groups reviews that name concrete curricular breadth and measurable postsecondary outcomes: AP/IB offerings, magnet/major/STEM tracks, dual-enrollment and career-technical breadth, formal academies (e.g., health/IB/tech/ Ski Academy), and explicit college matriculation examples (Harvard/Stanford/MIT acceptances, measurable test scores). Examples include: “IB offered…AP classes…accepted at Harvard, Stanford, Yale and MIT,” and “major-based STEM curriculum.” Circle reviews rarely provide this same level of program specificity or elite-college outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistently: This bucket captures reviews that emphasize uniformly positive, reachable, and effective teachers with low turnover and steady staff support (e.g., “The teachers are so passionate,” “highly qualified and truly work to help all of their students,” and repeated praise for caring teachers). By contrast, square entries tend to report wide variability in teacher quality, higher turnover, and classroom instructional problems, so inclusion means the review foregrounds consistent teacher competence and staff stability relative to the other group.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures or d: This bucket covers specific, actionable claims about inadequate special-education services, denial of 504/IEP accommodations, exclusion from honors because of disability or placement, and discriminatory treatment (race/gender/ socioeconomic cliques) — e.g., “discriminates against students on the 504 Plan,” “denied support because I am in AP,” and detailed accounts of being blocked from honors or being advised to transfer out of the district. Circle entries do not make comparable claims, so items here report concrete failures of inclusion, accommodation, or equity policy.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete claims about student-on-student harm and disorder (bullying, regular physical fights, gang activity, lockdowns, police involvement, drug/alcohol incidents, food‑safety/pest problems) that appear far more often in square reviews (e.g., “lock-down almost every day,” “many gang fights,” “police called on victim,” “multiple cases of drug and alcohol incidents,” “roach and rodent problem”) while circle reviews rarely describe comparable safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This groups statements about leadership and office-level practices (authoritarian or disconnected principals, punitive minute-level attendance rules, favoritism toward athletes or staff, dishonest or defensive district leadership, poor parent communication, legal/labor disputes) that square reviewers name explicitly (e.g., “principal favorites teachers,” “miss 5 days and your child gets all 59F's,” “principal lied to save money,” “guidance office is a joke”), whereas circle reviews emphasize engaged or at least neutral administrators and do not list the same breadth of governance failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a richer set of: This covers concrete programmatic evidence (AP/IB/honors breadth, magnet academies, Career and Technical Education, dual‑enrollment, alternative completion programs, formal academies) that square reviewers list by name and outcome (e.g., “International Baccalaureate Program,” “VASS grant pays for AP tests,” “CNA license, dual enrollment at Cabrillo,” “alternative program improved grades”), while circle reviews rarely enumerate this many distinct named academic pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries present more explicit, na: This bucket captures both lists of specific extracurriculars/electives (band, choir, DECA, JROTC, one-act, theater, many clubs) and program-level complaints about sports being prioritized (especially football favoritism, funding skewed to athletics, overlong/rule‑pushing practice) that square reviews repeatedly provide (e.g., “Son on the Golf Team, daughter on Crew,” “tons of APs and band,” alongside “this school is so ridiculously focused on sports (football especially)”), whereas circle reviews rarely enumerate such breadth and focus more narrowly on a few activities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more detailed, var: This groups classroom- and staff-level practices and outcomes — both positive and negative — that square reviewers give specifics about: teacher effectiveness and availability, inconsistent departmental quality, teacher morale and turnover, counseling and 504/Special Ed accommodations, and parent‑teacher communication (e.g., “teachers come in early/stay late to help,” “math dept low,” “guidance stood us up,” “best special needs program in area,” “Schooloop sends me an update DAILY”), whereas circle reviews provide far fewer concrete, multi-faceted claims about these staff/support behaviors.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews repeatedly describe daily/weekly violent fights, on-campus drug use and selling, gang activity, pervasive bullying and cyberbullying, vandalism, and claims that security/staff cannot or do not control it (examples: 'fights all of the time, violent fights. Drugs. Bullying.', 'the whole school smells like pot', 'students must fend for themselves against gang violence'). Circle reviews by contrast rarely allege sustained violence or drug markets and instead describe isolated incidents or improved safety.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: Many square reviews enumerate formal programs (full IB diploma, STEM academy, Early College AA, Cambridge or magnet programs, dual enrollment, abundant AP/honors offerings) and cite test scores/college placements as evidence ('offers full IB diploma', 'students earn AA in Early College', 'test scores continue to climb', graduates attending top universities), whereas circle reviews generally lack this level of concrete programmatic or outcome detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more detailed admi: Square reviewers frequently allege politicized principals/superintendents, favoritism/double standards, scapegoating or arbitrary teacher firings, board cover-ups, conflicts of interest, and threats of legal/media escalation (examples: 'new principal…not politics like the other one', 'double standard', 'reaching out to the board gets you nowhere'), while circle reviews seldom level sustained accusations against district governance or systemic lack of accountability.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational c: Square reviews provide concrete operational complaints—very large enrollment and divisional responses, crowded hallways/cafeterias, problematic bell/schedule formats, unknown bus routes and late busses, parking problems, building deterioration and safety-design concerns ('2700+ too large', 'impossible to find a seat at lunch', 'busses just now learning their routes', 'design is seriously flawed and possibly even a fire hazard'), whereas circle reviews rarely detail these kinds of system-level logistics.
candidate_defs.square entries include more concrete des: Square reviewers give named examples of tutoring centers, after‑school buses, guidance help, IEP accommodations, financial aid for homeless students, but also report guidance unresponsiveness or poor special-ed handling (examples: 'they have the tutoring center and study circles', 'financial help is great…when I was under the homeless category', and 'students with learning disabilities were often left behind'), while circle reviews seldom provide this level of concrete, programmatic detail about supports or special-education accommodations.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially br: This bucket captures claims that square schools offer more advanced/varied academic programming (AP, IB, honors, dual‑enrollment, specialized academies, upper‑level STEM) and produce quantifiable college outcomes (top‑tier scholarships, Ivy/military academy admits) compared with circle schools. Examples: numerous square reviewers list ‘robust AP program and dual enrolled program,’ ‘one of the only schools to offer an IB Program,’ or ‘students receive impressive scholarships to the best universities,’ whereas circle reviews rarely list AP/IB breadth or high‑tier matriculation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reports of physical fights, pervasive bullying, drug/vaping prevalence, weapons incidents, and weak or inconsistent disciplinary enforcement that square reviewers allege are common or inadequately handled—claims that circle reviews do not make. Examples: square reviewers recount ‘fights every day,’ ‘over half the kids vape,’ students bringing guns, and ‘administration does nothing about bullying,’ while circle contains no comparable pattern of daily violence or schoolwide enforcement failure.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: This bucket covers explicit, procedural failures—lost or unreviewed student records, incorrect scheduling/credit assignments, counselors described as ‘practically useless’ or only schedulers, clerical errors that jeopardize graduation, redistricting/overcrowding mismanagement, and wider district bureaucracy—that square reviewers report more often than circle. Examples: square cites ‘counselor forgot about UC‑approval, student had to redo courses,’ ‘records from old district not reviewed,’ ‘hard to transfer/enroll,’ and ‘ever‑changing superintendent causing negative trickle‑down,’ while circle reviews contain far fewer such operational complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report richer, award‑winn: This bucket groups square reports of strong/award‑winning extracurricular programs (state/national championships, All‑State band/chorus, outstanding JROTC), broad club/elective availability, and explicit facility investments (new buildings, 1:1 laptop program, renovated athletic facilities) that circle reviews do not enumerate. Examples: square reviewers name ‘award‑winning music department,’ ‘state titles in multiple sports,’ ‘Engineering Academy/robotics/world‑qualifying teams,’ and ‘1:1 Apple laptop program’ while circle seldom lists comparable program breadth, awards, or capital projects.
candidate_defs.square entries include more reports abou: This bucket captures concrete special‑education and inclusion evidence—both failures (IEP not implemented, expulsions without homebound services, records not transferred) and successes (effective accommodations, private lessons, college readiness for IEP students)—plus reports of racial harassment, class‑based exclusion, and minority‑ratio concerns that square reviewers raise much more often than circle. Examples: square contains statements like ‘they did not review special‑ed records,’ ‘they expel a special ed child with no homebound services unless you know your rights,’ alongside praise such as ‘they work hard to accommodate the disabled,’ and comments about ‘For someone of color… not a healthy environment,’ whereas circle reviews largely omit this body of special‑education and equity detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more exp: This bucket groups items where reviewers describe concrete, high‑level academic offerings and outcome evidence (AP/IB/honors growth, dual‑credit, vocational tracks, high SAT/ACT or National Merit counts, named alumni college/career successes) in square but not in circle (examples: repeated AP/IB lists, 'highest SAT average', 'plethora of AP/Honors', vocational programs, named alumni outcomes). It captures school‑level program breadth and measurable postsecondary results distinct from teaching style or general praise.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, better‑fu: This bucket covers concrete program and resource claims about after‑school life: square reviewers list many clubs, strong music/arts/theatre programs, renovated athletic facilities and protected sports funding, plus spectator culture and instances of nepotism or athlete favoritism (examples: 'club for every interest', 'incredible music program', '$20M capital improvements', 'sports are protected from cuts', 'athletes get leniency' and nepotistic team selection). It groups program breadth/funding and the distinct phenomenon of athletics‑dominant culture together because both are operational, resource‑level facts about extracurricular life.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket contains raw terms that describe tangible safety problems (fights, stabbings, shootings, bomb/gun threats, gangs, drug use, pervasive bullying, vaping in bathrooms) together with reviewers’ claims that school staff or district offices failed to respond effectively (examples: reports of stabbing/shooting, 'administration does nothing', security guards failing, SRO shortages, threats ignored). It bundles event severity and the school's failure to protect/respond as a single safety‑accountability climate feature.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups complaints about district/school governance and employment practices: board corruption or hiring cronies, superintendent resignations/scandals, cover‑ups, abusive principals toward staff, frequent teacher turnover and disruptive promotions (examples: 'superintendent resigned amid scandal', 'school board keeps hiring cronies', 'teachers fired after 2–3 years', 'promotion harmed program leadership'). It focuses on governance and personnel systems (hiring, promotion, turnover, oversight) rather than classroom instruction or single safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete stud: This bucket groups evidence about organized student supports (before/after tutoring, remediation classes, targeted counseling, career planning, free lunches/chromebooks) alongside reviewer accounts of guidance and special‑education failures (scheduling errors, unreturned counselor calls, IEP noncompliance, blocked accommodations) — e.g., 'before/afterschool tutoring', 'resource teachers tutoring', and 'IEPs not honored, won’t let son graduate'. It captures the dual pattern of visible support infrastructure coexisting with specific execution or access failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic stude: This bucket groups raw items where reviewers describe acute safety failures — daily/weekly fights, weaponized assaults (brass knuckles/knives), on‑campus drug dealing and vaping, self‑harm, hospitalizing assaults, and claims that staff/administration tolerate or cover up bullying (e.g., “fights almost every day,” “encouraged to sell drugs on the campus,” “ongoing bullying that is constantly covered up by school staff”). These are concrete, repeated safety and student‑behavior incidents that square reviewers report far more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures reports about leadership and governance: high principal/superintendent turnover, calls for replacement or charter conversion, allegations of dishonesty or nepotism, misuse of funds, poor front‑office responsiveness (unreturned calls, rude registration staff), and demands for budget transparency (e.g., “Conversion to a Charter School…”, “they don’t return calls,” “school keeps taking our money and uses it for useless things,” “nepotism”). These are operational/governance failures and instability that square reviewers emphasize relative to circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater availabili: This bucket groups descriptions of concrete programmatic strength: large AP/honors catalogs (e.g., ‘25 AP courses’), IB/magnet/STEM offerings, dual‑enrollment and guaranteed college credit, CTE/vocational credentials and internships (CNA, EMT, welding, aviation hanger), and named postsecondary outcomes (Cornell, Harvard, >90% college attendance, scholarships). These specific curricular, CTE and outcome claims appear much more often in square entries than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more prominent ext: This bucket includes accounts of strong, named extracurriculars (band, state championships, many clubs, competitive arts and athletics, community pep culture) alongside concrete evidence that athletics are prioritized (new football/track investments, pay‑to‑play fees, favoritism toward athletes) (e.g., “BEST BAND…state champions,” “new football field,” “you don’t play unless you pay $200–$400,” “athletes are favored”). Square reviewers both celebrate broader extracurricular success and report inequities/fees tied to athletics more frequently than circle.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete, op: This bucket groups specifics about day‑to‑day instruction and supports: teacher dedication and extra help, but also failures like no lesson plans, poor grading, substitutes mismanaging class, lost online assignments, extreme nightly homework loads, inconsistent or dysfunctional guidance/IEP handling, and mixed special‑education outcomes (e.g., “teachers stay after,” alongside “a few don’t even have lesson plans,” “no ACT/SAT prep,” “IEP forced on me” and “late for IEP meetings”). Square entries supply these concrete classroom‑level practices and student‑support details far more often than circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: These reviews repeatedly list concrete program availability and performance—AP/IB/dual‑credit, compressed/accelerated pathways, AVID/CTE/RoP, AP exam pass rates, high SAT/ACT scores, Ivy/elite college placements and multi‑million scholarship totals—while circle reviews omit such programmatic detail or measurable outcomes (examples: “RHS offers 18 AP classes,” “College Board recognized CHS for increasing AP access,” and “PHS class received over Seven Million in Scholarships/Grants”). This bucket groups items about explicit course pathways, test results, dual‑enrollment and documented college/career outcomes (not general teaching quality).
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many square reviews describe frequent fights, threats, drug dealing/use, lockdowns, racial slurs and pervasive bullying and say staff/admin often fail to intervene (examples: “violence, fighting is somewhat normal,” “drug deals...right next to the in house police officers,” “Students involved in bloody fights...”), whereas circle reviews contain few or milder safety complaints and note student respect or effective peer intervention. This bucket captures concrete safety incidents, prevalence, and lack/failure of protective responses or reporting mechanisms.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: Square reviews frequently enumerate large, successful extracurricular ecosystems—marching band winning state and performing nationally, JROTC, dozens/hundreds of clubs, travel trips, scholarship athletes—while also noting pay‑to‑play fees, coach favoritism or abusive coaching and selective casting in theater (examples: “band invited to China/Macy’s,” “over 200 clubs…,” and “you HAVE to pay at least $16 for every club,” “football gets most of the money”). This bucket groups concrete claims about program breadth/achievement plus described access barriers or inequitable treatment within those programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Numerous square reviews call out front‑office hostility or rigid residency checks, lost records/transcripts, punitive disciplinary culture, retaliatory responses to parents, funding inequities and prioritization of awards/athletics over student wellbeing (examples: “Told if I had a problem I can go across the street,” “lost her transcripts,” “school spends a horrific amount of money on sports,” and “Parents who post frustrations... get called in to the superintendent’s office”). This bucket covers leadership/operation issues, policy choices, transparency, and district/board funding or governance failures distinct from classroom instruction or program availability.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more specific, co: Square reviews supply detailed classroom and support descriptions—teacher variability (’half excellent, half atrocious’), rote vs. rigorous instruction, grade leniency/grade inflation, after‑school tutoring, counselor effectiveness or breakdowns, special‑education transition programs and slot shortages (examples: “teachers don't care about grades,” “Math tutoring is available EVERY day,” “transition program for special education students,” and “they run out of slots for those students”). This bucket captures classroom‑level pedagogy, grading/enrollment into accelerated courses, and concrete student supports (counseling, ESL, IEP implementation), separating those operational and curricular facts from admin leadership or extracurricular claims.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more advanced acad: This bucket groups raw terms that describe concrete academic program strength (AP, IB, many honors courses, dual‑enrollment, Math Academies, career academies), operational supports (tutoring, proactive college counseling, AP remediation, tracked AP diploma counts) and cited college placements/credit transfer; examples include 'International Baccalaureate program', '17 AP classes', 'tutoring before and after school', 'students into Ivy League/Notre Dame', and '15 college credits transferred via IB.'
candidate_defs.Square entries report broader and better: This bucket captures concrete program offerings and outcomes outside core classes—performing arts, marching band and black‑box theaters, journalism and FFA, competitive athletics and state championships, career/CTE tracks (culinary, auto, cyber), plus booster/alumni fundraising—evidenced by 'world‑renown theater program', 'band may be best in the state', 'South‑Western Career Academy', 'strong sports and music programs with huge booster support.'
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups allegations of pervasive climate and safety failures tied to student conduct and school response—bullying, racial harassment at events, weekly fights, drug culture and police seizures, bomb searches, and claims that administration 'won't do anything'—examples include 'a fight every week', 'drug issue is cultural norm', 'kids get jumped', 'video of bullying and nothing was done', and appeals to outside authorities.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more chronic facil: This bucket covers concrete infrastructure and resourcing problems—aging buildings, overcrowded classrooms/portables, leaks/rodents/bedbugs, old technology, lack of textbooks, cafeteria/heat/food complaints, parking/fees and crowded scheduling—that reviewers tie to capacity/funding and daily student experience (e.g., 'no math or spanish books', 'leaks everywhere', 'too crowded this year', 'parking passes $50/semester', 'bathrooms closed for vaping').
candidate_defs.Square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket groups personnel‑level operational practices: large variability in teacher effectiveness, staff unresponsiveness or active mistreatment (teacher bullying or sexism), favoritism toward athletes/popular students, punitive administrative behavior/retaliation, and leadership instability/turnover—examples include 'half the teachers are amazing and half are poor', 'they cater to athletes', 'administration may punish your child if you complain', '90 percent of teachers are quitting', and 'nepotism in hiring.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete program offerings and outcomes (AP/ honors counts, dual‑enrollment/Running Start, magnet and career academies, remediation and testing incentives, and named college placements), e.g. “17 different AP courses,” “dual enrollment…college credits,” “law and finance magnet,” and multiple reports of Ivy/UC/Full‑ride admits—features Circle reviews do not enumerate or support with metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety, bully: These entries document repeated student‑safety and conduct problems—bullying left unaddressed, vaping and routine intoxication, bathroom fights, locker break‑ins/theft, sexual activity and even shootings—e.g. “Drugs, sex and alcohol are rampant,” “watch fights in the bathrooms,” and “THIS IS THE SECOND TIME MY GRANDSON’S LOCKER HAS BEEN BROKEN INTO,” which Circle reviews largely omit.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: This group highlights systemic governance problems—leadership turnover and coups, abrupt policy rollbacks, public scandals, favoritism, unresponsive offices and slow dispute resolution—e.g. “vice principals tried to overthrow the principal,” “very public grade changing trial,” “office staff are rude,” and parents not being notified of ISS/lockdowns—patterns not present in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic facil: These reviews describe physical and operational constraints—overcrowded classrooms, run‑down or infested buildings, broken equipment/fields, lack of books/printing supplies, long lunch lines and heating/AC problems—e.g. “bathrooms are unusable…MONTHS!!”, “they do not have books…ask for ink and paper,” and “most classes were too big to control,” issues Circle does not raise.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: These comments document both standout teachers and serious in‑class problems—verbal abuse, inconsistent instruction (esp. math), lax discipline/phone use, locked doors limiting help, and also reports of ‘‘best teachers’’ who enabled college entry—e.g. “One teacher called me ‘dumb and stupid’,” “teachers let students stay on their phones,” and “some of the best teachers on earth,” contrasts that Circle’s comments do not produce.
candidate_defs.square entries report far stronger and b: These reviews name concrete, school‑level academic offerings and outcomes—IB/AP/Honors, dual enrollment, Running Start, college credits, CTE pathways and national rankings—e.g., “IB Program (which is EXCEPTIONAL)”, “Wildcat University where they earn 50+ college hours,” and claims of high college placement and National Merit scholars; circle reviews lack comparable program detail or measurable outcome claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: Many square reviewers recount recurring fights, sexual assaults, drug use/overdoses, riots and gang activity and note weak or punitive school responses and police involvement—e.g., “fights every single day,” “sexual assault happens…quite a bit,” “vaping epidemic…overdose,” and “recent riot in 2021”; circle entries do not document comparable recurring violence, drug epidemics, or large safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: Square reviews repeatedly allege incompetent district leadership, principal/office antagonism, favoritism toward elite students/athletes, biased discipline, toxic internal communications and teacher turnover—e.g., “Incompetent school board. Unqualified Superintendent,” “principal openly favors…same students,” and “reporting someone on the sports team…zero repercussions”; circle reviews contain far fewer or no such systemic governance accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive,: Square texts enumerate concrete non‑core offerings and capital projects—nationally ranked band/choir, robotics and cyber teams, accredited STEM/NAF/CAPA academies, pools/performing arts centers, booster fundraising and college partnerships—e.g., “choir and band are among the top in the nation,” “Cybersecurity team top 5% nationally,” and “new Olympic size pool,” while circle reviews rarely name comparable structured programs or partnerships.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: Numerous square reviewers describe weak/unavailable counselors, denied or poorly implemented IEP/504 accommodations, and poor college counseling—e.g., “The counseling department is weak…hard to reach them,” “getting support for them is tough…you must advocate,” and “I didn’t even know the counselor was the one to talk to about college”; circle reviews do not report these systemic support failures and sometimes describe proactive supports instead.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more student-safet: This bucket groups many square reviews that recount concrete safety problems (weapons found, stabbings, gang/drug presence, repeated fights, sexual harassment, severe injuries) plus failures in response (victims punished, ambulance not called, SRO misconduct). Examples: “a bullet was found in the bathroom,” “Drugs are everywhere, even in class,” and accounts that victims were suspended or ignored by administrators.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe stronger, more n: This captures square reviews that enumerate AP/IB/dual‑credit offerings, magnet/academy programs, explicit college-credit opportunities, high AP pass rates, scholarship totals and named post‑secondary placements. Examples: “The amount of AP classes that are offered are unbelievable,” “IB diploma,” “overall AP passing rate of 75%,” and reports of large scholarship awards and graduates attending top universities.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more administrat: These square reviews focus on concrete management and operational breakdowns—textbook/asbestos mishandling, scheduling errors, missing records, poor crisis handling, frequent principal turnover, cancelled specialized programs, and unkept administrative promises. Examples: “unavailability of textbooks due to an asbestos problem,” “screwed up my child's schedule,” and reports that administrators ‘make hundreds of promises and follow up on none.’
candidate_defs.Square entries report broader, better-su: This bucket groups square entries that list extensive extracurricular infrastructure and visible capital/support (many clubs, thriving band/theater, large sports rosters, named coaches, new gyms/fields, strong booster support and facility renovations). Examples: “dozens of clubs,” “marching band rated in the top ten,” “installing a new football field,” and “the boosterism is very encouraging.”
candidate_defs.Square entries show more evidence of une: These square reviews point to patterns where athletes, honors/AP students, or well‑connected/affluent families receive preferential attention while average, struggling, or special‑needs students are neglected, shipped out, or differently disciplined. Examples: “If you’re on the football team… teachers will pass you,” “students who are not ‘perfect’ get shipped off to alternative schools,” and allegations of nepotism and PTO favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: These reviews name specific curricular offerings and outcome metrics (AP/IB counts, dual‑credit, CTE tracks, arts/music excellence, vocational certifications) and cite college matriculation or rankings (e.g. “18 AP and numerous PreAP,” “CTE/medical/engineering tracks,” “98% graduation, Ivy accepts”), whereas circle reviews mostly lack detailed program lists or school‑level outcome statistics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain concrete eyewitness and incident claims — fights, lockdowns, guns, drug deals in hallways, vaping, vandalism, suicides, frequent truancy and unsupervised parking‑lot drug activity — while circle reviews rarely report such safety events and instead emphasize friendlier climates or isolated behavioral problems.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: Many square reviews enumerate a wide array of clubs, music/theater, JROTC, championships and niche programs, yet repeatedly assert an athletics‑first culture (football favoritism, special athlete privileges, large athletic capital projects and diverted spending, arts cuts), a pattern not present in circle reviews which either list fewer programs or do not document athletics‑favoring budget choices.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews frequently describe principal turnover, alleged abusive or incompetent leadership, admin unresponsiveness unless pressured by well‑connected parents, pressure to inflate grades, opaque class placement, and teachers forced out or protected by tenure — whereas circle reviews contain far fewer systemic governance or grade‑manipulation allegations and emphasize individual supportive staff.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Square reviewers report detailed operational shortcomings — overcrowded classes and trailers, closed bathrooms, cockroaches/mold, poor cafeteria food, broken/blocked Wi‑Fi and app bans, busing cuts, missing textbooks and online‑only classes — while circle reviews rarely describe pervasive facility, sanitation, or infrastructure failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more advanced acad: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete curricular offerings and outcomes (AP, IB, honors, AVID, STEM/Performing Arts Academies), claims about statewide/ACT/test rankings, scholarship/college matriculation evidence, and workload/rigor tied to those programs (e.g., “Lots of great AP classes,” “IB program,” “6th in the state for senior ACT scores,” “many students go on to college with academic scholarships,” and reports of heavy AP homework). Content belongs here when the primary difference is a school’s formal advanced-course structure or documented academic outcomes rather than teacher behavior or extracurricular strength.
candidate_defs.square entries report more prominent, aw: This groups reviews that emphasize high‑profile nonacademic offerings and the community/district resources that sustain them — band/JROTC/theatre state or national recognition, large JROTC battalions, performing-arts infrastructure, PTA fundraising, and documented capital projects or investments (e.g., “band traveled to China and the Inaugural Parade,” “JROTC battalion over 350 students,” “National Blue Ribbon,” “PTA is highly involved…huge donations,” and district fundraising/voter support). Use this bucket for programmatic, facility, or funding evidence that demonstrates strong extracurricular/community backing distinct from classroom instruction or administrative conduct.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This bucket covers concrete accounts of safety-related incidents and hostile peer behavior: repeated physical fights, guns/weapon threats, filmed racially‑motivated assaults, sexual‑misconduct allegations, pervasive bullying/targeted racial harassment, and related student trauma (e.g., “guns being brought to school,” “racially-motivated assault blew up on social media,” “20–25 fights,” “sexual abusers list on a bathroom wall,” and frequent self-harm references). Include items whose core distinction is the prevalence or severity of student safety/crisis events and intergroup hostility.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures operational and personnel dysfunctions: unresponsive or rude front-office staff and principals, failure to follow up on parent communications, favoritism toward athletes/‘favorites,’ arbitrary denial of privileges, inconsistent discipline or punitive counseling practices, and staff misconduct or gossip (e.g., “I called and emailed. I received NO Response,” “teachers pick favorites,” “they will call Child Services on parents for any little thing,” and “one teacher was fired for sleeping with a student”). Assign reviews here when the distinguishing fact is poor governance, biased enforcement, or broken parent/staff communication rather than curricular offerings, extracurricular acclaim, or specific safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit, con: This bucket groups reviews focused on how the school handles individualized supports: IEP/504 implementation and noncompliance, special‑education testing/accommodation failures, examples of strong counselors or excellent IEP teamwork, grief/crisis counseling, and college‑guidance errors (e.g., “they clearly do not know how to follow an IEP,” “IEP's were scheduled on time… daughter earned a 4.0,” “they refused to send transcripts… application was rejected,” and “amazing counseling staff”). Put content here when the primary difference concerns case‑level student supports and postsecondary advising rather than general curriculum, extracurriculars, or broad administrative culture.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures concrete reports of student-on-student and community-safety problems (fights, ongoing bullying, racialized harassment, drug/heroin/gang problems), frequent lockdowns/lockdowns-as-regular-events, and claims that staff/admin fail to resolve or mis-handle these incidents (e.g., “Lock downs are nearly a weekly event,” “Bad drug problem…heroin use is an epidemic,” “MAJOR bullying issues…right under administration noses,” and accounts of racialized harassment and administrative concealment). Circle entries contain little or none of this safety/bullying/crime evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups explicit program and outcome evidence—availability of AP, IB, dual-enrollment, Running Start, study-abroad, career-technical tracks and measurable alumni outcomes or college placement (e.g., “My Daughter is in the IB program,” “enough AP courses…many study abroad and scholarship opportunities,” and multiple reviewers citing college admissions and degrees). Circle reviews rarely list such named advanced pathways or concrete alumni matriculation data.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent spec: This bucket covers repeated, specific complaints about IEP/504 failures or inconsistent follow-through (e.g., “staff disregard 504’s,” “My IEP has been useless,” “IEP meetings were laughable,” or children being grouped/dumped into one room), as well as related claims of no ADHD support; while a few square reviews note good special-ed practice, the predominant pattern is documented procedural and support breakdowns that circle entries do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries document more staff and l: This bucket groups teacher-level misconduct and culture (teachers bullying students, gossiping during class, favoritism, discriminatory language) together with leadership/governance complaints (mass exoduses, hiring/firing for political reasons, nepotism, principal turnover and out‑of‑touch boards) as concrete personnel and accountability failures (examples: “teachers actually bully me,” “All the good teachers are leaving…fired for speaking out,” “administration is very biased,” and “put thousands in a bandroom while lacking classroom supplies”). Circle entries contain far fewer of these concrete accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups evidence about physical plant, budgeting and day-to-day operations: broken toilets, vermin, mold or brand-new buildings; austerity and funding cuts; contested spending priorities (paving, athletics equipment vs classroom needs); overcrowding and safety/code concerns; scheduling/grade-recording failures and poor parent communication; plus specific program changes (art cuts, added gym classes, laptop programs, large extracurricular breadth). Example claims include “ceilings with broken tiles…vermin,” “We are in our second consecutive year of Austerity,” “programs are suffering due to funding cuts,” and conversely “Every student gets a Macbook Air” or “new Performing Arts Center,” all patterns far more present in square than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report substantially more: These reviews describe specific, named program capacity at square schools (IB, many AP/Pre‑AP courses, dual‑enrollment, academies in medical/engineering/culinary, JROTC, strong arts/theater, AVID and measurable AP/IB exam and scholarship results), plus concrete claims of high college matriculation and accumulated college credit—features that Circle entries largely omit (Circle mentions general challenge or arts but gives no comparable AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/CTE lists or exam/college‑placement metrics).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: Multiple square reviews cite recurring fights, gang/weapon/drug activity (hallway drug deals, vaping, weapons), sexual/racial harassment, bomb threats and either ineffective enforcement or overly punitive responses (routine ISS, harsh detentions, security/police presence that does not stop incidents), whereas Circle reviews do not document the same level or frequency of safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers repeatedly recount concrete governance and operational problems—lost transcripts/credit‑scheduling errors that threatened diplomas, counselor overload, OCR special‑education complaints, cover‑ups/protectionism, nepotism, questionable budget priorities (athletic spending vs. textbooks), mandatory paid ID policies, and politicized board decisions—while Circle reviews contain far fewer such institutional‑level mismanagement allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater teacher/st: Square texts contain specific staffing problems (high turnover, many subs — e.g., eight algebra teachers in a year, teachers 'giving up,' absenteeism/empty classrooms, program implementation failures) and polarized teacher quality, whereas Circle reviews rarely mention chronic turnover or substitute reliance.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistently: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe teachers and counselors who work hard, offer tutoring/study tables, are accessible and supportive, and a small‑school sense of being known and supported; Square reviews are far more internally contradictory on staff warmth (praising some teachers while also documenting many instances of unresponsiveness or mockery).
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket groups reviews where square schools describe concrete safety failures (daily fights, suicides, sexual harassment, widespread drug use, police/armed responses, theft) and repeated claims that staff/administration fail to investigate or remediate (administrators ‘turn a blind eye’, bully incident reports ignored). Examples: reports of student suicide, shooting threats, overt drug use, repeated slurs and harassment, and parents obtaining attorneys after the school failed to act.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, broade: This covers reviews where square schools list concrete curricular offerings and outcome metrics—many AP/IB/dual‑credit courses, career academies, remediation programs, documented alumni attending Ivy/major universities, transferable college credits and scholarship evidence—while circle reviews give little or no comparable outcome/program detail. Examples: named AP/IB courses, MCAS remediation sessions that improved scores, alumni placements at Harvard/Princeton, and students entering college with dozens of transferable credits.
candidate_defs.square entries report more robust, award: This groups accounts of well‑resourced, competitive extracurriculars at square schools (state‑placing marching bands, award‑winning TV production, championship sports teams, show choir with live band) and facility investments for those programs (weight rooms, touring ensembles, well‑kept fields), whereas circle reviews rarely list comparable achievements. Examples: marching band state championships, Telly/Communicator awards for media, state athletic championships, and professional choreographers/costumers for show choir.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger teacher q: This bucket captures square reviews that emphasize highly qualified, caring, and invested teachers plus concrete in‑school supports (office hours, writing centers, targeted tutoring, frequent progress reports) that produce individualized help, whereas circle entries more often lack these kinds of instructional-support claims. Examples: teachers who give phone numbers and return emails, dedicated ‘Eagle Time’/smart‑lunch tutoring periods, and statements that staff go the extra mile to help students graduate on time.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete fac: This groups reviews that supply specific, actionable descriptions of the school’s physical and operational conditions—overcrowded classes, filthy bathrooms, underfunding or budget cuts, Pay‑to‑play fees, cafeteria policies denying meals, renovation/modernization projects, Chromebooks/iPad rollouts, and rigid or ad‑hoc discipline/handbook rules—details largely absent from circle entries. Examples: claims of major underfunding, 40‑student classes, broken HVAC/AC complaints, erased student progress records, and strict restroom/ID permission procedures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and stronger: This bucket captures concrete programmatic evidence that square schools offer formal advanced pathways and measurable postsecondary results (examples: repeated mentions of IB diplomas, many AP classes, Rochester/ Miami/Western dual‑enrollment partnerships, students graduating with 18+ college credits, and alumni admitted to selective universities), whereas circle entries rarely mention AP/IB/dual‑credit or concrete college‑credit outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater variabil: Count as this bucket reviews that give specific classroom-level failures or unevenness — e.g., 'hit and miss teachers', teachers who 'don't teach and don’t care', favoritism for athletes, grades 'adjusted to pass', teachers assigning pages of worksheets instead of teaching, or unqualified instructors — while circle entries tend not to list this mix of specific classroom malpractice or grade‑tampering.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This groups accounts of persistent bullying (student‑ and staff‑perpetrated), sexual assaults, student substance use/drug presence, gang activity, students coming home 'with bruises', plus allegations about security responses (random searches, on‑campus police presence, slow response or over‑punitive threats), all of which appear in square reviews far more than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete ad: Includes reviews documenting high principal/superintendent turnover, indictments or financial scandals, claims that leadership prioritizes image over students, school board not listening, or arguments over misallocated spending (e.g., stadiums/football vs classrooms), whereas circle reviews do not present this pattern of governance instability and contested resource allocation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit prog: This bucket captures concrete, non‑classroom programs and student supports: both positive and negative special‑education/IEP accounts, counselor shortages or accessible counselors, daily tutoring/late buses, PBIS or Early College pathways, plus detailed listings of band, choir, pottery, FFA, career academies and many clubs — contrasts with circle entries, which either omit such programmatic detail or focus on only one narrow program.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This bucket captures reports of acute safety problems and unaddressed peer harm in square reviews (fights 'everyday occurrence', an AR‑15 threat, recurring physical assaults, gang/drug activity, widespread bullying and alleged suicide attempts), often coupled with administrators who fail to stop or adequately redress those harms; circle reviews instead commonly describe a safe, respectful environment or do not report comparable safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive a: This groups concrete programmatic strengths reported in square reviews — AP/IB and many honors courses, dual‑enrollment/Running Start, Math/Science magnets, robotics, biotech and vocational shops, nationally‑recognized debate/theater and arts touring, and quantified college outcomes (Ivy/MIT/Caltech acceptances, large college‑credit totals) — features that circle reviews largely omit or describe only generally.
candidate_defs.square entries report larger disparities: Square reviews frequently include concrete facility/resource extremes (e.g., 'beautiful new building', 'state of the art sports complex' and community campus partnerships) alongside opposing accounts of overcrowded schools, leaking ceilings, vandalized restrooms, pest infestations, insufficient textbooks/substitutes and teachers buying technology for classrooms; circle reviews generally do not present this same range of acute facility or resourcing claims.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete fa: This bucket covers repeated square statements about special‑education breakdowns — cancelled IEP reviews, long delays to secure IEPs, segregation of special‑education classrooms, inadequate life‑skills supports, and confrontational SpEd administrators — a cluster of operational special‑needs failures not present in the circle set.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews frequently call out systemic management problems — 'numerous turnover of Superintendent...', politicized decisions, layoffs of experienced staff, prioritizing test/application counts or facilities over individual students, chaotic scheduling/enrollment, rigged favoritism and fundraising/pay‑to‑play pressure — while circle reviews lack comparable allegations of district‑level governance and policy dysfunction.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger special: These reviews repeatedly name concrete curricular programs and outcomes (IB, PLTW, SAS, ROTC, many AP/honors and dual‑credit classes, internships, PLTW, CNA/EMT/CNA certifications, college counseling, Naviance, free SAT/FAFSA help) and cite alumni college placements and scholarships; Circle reviews rarely list program names or outcome evidence and instead offer only general claims about academics. Examples: Square praises PLTW, IB, robust AP options, college‑prep counselors and student scholarships, whereas Circle offers no comparable named programs or alumni placement anecdotes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many Square reviewers detail ongoing safety incidents and substance use (vape epidemic, drugs easily accessible, bomb/gun threats, frequent fights, gang activity) and say anti‑bullying or discipline policies are not enforced; Circle reviews do not describe this level of persistent safety threats. Examples: Square notes vaping the school 'can’t control,' 'kids get high there,' 'bomb threats, gun threats, fights,' and repeated faculty inaction toward bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviews contain numerous concrete operational complaints—late/missing grades, scheduling errors, lost assignments, abrupt residency removals, ignored parent feedback, retaliatory complaint responses, board nepotism, and pandemic mismanagement—indicating leadership, policy implementation, and recordkeeping breakdowns; Circle reviews largely lack these systemic operational failures and sometimes praise leadership. Examples: Square reports 'grades not posted on time,' '48 hours to get children out of the school,' 'administration ignores feedback,' and 'when you file a complaint they make claims against you.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher‑level: Square reviewers describe concrete classroom problems (incompetent or burnt‑out teachers, public shaming, yelling, contradictory instruction), persistent failures in special‑education/504 accommodations and counseling (unhelpful or absent counselors, untreated mental‑health needs), whereas Circle tends to report more consistent teacher support and fewer severe special‑ed/counseling failures. Examples: Square cites teachers who 'scream at them and call them idiots,' 504 plans ignored by attendance, 'counselors hardly ever in their office,' and special‑ed departments described as 'horrible.'
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broader extracu: Square reviews enumerate extensive clubs, performing‑arts and elite music programs, competitive athletics, booster activity, pay‑to‑play inequities, and community pride or athletic primacy (sports as pathway to scholarships and social status), and also report ASB/athletics‑based favoritism and clique dynamics; Circle rarely lists this scale or variety of extracurricular programming. Examples: Square lists 'instrumental music, drama, crew, model congress, mathletes, band,' notes state championships and booster clubs, and also warns 'If you don't play sports ... you are nothing.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups raw terms where Square reviewers name concrete curricular offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/dual-enrollment/early-college, specialized STEM/engineering/health academies, vocational certifications) and cite college matriculation or AP credit — e.g., “Governors School of Engineering,” “IB Diploma,” “AP credits,” ‘students went on to Ivy League/UNC/PSU,’ and ‘$2M in scholarships’ — while Circle reviews generally lack district-level metrics or named advanced pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket covers allegations of fights, bullying, drugs, arrests, teen‑pregnancy, canine locker searches, unlocked doors, and school-police involvement plus claims that administration downplays or unevenly enforces responses — e.g., “every single day at least one fight,” “big drug problem…canine searches,” “students being arrested,” and administrators who ‘won’t enforce zero tolerance.’
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket groups reports of board resistance to change, administrators withdrawing credit/withholding communication, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, hiring/retention failures, and staff misconduct — e.g., ‘board will not approve change,’ ‘teachers favor popular kids,’ ‘administration withdrew my child’s credit without permission,’ and ‘board keeps unworthy teachers,’ contrasted with Circle’s relative absence of these governance failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and high: This bucket contains claims that Square schools run extensive clubs, award-winning performing-arts and music programs, varsity athletic success, and named extracurricular pathways (speech & debate, JROTC, ROTC, large club fairs) — e.g., ‘100+ clubs,’ ‘state championship athletic teams,’ ‘excellent choir and theatre,’ and ‘many arts scholarships’ — whereas Circle reviews typically report limited extracurricular breadth or primarily sports-focused activity.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete spec: This bucket groups specific, program-level evidence about special education/dyslexia services, mainstreaming/inclusion, organized tutoring/after‑school help, college counseling, and also explicit SPED failures — e.g., ‘special education department is wonderful,’ ‘autistic son mostly mainstreamed,’ ‘free math help after school,’ and conversely ‘special education system here is terrible’ — while Circle reviews rarely provide this level of detail about targeted student supports.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms describing recurring physical/psychological safety incidents at the school—daily fights, sexualized pranks, students bringing guns and multiple lockdowns, pervasive drug access and even drug‑related deaths—and reviewers’ accounts that administration/staff fail to protect victims (no follow‑up, punitive responses). Examples: 'in 2 months the school has been on lock down twice… kid brought guns,' 'There is a lot of violence, drugs, and alcohol,' 'If you want your kid to be bullied send them to this podunk school. They will not address it.' Circle reviews contain little or none of this severe incident/inaction evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and mor: This bucket captures claims of substantial academic program breadth and demonstrable outcomes at square schools—lots of AP/IB/honors offerings, dual enrollment, high average ACT/SAT scores, AP pass rates, and students earning full scholarships or Ivy placements—often with named programs and quantified results. Examples: 'He had a 30 on his ACT… full scholarships offered to the graduating seniors,' 'They offer more AP classes than many private schools,' and 'many students have gone on to receive full academic scholarships.' Circle reviews rarely provide comparable program detail or concrete outcome data.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and broader e: This bucket groups mentions of extensive after‑school life at square schools—large music programs (half the student body in band/choir), competitive DECA/FBLA and robotics teams, strong varsity sports and D1 pathways, and robust parent booster support—often with state/national accolades. Examples: 'DECA and FBLA chapters winning in international competitions,' 'one of largest music programs in the County,' and 'The basketball and soccer teams are very competitive.' Circle reviews generally do not list such wide-ranging, high‑achievement extracurricular infrastructure.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers complaints about leadership and district-level behavior at square schools—chronic unresponsiveness, favoritism/cronyism, inconsistent or punitive discipline, misallocated budgets (funding sports over academics), fake social‑media monitoring of students, billing/enrollment errors, and board/central office ignoring parent input. Examples: 'The Board of Education does their best to ignore the myriad of serious issues,' 'principal makes false profiles and adds students to keep an eye,' and 'they spend money on shiny buildings rather than books.' Circle reviews lack comparable evidence of systemic governance mismanagement.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: This bucket captures the mixed but pronounced teacher/staff patterns in square reviews: named teachers and counselors praised for deep mentorship and availability alongside reports of abusive paraprofessionals, protected incompetent teachers, high turnover, staff cuts (including SPED paras), and union disruptions. Examples: 'Mrs. Crandall… excellent in the English department' and also 'paras belittled that poor boy… and then yelled “shut up!”' or 'Jobs are cut including SpEd Para positions and not replaced.' Circle reviews are comparatively uniform in describing steady, caring staff and fewer such extremes.
candidate_defs.square entries report richer and more di: This bucket collects raw terms where square reviews list concrete program offerings and pathways (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment counts, career centers, welding/culinary/CTE tracks, STEM institutes, large AP catalogs, band/arts excellence, many clubs and college‑credit outcomes) that Circle either omits or does not document (examples: “25 AP/Dual Credit Classes,” “career center,” “Forensic science…Video Production,” “Band is spectacular,” “college readiness counselors”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups accounts of fights, regular threats, gang presence, drug problems, serious violent incidents, and failures in lockdown/incident communication that appear far more in square reviews than circle (examples: “significant number of fights… Drugs are also on an 'all time' high,” “thrown over the edge of a two story rotunda,” “we get threats every single week,” “when there’s a lock down we’re never told why,” plus camera‑surveillance usage described in square).
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket covers concrete governance/administration problems described more often in square: nepotism/family advantage and athlete favoritism, biased discipline or racialized treatment, refusal to admit or retain students, calls for firing principals/board scrutiny, and allegations of corruption or incentives‑for‑ratings (examples: “if your last name is not one of their well‑loved…,” “awards…based on popularity and favoritism,” “principal refused him admittance…my son eventually left,” “fire the administrative team,” “they only REALLY care about their yearly ratings so that they can make extra $$”).
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: This bucket groups raw terms about teacher instructional quality, morale, absenteeism, grading practices, reliance on paraprofessionals, and responsiveness of counselors/special‑education services — square reviews contain both strong praise and many detailed complaints (examples: “some teachers really do care while others couldn't care less,” “teachers are basically absent…rely on internet to teach,” “paraprofessionals delivering instruction,” “IEP not followed,” “therapists available on campus” and mixed notes on counseling responsiveness).
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: This bucket captures concrete operational and physical problems mentioned more in square: rapid enrollment and overcrowding, aging or damaged buildings, funding shortfalls and threatened program cuts, food/cafeteria complaints, bus accident/financial disputes, and device/schedule distribution failures (examples: “increase of student population from 1000 to 1600…overcrowding,” “bathroom stalls without the actual stall part,” “threats of bus cuts,” “Chromebook distribution requiring birth certificates/power bills”).
candidate_defs.square entries describe far more and bet: These reviews emphasize concrete, named programs and breadth of activities (e.g., “well over 30 clubs,” Phenomenal orchestra, marching band involving a quarter of the student body, Science & Technology internship/research program, ROTC, fashion major, no‑cut sports, robust band/orchestra travel, robotics/STEAM and dual‑enrollment partnerships) that Circle’s texts largely omit or only mention generically; falling in this bucket means the school narrative centers on distinctive co‑curricular offerings and program infrastructure rather than merely vague references to ‘activities.’
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: These items describe both high incidence and failed mitigation—examples include multiple suicides/attempts, ‘fights almost every day,’ pervasive drug use and students showing up drunk, Nazi/confederate graffiti and racial slurs, threats/assaults and staff who ‘turn a blind eye’ or ‘put it in writing their hands are tied’; a review belongs here when it centers on concrete safety incidents and/or explicit inability or unwillingness of staff/administration to protect students.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete admi: This cluster collects leadership‑level and governance issues (not classroom practice)—examples: misspending school funds, administrators encouraging falsified attendance for funding, entrenched nepotism and elitism, principal/superintendent turnover or obstructive leaders, zoning/rezoning harms, refusal to remove automated calls, and heavy-handed or inconsistent district policies—i.e., structural, fiscal, or ethical failures in how the school/district is run.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, more e: These reviews enumerate academic program strength and postsecondary results (e.g., many AP classes, IB/magnet programming, partnerships with community colleges, Presidential Scholars and Ivy admits, AP credit success, ACT/SAT claims) and also describe the effectiveness or breakdown of college/career counseling (examples: both praise—'guidance department is top notch'—and complaints—'guidance counselors are worthless' or blocking dual‑enrollment), so membership means the text focuses on concrete curricular pathways, outcomes, and counseling capacity rather than only general schooling claims.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: This bucket captures in‑class experience and staff delivery: reviewers cite extremes—some ‘great’ long‑tenured teachers and many ‘awful’ ones, teachers who ‘only care about a paycheck,’ punitive policies (harsh detentions, dress‑code policing), instructional harms (cramming, being tested on untaught material, overuse of videos), favoritism in grading/coaching, and inconsistent IEP/IEP implementation; a review fits here when it documents concrete instructional practices, teacher responsiveness, or classroom‑level supports (or their absence) rather than schoolwide programs or purely administrative governance.
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger, more con: This bucket groups reviews that name specific curricular offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, dual/concurrent enrollment, college partnerships, high AP scores, National Merit finalists, students graduating with college credits) and explicitly tie them to better college readiness; examples include ‘offers concurrent enrollment… graduate with an Associates Degree,’ ‘over 63% take IB classes,’ and ‘my AP scores allowed me to start college as a sophomore.’ Circle entries lack comparable program-level detail or measurable outcomes and instead offer only generic academic judgments.
candidate_defs.Square entries document worse on‑site st: This bucket captures reports of physical assaults, regular fights, weapons/drug incidents, pervasive bullying, and social exclusion (racial, religious, or wealth‑based cliques and segregated programs) along with claims administration ignores these problems; examples include a delayed‑notification concussion, ‘a student came to school with a loaded handgun,’ ‘bullying is a huge problem…when we report it NOTHING happens,’ and ‘elitism…Students form tight knit cliques.’ Circle reviews do not present the same pattern of chronic on‑campus violence or systemic exclusion.
candidate_defs.Square entries show more operational and: This bucket groups complaints about administrative and front‑office dysfunction (unreturned calls/emails, lost schedules/credits, long enrollment lines, refusal to release health records, mishandled medical complaints, defensive/secretive administration, and cases requiring lawyers or union escalation); illustrative items include ‘calling into the office is a lesson in patience,’ ‘I was informed about orientation by automated call…parents not allowed to attend,’ ‘refused to release school nurse records…subpoenaed,’ and ‘had to hire an attorney so my son could graduate.’ Circle reviews rarely report such systemic operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.Square entries reveal greater variabilit: This bucket covers concrete teacher and staff behaviors: one‑on‑one help, passionate dedicated teachers and outstanding counselors versus favoritism, public shaming, teacher laziness/absenteeism, adult‑on‑adult bullying, and discriminatory enforcement; examples include ‘Teachers are willing to spend 1 on 1 time,’ ‘counselors are outstanding,’ alongside ‘yearbook teacher would pick favorites and publicly shame students,’ ‘teachers not engaging…not even showing up for class,’ and ‘teachers have a favorites problem.’ Circle reviews tend not to contain this same mix of high variability and explicit unprofessional incidents.
candidate_defs.Square entries emphasize broader, higher: This bucket groups reviews that list concrete extracurricular strengths and accolades (award‑winning band/choir, Model UN, strong athletics, vocational/trade/STEM courses, AJROTC, culinary programs, large marching bands) and describe community/booster support for those programs; examples include ‘band program is second to none…24 state championships,’ ‘outstanding vocational/technical classes (SolidWorks, culinary),’ and ‘top music, top MUN team, top sports,’ whereas Circle reviews rarely enumerate such sustained programmatic accomplishments.
candidate_defs.square entries report more bullying, on-: These texts describe a pervasive student-safety problem at square schools — frequent bullying, fights, lockdowns, gang members and drugs on campus, routine searches and public PDA — paired with staff who are unaware or turn a blind eye (examples: “Bullying spreads like a disease,” “multiple lockdowns…kid brought a gun,” “Gang members are walking the halls,” “entering this school you will get search 30+ times,” and staff inaction or ineffective discipline). Circle entries lack these sustained safety/crime patterns or portray incidents as isolated with more adult intervention.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviews repeatedly report governance and accountability failures — ignored parental complaints, under‑reporting of violent incidents, conflicting attendance records, exclusionary discipline/pushing out students, nepotism and resource politics, and mishandling of safety/harassment claims (examples: “We tried to file report but administration did nothing,” “Students involved in bloody fights do not get reported to the state,” legal IEP noncompliance, and “Nepotism runs rampant”). Circle entries, by contrast, do not show the same pattern of systemic nonresponse, underreporting, or politicized favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and more: Square reviews enumerate concrete, expanded program portfolios and outcomes — many AP/IB/dual-credit courses, specialized pathways (MERIT, JROTC, biomedical), career centers/robotics, award‑winning arts and competitive teams, and cited college-matriculation/score evidence (examples: “Every student can take Pre‑AP and AP,” “Career Center and its awesome FIRST Robotics,” choir to Carnegie Hall, “Just got into Yale,” AP scores/GPA evidence). candidate_defs.square entries emphasize more extensive: This bucket covers concrete physical and resource attributes — new high‑tech buildings, Olympic pools and stadiums, fitness centers, extensive sports fields, specialized arts facilities, marching band resources, and community tax/levy support or alumni funding (e.g., 'new stadium and Olympic sized pool,' 'state-of-the-art facilities,' 'tax levies pass year after year'). Circle entries generally omit or do not evidence comparable facility scale, recent capital upgrades, or strong community funding ties.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews that describe operational and governance issues — unresponsive principals/counselors, transcript and scholarship deadline failures, counselor shortages/overwork, favoritism/nepotism in discipline and team selection, budget mispriorities, and district-level misconduct or staff turnover (examples: 'guidance counselor blew deadlines,' 'favoritism for faculty kids,' 'district more concerned with $$,' 'lost fantastic teachers due to leadership'). Circle entries do not present the same pattern of counselor/administrative operational breakdowns or district-level governance accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews attribute concrete, recurring safety problems to square schools (e.g., “Violence, drug abuse, and gang activity are rampant,” repeated fights, multiple overdoses, pervasive vaping causing fire-alarm evacuations, sexual harassment and hate‑crime reports), whereas circle entries rarely describe comparable violent or substance-related incidents and often omit safety concerns entirely.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, broader: Square reviews repeatedly name AP/IB/IBDP, honors, dual‑enrollment, specialized tracks (AG, University‑level, STEAM/Engineering) and cite college-placement evidence (top‑university admissions, scholarship totals, college credit savings), while circle entries generally lack comparable lists of advanced offerings or measurable postsecondary outcome claims.
candidate_defs.square entries document wider/more promi: Square entries enumerate extensive extracurriculars and high‑profile programs—award‑winning music/theater, FFA/ROTC, STEAM academies, sports championships—and also report resource/prioritization dynamics (athlete privilege, pay‑to‑play demands, sports getting new gear vs. arts undersupported), whereas circle entries describe far fewer or smaller extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Square reviews contain repeated, concrete complaints about leadership and policies—privacy/disciplinary abuses (breathalyze/photo incident), favoritism toward athletes/staff families, dishonest/inconsistent communication, chaotic registration, and systematic failures in counseling/special‑education/IEP/504 implementation—whereas circle entries include fewer or less severe examples of these governance and support failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: Square reviews simultaneously describe high teacher dedication and hands‑on remediation (teachers staying after class, named excellent teachers) and opposite complaints (many inexperienced/young or disengaged teachers, inability to control classrooms, inconsistent grading), presenting a broader spread of instructional experiences than circle entries, which tend to offer fewer, less variable classroom-quality anecdotes.
candidate_defs.square entries report systemic failure o: This bucket covers recurring claims that square schools ignore or mishandle IEPs and 504 plans, provide inadequate self‑contained special‑education curricula, and force families to “get a lawyer” to secure services (examples: “my child slipped through the cracks and her IEP was ignored,” “504 due to my color blindness that has been blatantly ignored,” “Complete failure with special needs… get a lawyer on retainer”), whereas circle entries include little or no comparable evidence of special‑education noncompliance.
candidate_defs.square entries document substantially ri: This groups concrete program and outcome evidence in square reviews: numerous AP/Honors/IB courses, magnet and CTE pathways, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit programs (SLU 1818, A+, Running Start), and cited college matriculation or test‑score gains (examples: “wide range of AP courses,” “4‑year BioMed program,” “took ACT from 18 to 25,” “students admitted to Harvard, Duke, NYU”), while circle reviews generally lack such sustained, specific advanced‑course offerings or quantified college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures square reviewers' repeated reports of bullying, widespread drug use, gang activity, frequent fights, arson/acute incidents, and a heavy law‑enforcement/punitive disciplinary approach (examples: “This school is full of drugs,” “a lot of violence including fights, gang activity,” “school resource officer will try to take u to jail,” “group punishment,” “security yell at students”), whereas circle entries contain far fewer or no comparable accounts of pervasive violence, drugs, or aggressive policing.
