candidate_defs.square entries allege administrative fav: This bucket groups claims that school/district leaders protect athletes and insiders, skew spending toward athletics/facilities at academics' expense, and engage in uneven enforcement or grade interference (examples: “administration doesn’t care unless they’ve got money or play football,” “principal told me to pass our star football player,” “$60 million stadium while books/computers lacking,” “superintendent gave himself raises”), whereas circle reviews do not present the same pattern of entrenched favoritism or large‑scale misallocation.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistent,: This bucket contrasts circle reviewers' concrete praise for reachable teachers/counselors and proactive parent communications (examples: “teachers are amazing and always ready to listen,” “communication with parents is exceptional,” “counselors were great at helping my daughter select classes”) with square reviewers' mixed but often negative reports of uneven instruction, burned‑out or incompetent teachers, overloaded/ineffective counselors, and missed/late communications (examples: “counselors are often too busy to be effective,” “some teachers are outright incompetent,” “They don’t inform you of anything going on”).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: This bucket captures claims that Square schools provide concrete, named academic offerings and outcomes (IB/AP/27 AP classes, dual‑enrollment, Advanced Learning Center, career/CTE certifications) and cite measurable college placement/scholarships (full tuition, alumni in law school/UVA/etc.), whereas Circle reviews lack comparable program lists or outcome evidence (examples: Square notes 'IB diploma', '27 ap's classes', 'dual enrollment' and alumni scholarships; Circle contains no parallel program/outcome detail).
candidate_defs.square entries describe a wider, higher‑: This bucket groups statements about breadth and prominence of out‑of‑class programs that Square reviewers emphasize—numerous clubs, nationally recognized marching band, state championships, specialized academies and strong arts/theater—while Circle reviews either mention few clubs, smaller/unstable programs, or no comparable competitive arts/athletics successes (examples: Square 'top national ranked band', 'State Champs in AA Football', '30+ academic teams'; Circle 'only thing ... lacks clubs', 'band program is very small').
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers descriptions of pervasive peer misconduct and uneven enforcement—explicit reports of bullying, physical fights, drug availability, threats and safety‑driven withdrawals/online enrollment paired with claims that staff/administration fail to stop or inconsistently enforce rules (examples: Square 'horrible bully problem... no support for victims', 'weekly fights, drug use', 'admin let bullies go unpunished; punish victims'), whereas Circle contains few or only isolated behavior complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries allege greater staff and: This bucket captures reviewer claims about adults and governance—slow or absent responses from counselors/administrators, rude front‑desk behavior, failed special‑education/IEP support, very high teacher turnover, favoritism/nepotism or data manipulation, and widely varying teacher competence—whereas Circle reviews more often report caring/helpful staff or do not allege systemic administrative corruption (examples: Square 'counselors don't return calls', '85% teacher turnover', 'it's all about who you know', 'IEPs not completed').
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: This bucket groups tangible infrastructure and operational constraints: overcrowded classes and portables, inadequate performance spaces, scheduling formats that cause lost instruction, limited AP sections or outsourced courses, and strict attendance/eligibility enforcement tied to athletics—features Square reviewers frequently raise whereas Circle reviews seldom report such facility/capacity or scheduling problems (examples: Square 'primarily portables (102)', 'gymnatorium', 'lost 6 months of schooling due to schedule', 'only one or two of each AP class', 'to play sports you HAVE to have a minimum of a 2.0 gpa and you can't be late more than 26 times').
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket collects concrete reports of on‑campus crises and hazards found far more often in square reviews — e.g., repeated fights, weapons and classroom assaults, lockdowns, student overdoses, gang activity, sexual assaults/harassment, bus bullying, and pervasive marijuana use — none of which Circle reviews describe with comparable frequency or severity.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially st: Square reviews repeatedly list programmatic evidence of academic rigor and college prep (AP/IB/Honors catalogs, Cambridge/PTECH/Math‑Science magnets, dual‑enrollment partnerships with colleges, freshman academies, Naviance/counseling supports) and named college acceptances (Ivy/flagship/MIT examples), whereas Circle reviews lack that level of articulated advanced program breadth or concrete college‑placement evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑le: Square reviewers name extensive specialized activities — top robotics, renowned band/theatre/PAC, large CTE/aviation/CTE academies, and established DIV‑I athletic pipelines (including heavy athletic spending, recruiting, and scholarships) — and also note funding/prioritization tradeoffs (athletics favored over academics), a level of extracurricular scale and specificity absent from Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more evidence of u: This groups systemic treatment and equity complaints concentrated in square reviews — e.g., athletic or insider favoritism, racially disparate/punitive discipline, politicized/choosey enforcement, students with IEPs/504s ignored or forced into punitive tasks, residency rezoning/forced transfers — patterns of unequal treatment and compliance failures not raised in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistently: Circle reviews emphasize an inviting, safe environment with accessible/caring teachers, effective counselors, stable/prized principals and pastoral support for students (e.g., responsive counseling around grief, steady teacher availability), features that Circle reviewers cite repeatedly and that are generally absent or contested in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe concrete threats to student safety—regular fights, stabbings, gangs, on‑campus drug and vaping use, sexual harassment by SROs, pepper‑spray episodes, and K‑9 searches—and repeatedly claim administration fails to address them (e.g. 'food fights... occasional stabbing', 'drug infested', 'SROs sexually harass', 'administration does nothing about threats or fights'). Circle reviews rarely cite comparable violence, gangs, drugs, or claims of official nonresponse.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, more sp: Square reviews enumerate curricula and programs (AP/IB/honors, CTE/vocational shops, multiple languages, robotics, performing‑arts academy, JROTC, VoTech, extensive electives), cite scholarships and elite college placements, and note program caps/selective auditions—e.g. 'AP courses, 4 languages, New Tech, music program, several Ivy league students'—while Circle reviews provide far fewer concrete program lists and less measurable postsecondary evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more detailed st: Many Square reviews allege leadership problems and problematic staff conduct: 'administrators love to abuse their authority,' 'good‑ol‑boys club', transactional favoritism, punitive suspension policies, staff flirting with students, and replacement/turnover tied to low pay; they also include allegations of staff physical aggression and hypocrisy. Circle reviews rarely raise these specific governance/facility‑misconduct claims and instead focus on other issues.
candidate_defs.square entries include more specific acc: Square reviewers provide concrete, often conflicting, descriptions of guidance and support—full‑time school nurses, GEAR UP, co‑taught inclusion classes and strong IEP teams in some reviews, but also 504/IEP non‑enforcement, understaffed/ineffective counselors, guidance encouraging dropouts, and poor college counseling—e.g. 'they refused accommodations for my disability', 'guidance told him to drop out', 'co‑taught classes are a big plus'. Circle reviews rarely contain such detailed special‑education or counseling accounts.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: These reviews list overcrowding, high student:teacher ratios, unstaffed classes, unreliable wifi/technology blocks, outdated textbooks, scheduling/start‑time complaints, ID lines, bus/transportation failures, and renovation/status details—e.g. '1 teacher to 30 students', 'outdated books from the 1970s', 'wifi extremely unreliable', 'two hour ID line'—whereas Circle reviews seldom enumerate multiple operational or infrastructure specifics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe concrete student-safety harms (daily fights, gang activity, bomb threats/lockdowns, sexual harassment), pervasive bullying and homophobia/racism, and easy access to drugs/alcohol—examples include “fights breaking out almost daily,” “students even bring in certain drugs and deal in the hallways,” and ‘bomb threat and a soft lockdown.’ Circle reviews contain little or no comparable reporting of violence, drug dealing, or sustained bullying problems.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and more: Many square reviews list concrete programs and pathways (IB/AP/honors/dual enrollment, magnet/STEM/ROTC, extensive band/choir/arts and dozens of clubs) and often strong college‑prep outcomes or heavy homework loads—e.g., “IB Diploma Program…more than prepared for college,” “award‑winning band,” and “at least 19 college level classes.” Circle reviews generally omit such a wide catalogue of advanced courses, international exchanges, or high‑impact extracurricular breadth.
candidate_defs.square entries document more variable an: Square reviewers frequently report bimodal teacher quality (either exceptional or ‘do not teach’), frequent departures, teacher apathy, and administrators who protect poor teachers—examples: “teachers are either hit or miss,” “teachers have all but given up,” and “administration supports the inept teachers.” Circle reviews, by contrast, more often describe consistently caring or energetic staff without widespread turnover/abandonment claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced fa: Concrete operational complaints recur in square reviews—active cockroach infestations, collapsing ceilings, persistent foul odors, overcrowded classrooms (30–40+ students), poor food, and malfunctioning enforcement/IT systems—e.g., “roaches everywhere,” “the building is falling apart,” and “there are about 40 kids in every class.” Circle reviews rarely raise these systemic facility or capacity failures.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly accuse leadership and the school board of protectionism, coverups, corruption, inequitable favoritism (to prominent families, athletes), punitive or inconsistent discipline, deliberate transfer/enrollment barriers, and record‑keeping errors—examples: “school answers to the school board…one hand washes the other,” “money talks here,” and “they erased all his credits.” Circle reviews do not contain the same pattern of board‑level concealment, systemic favoritism, or deliberate policy manipulation.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit substantially bro: This bucket captures reviews that list concrete program breadth and formal pathways (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment/SUPA/CHS, extensive CTE/ROP classes, JROTC, robotics/biotech labs, award‑winning band/theater, dozens of clubs and sports, offsite vocational centers like Bechtal) — e.g., many Square reviews name AP/IB/dual-credit, nearly 30 after‑school clubs, strong JROTC and robotics, and explicit college‑credit partnerships that Circle reviews do not.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This groups reviews describing day‑to‑day physical-safety crises and institutional failures to protect students — fights every day, gang activity, pervasive drug/vaping use, heavy police/SRO presence, campus assaults and threats, and explicit claims that sexual‑assault reports were ignored or victims punished; those concrete safety and mishandling accounts appear far more often in Square than in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger pattern: Reviews here name administrative practices and policy choices (administration focused on test scores/rankings or money, 'cleansing' of students, staff married to superintendents, curriculum secrecy, mandatory IB fees, rehiring after alleged abuse, punitive dress/code/attendance enforcement, and leadership-by-intimidation) — concrete governance behaviors and policy decisions emphasized in Square reviews exceed those in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater inequity o: This bucket covers concrete exclusionary practices and broken inclusion supports — IEP non‑enforcement/altered notes, counseling barriers, segregation across PTAs and student groups, resource and attention concentrated on IB/high‑achieving tracks while regular or special‑needs students are neglected, and explicit anti‑LGBTQ or disability mistreatment — patterns that Square reviews call out far more than Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pronounced: These reviews report day‑to‑day functioning shortfalls: slow or minimal grading, chronic substitute use and math‑department turnover, inconsistent teacher engagement but also before/after tutoring in some cases, large enrollment/crowded classrooms (2,800–3,000 students, 35–40 class sizes), construction, poor custodial upkeep, bus‑driver shortages and levy-driven cuts — concrete operational outcomes and variability that Square reviewers highlight more often than Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent/seri: This bucket captures accounts of recurrent fights, on-campus drug use, police/tasing incidents, sexual harassment, student suicides, gang activity and severe harassment — paired with staff inaction or ineffective anti-bullying efforts (e.g., “fights every day,” “kids doing drugs in the bathroom,” “2 suicides… principal said nothing could be done,” “assemblies to raise awareness of bullying but they don’t do anything”). These square reports indicate an elevated safety/crisis problem plus inadequate supervision or follow-through that circle reviews do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive,: This bucket groups mentions of formal programmatic offerings and outcomes such as IB/AP/honors, dual-enrollment, Early College, numerous CTE pathways (cosmetology, CNA, robotics, HPA/health programs), partnerships with universities, and documented college placements/scholarships (e.g., “IB program… accepted to 7/8 schools,” “AP and Dual Enrollment… students got scholarships,” “kids went to MIT, Stanford, Johns Hopkins”). These square items emphasize availability of accelerated tracks, credentialing, and tangible college/career results that Circle reviews generally do not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and more n: This bucket covers both the volume/variety of extracurriculars (many clubs, select strings, marching band, theater, 40+ clubs, multiple sports, internships, off-site technical courses) and critiques that athletics/band often receive outsized attention or preferential treatment (e.g., “more than 40 clubs,” “music program is top‑notch,” alongside “they are solely focused on sports… unless you’re a sports prodigy you’re just a number,” and coach/grade-favoritism allegations). Square reviewers therefore describe a rich extracurricular ecosystem but also frequent complaints that resources or grading are skewed toward athletes; circle reviews generally lack comparable program breadth or these favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more punitive, sec: This bucket captures concrete governance and process failures: punitive discipline and expulsions, secrecy/cover-ups of incidents, refusal to cooperate with parents, lost/ignored academic paperwork, fee enforcement blocking graduation, and leadership churn or calls for wholesale replacement (e.g., “admins hide problems… will not cooperate,” “fees over $300 prevented graduation,” “administration shows more interest in expelling children than educating them”). These are administrative-level practices and politics that square reviewers raise far more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extreme and: This bucket groups physical-plant and operational evidence — both negative (crowded hallways, 2½ minute passing, filthy restrooms, rats/cockroaches, broken HVAC, makeshift 5‑gallon toilets, underfunded levies) and positive/explicit investments (new science wing, fab lab, distance-learning lab) and concrete operational details (short lunches, multi-line cafeterias, locker searches). Square reviews contain many more named facility/funding/operational specifics (and funding disputes) than circle reviews, which rarely report comparable concrete infrastructure narratives.
candidate_defs.square entries report more numerous and: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete programs (many AP/IB courses, 25 APs or 10 STEM APs, IB magnet, engineering/medical/Collegiate Academies, dual‑enrollment/college credit, AVID/GearUp/CATE) and cite measurable outcomes (state/national rankings, Ivy/college acceptances, scholarships, AP/IB scores). Examples: multiple Square items list high AP counts, named magnet/academy programs, dual‑enrollment centers, and explicit college-placement or scholarship evidence that Circle reviews do not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries report a wider, higher‑pr: This bucket groups reviews noting concrete extracurricular breadth and public successes—robust band/choral/music programs, theatre/musicals, ~40 clubs, Ag/Ag‑mechanics, award‑winning marching bands, community performances, and visible event turnout/traditions (homecoming spirit, packed football crowds). Examples: many Square reviews catalogue named arts and club programs, state competitive achievements, and strong parent/community attendance that Circle reviews largely omit.
candidate_defs.square entries report an athletics‑domin: This bucket covers comments that athletics not only are strong but also dominate culture and resources—athletes protected from discipline, coaching/relative nepotism, athletics as a college pipeline, unequal treatment of girls' teams, out‑of‑pocket sports fees, and claims 'money goes to athletics.' Examples: Square reviewers allege children of coaches 'get away with anything,' athletes allowed to play when failing classes, and budget choices favoring football/band at expense of other programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete safety and climate failures described in Square reviews: repeated lockdowns for guns, in‑class fights and chokes, pervasive drug use, widespread verbal and physical bullying, staff indifference or victim‑blaming, and administrators withholding evidence or mishandling incidents. Examples include reports of weapons on campus and multiple lockdowns, teachers laughing at bullying of a student with autism, and administrators failing to act or reversing expulsions—patterns not present in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: This bucket groups concrete governance and operations problems described in Square reviews: frequent principal/assistant turnover, opaque or inconsistent discipline, program cuts and budget scandals, overcrowded halls and scheduling issues (A/B days, restroom breaks), hazardous facilities/AC failures, cafeteria/food complaints, poor responsiveness to parents, and counselor/mental‑health shortfalls. Examples: Square reviewers cite 'constant admin changes,' missing millage money, heat‑stroke incidents from no A/C, long detentions/suspensions and unreturned parent safety emails—issues Circle reviews rarely raise.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe safety: These reviews describe repeated, concrete safety incidents (gangs in the halls, daily fights, lockdowns, bomb threats), pervasive identity‑targeted harassment and bullying, drug/vape problems, sexual‑assault complaints, and claims that staff/administration failed to stop or adequately remedy them (e.g. “gang members are walking the halls,” “there’s fights every day,” “my child was bullied and nothing was done”).
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive a: Square reviewers list specific rigorous offerings and outcomes—AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, many honors courses, engineering/STEM/medical/career academies, college‑credit partnerships, and concrete matriculation evidence (high AP pass rates, Ivy/Top‑tier acceptances, measurable test scores)—while circle reviews rarely cite comparable program breadth or strong college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly cite understaffing and high turnover, broken office/registration systems, poor parent communication, counselor shortages or unresponsiveness, budget cuts or misallocated funding, overcrowding/large enrollment and dilapidated facilities, and examples of administrative concealment or inconsistent policy enforcement (e.g. “communication is terrible,” “GOT TO HIRE MORE GUIDANCE COUNSELORS,” “building is dilapidated”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more favoritism, d: Square reviewers allege targeted bias and unequal treatment—racial profiling and homophobic harassment, dress‑code or gendered enforcement, favoritism for wealthy or influential families and athletes, exclusion of outsiders or military families, and donor‑/influence‑driven discipline/team decisions—describing patterns of unequal discipline and social stratification not present in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, more n: Many Square reviews name discrete programs (IB, wide AP/honors offerings, accredited STEM/NAF/CAPA academies, JROTC, vocational shops, dual-enrollment/LCTC) and cite measurable outcomes (high AP pass rates, IB diplomas, US News rankings, students admitted to selective colleges) that Circle reviews do not; examples include students graduating with IB diplomas, AP BC score-5 reports, PLTW/NAF accreditation, and college matriculation to Northwestern/USC/Villanova. (This bucket is about program availability/rigor and documented outcomes, not classroom teaching style or counseling quality.)
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical-pla: Square reviewers more often describe facility and operational failures — unsanitary bathrooms, pests and cockroaches, roof leaks, construction disruptions, overcrowded classrooms/lunchrooms, terrible cafeteria food, unreliable buses, high parking/lunch fees — e.g., "cockroaches everywhere," "impossible to find a seat at lunch," and buses that fail to pick up students. (This bucket covers tangible facilities, food/service hygiene, space/capacity and transportation/logistics issues.)
candidate_defs.square entries show greater polarity and: Square reviews frequently report a wide spread—exceptional, award-winning or highly supportive teachers and AP instructors on one hand, and chronic teacher incompetence, absenteeism, cancelled classes, or subject-specific weakness on the other (examples: named outstanding AP teachers vs "teachers don’t know what they are teaching," substitutes covering many classes, and teachers staying after school to tutor). (This bucket addresses classroom instruction quality and teacher availability distinct from administrative or programmatic issues.)
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers more often allege poor leadership, unresponsive or error-prone counselors (missed scholarship deadlines, transcript delays), punitive or inconsistent discipline (Saturday School, harsh punishments), favoritism/nepotism (athlete/legacy bias, secretive boards), and governance problems (turnover, opaque hires), e.g., counselors "blew deadlines," "Board of Education does not solicit feedback," and claims that administration is "self‑serving." (This bucket groups leadership/governance, counselor effectiveness, communication responsiveness and biased or opaque administrative practices, separate from teacher-level or student-behavior issues.)
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms that describe concrete safety problems inside/around the school (fights, lockdowns, guns/knife threats, frequent fights, vandalism, theft, visible drug dealing including on buses, student cyber-harassment that led to sheriff involvement, and repeated police visits). Examples: multiple square reviews list 'frequent fights,' 'kids selling drugs behind the school,' 'lockdowns,' 'vandalized restrooms,' and 'felony-level email hacks confirmed by sheriff,' whereas circle reviews do not report comparable criminal/safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive for: This bucket captures concrete curricular/program offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/AVID/dual-enrollment/Early College, wide AP breadth, magnet/CIS programs, demonstrable college matriculation and high test scores, and specialized rigorous coursework). Examples: square reviews enumerate 'Early College program,' 'AP/IB/AVID and many AP classes,' 'dual-credit,' 'students admitted to top colleges/Georgia Tech,' and explicit claims of high testing performance, while circle reviews rarely document these formal program credentials.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups governance and policy failures reported as concrete practices (administrative protection of staff, favoritism toward athletes/high-achievers, delayed/inconsistent discipline, arbitrary/punitive attendance policies, grade manipulation, failure to follow Ed Code/IEP law, and leadership turnover). Examples: square reviewers allege 'teachers and staff protect one another... protectionism goes to the top,' 'punishments meted out days or weeks later,' 'principal causing teacher morale to plummet,' 'cheating/AP testing scandals brushed under the rug,' and 'IEP/IDEA noncompliance,' while circle reviews lack these systemic governance accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, more nume: This bucket groups concrete programmatic and physical-resource claims (wide clubs and competitive teams, award-winning band/arts/ROTC, elite/privileged sports, large campus amenities, new stadiums, 1:1 Chromebook programs, and detailed facility inventories or recent capital upgrades). Examples: square reviews list 'Cybersecurity team top 5% nationally,' 'award-winning band and ROTC,' 'Fitness Center, Olympic pool, multiple gyms,' 'new high school and stadium,' and 'every student 5–12 has a Chromebook,' whereas circle reviews typically do not enumerate comparable extracurricular breadth or facility inventories.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more small-school/: This bucket groups concrete positive climate and support practices emphasized by circle reviewers (teacher caring and responsiveness, close-knit/small-community character, improving safety under new leadership, clinical supports, and examples of successful college preparation tied to staff support). Examples: circle reviewers say 'teachers are awesome/helpful,' 'typical of a small town — everyone knows everyone,' 'well prepared for university,' and note improvements under a principal or presence of clinical child psychologist—features that are reported far less often in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more robust and cl: This bucket captures concrete program availability and measurable outcomes: Square reviews repeatedly name AP, IB, dual‑enrollment, career academies, large AP/Dual Credit counts, internship pathways and explicit college credit/transfer metrics and alumni placements (e.g., 'IB Diploma Programme', '25 AP/Dual Credit Class offered', 'started at ISU with 78 transferable credit hours', 'full ride scholarships'), whereas Circle reviews lack or omit these programmatic/outcome details.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive ext: This groups descriptions of breadth and success in outside‑class programs: Square lists many clubs, marching band/ensembles, JROTC/AFJROTC, robotics, vocational programs, numerous varsity sports and booster activity and notes facility upgrades tied to athletics (e.g., 'band invited to play in Normandy', 'upgraded Bleachers and Gym floors', 'plethora of opportunities to get involved'), while Circle contains few comparable program lists or site‑level extracurricular achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket includes repeated firsthand accounts of on‑campus peer harm and public‑safety incidents: Square reviews document daily fights, assaults requiring hospitalization, routine vaping/drug use, bomb threats, gang proximity, multiple suicides and families withdrawing for safety ('fights EVERY day', 'my friend... now she is in the freaking hospital', 'multiple suicides'), whereas Circle reviews do not describe this level or frequency of student safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This groups complaints about leadership, district governance, and systemic non‑instructional failures: Square reviews allege poor responsiveness, fabricated allegations by staff, unlawful phone searches, superintendent leave/indictment, budget misprioritization toward athletics, and tenure‑protected poor teachers ('superintendent was put on leave... business manager resigned and has been indicted', 'they unlawfully taken my cell phone and read my text messages', 'spend money on artificial turf instead of coaches'), whereas Circle reviews rarely report such governance scandals or privacy violations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more uneven teache: This bucket covers classroom‑level instructional and professional practice issues: Square reviewers cite large variability in teacher quality (standout AP instructors vs. inexperienced/unprofessional teachers), inconsistent/punitive grading and promotion practices, failure to follow IEPs, classroom practices that impede learning, and teacher misconduct (favoritism, verbal abuse, throwing objects) ('AP teachers excellent but level classes terrible', 'they are not doing the IEP guidelines', 'teachers would call students slow and stupid', 'passed with a D so they’re not left behind'), while Circle reviews generally present more consistent, caring faculty assessments and do not document these specific instructional failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: These reviews enumerate durable, named program structures and college supports (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/Running Start, explicit AP counts like “27 APs,” IB programs, engineering/aviation/ROTC/technical academies, FLVS, on‑site college classes, dedicated college counselors, FAFSA/free SAT) that square reviewers use to signal real program breadth and college preparation—features Circle reviews largely omit or only mention generically.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain many concrete safety incidents and patterns (gang targeting, recorded racist threats, stabbings/threat threats, fights, regular drug availability, underage smoking/vaping, K9 lineups) and explicit requests for police/security; Circle reviews either lack these reports or confine safety complaints to theft or isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more governance/di: Square reviewers repeatedly cite systemic leadership problems—administrators who ignore complaints or lie, demands for students' off‑campus texts, nepotistic cash‑for‑service allegations, inconsistent or punitive discipline (prison‑like policies, arbitrary suspensions), micromanagement of teachers, and board decisions displacing experienced staff—while Circle contains fewer or only isolated governance complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Square texts point to chronic physical and operational problems (severe overcrowding and dozens of portables, lack of AC, crowded lunchrooms, pest/cleanliness issues, outdated or insufficient labs/textbooks, delayed yearbooks, rarely‑updated websites and broken parent communication systems, scheduling problems and half‑day time loss) that Circle reviews do not document at the same scale.
candidate_defs.square entries report more variable inst: Square reviews combine claims of wide teacher quality variance and poor classroom practice (many ‘not teaching,’ movies in class, inconsistent grading) with programmatic failures for vulnerable students—IEP/504 noncompliance, Special Ed seen as ‘glorified study hall,’ minorities tracked into lower classes, and staff‑communicated low expectations—whereas Circle reviews rarely document systemic SPED or tracking failures and show more consistent instructional endorsements.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse safety and m: This bucket captures differences where square reviewers describe pervasive safety problems and harmful student behavior (bullying, fights, drugs, gangs, arrests, targeted harassment of queer/POC/disabled students, self‑harm) that circle reviewers do not. Example evidence: numerous square lines about “huge drug problem,” “bullying happens at least four times a day,” repeated fights, gang activity, locker thefts, and students being arrested versus circle’s lack of comparable violence/drug claims.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This groups contrasts in concrete programs and measurable outcomes where square reviews list more AP/Honors/IB/dual‑enrollment/college‑credit pathways and explicit college matriculation/scholarship evidence that circle reviews lack. Illustrative items: square mentions wide AP/Honors catalogs, College Credit Plus/dual enrollment, IB debates, graduates at elite universities and scholarship totals; circle reviewers explicitly report missing AP or weaker advanced offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket covers classroom-level delivery and support differences: square reviewers more often document problems like teachers not teaching, excessive in‑class phone use, missing labs, homework practices (none or overload in honors), and uneven special‑education/IEP responsiveness as well as examples of both helpful and neglectful teacher behavior. Representative raw evidence: “teachers do not teach… students stay on the phone,” “chemistry class didn't perform any labs,” IEP delays and also isolated reports of strong teacher help—contrast with circle’s generally fewer classroom‑instruction failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This bucket captures differences about leadership, staffing morale, and governance where square reviewers more often cite leadership turnover, calls for wholesale leadership change, unresponsive or punitive administration, board/fiscal complaints, and teacher morale/turnover. Examples include “third principal in three years,” demands for new leadership, “administration is horrible,” budget transparency calls, and widespread teacher exits—conditions circle reviews largely do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive fac: This groups concrete physical, operational, and program‑infrastructure differences: square reviews more frequently mention building age/modernization plans, extreme overcrowding or new‑build plans, take‑home laptop programs, transportation/meal systems, security cameras/police, large music/arts programs, championship athletics, and pay‑to‑play fees or visible athletic spending. Examples: “3500+ students / need for second high school,” “brand new, state of the art building,” district laptop program, international‑traveling music program, athletics stadium spending and ‘pay to play’ sports—topics circle reviews tend not to report.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers concrete reports of physical harm and health risks at school (fights, assaults, gangs, drug sales/use, sexual‑misconduct incidents, pest infestations, food poisoning, and serious medical events) — e.g., reviewers say students were "shoved into lockers," the school is "infested with gangs," staff tolerated "drugs in children's bags," a student was "fondled by a teacher's son," there were claims of "roach and rodent problem" and "food poisoning," and even seizure‑like illnesses tied to mold. It groups items that document actual harm or ongoing safety/health exposures (frequency, types, and reported on‑site incidents) rather than perceptions of climate or administrative handling alone.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket captures concrete programmatic and outcome evidence of academic rigor and college preparation: availability of AP/IB/honors tracks, diploma levels, college credits, awards, and measurable matriculation/scholarship outcomes — e.g., mentions of an "IB Programme," "6 national merit finalists," many AP classes and students earning college credit, students admitted to Ivy/competitive colleges, and named scholarship/placement examples. It groups claims about formal advanced curricula and verifiable student outcomes rather than general statements about teaching quality.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher-: This bucket covers named, concrete extracurricular offerings and capital/facility strengths (large rosters of clubs, music/theatre excellence, JROTC, competitive sports success, dorms/recruitment, new gyms/pools, auditorium and stadium quality) — e.g., "almost 100 different clubs," "girls' water polo made States 30+ times," an "outstanding JROTC program," "brand new Olympic sized pool," and a "best performing arts center auditorium." It groups tangible after‑school pathways, competitive program achievements, and facility investments distinct from classroom or staffing issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report more variable and: This bucket groups reviewer claims about personnel behavior, stability, and support services — leadership turnover, role‑specific praise mixed with criticism, poor counselor/IEP compliance, tenure‑protected bad teachers, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy students, staff mistreatment and low morale — e.g., "too many principals," "counselors do very little," "teachers flirt with female students," and "administration suspended the attacked student." It focuses on how staff and leaders behave, how consistent and competent supports (counseling, special education, discipline) are, and documented failures or favoritism in personnel actions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational,: This bucket includes concrete operational practices and resource/policy effects that impede schooling: scheduling and enrollment failures (excessive closures, finals scheduling, block schedules, huge class sizes), overcrowding/HVAC/construction issues and odors, program cuts and funding choices (money for sports/tech over books), communication failures, and punitive revenue‑linked enforcement (dress‑code fines) — e.g., complaints about "extending school into summer because of finals," "no books allowed to take home," "lots of money for sports and tech gadgets, but books... second priority," "AP classes canceled due to low enrollment," and "Calendar of events has not been updated." It groups infrastructural, scheduling, fiscal, and policy constraints separate from safety incidents, academic program content, extracurricular breadth, or staff conduct.
candidate_defs.square entries document substantially st: These reviews name concrete, school‑level offerings and outcomes that square reviews list far more often—AP/IB/Honors tracks, named magnet programs, dual‑enrollment and test‑prep, paid AP exams, external college partnerships, CTE/associate‑degree pathways and explicit alumni placements (e.g., Ivy/UC admits, transferred college credits). Circle reviews lack these programmatic specifics and instead offer only generic academic commentary or note limited curricular choice.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews include repeated, concrete accounts of fights, gang presence, drug/vaping problems, student assaults, suicides, teacher/student sexual misconduct and lockdowns, often describing police involvement or social‑media amplification; circle reviews rarely contain such incident‑level reports and more often emphasize safety or only interpersonal drama.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Square reviewers repeatedly accuse leaders of mismanagement, inconsistent rule enforcement, punitive or lenient retention policies, nepotism/favoritism, record‑keeping failures, silencing parents, aggressive attendance documentation, PR spectacles (e.g., helicopter pep rallies), and explicit resource allocation choices that privilege athletics or rankings over individualized supports; circle reviews offer far fewer such management‑level allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher‑: Square reviews enumerate many concrete activities—large marching bands, award‑winning music/choir programs, competitive sports teams, numerous clubs, and formal academy/magnet extracurricular pathways—plus strong descriptions of school spirit and traditions; circle reviews rarely list comparable breadth or marquee extracurricular achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete acc: Square reviews include explicit operational details about special‑education supports or failures (IEP/504 implementation, inclusion practices), tutoring structures and one‑on‑one teacher help, counselor proactivity or neglect, mandated remediation sessions, and mental‑health support gaps—whereas circle reviews largely omit such detailed descriptions of SpEd/counseling practices.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures descriptions of concrete on-campus danger and peer harms that appear much more often in Square: fatal overdoses, confirmed weapons, hallway drug-dealing and vending, frequent fights and assaults, pervasive bullying and sexual coercion, and suicide clusters/mental‑health crises (e.g., “two kids OD…died,” “loaded handgun…that was my son’s last day,” “highest suicide rate in the area”). Circle reviews rarely document comparable specific safety incidents or systemwide student‑harm patterns.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete ad: This groups claims about formal academic programs, tracking, and postsecondary evidence that Square reviewers name more: AP/IB offerings, honors/gifted programs, dual‑enrollment, tracking policies, and explicit college placements or AP-credit counts (e.g., students accepted to Berkeley/Cornell/Stanford, graduates with 48 AP credits, ‘AP classes and honors classes are normally challenging’). Circle reviews typically lack comparable documented college‑placement evidence or named extensive advanced‑course inventories.
candidate_defs.square entries report more detailed alle: This bucket covers leadership and governance practices described in Square: nepotism, targeted harassment (by principals or SROs), grade/athlete favoritism, routine suspension/authoritarian discipline, cover‑ups of incidents, misused funds, and claims of leadership intimidation (e.g., “Nepotism galore,” “police guard always accompanies a principal,” “they go to great lengths to cover up what really goes on”). Circle may note general administrative problems but lacks the same volume of named misconduct, structural favoritism, or coercive enforcement examples.
candidate_defs.square entries document more and more sp: This bucket groups concrete in‑school services and how they operate: ELL one‑on‑one tutors, teen‑center homework supports, formal PBIS implementation, documented IEP/resource‑teacher teams, counseling availability or failures, and school‑level intervention programs (e.g., ‘district give great interventions for all types of learners,’ ‘hired special tutors for ELL’). It also includes programmatic misuse claims (e.g., special education used as a catch‑all or push‑out practices). Circle reviews seldom enumerate comparable student‑support programs or targeted intervention structures.
candidate_defs.square entries provide far richer, more: This bucket groups described non‑academic offerings and physical/resource choices: extensive band/theatre/music, vocational/MBIT programs, high‑profile athletic funding or state championships, costly class trips, capital projects and modernization plans, and concrete equipment/facility comparisons (e.g., ‘nationally recognized Show Choir,’ ‘$1M football field,’ ‘newly renovated, latest in tech’ and complaints about arts cuts vs. athletic spending). Circle’s reviews are comparatively sparse about in‑person extracurricular breadth, large capital projects, or detailed resource allocation narratives.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures reports of violence, frequent fights, stabbings/arson, rampant vaping/drugs/alcohol, daily racial slurs, unchecked bullying that led to therapy/protective orders/attorney involvement and even deaths — e.g. “a student was stabbed in the hallway,” “we have obtained an attorney…protective order,” “the N word is used a lot… I hear it daily,” and “so many deaths of drug overdoses and drunk driving.” These are concrete in‑school safety and student‑behavior problems square reviewers cite far more than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger/more nume: This bucket groups concrete program availability and outcomes: AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, named academies/CTE pathways, district‑paid AP exams, and documented college acceptances/scholarships — e.g. “IB program is awesome,” “28 AP credits,” “UCONN ECE courses,” and students admitted to Cornell, Berkeley, HYPSM. Square reviewers repeatedly cite specific course lists, academies, and measurable college results that circle reviewers generally do not.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater administra: This bucket covers operational and leadership behaviors: ignored parent letters/phone calls, principals/yielding to image protection, admonishing victims, retaliating against reporters, grade‑changing, and frequent police escalation — e.g. “My letters are completely ignored,” “the principal yelled at my daughter for not being more kind to the perpetrator,” and “known for frequent, unnecessary use of police presence in parent disagreements.” These governance/response failures are described far more often in square texts.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistently: This bucket captures repeated classroom‑level praise in circle reviews: teachers who “bend over backwards,” return phone calls, offer extra help before/after school, and a generally respectful, helpful staff — e.g. “teachers and staff truly do care,” “phone calls were returned quickly,” and “teachers make lessons creative and fun.” Circle reviewers describe steady, personal instructional support that square reviewers either report less often or describe as uneven.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑vi: This bucket groups concrete programmatic prestige and breadth outside core classes — strong music/theater/Journalism/Model UN/NJROTC, state/national competition results, stadium/community pride, and numerous clubs/CTE offerings — e.g. “music program is world class,” “football team to state play‑offs… cheerleading to nationals,” “Journalism department is nationally recognized,” and many named CTE pathways. Square reviewers more often enumerate these high‑visibility extracurricular strengths and community reputation than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more acute student: This bucket groups raw terms that describe frequent fights, drug use/overdoses, gang activity, K-9 locker searches, students ‘out of control’, ceiling/physical-safety incidents, late or absent security response, and ineffective bullying remediation (e.g., 'Extremely high gang activity', 'k-9 teams... bust a few people', 'students throwing desks/chairs', 'bathrooms smell like pot', 'lockdowns and overdoses'). These are concrete safety/supervision failures inside the building and on campus that square reviewers document far more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more concrete ad: This bucket captures statements about explicit program offerings and measurable results: AP/IB/Dual Enrollment counts, specialized academies (CTE, aviation, fire science, Cambridge AICE), vocational offsite centers, competitive achievements and quantified college placement/scholarships (e.g., '24 AP and Honors courses', 'full IB diploma program', 'Seven Million in Scholarships/Grants', 'state and national championships', 'early admits to Columbia/Stanford'). These are concrete descriptions of what the school provides and the outcomes produced — reported more often and with specific metrics in square entries than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report stronger, consiste: This bucket groups claims that circle reviewers give more concrete evidence of effective counseling and in‑class/extramural academic support: timely counselor/principal email responses, walking into college with credit, teacher‑run AP review sessions and hands‑on help (e.g., 'walked into college with 12 credit hours', 'teachers offer review sessions on their own time', 'timely counselor responses'). These are descriptions of consistent delivery of college‑prep services and proactive teacher support that circle entries emphasize relative to square.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more concrete ad: This bucket covers operational leadership and procedural failures reported more in square entries: ignored emails, denied/blocked graduations and mis‑calculated credits, biased discipline or favoritism (sports/wealth), withheld incident records, and mishandled sexual/harassment complaints (e.g., 'principal never responds', 'had to hire an attorney', 'office staff clearly hold favorites', 'complaints about black face were ignored'). These are specific administrative behaviors and policy/discipline mishandlings, distinct from general safety problems or program availability.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more operational f: This bucket collects concrete day‑to‑day infrastructure and systems problems square reviewers document more often: broken A/C and bathrooms, short lunches/long lines, overcrowded classes, LMS/gradebook sync failures (Canvas/Infinite Campus), budget cuts/mandatory fees, and declining maintenance (e.g., '20 minutes for lunch... waiting in the line', 'Canvas synch's with Infinite Campus is VERY ANNOYING', 'bathrooms don't work', 'underfunded robotics/tech shop'). These are tangible resource, facility, scheduling and technology failures that affect routine instruction and student experience.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute student: These reviews describe repeated, tangible safety incidents and heavy disciplinary responses: e.g., “so many incidents of bullying,” “There are fights literally every single day,” reports of drugs/knives/sexual acts, on-site police and metal detectors, and claims of administrative inaction — contrasts with circle entries that do not document chronic violence, drug problems, or constant police presence.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more and broader: Square reviews list concrete, high‑level academic pathways and results (IB, many AP/honors classes, dual enrollment, Early College, multiple CTE tracks, STEM partnerships, ‘students start college with several college credits’), while circle reviews lack comparable named program breadth or consistent evidence of earned college credit.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: Square texts repeatedly cite a split between a few excellent teachers and many weak ones, tenure/turnover issues, administrators accused of favoritism or bullying, firing/gerrymandered staffing decisions, and unanswered parent communications — a wider and more conflictual pattern than circle, which mostly portrays consistently supportive teachers and engaged administrators.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger extracurr: Square reviews catalogue abundant extracurricular offerings and high‑profile successes (award‑winning band, championship teams, dozens of clubs, ROTC, strong CTE/FFA), but also describe a sports‑centric status system and coach favoritism that marginalizes non‑athletes — features circle reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: Square reviewers provide specific facility/resource evidence — roach infestations, ‘way too crowded’ buildings, lack of science labs or textbooks, no public transportation to campus, and both complaints about misallocated stadium spending and examples of bond-funded upgrades — whereas circle entries rarely report this mix of operational deficits or named capital projects.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, more ri: These reviews name concrete curricula and outcomes (30+ AP credit hours; IB programmes, Cambridge/dual‑enrollment, CU Gold/college credit, measurable ACT/AP results, alumni matriculation to Ivy/U‑lists, and vocational certifications) that square schools report more often, whereas circle reviews typically lack AP/IB/dual‑credit metrics or explicitly state limited AP options.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews repeatedly document incidents and day‑to‑day safety threats (drugs in class and on campus, vaping in restrooms, frequent fights, racial harassment, even fires) plus claims that administration or police ‘turn a blind eye’ or only act after escalation; circle reviews do not describe these sustained safety and substance‑use patterns.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Multiple square comments cite withheld information, poor parent communication, chaotic scheduling needing district intervention, nepotistic pay/raise decisions, inconsistent discipline, and appeals to outside authorities—concrete governance and transparency failures that circle entries do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries evidence greater variabil: Square reviews contain repeated specifics about high teacher turnover, low pay, uncertified or long‑term substitute coverage, teachers on phones, punitive grading or group punishments, and both excellent named teachers and many ‘trash’ teachers—showing inconsistent instructional delivery and staffing problems that circle entries rarely describe.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize richer extracur: Square reviewers list extensive clubs, award‑winning music/performing‑arts programs (even Carnegie Hall mentions), strong sports traditions and new athletic facilities, while also accusing schools of prioritizing athletics (multi‑million sport facilities, favoritism in team selection/recruiting) at the expense of academics and equitable resources—patterns largely absent from circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: This bucket captures reports of on‑campus harm and day‑to‑day safety failures in square texts (e.g., “fights near everyday,” vaping/drugs sold openly, weekly lockdowns, thefts, homophobic/Neo‑Nazi threats, sexual misconduct, SRO bullying) together with claims that staff/administration fail to protect victims or follow up (bus‑bullying ignored, assaults not prosecuted, victims put on homebound). Circle entries lack comparable incident-level safety allegations or pervasive substance/use claims.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, higher‑: This groups concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes that square reviewers enumerate (many AP/IB/dual‑credit courses, multivariable calculus/linear algebra/linguistics, nationally ranked debate/band, state championships, ROTC/JROTC, college credits and scholarship counts, Ivy/Top‑tier admits), whereas circle entries generally do not list comparable advanced course inventories, program prestige, or measurable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: This bucket captures claims that leadership privileges elite athletes/favorites, practices nepotism in selections and events, places image/athletics above student welfare, or enforces discipline inconsistently or for political reasons (examples: coaches picking favorites, principals ‘play favorites,’ grade‑changing scandals, 'image before mental health'). Circle entries do not make these systemic favoritism/nepotism allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: This covers logistical and physical‑plant complaints in square texts—severe overcrowding and hallway standstills, insufficient passing time and locker access, chaotic registration, broken desks/intercoms, closed bathrooms from theft, poor food service, no student wifi, and bus/transport mismanagement—issues that circle reviews do not raise at comparable scale.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: This bucket groups reports of uneven instructional quality and unstable staffing plus failures in counseling and special‑needs supports in square reviews (examples: 'some excellent teachers but many who just collect paychecks,' high teacher turnover, 'guidance is beyond useless,' counselor overload, IEPs ignored, lack of mental‑health peer supports) while also noting occasional named exemplary staff; circle entries do not evidence the same breadth of inconsistent or failing student‑support systems.
candidate_defs.square entries report far worse student: This bucket groups reports of on-campus danger and peer misconduct—drugs, vaping-triggered fire alarms, fights, weapons, sexual assaults, chronic bullying (including suicides), thefts and pervasive clique/gang dynamics—that reviewers attribute to an unsafe climate and poor victim protection (e.g., “riddled with drugs…kids bringing guns…few suicides due to bullying,” locker thefts, repeated fights); circle reviews either omit these incidents or describe only isolated discipline/bullying issues.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and mor: This captures concrete program availability and outcomes—AP/IB/STEM magnets, many APs/honors, dual‑enrollment and summer credit courses, high test scores and detailed college matriculation examples (e.g., 'many AP classes…national merit scholars', 'accepted to UCLA/Stanford…'), whereas circle entries generally lack such named advanced course breadth, test statistics, or concrete college-placement evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more explicit cl: Includes reports of classroom-level teaching practices and curriculum delivery—reliance on videos, little homework or poorly integrated assignments, honors classes that don’t teach new material, wide variability in teacher competence and unprofessional in-class behavior (phones, texting), and blended‑learning tech deployments—contrasted with circle entries that rarely allege systemic passive instruction or such uneven instructional rigor.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This groups leadership- and policy-level complaints tied to inequity—unresponsive or rude principals, board politics/nepotism, ideological enforcement, athlete/district‑employee favoritism, retaliation against complainants, failure to follow IEPs or support special‑education students, and racially/sexually hostile incidents (e.g., 'administration stacked with favoritism…SpEd pushed out…racial incidents ignored')—while circle reviews contain fewer or no such governance/fair‑treatment allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete reso: Covers physical and fiscal realities: overcrowded classrooms/short passing periods, aging or hazardous facilities (falling ceilings, foul odors), onerous fees, visible fundraising that prioritizes turf/athletics over arts, arts underfunding, and cancellations due to budget shortfalls—circle entries typically praise facilities or mention only limited operational/policy concerns rather than chronic disrepair or explicit athletics‑over‑arts resource allocation.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more advanced/st: These reviews emphasize concrete curricular offerings and outcomes (AP, IB, dual-enrollment, honors tracks, Academic Decathlon, sustained AP/IB rigor) and cite measurable results (high test/API scores, Ivy/elite college acceptances, large scholarship totals), whereas circle reviews lack such named advanced programs or outcome evidence (examples: 'IB, AP & dual credit', 'started college the equivalent of sophomores with AP/IB', 'graduates go to Princeton, Dartmouth...').
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These items document recurring safety incidents and substance problems plus failures to remedy them (daily bullying, physical assaults, in‑school drug dealers, vaping, assaults with weapons, police involvement) and describe administration/counselor nonresponse or wrongful discipline; circle reviews mention behavior more generally but do not provide the same volume of concrete violent/drug incidents or chronic nonresponse (examples: 'kids are out of control, high drug use', 'I was bullied constantly... No one even tried to stop the bullying', 'students are harrassed and even arrested').
candidate_defs.square entries highlight a broader, high: These reviews enumerate extensive extracurricular offerings and spectacle (marching band, state championships, many clubs, JROTC, FFA, strong drama/music programs, large sports facilities) and sometimes note athletic/performing-arts favoritism (special treatment for football players), while circle reviews rarely list comparable breadth or competitive achievements (examples: 'marching band is amazing', 'multiple state-championship winning athletic teams', 'there is literally a club for every interest').
candidate_defs.square entries contain more explicit com: These items allege structural and leadership problems—nepotism, administrators defending ineffective teachers, hiring/screening failures, bullying by administrators, textbook/asbestos mismanagement, district policy-driven staff time cuts, and even alleged faculty‑student misconduct—that go beyond isolated teacher complaints present in circle reviews (examples: 'administration will stick behind bad teachers', 'suffering from an intense level of nepotism', 'unavailability of textbooks due to an asbestos problem').
candidate_defs.square entries describe more explicit pa: These reviews give concrete, named examples of school-to-family systems and student supports—parent portals, teacher blogs/emails, named college counselors, Link Crew/Sources of Strength, detailed IEP/504 program descriptions and specific accommodation failures or successes—whereas circle reviews rarely name these systems or give equivalent service detail (examples: 'The Parent Portal is a secure online database of your child's grades', 'they offer specialized classes iep and 504 programs', 'Ms Janet Turner... My eldest Is now doing her best at one of the best public universities').
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures reports of concrete student‑safety harms and weak safety follow‑through: many square reviews cite rampant bullying, daily fights, drug/alcohol use, sexual harassment, teen suicides, and explicit cases where victims were ignored or even arrested (e.g., 'Bullying is rampant…2 suicides in past couple of years', 'The principal called the police on the VICTIM of bullying'). Circle entries lack these severe safety incidents or frame conflict as isolated student drama rather than systemic failure.
candidate_defs.square entries document more formal adva: This bucket groups descriptions of concrete curricular pathways and outcome metrics: square reviews routinely name IB/AP/Pre‑AP, PLTW/RIT credits, dual‑enrollment (Cabrillo, Montgomery College), CTE shops (auto tech, welding, woodworking), TRIO/Upward Bound, and college‑placement evidence (Ivy admits, National Merit counts, AP exam %), while circle reviews generally do not enumerate these formal programmatic offerings or measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater variabili: This bucket covers repeated square claims that teacher effectiveness is uneven—'hot or cold' instructors, frequent teacher turnover or long‑term subs, tenured complacency, inattentive or incompetent teachers, and honors/AP classes taught poorly—contrasted with circle reviews which more often describe consistently effective or passionate teachers; it captures personnel stability and day‑to‑day instructional reliability as distinct from program availability.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more administrativ: This bucket captures governance and conduct complaints: square reviewers report biased administration ('good‑ol‑boys club'), favoritism for athletes, blacklisting or retaliation, refusal to investigate complaints, cover‑ups, union/board tensions, rude/unresponsive front offices, and legal/police escalations (e.g., 'administration…sweeps things under the rug', 'so much tension between the union and the school board'), whereas circle entries offer far fewer or none of these allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete fac: This bucket groups square reviews' specific descriptions of physical and operational resources: building conditions and bond‑funded renovations or neglect, tech rollouts or rich labs ('Apple Distinguished School' vs broken iPads), overcrowding and blocked classes, modular/block schedules and open mods, locked bathrooms/bussing problems, and named extracurricular programs (marching band, JROTC, robotics, many clubs); circle reviews rarely provide this level of concrete facility/operational or activity detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger formal ad: These reviews describe concrete program availability and results (AP/IB/honors, dual‑credit/early‑college, Cambridge/AVID, formal engineering/STEM tracks, high AP credit accrual, measurable college acceptances and rankings) far more often in square than in circle (examples: “solid AP programs…left with enough AP credit to fill a full year of college,” “IB or nothing…IB Diploma,” “many dual credit courses…graduating college a year early,” and top‑university placements).
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, better‑: Square reviews repeatedly name a wide variety of supported extracurriculars and campus facilities (speech & debate ranked nationally, theater/choir/band excellence, pottery studios, aviation hangar, cross‑country ski trails, extensive clubs, no‑cut sports policies) and also call out explicit budgetary/priority choices for athletics (football‑centered culture, athletic scholarships, money funneled to sports at expense of other programs), a pattern not present in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews document concrete safety incidents and student behaviors—physical assault and repeated fights, gang activity, vaping/drug use, sexual misconduct allegations, and even alleged violence by a school resource officer—and describe administration failing to address them or using inconsistent/punitive discipline (examples: 'bullying is a huge problem...nothing happens,' 'Pot is a pretty big problem,' 'officer slamming a student,' and families withdrawing/homeschooling after unresolved assaults).
candidate_defs.square entries show greater internal pol: Square texts more often contain sharply conflicting accounts from the same school—simultaneous high praise for programs, college outcomes, or caring staff and equally severe accusations about safety, bias, or instructional neglect—producing a polarized picture (examples: 'one reviewer: this school is great… Ivy placements' vs another: 'this school isn't a good school at all' with violent incidents), while circle reviews are more internally consistent.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: Square reviews repeatedly cite concrete administrative and support breakdowns—IEP not followed or goals reset, counselors ineffective or favoring IB students, erased credits/lost AP paperwork, mandatory parent‑presence policies, poor online grade posting, nepotism/favoritism, and calls for teacher/leadership accountability—whereas circle contains far fewer such specific procedural or special‑education compliance complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, broader: These reviews describe concrete programmatic assets (AP/IB, Early College/dual‑enrollment, specialized academies/magnets, award‑winning arts, Jr. ROTC, DAAPS, CTE) and documented outcomes (SAT averages, associate degrees, large scholarships, Ivy/Selective admits) that circle reviews do not; e.g., square mentions “Dual Enrollment…gets college credits,” “IB program has attracted many quality students,” and students with “full academic scholarships,” whereas circle lacks comparable named programs or measurable results.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: Many square reviews recount concrete safety incidents, daily fights, racial slurs, on‑campus substance use, medical‑vulnerable assaults, and both lax and punitive responses (overuse of ISS, suspensions that amount to expulsion), e.g. “every day i go to school and someone’s saying the n word,” “there is a big alchohol and drug problem,” and “suspend her til the end of the school year,” while circle reviews rarely document this pattern.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers repeatedly cite concrete administrative failures—unanswered parent calls, alleged cover‑ups, income/connected‑family favoritism, lost transcripts and scheduling/placement broken promises, and manipulations of graduation statistics—(“They will say anything…to make parents go away,” “constantly messing up students transcripts,” “Parents are given attention, but seemingly only based on their income”), claims that circle reviews generally do not present at the same scale.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher/instr: Square reviews contain repeated, specific classroom complaints—math department instructional failure, teachers who won’t help, inconsistent grading and favoritism, coaches teaching academic classes without certification, and overloaded teachers relying on online portals—e.g. “The math department is horrible…they refuse to help you,” “teachers having 180 kids…assuming parents will use online ability to check grades,” whereas circle reviews emphasize caring teachers and do not document this pattern of instructional breakdown as often.
candidate_defs.square entries report more resource/spac: Square reviewers frequently note overcrowding and scale strain (multi‑thousand enrollments, few counselors), budget cuts or misallocated spending, district debt/tax impacts, and facility problems or contentious modernization tradeoffs—e.g. “For a school with 3,300 students…just 8 overworked counselors,” “programs…cut…due to cuts in state education funding,” and “disintegrating infrastructure, outdated textbooks”—issues circle reviews do not consistently raise.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive a: These reviews repeatedly name concrete programmatic offerings (AP/IB/ Honors, dual‑enrollment/CCP, College Now, AVID, PLTW, pre‑AP tracks, academy/major systems) and cite quantifiable postsecondary results (students admitted to Ivies, millions in scholarships, college credit hours) that circle reviews lack; examples include 'over 20 APs offered', '18 college credit hours under her belt', and alumni matriculation to Harvard, MIT and state universities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews describe violence, fights, gang activity, drug use, vandalism, hazing, suicides and physical assaults — and document insufficient supervision or safety failures (hallway violence, outsiders on campus, daily fights, metal‑detector/K9 searches) — contrasts with circle reviews that largely do not report comparable safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive e: Square reviews enumerate rich, well‑resourced extracurricular life (marching band, competitive sports, show choir, orchestras, abundant clubs), specific athletic and arts facilities (weight rooms, championship fields, new campuses), and booster/fee structures (season fees, large donations), while circle reviews seldom list comparable programming or capital investments.
candidate_defs.square entries provide more concrete evi: Square reviewers routinely reference operational IEP/504 actions, counseling scheduling and outcomes, remediation/AIS programs, but also document denial/cutting of services, ADA noncompliance, stigma and therapy costs (e.g., 'IEPs scheduled on time... my daughter earned a 4.0' vs 'they will cut your child's services... no support for mental health'), a level of programmatic specificity absent from circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews frequently allege leadership churn (multiple principals), pervasive favoritism or nepotism, unresponsive or defensive administration and staff, substitute/coach turnover, and arbitrary or punitive discipline/communication failures (e.g., '7 principals over 4 years', 'nepotism runs rampant', 'no communication between parents/teachers', frequent substitutes), patterns that circle reviews do not generally describe.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive for: These reviews repeatedly list concrete school offerings—IB and AP curricula, dual‑enrollment partnerships, STEM/vocational academies, award‑winning band/music, many clubs, and named programs (e.g., culinary, auto‑body, ROTC)—that circle reviews generally do not describe; examples include explicit IB/AP/dual‑enrollment references, many named clubs and academy programs, and multiple award‑winning arts/music claims.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more frequent an: Many square reviews describe fights, recorded student‑on‑student assaults, arson/vandalism, bomb threats, weapons incidents, pervasive drug problems, organized suspension‑seeking to avoid school, and severe harassment with mental‑health impacts—claims far more frequent and more extreme than the safety/teasing references in circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews provide concrete governance failures—transcript and record mishandling, principals demoted or frequently replaced, administrators who ignore parent emails, inconsistent discipline, explicit accusations of lying/favoritism, and policy confusion (70% rule, grading/retake controversies)—whereas circle reviews rarely document such operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more physical‑plan: These reviews cite tangible infrastructure and safety problems—mold outbreaks, pest/rodent infestations, rotten or contaminated lunches, exposed wiring/leaks, overcrowded classrooms and fire‑code concerns, aging buildings or urgent remodeling needs, plus difficult site logistics and parking/transportation constraints—noted much more often in square than circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries show more internal inequa: Square reviewers repeatedly allege selective access and unequal treatment—favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, program/track segregation (IB vs non‑IB, specialty centers), punitive or inadequate special‑education treatment, grade inflation/promotion despite failing, and widely divergent family outcomes and college matriculation—patterns that portray stratification and inconsistent support across student groups absent in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: These reviews recount concrete safety failures—frequent fights, lockdowns, bomb threats, pepper‑spray events, gang activity, arrests, heroin/drug use, pervasive vaping/smoking and bathroom assaults—that Circle reviews do not describe (examples: “bomb threat and sweep,” “parents went on campus fought kids, someone peppered sprayed,” “drug infested… High drug use including heroine”).
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviewers report systemic operational breakdowns—unresponsive offices, billing and registration errors, chronic guidance/counseling failures, FAFSA/college‑counseling gaps, scheduling/schedule‑change failures, and alleged misuse/mishandling of IEPs—that impede student placement and parent advocacy (examples: “The Office doesn't return calls…treasure office keeps saying there is balance,” “counselors are not prepared…do not know how to interpret transcripts,” “students disqualified from graduating with a diploma due to IEP errors”).
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger and mor: Many Square reviews list concrete academic offerings and outcomes—IB/Cambridge magnets, many AP and honors classes, specialized academies (engineering, biomedics, AOIT), high AP participation and named college matriculations or rankings—whereas Circle lacks comparable program/offering evidence (examples: “My daughter is in the IB program,” “Most students take at least one honors or AP class,” “many students make it into Harvard, Duke, and NYU”).
candidate_defs.square entries highlight more robust ext: Square reviewers frequently name extensive clubs/teams, award‑winning arts and athletics, recent capital projects and specialized equipment (new science/arts wings, STEM labs, TV production gear, auditoriums, state championships), and also explicit allocation choices (fundraising favoring football) that Circle reviews do not enumerate (examples: “renovated … $14 million science and arts wing,” “Sports program is awesome…many state championships,” “our television opportunities … unparalleled”).
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: Square accounts often name individual teachers and counselors who go above and beyond alongside repeated allegations of unprofessional conduct (swearing, proselytizing, threats), staff collusion/favoritism, protected underperforming staff, and biased enforcement, producing a polarized portrait of adult behavior that Circle does not (examples: “They curse at you,” “Teachers complain behind students' backs,” “staff covers for each other,” and also “Several teachers…went above and beyond” and named mentors who changed students' trajectories).
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete safety and harm: frequent fights, gang activity, on-campus drug use and vaping, sexual harassment between students, physical assaults and vehicle vandalism, plus extreme staff misconduct (corporal punishment, sexualized comments) and even toxic mold/health crises — problems that Circle reviews do not raise (examples: “too many fights to count,” “Vaping is rampant,” “I was beaten and slapped around by Brother Paul,” and reported Stachybotrys/mold illnesses).
