candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: Square reviews repeatedly list specific curricular pathways and results — abundant AP/Pre‑AP offerings, AP pass rates and heavy AP participation, National Merit semi‑finalists and Ivy/MIT acceptances, Early College/vocational certifications, guest‑speaker STEM series, and measurable accountability ratings — while Circle contains few or no comparable program details or outcome metrics (examples: “offer over 21 AP courses,” “overall AP passing rate of 75%,” “full ride to Stanford,” “FVMA CVA certification,” and “best possible rating from the state eight years running”).
candidate_defs.square entries describe more governance: Many Square reviews allege leadership churn and unresponsiveness, favoritism tied to donors/athletics/teacher families, arbitrary or reputation‑driven punishments, policy-driven limits on expulsions, and obstruction of services (counseling/special‑ed), whereas Circle rarely levels these organizational/governance charges (examples: “it all depends on who you are…families donated lots of money,” “leadership turnover is ridiculous,” “3/4 VP's could care less…,” and “they deflect [special‑ed] as a cost saving measure”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more hands-on indi: Square reviews frequently cite one‑to‑one supports that enabled student success — dedicated counselors, teachers offering before/after‑school tutoring, long mentorships, individualized schedule fixes and staff who helped transfer or at‑risk students graduate — often paired with named postsecondary outcomes; Circle mentions caring teachers but lacks comparable concrete examples of sustained individualized interventions (examples: “great counselor… I received a full paid scholarship to attend SDSU,” “teachers would leave at 7:00 if I needed that help,” and “without them I would not graduate”).
candidate_defs.square entries provide richer, more deta: Square reviews give specific facility and resourcing facts — overcrowding and modular classrooms, lack of desks/lockers, sanitation or sewer/mold problems, traffic/parking hazards, capital spending choices (big stadiums vs. textbooks), and a broad catalog of extracurriculars (performing arts centers, huge bands, many clubs) including access costs or barriers — while Circle mostly omits or contradicts these particulars (examples: “8 modular buildings…THERE WEREN'T ENOUGH DESKS,” “a stadium of a staggering $60 million,” “bathrooms are very unsanitary,” and “tons of extracurricular options but you HAVE to pay $16 per club”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more bullying, fig: This bucket captures school-safety and supervision problems: multiple square reviews recount pervasive bullying, daily hallway fights, gang fights, student intoxication/contraband, and staff who ‘do nothing’ (e.g., “Bullying is prevalent and no one does anything,” “all there is bullying, and gang fights everyday,” “students come to school everyday intoxicated”), whereas circle reviews contain little or no comparable evidence of persistent violence, drug culture, or chronic supervisory failure.
candidate_defs.square entries report more advanced/rigo: This groups concrete program- and outcome-level academic strengths: many square reviews list IB/AP offerings, free/accessible AP exams, AP/IB rigor, named AP outcomes and college acceptances, and graduation/college-continuation rates (e.g., “numerous, challenging AP courses,” “IB program... a ton of work,” “98% graduation rate... 97% continue on to college,” and named alumni placements), while circle reviews rarely provide comparable program inventories, AP/IB evidence, or measurable school-level college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑ac: This bucket covers breadth and performance of non-academic offerings: square reviews frequently enumerate many clubs, mandatory arts participation, outstanding band/music/forensics results, vocational certificates (CNAs), and community-engaged programs (e.g., “half the student body in band,” “forensics has won state three years,” “many students graduate with jobs waiting in the health fields”), whereas circle reviews generally report sparse extracurriculars or lost arts programs and do not cite comparable competitive achievements.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic raci: This captures equity-related practices: square reviewers allege tracked segregation by race/SES, racial profiling and harassment, differential discipline toward Black/Latino students, favoritism toward wealthy/longtime families, and exclusion of newcomers (e.g., “By 4th grade the students are segregated in math and English classes,” “Racial profiling…”, “you pay to play… unless you have rich, white parents”), while circle reviews contain few or no parallel allegations of institutionalized racial/SES discrimination or profiling.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects concrete governance and support failures: square reviews document long grading delays, scheduling mishaps that block classes, mishandled 504/IEP accommodations, counselors who ‘hide in meetings,’ transcript/fee withholding, poor event/test communication, and inconsistent policy enforcement (e.g., “attendance office blows me off... marks her absent,” “principal revised schedule making AP Biology impossible,” “They will hold your transcripts... send you to collections”), whereas circle reviews typically emphasize proactive teacher help or describe fewer multi-level administrative/operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports of fights, pervasive drug/alcohol use and dealing, sexual misconduct allegations, arson/false alarms, repeated threats, and police responses described in square reviews (e.g., “multiple fights each day,” “someone set fire to the bathrooms,” “students bring alcohol/drugs; police raided my home”), while circle reviews do not document comparable acute safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger and mor: Square reviews repeatedly name concrete offerings and measurable outcomes—AP/IB/Cambridge, many AP classes, Project Lead The Way, metals/welding labs with credentials, dual-enrollment/PSEO interest, Student Success/Career Centers, and lists of elite college acceptances—whereas circle reviews lack or downplay such structured advanced-program infrastructure and college-prep services.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater internal: Square texts frequently include dual evidence in the same school—named teachers praised for after‑hours help, mentorship, and rigorous classes alongside named staff accused of ideological bias, rudeness, favoritism, unfair grading, or neglect (e.g., ‘Mrs. Hernandez stays after school’ vs. ‘Jeffrey Daucher … unprofessional’), producing a wider spread of teacher performance than circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This covers allegations of corruption or auditing irregularities, refusing records or legal avoidance, mishandled emergency procedures, opaque budgeting/athletics revenue diversion, poor recordkeeping and counselor access problems (e.g., principal resigned over auditing irregularities; school refused nurse records even after subpoena; athletics concession revenues diverted), complaints largely absent from circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a more status-dr: Square reviews frequently describe clique-based ostracism, racial and gender bias, family-name/nepotistic advantages, athletics-as-gatekeeping, and counselor/discipline favoritism (e.g., ‘students form tight knit cliques…treat those that cannot afford nice things less than human,’ ‘advancement…based on your last name,’ and ‘rules do not apply to those with influential parents’), while circle reviews do not present this same pattern of systemic social exclusion.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete, recurring safety and wellbeing failures (fights, stabbings, drugs, regular police presence, pervasive bullying, sexual harassment, and linked self‑harm/suicide) — e.g., “Every single day there are at least 2‑3 fights minimum,” “Drugs are a big problem here,” and reports of suicide/self‑harm — while circle entries do not recount comparable violent or self‑harm incidents and instead emphasize neutral/positive student climate.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more concrete, n: Square reviews enumerate specific program offerings and college pathways (AP/IB, STEAM academies, magnets, dual‑credit at Dickinson, science research, vocational academies) and cite explicit alumni acceptances/scholarships/outcomes (Ivy/UC placements, scholarships), whereas circle reviews typically give only general claims about being 'well‑prepared' or an 'advanced track' without the same program names or outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Many square reviews allege administrators and counselors ignore complaints, protect favorites (athletes/wealthy families), manipulate grades/ratings, or exhibit abusive behavior (e.g., “the true bullies... are the principals and coaches,” counselors favor advanced/wealthy students, claims of forced passing to keep ratings), while circle entries do not contain the same pattern of systemic unresponsiveness or manipulation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced fa: Square reviewer evidence repeatedly points to capacity/operational failures and resource strain (severe overcrowding, 'only two counselors', filthy restrooms and cockroaches, outdated computers, long ID lines, paid parking without cameras) and occasionally to new‑building or tech upgrades as counterpoints, whereas circle reviews rarely document these facility or operational crises.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and broader e: Square texts both list many concrete extracurriculars (marching band, award‑winning arts, JROTC, debate, wide athletic teams, vocational clubs) and document cultures that privilege athletes (funding and teacher favoritism toward football players), while circle entries either omit such breadth or describe fewer extracurricular supports and note different prioritization patterns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe concrete, recurrent safety incidents—weekly or daily fights, pervasive drug/alcohol use in-school, gang presence, sexual harassment/assault, arson, racial slurs, and LGBT-targeted bullying—and link them to transfers and dropouts (examples: 'fights at LEAST once a week', 'students offered illegal drugs daily', 'sexual harassment/sexual assault', 'I've never heard more racial slurs...'). Circle entries lack comparable evidence of systemic violence or targeted abuse and instead focus on isolated peer conflicts or non-safety critiques.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more concrete aca: Many square reviews name specific offerings and outcomes—AP counts and norms ('taking 5 AP classes is the norm', students taking eight APs), dual-enrollment/college-credit classes, programmatic pathways and capstones, and measured gains (API jumped mid-600s to 800+, A-G rate 35%→71%, alumni at UCLA/Stanford)—whereas circle reviews generally do not provide such explicit program lists or quantified outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries document more explicit sp: Square reviewers repeatedly report formal IEPs and concrete compliance breakdowns or FAPE denials ('IEP accommodations are not granted', 'refuse to comply with federal laws', 'shunt kids into a catch-all class called "Strategies"') and note special-needs students being bullied or forced out; circle reviews rarely mention formal SPED processes or these legal/non‑compliance problems.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, named e: Square texts enumerate many specific clubs, award-winning band and theatre, state championships, career-technical pathways, and facility investments (new gym/pool, $14M arts wing), and simultaneously report favoritism or resource tradeoffs (football-funded over academics, athletes/band getting special treatment); circle reviews rarely list this breadth of programs or the same pattern of funding/priority favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more intrusive, pu: Square reviews document concrete administrative practices and failures—internet/blocking policies, bars on windows, ID-based restroom protocols, security guards invading privacy, license-plate discipline, wrong-parent calls, scheduling/website shutdowns, and parents needing relentless follow-up to get services—whereas circle reviews do not present the same mixture of intrusive surveillance plus operational negligence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive saf: These reviews describe repeated physical fights, guns/overdoses/vaping, bathroom vandalism, rampant harassment, and frequent disciplinary failures (e.g., “guns being brought to school,” “harassment and threats of violence are rampant,” “bathrooms never have soap… kids smoke in them”), often paired with security incidents and calls for hall sweeps or cameras — problems that Circle reviews do not portray at the same scale or frequency.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, more f: Square reviewers list concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes (AP/IB, academies, dual‑enrollment, specialized academies like Justice or Environmental Innovation, College Center, National Merit finalists, Ivy/college matriculation) and name counselor/college supports, whereas Circle reviews either do not mention these structured pathways or explicitly report weak college preparation and low HSA/AP access.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Many Square reviews allege systemic leadership failures—nepotistic hiring, rehiring after alleged abuse, covering up complaints, rude/unresponsive office staff and counselors, inconsistent discipline and favoritism (e.g., ‘‘create positions for friends and family,’’ ‘‘the Principal and Assistant Principal cover up any and all complaints’’) — alongside some reviews that name individual supportive staff, a pattern of polarized administrative conduct absent in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater breadth,: Square reviews repeatedly enumerate large, successful co‑curricular ecosystems—dozens of clubs, multiple orchestras/bands, award‑winning theatre, championship teams, booster activity and high student participation (e.g., ‘‘well over 30 clubs,’’ ‘‘four orchestras,’’ ‘‘track program has won numerous district championships’’) — features Circle reviews generally do not emphasize or present as extensively.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviewers describe overcrowding, dilapidated or recently renovated buildings, missing amenities (no auditorium/pool/intercom/AC), sanitation and lunch/food safety issues, textbook/fee problems, and contested budget/prioritization choices (e.g., ‘‘old, small and crammed,’’ ‘‘bathrooms are horrible,’’ ‘‘ASB spends too much on pointless things leaving students without planners’’), whereas Circle rarely reports such pervasive facility/resource deficits.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete on-campus safety problems and weak or punitive responses — e.g., frequent fights, gang and weapon presence, pervasive bullying, student vaping/drug use, pepper‑spray or dog searches, and reports that staff ignore or enable bullies. Falling into this bucket means the review gives specific incidents or recurring counts (2–3 fights/week, bathroom sexual incidents, weapons, police activity) or documents failed safety enforcement rather than only general social complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, san: This bucket captures concrete descriptions of the physical plant and space constraints: overcrowded classrooms and cafeterias, single bathroom stalls for hundreds of students, leaky roofs, rats/roaches, moldy/spoiled food, closed facilities due to vaping, and new buildings already over capacity. A review fits here when it details tangible facility breakdowns or space shortages affecting daily student life, not abstract facility praise or generic comments.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and broader p: This bucket groups statements about concrete curricular and extracurricular programs and results — e.g., plentiful AP and Honors classes, IB and College‑in‑High‑School credit, dual enrollment and 12+ college credits, strong music/band/show choir programs, robotics/Mock Trial/FFA, career certifications, and Ivy/conservatory placements. Reviews in this bucket enumerate named programs, advanced-course participation counts, college matriculation examples, or credentialed career pathways rather than just vague praise.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket covers reviews detailing how instruction and assessment are delivered: teachers playing videos or being absent, whole-class penalties, grade curving and grade‑floors that lower accountability, tolerated plagiarism/outsourced credit recovery, intra-course rigor variability, and complaints about honors/AP not preparing students. A review belongs here when it cites specific classroom practices, grading policies, or academic integrity problems affecting learning, rather than program availability or administrative policy alone.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket contains reviews that describe leadership and operational governance problems: counselors overloaded or not helping with college/IEP compliance, parents reprimanded or facing retaliation, 'good old boys' favoritism, denial of transfers for funding reasons, arbitrary policy changes that weaken rigor, and active refusal to follow IEPs. A review fits here when it documents how school or district leadership decisions, communication breakdowns, or biased enforcement shape student support and discipline.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete reports of fights, assaults, weekly threats, weapon/gun rumors, pervasive bullying, racialized harassment, on-campus drugs/vaping/sex/alcohol, and slow or absent incident response (e.g., “There’s fights weekly,” “drugs at school,” “My daughter was beaten…concussion…and I was not notified”). These items are about actual student safety/behavior occurrences and their immediate handling, not broader policy or leadership critiques.
candidate_defs.square entries document stronger, more n: This groups concrete program- and outcome-level evidence: AP/IB/honors availability, concurrent enrollment, vocational apprenticeships, documented college matriculation and test-score achievements, and named partnerships (e.g., “offers over 21 AP courses and a medical apprentice program,” “outscore peers…in BOTH ACT and AP assessments,” “partnership with Sacred Heart University”). These items refer to specific course offerings, credentials, and measurable academic results rather than general perceptions of teaching quality.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive e: Includes explicit inventories and achievements (marching band nearly 25% of students, state champion teams, award‑winning theater/band, many clubs) plus linked issues like coach favoritism or athletics prioritized over academics (e.g., “championship sports teams,” “We spend SO much money on athletics,” “teachers favor students who are popular and usually athletes”). This bucket covers the presence, scale, successes, and the contested role of extracurricular programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Encompasses leadership turnover, micromanagement, unethical actions (manipulating attendance/funding or review scores), harsh attendance/truancy regimes, arbitrary denial of privileges, biased discipline targeting (race/disability), front-office rudeness, and evidence of systemic mismanagement (e.g., “turned a deaf ear towards toxic mold,” “If you miss ~6 days...you will be forced to sign a contract…fail,” “same administrators writing up review to jack up the score,” “Brown and black students...are unfairly targeted”). These are concrete governance and policy failures that structure school life.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, res: Captures physical-plant and resource realities: dirty/neglected buildings, closed bathrooms, overcrowding and large class sizes, lack or abundance of technology, fundraising pressures, and renovation/underfunding descriptions (e.g., “it was dirty… bathrooms are never clean,” “Class size (Over 50 students) is common,” “Smartboards in every classroom” or “no computers at all,” “Parents are always left to scramble and raise money”). These items concern tangible infrastructure, space, and material supports rather than instructional programs or personnel behavior.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more c: This bucket groups reviews that report explicit, programmatic academic offerings and measurable postsecondary outcomes at square schools (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/PSEO, CTE/health/engineering tracks, internships, college advisors/recruiter visits, high API and stated college matriculation) that circle entries do not mention — for example: “AP, IB, dual enrollment…internships at USC,” “early college…many graduates went to amazing colleges,” and “one of the best CTE departments,” contrasted with circle’s claims of limited AP/college readiness.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent safe: This bucket captures reports of concrete safety incidents and school‑response failures in square reviews (daily slurs and targeted bullying, on‑campus drug use, gang activity, fights, police presence, death threats) and accusations that discipline is inconsistent or protects athletes/perpetrators — e.g. “I got called the F slur…every single day,” “They have a drug problem,” “police officer on duty…a lot of fights,” and claims that victims were punished the same as bullies — which circle reviews do not describe.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket groups concrete process failures and harmful policy changes reported at square schools (lost/misplaced paperwork denying opportunities, PowerSchool/gradebook mismanagement, attendance/credit record errors, scheduling instability, rezoning impacts, removed senior release, charging/meal policies, failure to transfer SPED records, alleged test‑score manipulation or nepotism) — e.g. “they lost the paperwork…board could not approve it,” “teachers not entering grades in PowerSchool,” “days marked absent that weren’t true,” and “administration raising test scores,” which circle reviews do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize facility, capac: This bucket covers concrete physical‑plant and resourcing issues in square reviews — overcrowded classrooms and large cohorts, outdated or unsanitary facilities (rats, mold, cockroaches), awkward/addition circulation, open‑campus lunch/traffic risks, and explicit prioritization of athletics/facility upgrades over academic materials (new turf fields, big athletic complexes vs. lack of textbooks/labs) — e.g. “40 kids in every class,” “rats, cockroaches, mold,” “new turf field…money could've gone to new textbooks,” contrasts with circle’s absence of such combined facility/crowding/resource claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced cu: This bucket groups reviews describing systemic cultural or interpersonal problems at square schools (racial and LGBTQ discrimination, political homogeneity that silences dissent, socioeconomic elitism and cliquishness, staff hypocrisy/offensive language, staff crossing professional boundaries, wide swings in teacher quality and counselor support, and mental‑health harms) — examples include “If you are a person of color, be prepared to be treated differently,” “teachers use offensive language,” “very toxic…driven me to suicide,” and repeated notes that some teachers care deeply while many are uncaring; these cultural/professional systemic claims are largely absent from circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater programmat: This bucket groups raw terms describing concrete curriculum and pathway offerings and documented outcomes (AP/Pre‑AP, IB, honors, dual‑enrollment/PSEO, AVID, ROP/CTE, magnet/academies) and explicit college matriculation or scholarship evidence (e.g., “offers many AP classes,” “IB and Health Academy,” “full scholarship,” “ranked nationally,” “90% go to college”). Items here are about what formal programs the school provides and measurable postsecondary results, not about casual praise of teachers or school climate.
candidate_defs.square entries document more safety, bul: This bucket captures concrete incidents and system failures tied to student safety and discipline—bullying, sexual harassment, daily fights, weapons/weapons finds, vaping/drug use, increased violence, ineffective security or selective enforcement, and punitive or exclusionary discipline practices (e.g., ‘vaping epidemic,’ ‘a bullet was found,’ ‘sexual harassment brushed under the rug,’ ‘the green school’ segregation, ‘students skip metal detectors’). Reviews in this group focus on actual safety incidents and how the school enforces (or fails to enforce) rules.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staffing shor: This bucket groups concrete personnel and support‑system problems: teacher shortages, high turnover/unqualified substitutes, burnout or low instructional effort, overloaded counselors, and failed IEP/504 implementation (e.g., “no chemistry teacher first semester,” “teachers burned out,” “counselors each have 300 kids,” “IEP not followed”). It covers the operational capacity of adults who deliver instruction and specialized supports, and the downstream effect on students needing accommodations or counseling.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, higher‑v: This bucket collects references to well‑resourced, externally recognized extracurricular strengths and partnerships—nationally recognized band/choir/theater, recurring state championships/scholarship athletes, strong boosters, on‑campus internships or local bank branches, university partnerships, or a dominant athletic/music culture (e.g., “band traveled to China,” “many scholarship athletes,” “state champions,” “parent booster support,” “bank branch in the school”). These items describe program prominence, competitive outcomes, and community backing outside the classroom.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: This bucket groups items about physical plant, space and logistics, and school finances: overcrowding and rezoning impacts, aging or newly renovated buildings, broken fixtures and custodial problems, lack of supplies and fundraising dependence, transportation crowding, and allegations of budget mismanagement (e.g., “over capacity building,” “need more counselors,” “books falling apart,” “budget cuts, parents must fundraise,” “reconstructing the large gym”). These are concrete, material constraints or investments that affect daily operation and access.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater advanced/t: This bucket captures claims that Square schools offer more concrete programmatic pathways and documented student outcomes — e.g., many AP/IB/dual‑enrollment options, vocational certificated programs (Automotive, Culinary, Engineering, JROTC), robust arts/band/athletics programs, and named college scholarships/credit (e.g., full rides, SUPA credits, associates on graduation) — whereas Circle reviews lack comparable named programs or concrete post‑secondary outcome anecdotes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This groups descriptions of on‑campus danger and peer harm in Square: recurring bullying, relational/social bullying, daily fights/riots, pervasive drug/alcohol/tobacco use, sexual misconduct/creeping by staff, gang/theft activity, and racially/homophobically hostile remarks — Circle entries contain few or no parallel reports of these safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more variability a: Includes reports of uneven teacher quality, chronic substitute/teacher absences, instructors not posting grades/neglecting lesson plans, overloaded or ineffective counselors, and failures to implement IEP/504 accommodations — concrete instructional and student‑support breakdowns that Circle reviews do not describe to the same extent.
candidate_defs.square entries report more governance, a: Covers leadership and policy problems in Square: alleged nepotistic hiring and coach/team favoritism, administrators publicly shaming students, claims of under‑reporting fights to protect ratings, expulsions/pushing out low performers to improve stats, botched scheduling/arena‑scheduling and misfiled records, and demands for wholesale administrative reform — issues Circle reviews rarely raise.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced fa: This bucket groups physical‑and‑logistics evidence in Square: overcrowded campuses and parking shortages, outdated or uneven technology, broken HVAC/bathroom/food issues, long school days/commutes and scheduling bottlenecks, mixed reports of major renovations/field upgrades or new labs; Circle reviews generally do not document this same mix of resource/space problems or named capital partnerships.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent fights, police involvement, guns/drugs/thefts, sexual harassment, pervasive bullying or discriminatory climates and repeated claims that administrators fail to act (e.g., “guns on campus… Police walk students out on a daily basis,” “The bullying is OBSCENE and nothing is done,” “sexually harassed… admin fails to take action,” “students with weapons”), distinguishing these safety-and-discipline incidents and the school’s ineffective response from Circle reviews that rarely mention weapons/substance incidents and generally report a calmer, safer environment.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete adva: This bucket groups reviews that enumerate named advanced offerings and measurable outcomes—large AP portfolios and AP test grants, IB/medical magnets, dual-enrollment programs, honors classes, internships and specific college placements (e.g., “most AP classes in the area… VASS grant pays for AP test,” “excellent dual enrollment… 95% of credits transfer,” “graduates to MIT/Carnegie Mellon/Uni. of Pennsylvania”), whereas Circle reviews lack similarly detailed, systemic evidence of these structured college-prep pathways.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more and more-deta: This bucket captures mentions of many named co-curricular programs, external awards and accessibility (no-tryout teams, widespread clubs, championship results)—for example, “marching band wins 1st…,” robotics/regional recognition, National Honor Society and community leadership awards, and comments that many sports/clubs do not require tryouts—while Circle reviews do not enumerate or document comparable program variety, achievements, or low-selectivity access.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete oper: This bucket groups facility, logistics and resource-allocation evidence such as overcrowded classes/hallways, filthy restrooms/rodent/roach reports, busing and parking chaos, inconsistent scheduling/block-schedule credit loss, and explicit budget/prioritization complaints (e.g., “spends a horrific amount on football,” “not enough books or computers,” “$20M capital improvements” or conversely near-bankruptcy and odd spending choices), distinguishing these tangible, operational/resource facts from Circle reviews that rarely report the same combination of physical degradation, logistical strain, and sport-focused budget choices.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more failures and: This bucket covers reviews that document special-education denial/manipulation, late or missing transition/IEP plans, inadequate 504 support, overloaded or unhelpful counselors, uneven placement of students and teachers, and poor parent-office responsiveness (e.g., “manipulated beyond detriment… keep your educational attorney on speed dial,” “I would call and leave messages and not get any return calls,” “counselors are super-busy and often hard to get answers from”), separating concrete student-support and case-management failures from other topics such as academics, facilities, or extracurriculars.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic stude: This bucket captures concrete safety and behavior complaints emphasized by square (bullying, frequent fights, gang/drug activity, students 'on drugs', students jumped at lunch) plus failures or perverse outcomes in discipline (administration does nothing, victims also punished, lack of truant officers, open-door security/trespass). Circle reviews by contrast repeatedly describe a safe, supervised environment and zero‑tolerance or effective enforcement, so items that document recurring violence plus ineffective or punitive handling belong here (e.g., 'This school does NOTHING about bullying', 'fighting inside classrooms', 'they punish the victim').
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ac: This bucket groups square reports that enumerate specific curricular and credential offerings and outcomes—AP/IB/honors, dual enrollment, CTE pathways and certifications (Cuyahoga Valley Career Center, nursing/EMT/dental certifications), named college matriculations, scholarship totals and numeric AP/OK Scholars figures—whereas circle tends to make general statements about college readiness without the same program-level evidence (e.g., 'IB most prominent', 'dual enrollment', 'students now pre‑med', 'received thousands of dollars in scholarships').
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects square allegations about governance and resource choices: coach/athlete favoritism and nepotism (varsity locker for coach's son), diversion of capital to stadiums at expense of basic infrastructure, deliberate cover‑ups during inspections, superintendent hostility toward parents, billing/enrollment mishandling and claims of corruption—while circle does not raise these systemic favoritism/corruption claims. Include reports that administration prioritizes athletics or optics over academics or safety (e.g., 'spent millions on a football stadium instead of removing asbestos').
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistentl: This bucket captures circle's repeated evidence of supportive, reachable staff and organized parent channels—'excellent teachers who really care', effective mentoring, strong PTO/parent advisory relationships and active counselor/tutoring support—contrasted with square reports of unresponsive counselors, poor parent communication, counselor turnover and families escalating to advocates/attorneys. Items about reliable teacher outreach, helpful counselors, and active parent governance belong here (e.g., 'teachers go out of their way', 'Coffee Talks', 'PTO, School Site Council').
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive e: This bucket groups square's concrete lists and evidence of broad extracurricular life and capital investment—dozens of clubs and competitive teams, award‑winning band trips, STEAM/performing‑arts academies, recent campus renovations, PTSA/FoSOTA fundraising and community partnerships—whereas circle generally lacks that catalog of activities or notes weaker athletics and fewer clubs. Include mentions of large activity rosters, new auditoriums/STEAM labs, fundraising drives and explicit facility projects (e.g., 'over 80 clubs', 'band traveled to China/Paris', 'brand new school opening').
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures claims about on-campus violence, frequent fights, drug/alcohol use, sexual/physical assaults, pervasive bullying (including cyberbullying), and school failure to punish or protect students — e.g., 'I've been jumped twice... I DIDNT feel safe,' 'one of the most severe drug problems,' 'bullying happens here…adm.& some teachers included,' 'not uncommon to witness 2-4 fights a week' and reports that administrators do not follow through or ignore reports; Circle reviews lack these systemic safety/discipline allegations and often portray a safer, more contained environment.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: This groups claims about AP/IB/dual-enrollment courses, honors tracking, high AP/IB/ SAT scores, scholarship dollars, and alumni college placement (e.g., '4/5 on the AP exam,' 'dual enrollment... high school AND college credit!!!', 'gave out millions of dollars of scholarships', '90 percent of the senior class was accepted'); Circle reviews generally lack verified outcome metrics or formal college-credit program descriptions and instead focus on experiential/personal growth or report poor preparation.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a broader and mo: This covers enumerated, named offerings and achievements (award‑winning band and theatre, NJROTC, robotics, Science Olympiad, many clubs, internships, private‑sector partnerships, D1 athletic pathways) — e.g., 'Best theatre department... competed and got 1st place,' 'NJROTC,' 'about 100 different student clubs,' 'private sector invests with internships'; Circle reviews rarely list comparable program breadth or high-level competitive/artistic success and instead emphasize a smaller set of activities or experiential opportunities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete staf: This bucket groups complaints about teacher disengagement or abuse, favoritism, tenure-protection, micromanagement, rude or dishonest office staff, and inconsistent application of rules (e.g., '90% of teachers only seem to be there for the paycheck,' 'teachers pick favorites,' 'administration is horrible and you are always lied to as a parent,' 'dress code over-enforced by some but not others'); Circle reviews more often describe caring, available staff and do not make pervasive claims of institutional deception or systemic favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries contain more detailed fac: This bucket captures concrete, operational facility claims (new state‑of‑the‑art buildings, athletic complexes, cameras, elevators) alongside specific hazards and capacity issues (asbestos, mold, rodents, filthy restrooms, extreme overcrowding, dismissal/busing delays) — e.g., 'gorgeous, updated new building' and also 'asbestos hanging from their ceilings,' 'classes so over full that teachers can't effectively teach,' 'bathroom stalls without the actual stall part'; Circle reviews generally do not report the same level of specific facility investments or acute maintenance/health/capacity incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe safety: This bucket captures concrete safety and discipline failures that reviewers attribute to the school: frequent on‑campus fights (weekly/daily), stabbings/near‑abductions, on‑site drug/alcohol use and gang activity, emergency‑procedure breakdowns, and repeated claims that anti‑bullying programs and administrators fail to stop or appropriately communicate about incidents (e.g., gummy‑bears laced with substances, a student almost abducted, a 9th grader allegedly trying to stab staff, and reports that bullying is ignored). These are substantive campus safety problems (incidents + poor remediation) that appear far more often in square than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger advance: This bucket groups concrete programmatic evidence of academic pathways and outcomes: abundant AP/IB/PSEO offerings, named specialty academies (Math & Science Academy, Cambridge), dual‑enrollment partnerships and huge college‑credit accruals (examples: 12 college credits, 125 college credits, Running Start AA), and repeated alumni admissions to elite universities (MIT, Stanford, Johns Hopkins). These are factual, trackable program and outcome claims (course availability, partnerships, credit counts, college placement) that square reviews report far more than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers operational governance and staff‑accountability problems: unresponsive front office/registrar and communication failures, alleged grade tampering, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy/prominent families, insults and staff bullying of students/parents, misuse of funds, arbitrary enforcement (e.g., drawing names from a hat, selective punishment), and coercive tactics (extortionate fundraising tactics or withholding yearbooks). These are governance, equity and accountability problems—distinct from classroom instruction or facilities—that are repeatedly documented in square but not in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extreme var: This bucket captures tangible resource and extracurricular patterns: square reviews simultaneously report award‑winning arts/athletics, broad clubs, robotics/DECA successes and state‑of‑the‑art tech or large stadiums, while also reporting facility deficits or decay (mold, roaches, no AC), overcrowding, budget cuts (cancelled tutoring, closed library), pay‑to‑play fees, and contested spending priorities (sports vs. arts). In short, square reviews focus far more on concrete, often contradictory, physical resources, capital projects, extracurricular offerings and how funding choices are allocated than circle reviews do.
candidate_defs.square entries show more inconsistent cl: This bucket groups teacher‑level instruction and student support realities: reviewers describe specific classroom instructional deficits (unqualified or ineffective regular‑track teachers, poor lesson structure) alongside concrete school‑run supports (math labs, free after‑school tutoring, study halls, special‑needs services, college counseling), and also document gaps in guidance/mental‑health services (overworked counselors, dismissive deans). These are front‑line instructional and student‑support practices and failures—present in square entries with strong, detailed examples—distinct from governance, facilities, or academic program availability.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent safe: This bucket groups raw items where reviewers describe concrete safety incidents (weekly or mass fights, on‑campus drug/alcohol use, gang presence, police/SHERIFF patrols) and school responses that are punitive, absent, or biased (staff condoning bullying, racialized discipline, students withdrawn for safety). Examples: 'fights every day,' 'DRUGS.ARE.EVERYWHERE.HERE,' 'two full time sheriffs... to break up the weekly fights,' 'we had to take her out of the school due to her being excessively bullied,' and allegations that 'majority... reprimanded are black' — all appear in square but not in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe broader, concret: This bucket captures explicit inventories of curricular, CTE and extracurricular programs (AP/IB/STEM academies, Project Lead the Way, dual enrollment, career centers, large JROTC/band programs) and linked outcomes (National Merit, scholarship totals, college matriculation, external rankings). Examples: 'IB classes offered,' 'Honors, AP, ACP, IB, AVID, Spanish Immersion,' 'Project Lead the Way and biomed,' '8 National Merit Scholarship winners' and '$16 MILLION in scholarships' — program breadth and measurable outcomes are repeatedly documented in square reviews but largely absent in circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries mention facilities, maint: This bucket covers concrete statements about the physical plant — new construction/renovations/modern tech and athletic infrastructure as well as maintenance failures (bathrooms locked/out of supplies, litter, graffiti). Examples: 'brand new facilities,' 'new stadium and Olympic sized pool,' 'air conditioning... technology is very modern,' alongside 'the bathrooms are always out of toilet paper' and 'building is in need of repairs' — square reviewers supply facility details much more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.Square entries report greater administra: This bucket groups claims about leadership and personnel practices: unresponsive or dismissive administrators, punitive/erroneous administrative actions (credit withdrawals, expulsions), staff favoritism (athlete/wealth bias), privacy/stalking allegations, high turnover and morale problems, and broken parent‑school communication. Examples: 'administration withdrew my child from the class with no credit,' 'favoritism... they show it,' 'teachers leaving in droves,' 'they do not return parent phone calls' and 'Im considering a lawsuit' — these operational leadership/staff failure reports are concentrated in square.
candidate_defs.Square entries report overcrowding, larg: This bucket captures repeated citations of enrollment/space pressure and its instructional consequences: packed hallways, classes with 30–35 students, two‑campus logistic hazards, and mid‑level students receiving insufficient individualized attention as resources are stretched. Examples: 'incredibly overcrowded,' 'over fourteen hundred students,' 'class sizes with as many as 35 students,' and 'unless you are one of the very top students... you do not receive the attention' — these capacity and class‑size problems appear in square far more than in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents and supervision lapses (fights with broken noses, sexual harassment, a locker set on fire), systemic bullying and homophobia, easy access to drugs (sold in bathrooms/parking lots), and staff or security who fail to intervene (attacker picked unsupervised areas, nurse didn’t call ambulance). Example evidence: 'there's fights a lot… a girl had her face slammed into a table', 'Drugs are a HUGE problem… give them out in the bathrooms', and 'staff… would look the other way.' Circle entries contain few or no comparable reports of violence, drugs, or tolerated bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more num: Many square reviews list concrete academic programs and outcomes—AP/IB offerings, named dual‑enrollment partners, high participation rates, rising test scores, and top‑university matriculations or quantified program growth (e.g., 'over 63% of Juniors and Seniors take at least 1 IB class,' 'DMACC partnership,' 'MCAS scores higher than state average,' 'graduated with almost 60 college credits'). Circle reviews generally lack these program details and instead report inadequate AP/college preparation or inconsistent advanced-course success.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive tea: Circle reviews repeatedly allege broadly poor instruction and unhelpful staff (teachers 'lazy,' 'didn't care,' students 'unprepared for AP tests and for college'), slow or missing grading, and a uniform negative view of classroom teaching, whereas square reviews more often describe variability and named pockets of excellent teachers or departments. Example circle evidence: 'Yerington High School is a terrible school. The curriculum and teachers leave something to be desired,' and 'my teachers didn't care... they were not hands on.'
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical fac: Square reviewers provide concrete facility complaints—leaking ceilings, mold, roaches, unsanitary bathrooms, mice in gyms, run‑down buildings, and overcrowded classrooms (advertised 10:1 but classes of 28)—plus operational issues like shortened lunches; Circle reviews rarely report comparable maintenance or sanitation failures and sometimes state the campus is clean. Example evidence: 'leaking ceilings… mold in some of the bathrooms,' 'The grossest classrooms or bathrooms,' and 'They tell you the teacher/student ratio is 10:1… classes average 28.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews document systemic governance problems and specific administrative policies—corruption or favoritism for established/donor families, athletic-first funding decisions (e.g., 'Invest more in students needs, less on 400,000 turf and track!'), unpaid contractors, inconsistent enforcement (closed female bathrooms, unequal concussion treatment), scheduling/credit errors, high turnover, and opaque athletic tryouts. Example evidence: 'Corruption in the city… established families being favored,' 'over 100 hours of work from THEATER PROFESSIONALS went unpaid,' and 'They will harass your student before contacting you.' Circle reviews do not present this same pattern of entrenched mismanagement or nepotistic resource allocation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: These reviews describe named programs, articulated course sequences and explicit outcomes (AP/IB classes, CAS, dual‑credit, STEM/CTE academies, junior/senior internships and alumni attending elite colleges) that circle reviews do not; examples include claims of a full IB program, many AP classes, dual‑enrollment with community colleges, and specific college acceptances and scholarship awards. Falling into this bucket means a school review emphasizes programmatic availability and documented postsecondary results (course names, credit pathways, test/placement evidence) rather than only vague statements about being “academically good.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive ext: These entries list abundant clubs, performing‑arts offerings, varsity sports, championships and active booster/PTO fundraising that circle lacks—e.g., detailed lists of Model UN, robotics, outstanding choir/theatre, undefeated soccer seasons, district titles, and parent-funded amenities. Content in this bucket focuses on concrete extracurricular breadth, performing‑arts/public performance activity, and documented athletic achievement (including boosters/donor support) rather than generic mentions of opportunities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Reviews here document frequent, severe student misconduct and health/safety incidents—bullying that persists despite reporting, on‑campus vaping/drug use, fights, sexual activity/assaults, suicides and police involvement—and assert inadequate school response or supervision. A review falls into this bucket when it details specific safety incidents, substance problems, or recurring peer‑violence and frames school protection/discipline as failing or absent.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These items describe unresponsive or dishonest administration, inconsistent rule enforcement, punitive attendance/tardy/make‑up policies, favoritism toward athletes or local families, lost/incorrect records, litigation or concealed scandals, and technology/parent‑portal failures—examples include locked‑out penalties, $5 make‑up fees, missing fire alarms, grade/credit misreports, and claims of closed investigations into racism. Put simply, this bucket captures concrete governance, procedural and policy breakdowns (or abusive policy enforcement) attributed to leadership or district operations.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistentl: These reviews emphasize warm, accessible teachers and counselors, individualized attention, strong guidance/tutoring supports and a close community (principal visibility, smooth enrollment, bilingual staff and parents able to access data), with explicit praise like “amazing staff” and “counseling center is amazing.” A review fits here when it documents dependable, student‑centered daily support and an inclusive school climate rather than listing program inventories or administrative failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive, co: These reviews name specific, high‑level academic pathways and outcomes (IB, many APs, dual‑credit, Governor's‑school links, PTECH/CTC, vocational programs like cosmetology/auto/welding) and cite concrete matriculations (Harvard, UPenn, Carnegie Mellon) and credit transfer success; Circle reviews lack IB/explicit AP/dual‑credit detail and measurable college placements, instead offering general claims about academics without program evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report a more pervasive u: Many square reviews document frequent physical fights, gang/drug activity, cyberbullying and unauthorized photos, locker‑room supervision failures, arrests and PTSD‑level harms; Circle reviews do not describe this level of routine violence or drug/illegal‑behavior incidents, instead mentioning only intermittent slurs or isolated bullying in a few cases.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers repeatedly describe unequal discipline (protecting athletes/white students), racial/homophobic staff bias, IEP/special‑education mishandling, counselors who are unresponsive or make scheduling errors, punitive retaliation against students whose parents complain, and frequent principal/teacher churn; Circle reviews more often praise administrators and do not raise the same breadth of biased enforcement, IEP misconduct, or retaliatory claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, larger,: Square texts list abundant clubs, massive participation (e.g., 1/3 in music, 214‑member marching band), state championships, near‑Broadway musicals, Normandy trips, and high‑quality performing arts facilities—concrete program depth and competitive success that Circle reviews do not document or that Circle only references in passing.
candidate_defs.square entries report visible facility/t: Square reviews recount campus modernization and 1:1 laptop programs alongside problems like roaches, disgusting bathrooms, reduced janitorial staff, parking fees, contracting choices (alleged $170k fruit‑cake spending), lack of textbooks, and opaque budgeting or austerity cuts; Circle reviews focus on crowding/tuition pressures but do not show the same mixture of capital upgrades paired with operational mismanagement and fee‑shifting.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe concrete, repeated safety crises—e.g., “I've seen more fights than on Jerry Springer,” “Drugs everywhere… shooting threats,” and an allegation of sexual assault and multiple suicide attempts—whereas circle entries rarely mention such extreme incidents and focus on milder conduct or camaraderie.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more punitive, a: Many square reviewers report inconsistent or punitive enforcement and biased exemptions—examples include ‘students always get suspended for some invalid reason,’ athletes being exempted from ‘random’ drug tests, punitive zeros for long hospitalizations, and claims of racially disparate discipline—claims that circle entries do not raise or that circle frames discipline as less arbitrary.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive a: Square reviews frequently list concrete programmatic college‑prep offerings and outcomes—‘15 AP classes and over 30% enrolled,’ IB programs, dual‑enrollment partnerships, students leaving with 20–33 college credits and full‑ride scholarships—while circle reviews rarely cite comparable AP/IB breadth or quantifiable postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight broader, higher: Square texts enumerate thriving extracurricular ecosystems and capital amenities—marching band national placements, thriving athletic attendance, vocational centers, many clubs, and stadium/field upgrades—whereas circle entries either omit such breadth or criticize an overemphasis on athletics without comparable program diversity or facility investment.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers document concrete operational failures—inconsistent visitor/entry enforcement, missed attendance causing grade drops, scheduling/counselor mismanagement, mass teacher turnover, board-level resistance and nondisclosure of issues like mold—while circle entries tend to emphasize organized operations or do not report these systemic administrative failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete, repeated safety failures in the building and community (frequent fights, multiple lockdowns, weapons/threats, widespread drug sales/use, suicide attempts, heavy police presence) combined with ineffective adult response (ignored bullying, punished victims, nonfunctional cameras). Examples: 'weekly fights', 'more than 6 bomb threats', 'drugs are a HUGE problem', 'bullied to the point of attempting suicide' and 'videos on social media showing these fights.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive a: These reviews enumerate concrete program infrastructure (IB diploma and STEM academies, AP and dual‑enrollment partnerships, strong CTE/vocational pathways, aerospace/aviation and specialized centers) and link them to measurable outcomes (students earning free college credit, AP exam success, alumni at selective universities). Examples: 'offers a full IB diploma', 'dual enrolling at Western', 'tremendous amount of opportunity through CTE', and 'one child received a Fulbright; another at UVA/NYU.'
candidate_defs.square entries depict abundant, organize: These comments list named, well‑organized extracurriculars (phenomenal band/music, theater companies, JROTC, academic teams, international trips, many clubs) and documented competitive success in arts and sports (state championships, national titles, decades‑long rival dominance). Examples include 'the band program is phenomenal', 'Blue Roses Theatre Company', 'won 3 State Wrestling tournaments in a row', and 'yearly trips…Europa.'
candidate_defs.square entries report greater inconsiste: Reviews emphasize a polarized academic experience—strong AP/honors instruction and supports for high‑achieving students versus weak mainstream teaching, low rigor/easy passing, limited in‑school remediation, grade‑inflation or cheating, and misplaced placements for struggling learners. Illustrative claims: 'strong AP program but other 4/5 of the school provides a very low education', 'You really don't need to study to PASS... pass and play', 'no extra services during school for kids who struggle', and 'teachers give answers to tests to boost scores.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews describe concrete management and operations failures (punitive public discipline, locked/ID‑scanned bathrooms, inconsistent rule enforcement, visible favoritism to athletes/children of staff, underqualified or understaffed counselors/psychologists, PTA monopolies, overcrowding, aging facilities, and budget misallocation). Examples: 'they locked the bathroom', 'School psychologist... utterly unqualified', 'pay to play and favoritism', 'no PTA allowed', 'building falling apart but new tech bought', and '36:1 class ratios; kids standing in back.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe and pe: These reviews describe concrete safety failures (hospitalizing assaults, sexual harassment, monthly drug‑dog searches, students planning 'jumping' someone, students leaving campus unnoticed, bathroom drug/smoking use) and repeatedly say administration did little or stayed silent; examples include “multiple kids were beaten up so badly they were hospitalized,” ongoing band bullying with no help from the principal, and students selling drugs via school laptops—phenomena not reported in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, named a: Square reviews list formal pathways and outcomes (IB program and diploma, Business/Engineering/BioMed academies, 20+ AP courses, CLEP/dual enrollment, 90%+ graduation and alumni at Stanford/Harvard) as evidence of college-prep infrastructure and alumni success, whereas Circle rarely names such programs or long‑term postsecondary metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries combine stricter, more pu: Square reviewers report blanket suspension practices, lunch detentions for tardies, ID citations, students denied meals for low accounts, plus contradictory application or favoritism (athletes spared, inconsistent tardy discipline, deans pushing suspensions that hurt coursework), showing both harsher rules and biased/irregular application absent from Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete extr: Square reviews enumerate specific extracurricular assets and facilities—32 sports, award‑winning band/ROTC, engineering institute, aquaculture lab, new pool/track, 1:1 laptops and recent rebuilding projects—while also documenting overcrowding, sanitation or asbestos incidents and maintenance problems tied to growth; Circle contains far fewer named programs or facility upgrade descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries describe greater operatio: Square includes multiple operational complaints—teachers not updating grade portals, missed/late grades and lost assignments, guidance counselors giving wrong information, high turnover, rehiring problematic staff, allegations of staff sexual misconduct and rude front‑office behavior—whereas Circle’s reviews contain fewer examples of these systemic personnel and communication failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: These reviews describe concrete safety and conduct problems (daily fights, gang activity, drug offers, weapons incidents, bomb threats, student sexual/physical assaults, and staff who fail to intervene) and link them to supervision gaps (open-campus lunch, security ignoring incidents, students leaving campus). Examples: reports that bullying led to depression/suicidal ideation, ‘multiple fights a day,’ students bringing guns, and repeated accounts that ‘no one does anything’ when misconduct occurs—claims absent from circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and broad: These reviews list tangible curricular and programmatic offerings and outcomes—named IB/AP/honors tracks, robotics, biotechnology labs, vocational certificates, marching band achievements, College & Career Centers, and objective awards/test scores—plus alumni college-placement claims. Examples: multiple mentions of IB/AP programs, ‘#1 robotics program,’ a new biotech lab and drones, US News rankings/National Blue Ribbon, and active college counseling; circle entries do not provide comparable program, facility, or outcome evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews document governance-level failings—unresponsive or rude principals and central office staff, inconsistent or punitive discipline policies, favoritism toward athletes/alumni/wealthy donors, grade interference, broken scheduling/policies, and formal complaints—often describing systemic or district-level causes. Examples: administration told a teacher to pass a failing athlete, parents filing personnel complaints, widespread reports of ignored emails and disorganized front offices, and budget‑driven program cuts; circle entries lack this pattern of governance failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: Multiple square reviews describe frequent one‑on‑one teacher support, named exemplary teachers, active guidance counselors (GED planning, targeted case carriers), and teachers meeting students after school/weekends—whereas circle reviews tend to note only a few isolated excellent teachers or general lack of support. Examples: teachers who ‘meet for hours during free hour’ or guidance counselors helping arrange GEDs or college resources, contrasted with circle’s ‘some teachers are wonderful but only in a couple classes.’
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced pa: These reviews emphasize community-level dynamics—high local affluence, active PTO/donor-funded roles (even a donor-funded historian), routine private tutoring, families moving or open‑enrolling for school quality, and fundraising pressure—that shape programs and access. Examples: comments about ‘parents hiring private admissions counselors,’ ‘parents moved neighborhoods for the school,’ strong PTO and alumni endorsements, and explicit donor-funded staff roles; circle entries do not report this concentrated parental/donor influence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reviews describing concrete student‑safety failures (daily fights/lockdowns, gang/drug/alcohol use, sexual assaults, racial harassment) together with explicit staff inaction or protection of perpetrators (e.g., “fights every day,” “several rapists attend… administrators did absolutely nothing,” “drug use at football games,” “Racism… staff is aware but chose not to punish”). These accounts are about threats to student physical/psychological safety and the school’s failure to remediate them, distinct from operational or programmatic problems.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: This bucket captures concrete programmatic academic evidence: availability of many AP/IB/Honors courses, formal tracking or restricted access to advanced pathways, and measurable college outcomes (e.g., “many AP classes,” “the only school in the state with the entire IB Programme,” multiple Ivy/MIT/Caltech acceptances), plus the countervailing claims about gatekeeping or limited AP access to protect averages (e.g., “will not put them in an AP… to protect mid‑90s”). It groups supply/structure of advanced coursework, tracking policies, and documented post‑secondary outcomes as a single academic‑program theme.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑pr: This bucket gathers descriptions of extracurricular breadth and prestige (hundreds of clubs, award‑winning band, international trips, NCAA/competition pipelines, distinguished music/drama programs) along with claims sports receive outsized priority and preferential treatment (e.g., “over 200 clubs… band performed in Macy’s/Carnegie Hall,” alongside “Football is all they care about,” special hires and huge coach pay, favoritism in tryouts). It groups program scale/visibility and resource/prioritization imbalances toward athletics rather than general school culture.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups concrete governance and operations failures: rude/uncooperative front office, registration/placement errors, mishandled field trips/refunds, governance cronyism and purges, pandemic‑policy failures, poor communication, and weak complaint resolution (e.g., “front‑desk laughed in my face… registration routing problems,” “superintendent replaced dissenting staff,” “took 3 months for my refund only after legal threats,” “no masking, no contact tracing”). These are institutional/management practices and record‑keeping/response problems distinct from student conduct or program offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more personalize: This bucket contains reviews that foreground attentive, student‑focused adults and a close community (e.g., “teachers go above and beyond,” “counselors are very engaged,” “this community is one big family,” “teachers take time with students”), emphasizing individualized support, counseling accessibility, and small‑school community bonds rather than the large‑scale programmatic or safety issues highlighted in other buckets.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, concrete: These reviews list specific curricular and pathway offerings (e.g., 17 AP classes, IB/AICE, science magnets, medical magnet, Work‑Based Learning/Career Center, dual‑enrollment/college credit, JROTC, robotics, extensive electives) and cite named alumni/college placements and AP/college‑credit success as evidence (examples: ‘‘17 AP,’’ ‘‘BASA dual credits,’’ ‘‘kids going to Harvard/Cornell/West Point,’’ ‘‘15 college credits at graduation’’), whereas circle reviews rarely enumerate such program breadth or concrete outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent an: These reviews describe concrete safety events and failures (bomb threats, lockdowns, repeated fights, sexual assaults, weapons/drug access, theft, chronic bullying/hazing) and lapses in security or supervision (weapons/assaults entering/exiting campus, slow incident response), e.g. ‘‘bomb threat and a soft lockdown,’’ ‘‘drugs are easily accessible,’’ ‘‘weapons have entered and exited the school,’’ whereas circle reviews do not report comparable severe safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries reveal more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly document operational/admin breakdowns—unreturned parent emails/calls, counselors hard to reach or scheduling failures, failure to act on reported assaults/weapons, opaque grading/rezoning/board decisions, and punitive attendance/discipline rules (suspensions for tardiness, exclusionary expulsions), e.g. ‘‘counselors don’t reply,’’ ‘‘they dropped her to 22 credits and she lost graduation,’’ ‘‘board ignored 600 petitions,’’ whereas circle reviews more often describe accessible leadership or do not report these systemic responsiveness failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more uneven teac: These reviews name patterns of teacher misconduct or low performance (bullying teachers, refusing accommodations for special needs, physical aggression, staff sexual misconduct), retention of ineffective staff, and biased treatment/nepotism (preferential treatment for athletes or wealthy families, political selections), e.g. ‘‘teachers mock disabled students,’’ ‘‘faculty bias toward sports/funders,’’ ‘‘nepotism is rampant,’’ while circle reviews rarely document this combination of tolerated abusive staff plus institutional favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: This bucket collects reviews where square schools list concrete academic pathways (IB/AP/honors, dual enrollment, transcripted college credit, Career Pathways) and cite measurable outcomes (higher graduation rates, scholarships, Ivy/top‑college placements) that circle reviews do not. Examples: multiple square notes of wide AP/IB offerings, RIT/University transcripted credits, SLU 1818/DMACC dual‑credit, district‑paid AP exams and claims of strong graduation/college acceptance statistics versus Circle's lack of such programs or claims of poor college prep.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑qu: This bucket groups reviews that enumerate extensive extracurricular, arts, music, athletic and vocational offerings at square schools (large club rosters, award‑winning band, music tours, robust sports, STEM buildings, health academies, CTE certifications) while circle reviews lack comparable program breadth. Examples include squares listing 100+ clubs, marching band tours, biomedical/health academies, robotics/woodshop, CNA/servsafe certifications, and magnet/STEM programs versus Circle's sparse or athletics‑only descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries document more pervasive s: This bucket covers reviews describing frequent fights, police calls, on‑campus drug use and smoking, violent assaults, pervasive bullying (including staff‑perpetrated/targeted harassment), and ineffective enforcement of policies at square schools; Circle reviews generally do not report these systemic safety failures. Representative evidence: square mentions students using drugs at 8:30am, vaping/closed bathrooms, police interventions, racial/homophobic slurs, and administration/teachers failing to act — contrasts with Circle's lack of such safety incident reporting.
candidate_defs.square entries report concrete facility,: This bucket captures reviews where square schools give specific, actionable details about the physical plant and daily operations — overcrowding, multi‑campus splits, broken escalators, mold/rodent/asbestos problems, cramped lunch logistics, or conversely recent rebuilt/new STEM/theater facilities and upgrades — while Circle rarely provides such facility detail. Examples: square complaints about mold, cockroaches, 10‑minute lunches and overcrowded classes, plus other squares noting brand‑new buildings, new STEM centers or theater upgrades; Circle lacks comparable facility/capacity narratives.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews detailing administrative incompetence or hostility, front‑office failures, enrollment/paperwork barriers, ‘good ol’ boy’ governance, inconsistent/punitive policies (strict tardy/attendance/discipline), and patterns of teacher retention problems at square schools; Circle reviews typically do not allege systemic governance malfeasance and often describe more supportive counselors/leadership. Examples: square cites missing VOE paperwork, refusal to help transfers/military families, administrators who ignore bullying, principals blamed for running off good teachers, and minute‑level tardy suspensions versus Circle's absence of these administrative failure accounts.
candidate_defs.Square entries report far more concrete: These reviews name specific curricular and co-curricular offerings (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, Highly Gifted/Magnet/HGM tracks, career academies, trade/vocational classes, robust arts programs, JROTC, many clubs, and 1:1 laptop/iPad rollouts) and discuss program capacity and outcomes (College Board recognition, scholarship/college placements), while Circle reviews generally do not list or document these formal programs or measurable program outcomes (examples: Square mentions AP/IB/HGM, CECA, Academy of Health Careers, 1:1 laptops/iPads and many named clubs; Circle provides no comparable program inventory).
candidate_defs.Square entries report far more pervasive: Many Square reviews describe drugs on campus, frequent fights, gang issues, sexual assault reports, weaponized attacks, targeted bullying (including racialized harassment), and concrete examples of administrators ignoring or inconsistently responding to incidents (students forced to withdraw, outsiders entering campus, ‘‘turns a blind eye’’), whereas Circle reviews largely lack reports of widespread drug use, weapons/fights, or systematic administrative indifference to safety.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain enumerated staff misconduct examples, allegations of unqualified teachers, rapid turnover, calls to fire principals, biased enforcement or discrimination by officers/administrators, grade‑manipulation allegations, and repeated complaints about unreturned emails/office rudeness; Circle contains far fewer or only milder instances of these detailed staff or leadership failures and more often describes staff as caring or mixed in tone (examples: named teacher credential failures, 'pedophile' allegation, principal bullying then replacement, IEP non‑compliance claims in Square).
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviewers repeatedly cite overcrowded classrooms, broken infrastructure (leaking roofs, pests, unsanitary incidents), transport/busing failures, missing textbooks and supplies, substitute‑driven instruction, budget constraints and vendor complaints — and sometimes the opposite (recent rebuilds or new construction) — while Circle reviews rarely document these granular facility or district‑level operational logistics (examples: leaking roof, dead rat left a week, 630am bus pickups, 30‑student classes with no desks; Circle lacks comparable facility/transport specifics).
candidate_defs.Square entries report more stratified, e: Square reviews repeatedly describe clique cultures, socioeconomic/heritage‑based advantage, athletic favoritism (grades/promotions for athletes), tracking that limits mobility, public shaming of lower‑performing students, and racialized exclusion or harassment — concrete social‑equity problems that Circle reviews do not substantively report (examples: 'elitism', 'if you’re not athletic you are shunned', 'success determined by heritage', biased resource/discipline for athletes, racial slurs and administrative inaction).
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more num: This bucket captures content where square reviews list concrete advanced offerings and downstream evidence (AP/Honors/IB, STEM/ AICE/accelerated tracks, dual‑enrollment, college credits, scholarships, and specific college admissions) that circle reviews do not. Examples: square mentions “Honors/AP,” “IB curriculum,” “dual enrollment at Cabrillo College,” “pilot CNA program,” explicit AP counts and AP pass rates, and scholarships/full‑ride acceptances, whereas circle contains no comparable AP/dual‑enrollment/program counts or concrete college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize broader, higher: This bucket groups descriptions of wide extracurricular breadth and high-achievement programs plus claims that athletics (or flagship activities) receive outsized attention/funding or favoritism. Examples: square names award‑winning band/robotics/ROTC, “one of the largest music programs,” robust clubs and community events, and also accuses the school of “all the income goes to football,” athletic recruitment and favoritism (“If you don’t buy softball coach gifts sit the bench”), while circle rarely lists comparable extracurricular program breadth or alleges athletic favoritism.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This bucket covers recurring concrete safety incidents (fights, assaults, stabbings, bomb threats, in‑school drug sales/vaping) and reviewers’ claims that the school/district fails to respond effectively. Examples: square texts cite “fights all of the time, violent fights…trash can fire…a stabbing…bomb squad search,” “girls doing coke in the bathroom,” and claims like “Nothing is ever done about a bullying situation,” while circle contains far fewer or only isolated bullying/security complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete fa: This bucket captures tangible infrastructure and administrative failures: physical plant neglect or upgrades, overcrowding and trailers, routine logistical breakdowns, confusing tech/assignment platforms, burdensome program fees and local budget shortfalls. Examples: square reviewers report “no AC/no working water/bathrooms smell,” classes in trailers and long walks between buildings, “several different computer based platforms…a fistful of logins,” billing/fee complaints ($200/class IB fee, $1000 sports fees), lost lockers, scheduling that causes credit loss, and explicit budget constraints not present in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document greater staff‑le: This bucket groups reviewer evidence about teacher/counselor/admin behavior and workforce practices — from exemplary named mentors to allegations of misconduct, dishonesty, grade inflation, poor recordkeeping, high turnover, and differential staff access for program cohorts — that circle reviews rarely report. Examples: square includes named supportive staff (“Andrea Hormuth, Director Of Student Services”), claims of transphobic remarks and sexual‑misconduct mishandling, “teachers passed my child with ‘A’s rather than requiring learning,” “revolving door with teachers,” counselor inequities (dedicated counselor for Cambridge), IEP noncompliance and special‑education slot shortages, and both strong and poor teacher responsiveness in concrete terms; circle lacks comparable detailed staff‑misconduct, turnover, or program‑access allegations.
