candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reports that schools labeled “square” describe normalized bullying, frequent physical fights, substance abuse/overdoses, gang activity, thefts and visible police/security failures — often paired with adults failing to stop or document incidents (e.g., 'Bullying and harassment is heavily normalized', '5 freshman overdosed', 'La Ganga Crips muve todo adentro de la escuela', 'Twice now his gym locker was broke into... cameras didn't catch anything', and 'The teachers don’t do anything... It’s even worse on the bus'). These items emphasize concrete student safety incidents and ineffective on‑site protection/response — a distinct operational reality from teacher skill, facilities, or program offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive,: This bucket captures concrete program availability and outcomes that reviewers tie to the school: AP/IB/magnet/dual enrollment courses, vocational/CTE certifications, strong band/arts programs, and specific high‑value results (e.g., 'wide variety of top notch AP courses', 'This school is a IB school', 'opportunities to earn CNA, EMT, IT', 'My oldest two scored 34 and 36 on their ACTs', 'over 1.2 million dollars received in scholarships', 'students playing at Carnegie Hall'). These items are about what programs/courses/credits the school offers and the measurable student outcomes produced, not about daily instruction or tone.
candidate_defs.square entries report more variability a: This bucket groups teacher‑level delivery and conduct issues described in square reviews: broad variation from 'very strong teachers' to 'teachers don't teach', examples of mean or unprofessional behavior ('teachers belittle the students', 'one teacher threw a phone across the room'), punitive grading or retaliation, chronic tardiness, and reports of work‑to‑rule or underqualified instructors ('teachers are stressed... work‑to‑rule', 'teachers who can't teach their own subject'). These items are about how instruction is delivered and how staff behave day‑to‑day, distinct from high‑level program offerings or district governance.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures structural and leadership problems named in square reviews: alleged coverups, alumni‑controlled hiring, favoritism based on money/connections, district/board mistrust and levy battles ('The administration is very good at coverup', 'UNLESS YOU HAVE MONEY... THEY WILL NOT ACKNOWLEDGE YOU', 'Do not vote this levy in!'), elimination of supervisory positions that precipitated staff exits, and explicit calls to replace principals/administrators. These are governance and policy‑level failures distinct from teacher conduct, facility condition, or program availability.
candidate_defs.square entries report more active parent: This bucket groups concrete community actions and involvement described more often in square reviews: parents relocating or buying in particular attendance zones, organized PTA/booster activity and volunteerism, alumni pride and multigenerational continuity, community warnings or social‑media safety alerts, and municipal/district support programs (e.g., 'parents were super‑involved', 'we were purposeful about purchasing our home... to attend', 'active PTA and sports booster program', 'the care the school district takes for affordable learning and housing are amazing'). These items describe external community/demand dynamics and civic engagement around the school, distinct from in‑school staff, facilities, or program content.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: These reviews describe concrete safety problems (bomb/gun threats, stabbings, shootings, gang fights, daily brawls), pervasive bullying and harassment (racial slurs, targeted new‑student harassment, coach bullying), and frequent claims that staff/administration fail to investigate or protect victims (K9 searches, protests, student suicide linked to bullying). Example evidence: “Bomb threats, gun threats, Fights,” “Kids have been stabbed during fights,” “bullying runs rampant,” and administrators ‘turn their sight and wash their hand.’
candidate_defs.square entries describe richer extracurr: Many square reviews enumerate specific, high‑level extracurricular offerings, named arts/music staff, competitive teams and championships, booster organizations, and school‑spirit traditions—details that circle reviews generally omit. Example evidence: named successes and programs such as “Five time golf state champions,” “TSA, Model UN and Mock Trial,” “choir, band, orchestra,” supportive coaches and Ram Fans/Wilson Music Boosters, and large traditions (homecoming rallies, powderpuff).
candidate_defs.square entries report more advanced/rigo: Square reviews repeatedly list concrete college‑preparation and credential pathways—AP/Honors/IB, dual enrollment, specialized magnets/STEM tracks, CTE certifications and internships—often with documented outcomes (SAT/ACT, college acceptances). Example evidence: “enough AP courses…study abroad and scholarship opportunities,” “dual enrollment credit is guaranteed college credit,” “Project Lead the Way…IDEA Academy,” and many accounts of students accepted to selective colleges.
candidate_defs.square entries allege more administrativ: Square reviewers frequently accuse leadership of nepotism or favoritism (e.g., principal protecting a relative, athletics favoritism), inconsistent or punitive discipline, poor recordkeeping and procedural failures, and district‑level mismanagement or scandal. Example evidence: “His son…can literally walk out…not get in trouble,” “the wholesale dismantling of gifted programs,” erased progress/records, and references to superintendent resignations and ‘money hungry’ district behavior.
candidate_defs.square entries report more material/infr: These reviews call out concrete facility and operational deficits—severe overcrowding, aging HVAC/building problems, outdated or inaccessible technology, poor cafeteria food/pricing, unsafe pickup/bus conditions, and contested spending priorities (athletics vs academics). Example evidence: “packed like a sardine can,” “Technology is severely out of date,” “awful lunch…the prices,” “not enough safety on the buses,” and debates about levies/new campus funding.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: These reviews emphasize concrete advanced-program availability and outcomes (rich AP/IB/pre‑AP offerings, magnet tracks, high AP scores and National Merit counts, college matriculation examples) that circle reviews do not; e.g., square texts list IB/AP/magnet curricula, ‘almost every year… highest number of National Merit semifinalists,’ and students exempting college courses from AP credit, whereas circle contains no comparable program lists or measurable college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: Square reviewers repeatedly name many specific co‑curricular offerings and strong programs (marching band, career academy, CNA/welding certificates, robust sports with college recruiting, many clubs and music/drama honors) that circle reviewers do not; examples include ‘career academy is awesome,’ ‘band program is the best,’ extensive club lists, and vocational certificate pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews contain numerous concrete safety incidents and claims of institutional failure to protect students (regular fights, drug deals, gang presence, cyberbullying, random canine searches) and administrators either ignoring or punishing victims — e.g. ‘bullying every single year,’ ‘drugs and fights... are true,’ and ‘they let people get bullied and then punish the people that get bullied’ — whereas circle reviews generally omit or deny such pervasive safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square texts catalog operational breakdowns and inequitable governance: chaotic registration/scheduling, counselors who don't return calls, strict/uneven attendance or punishment policies, favoritism toward faculty families or athletes, and politicized decision‑making (e.g. ‘registration was a mess,’ ‘counselors do not return phone calls,’ ‘they give athletes rigged grades,’ and ‘faculty favoritism’); circle reviews do not exhibit this pattern of systemic administrative failure.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures and: Multiple square reviews give concrete examples of special‑education breakdowns (IEPs/504s ignored, OCR complaints, inadequate assistant support, forced inappropriate placements) such as ‘they don't follow the IEP accommodation,’ ‘OCR has been contacted,’ and ‘assistant teachers were too busy,’ while circle entries lack parallel evidence of systemic special‑education noncompliance or denial of required services.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute safety: This bucket groups reports about on-campus and community safety: frequent fights, visible gang shirts, drug use, monthly lockdowns/shelter‑in‑place events, regular police presence or tasing, and even multiple suicides/attempts (e.g., “fights break out nearly every day,” “gang-related shirts… smoking,” “3 suicides in 3 yrs”). It also includes failures of supervision or inadequate responses to violence and bullying described together in the reviews; circle entries lack these recurring, high‑severity safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: This bucket captures concrete program offerings and measurable postsecondary results: AP/IB/dual‑enrollment counts, magnet/academy options, vocational/CTE tracks, early‑college pathways, documented scholarships and top‑tier college matriculation (examples: “18 AP…as many as two full years (60 college credits)”, “full tuition scholarship”, magnet/Governor’s School). It describes program availability and outcome evidence (not teaching style); circle entries do not provide comparable breadth or documented college outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic admi: This bucket groups complaints about administration and district governance: alleged district cover‑ups/manipulation, administrator harassment of parents, favoritism/nepotism, punitive fee/ID/graduation policies, lost credits/transcript delays, scheduling and placement breakdowns, and calls for admin replacement (e.g., “covering up…manipulating law enforcement,” “fees…could not graduate,” “they lost some of my credits”). Circle reviews do not show the same pattern of district‑level manipulation or pervasive operational failure.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent spec: This bucket covers specific special‑needs and counseling evidence: IEP noncompliance and legal noncompliance claims, poor identification/support for dyslexia/ADHD/ASD, counselors who fail to act or are inconsistent, alongside mentions of credit‑recovery or summer supports when present (examples: “Have an IEP? Good luck…,” “Special Education in Crystal Lake is awful…,” and also “offering credit recovery and summer school”). It groups both systemic failures and the contrasting reports of some functioning supports; circle entries largely omit special‑education/counseling issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater extracurri: This bucket aggregates reports of wide elective/extracurricular offerings (band, orchestra, theater, JROTC, FFA, trade programs), strong athletic programs and championships, arts‑magnet/cluster specialization, and community/alumni backing or tax‑levies (e.g., “clinched five sports titles,” “arts magnet… I wake up excited to go to school,” “Schools ARE a priority in Lebanon… tax levies”). It also includes notes about program funding disparities (underfunded arts vs. strong athletics) and parental/alumni involvement; circle entries do not exhibit comparable program breadth, athletic success, or organized community funding.
candidate_defs.Square entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket captures school-level curriculum and outcome evidence: square reviews repeatedly name more AP/Honors courses, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit options, specialized academies (STEM/pre‑med/engineering), concrete AP exam and scholarship success, internship pipelines, and documented college placements (Ivy/University acceptances), while circle reviews lack these program- and outcome-level details. Examples: square cites "many AP and honors classes," "dual enrollment… over 30 hours of credit," "internship program for seniors," and alumni admitted to top universities; circle contains no comparable program lists or measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.Square entries report broader, higher‑pr: This bucket covers scope and prominence of out‑of‑class programs plus sports-related staffing/favoritism: square reviews list extensive clubs, award‑winning band and state‑championship athletics, arts magnet programs, JROTC/Running Start and other competitive teams, and also describe coach misconduct, recruited out‑of‑district athletes, or unequal discipline favoring athletes; circle reviews generally do not enumerate comparable extracurricular breadth. Examples: square mentions "marching band… state title wrestling," "many clubs… environmental club, journalism," plus claims like "kids with names can do whatever while the rest are punished" or "coaches focus on sports over academics."
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent seri: This bucket groups concrete claims about student safety, rule enforcement, and disciplinary practices: square reviews document fights, stabbings, guns/bomb threats, widespread drug use, victim‑blaming, expulsions for social‑media content, lockdowns, and either lax enforcement (kids roaming, wellness‑room misuse) or heavy‑handed punishments; circle reviews do not present the same density or severity of safety/discipline incidents. Examples: square cites "fist fights… occasional stabbing," "gun found in backpack… code red lock downs," "victim was attacked… administration did nothing" and policies like "students are treated like prisoners" or "no consequences/teachers give credit late."
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers back‑office and leadership practices that affect student progression: square reviews describe lost enrollment/transcript paperwork, unreturned phone calls, missed deadlines/cost surprises, overloaded or absent counselors (college applications harmed), guidance failures that jeopardized graduation/admissions, and disorganized front‑office behavior — sometimes alongside accounts of new principals improving enforcement — while circle reviews do not report these repeated operational failures. Examples: square gives "They doNot return phone calls on any level," "refused to send transcripts… application rejected," "guidance program is awful… only way to get a meeting was to wait outside their door," and also "new principal… more rules are enforced."
candidate_defs.square entries report worse and more fre: This bucket captures reports of physical danger and peer harassment that square reviewers describe but circle does not: concrete claims like “There are fights every day… My daughter was assaulted…”, “The police are at this school almost everyday,” gang violence, rampant drug/alcohol use, and long‑term unaddressed bullying or retaliation for reporting. It emphasizes both the incidence (fights, assaults, police presence, substance use) and failures of staff to intervene, which distinguish square schools from the generally ‘clean and safe’ accounts in circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This groups reports about how the school is governed and managed — concrete practices like teachers/admin ‘following rules… the student be damned,’ athlete favoritism (‘if you are a football player, you receive immunity’), lost files and counselor recordkeeping failures, administrators only responsive when parents escalate, repeated calls to the superintendent, and calls for board oversight or removal of administrators. These are operational/leadership failures (biased discipline, politicized leadership, poor parent communication, transparency problems) that square reviewers describe far more than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑ac: This bucket covers concrete program availability and measurable results: square reviewers name AP/IB/Pre‑AP, dual enrollment, CTE tracks (EMT, cosmetology, tech), SAS/college‑prep programs, AP scores/college credit, scholarship totals and West Point appointments — claims of “many AP classes,” “IB program,” and “$7M in scholarships” that circle reviews do not provide. It captures availability and documented academic outcomes (rigor, course breadth, credentials) as a distinguishing programmatic feature.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more extensive: This bucket groups concrete extracurricular strength and community support: square reviews repeatedly list championship band/drumline/colorguard, outstanding theater programs, many sports teams and rivalries, active booster clubs and parent involvement (e.g., ‘band, chorus, marching band WGI champs,’ ‘softball state championships,’ ‘hundreds of clubs’). These specific, high‑achievement arts/athletic offerings and visible school‑spirit infrastructure appear frequently in square and are largely absent from circle.
candidate_defs.square entries document more and more‑de: This bucket includes references to formal student supports and their implementation: square reviewers mention social workers/counselors being ‘top notch’ or ‘extremely accommodating,’ on‑campus child care, military‑family guidance, plus detailed IEP/504 experiences (both successful college‑prep outcomes from IEP services and instances where 504s were ignored). The key distinction is that square reviews provide far more concrete evidence—positive and negative—about special‑education, counseling, and individualized support processes than circle reviews do.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete, spe: This bucket captures statements that name real, structured programs and course pathways found in the building — e.g., Square lists Wall‑to‑Wall IB, many AP/Double Honors/Calc III/multivariable courses, Early College/dual‑credit, MERIT/gifted magnets, Career Center/CTE offerings, FIRST Robotics, band, theater and extensive club lists — whereas Circle reviews rarely enumerate comparable program pathways or specialized course catalogs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This groups accounts of repeated, concrete safety incidents and ongoing student‑behavior problems (e.g., 'drugs on campus and at football games', 'fights every single day', 'very big problem with bullying', 'high teen pregnancy and dropout rates', reports of physical assaults) that Square reviewers raise far more often than Circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers concrete operational and governance failures described by reviewers: multiple scheduling errors and counselor understaffing, swapped or missing classes, refusal/fees for homeschooling or remote options, inability to get transcripts, inaccurate attendance/absence records, and administrators who 'do not return calls' or ignore survey results — problems Circle reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.square entries describe a sharper within: Capture of the repeated pattern where Square reviewers say 'AP/Honors/IB students thrive, lots of APs and individualized AP support' alongside contrasting reports that 'regular classes are easy/poorly taught, large gulf between AP and non‑AP students, uneven teacher quality,' a polarized outcome pattern that Circle reviews do not present as strongly.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistent,: This bucket groups Circle's recurring claims that staff and leaders are organized, accessible and supportive (praising principals, teachers, front office and required parental involvement), and that the campus feels safe, family‑like and community‑oriented — a consistent, uniformly positive climate Circle reviewers emphasize more than Square reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive a: These reviews repeatedly name concrete program offerings and results (AP/IB, multiple APs, PLTW with RIT credit, dual‑enrollment partnerships, Wildcat University, large transferable credit totals, National Merit and scholarship dollar amounts, valedictorians and top‑tier college matriculation) that circle reviews do not provide; examples include 'He received 3 credits from RIT,' '12 college credits through dual enrollment,' and 'students with PERFECT SAT scores.' This bucket captures differences about formal course availability, external credit articulation, and documented post‑secondary outcomes (not general teaching quality).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many square reviews describe concrete safety failures—ongoing bullying, slurs, fights, drugs/vaping on buses and in bathrooms, trespasser incidents, and slow/poor security response—plus failures to follow up on incident reports (e.g., ignored emails or video evidence), which circle reviews rarely mention; representative lines include 'major drug problem on the buses,' 'kids are very cruel...the bullying...is never dealt with,' and 'a former student sailed right through the paper‑thin security.' This bucket groups student‑safety events, substance use on campus/transport, and operational security/response breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries document more special‑edu: Square reviews contain numerous concrete allegations about special‑education breakdowns (lost or untransferred records, IDEA noncompliance, teachers ignoring 504 plans), plus criticisms of college guidance and mental‑health counseling (uninformed college advising, 'counselors are terrible,' and students leaving due to depression), examples include 'Have an IEP? Good luck getting the school to follow it' and 'The way they deal with mental health is god awful.' This bucket groups compliance and operational failures in formal accommodations and allied student support services.
candidate_defs.square entries report more visible admin: Square reviewers more often name higher‑level governance problems—superintendent/district mismanagement, budget/fiscal mishandling, alleged corruption or athletic favoritism, administrative rudeness or retaliation, name‑calling leaders, legal avoidance, and repeated principal turnover—evidenced by comments like 'the superintendent's office is severely lacking in leadership,' 'budget miscalculations,' and 'the administration can be corrupt and value athletics over education.' This bucket covers governance, staffing churn, fiscal decisions, favoritism/nepotism, and communication failures at school and district leadership levels.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: Square reviews frequently portray a wide spread—some teachers described as exemplary and providing tutoring/targeted help, while many others are accused of incompetence, poor classroom management, getting behind on curriculum, or high turnover—examples include 'half excellent, half atrocious,' 'teachers go beyond expectations with tutoring,' and 'teachers who can't teach their own subject.' This bucket captures differences in teacher effectiveness, consistency across grades, turnover patterns, and the presence of teacher‑provided remediation/supports (distinct from program availability or administrative issues).
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews document concrete safety failures (drugs/sex/alcohol "rampant," repeated physical fights, thefts, sexualized pranks, students calling themselves 'Neo Nazis', police called to campus, student self-harm conversations) and often allege administrators fail to stop or properly investigate them ("principals do absolutely nothing," "never gets punished"). Circle entries lack comparable reports of pervasive violence or organized hate and more often describe problems as limited cliques or isolated incidents rather than systemic safety crises.
candidate_defs.square entries describe substantially br: Many square reviews list named, structured offerings—IB and magnet tracks, many AP/dual-enrollment courses, vocational/CNA pathways, award‑winning marching band and performing-arts centers, AVID/GSA, college partnerships and scholarship outcomes—presenting both facility investments and competitive extracurricular success. Circle reviews rarely enumerate comparable formal programs or college-access pathways and instead focus on a small set of offerings or local initiatives.
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: Square reviewers repeatedly report counselor overload or ineptitude ("200+ students," "counselor was clueless"), slow or missing grade/attendance corrections, denials of appeals that block graduation, high teacher turnover, and poor responsiveness to parents ('no one returns calls'). Circle entries contain fewer operational failures and more remarks about stable, involved leadership and functioning administrative practices.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more problematic: Evidence in square includes teachers 'teaching to the test,' 'explosive amounts of tests,' refusing make‑ups or extra credit, punitive grading/attendance enforcement, and descriptions of many teachers as disengaged or burned out—while some square reviews also praise rigorous tracks, the dominant instructional complaints contrast with Circle's reports of helpful, committed teachers and constructive college-prep advising.
