candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This covers complaints about school/district communication failures, nepotistic hiring/protectionism, ad‑hoc or punitive rules (harsh tardy/meal/credit policies), micromanagement, and administrators who protect staff or invent allegations; representative raw claims include 'very poor communication,' 'nepotism runs rampant,' punitive ISS/tardy rules, charging policies that deny meals, and administrators who side with or shield staff.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: This bucket groups evidence that the same school has both standout, named supportive teachers and many ineffective or ideologically driven instructors, high turnover/substitute reliance, inconsistent grading/AP rigor or grade inflation/deflation, and some teachers refusing standard curriculum (e.g., evolution); examples include '8 algebra teachers this year,' named teachers who tutor before/after school, claims that ‘many AP courses did not prepare me,’ and teachers who 'won't even explain' lessons.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: This groups specific mentions of renovated/new buildings, large capital investments, 1:1 device rollouts, modern tech/AV facilities, extensive arts/athletics/club offerings, block/advisory schedules, AND operational problems tied to resources—overcrowded classes, parking/traffic hazards, high extracurricular fees, unreliable bussing and many half‑days; examples include '$20M capital improvements,' 1:1 iPads, new block schedule descriptions, strong band/arts programs, alongside 'classes packed to the max,' parking nightmares, and 'donate an extra $5k a year' athletic costs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: These reviews repeatedly name concrete program offerings and college-credit pathways (AP classes, Advanced Placement Academies, IB, PSEO/dual‑enrollment, career academies, A+/college at high school) and cite student outcomes (AP credit accrual, students entering UNC with 25 credits, associates by graduation), whereas circle reviews praise academics only generically without listing specific advanced/dual‑credit programs or measurable postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Many square reviews document violent fights, stabbings/tazings, overdoses, gang/drug problems, frequent police presence or under‑reported incidents and systemic bullying, often paired with claims that administration/staff fail to resolve or underreport these incidents; circle reviews lack comparable concrete reports of violence, substance crises, or pervasive bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, more nume: Square reviews enumerate many clubs, award‑winning band/choir/theatre programs, competitive academic teams, vocational/arts specialties and strong athletic traditions (state championships, All‑State Band), while circle reviews mention far fewer organized extracurricular offerings (primarily JROTC/community service) and do not document the same breadth or competitive accolades.
candidate_defs.square entries document frequent adminis: Square reviewers recount concrete operational breakdowns — rude/inefficient registration offices, counselors hard to reach or transcript delays, scheduling mistakes and limited passing/locker access, overcrowding/parking/traffic hazards, renovation/maintenance problems, inconsistent rule enforcement and delayed grading — whereas circle reviews more often describe responsive staff and fewer logistical breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries describe uneven instructi: Square reviews frequently contrast strong AP/honors teachers with weak general classrooms, report tracking by race/socioeconomic status, athlete/wealth favoritism, grade‑inflation concerns, and explicit special‑education/IEP neglect or mistreatment, while circle reviews do not present this constellation of tracked inequity and systemic special‑needs failures.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures accounts of daily fights, drugs and alcohol on campus, gun/lockdown incidents, physical assaults and sexual harassment, claims of high suicide rates, and pervasive bullying that is either ignored or punished unfairly (examples: ‘several lockdowns for guns,’ ‘students offered illegal drugs daily,’ ‘I was shoved into lockers,’ ‘suicide rates are high!’ and ‘bullies get a mere warning’). Falling into this bucket means reviewers describe repeated, concrete safety/discipline incidents plus ineffective or punitive staff/administrative responses (retaliation for reporting, victims disciplined, security described as ‘horrible’), a pattern largely absent or far less frequent in circle entries.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more concrete ad: This bucket groups mentions of AP/IB/honors breadth, dual-enrollment and early-college pathways, named magnet/academy programs, internships/research experiences, and explicit outcomes (AP pass rates, college acceptances) — e.g., ‘offers over 21 AP courses,’ ‘AP Physics pass rates higher than anywhere in the state,’ ‘dual-enrollment resulting in a two‑year AA,’ and ‘students accepted to top universities.’ Being in this bucket means reviews report specific, structured college-prep offerings and measurable postsecondary results or partnerships that circle entries rarely enumerate.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers systemic governance problems: favoritism and ‘good ol’ boy’ nepotism, arbitrary or inconsistent punishments (drawing names from a hat, punitive isolation), exclusionary transfer/retention policies for low‑GPA students, transcript/record-keeping errors, administrators ignoring complaints, and rapid principal/district leadership turnover (examples: ‘force any students with a GPA 2.0 and under to transfer,’ ‘they screwed up my daughter's transcript,’ and ‘administrators never bother to verify if anything is true’). Reviews in this bucket describe institutional practices or governance failures that create unfair outcomes and lack accountability, a set of concrete complaints much more frequent in square than circle entries.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more teacher-lev: This bucket aggregates teacher-centered problems distinct from administrative policy: mocking or refusing to accommodate students with disabilities or 504/IEP plans, teachers not returning graded work or posting grades, unqualified instructors or high teacher turnover, favoritism/gossip among staff, and classrooms out of control or mismanaged (examples: ‘teachers will even refuse to work with some students with disabilities,’ ‘few teachers return completed work,’ ‘most teachers are good coaches and not certified,’ and ‘some classes are wild, out of control’). A review falls here when it documents recurring, specific teacher-level failures in instruction, professionalism, or special‑education compliance — not broad program availability or admin behavior.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups explicit statements about physical assets and capacity — new gyms, stadiums, performing arts centers, vocational labs with industry credentials, renovated science/math buildings, bond-funded projects, or conversely aging buildings, cockroaches, overcrowded classes and maintenance problems (examples: ‘new gym floor…artificial turf football field…performing arts center,’ ‘metals lab with nationally recognized credentials,’ and ‘class sizes were huge…ceilings falling down, cockroaches’). Falling into this bucket means reviewers give concrete, named evidence about capital projects, extracurricular facilities (band/theater/athletics), vocational offerings, or space/maintenance constraints; circle entries rarely provide this level of facility/program infrastructure detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety incide: This bucket captures school safety and student behavior problems: square reviews describe concrete violent and safety incidents (bullets found, stabbings, frequent fights, lockdowns, police involvement), pervasive bullying, gang/drug/vaping culture and overdoses, and hazing or daily-targeted aggression — examples include “Every day I see at least one fight,” “Last year, 5 freshman overdosed together,” and “she was bullied daily.” Circle reviews do not contain comparable reports of weapons, overdoses, pervasive fighting, or chronic gang/drug activity.
candidate_defs.square entries document more organized a: This bucket groups concrete academic/program offerings and measurable outcomes: square reviews explicitly name IB/AP/honors curricula, academies and CTE/trade pathways, one‑to‑one laptops, free AP exam policies, and quantifiable college credits/placements (e.g., 'IBDP prepares you for university', 'graduated with 18 college credits', 'AOIT participation'), as well as sustained arts/athletics achievements; Circle contains only generic academic praise and lacks these specific program details and outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries reveal more administrativ: This bucket covers governance, leadership, accountability and back‑office failures: square reviews report frequent principal/superintendent turnover, indicted business managers, opaque/ wasteful budgeting, manipulated review scores, credit/records errors that blocked graduation, cover‑ups and extreme administrative defensiveness — e.g. 'business manager resigned and has been indicted on stealing 400k', 'we never received his report cards ... student dropped out', and 'administration created defensive barriers.' Circle contains no comparable sustained allegations of fiscal scandal, systemic recordkeeping failure, or governance cover‑ups.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more physical ov: This bucket groups concrete space/operations issues: square reviews report overpopulation and crowded hallways/classes, confusing or unstable schedules and drill confusion, inadequate computing/testing logistics, parking shortages and poor restroom/cleanliness/odor/maintenance, and archaic paper processes — examples include 'class sizes 44', 'school website is rarely updated', 'parking passes $50', and 'horrible bathrooms with graffiti.' Circle reviews do not raise comparable chronic crowding, scheduling chaos, or facilities upkeep failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures in s: This bucket captures breakdowns in supports and fairness: square reviews allege IEP/special‑education noncompliance and also testify to long‑term effective special‑ed in other cases, inconsistent or punitive counseling (including using counseling to 'correct' nonconformity), athlete/wealth/nepotistic favoritism, racial and homophobic hostility, newcomer exclusion and socioeconomic cliques — e.g. 'They do not make arrangements to comply with IEPs', 'students involved in sports are given priority', and 'Aynor is a very tight community — do not go here if you are new.' Circle reviews do not present the same breadth of systemic support failures, targeted discipline, or exclusionary social hierarchies.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, better‑d: This bucket groups differences where square reviews name concrete academic pathways (AP, IB, Running Start, CTE, Career Center, academies, honors/IB expansions), institutional partnerships (university partnerships, TRIO/upward bound), and quantifiable outcomes (API/test scores, graduation rates, scholarship/college placements) that circle reviews do not; examples include 'adding an IB program,' 'CTE certifications (EMT, cosmetology),' 'Took at Least One AP® Exam 46% and Graduation Rate of 94%,' and 'students moving on to college athletics.'
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize athletics‑cente: This bucket captures instances where square reviewers describe visible prioritization of sports (new football field, gym floor, high athletic budgets), favoritism toward athletes, large/award‑winning athletic and performing programs, and extensive club/booster activity, contrasted with circle’s lack of comparable program breadth; illustrative evidence: 'Most of the funding goes towards sports,' 'new Football Field & Gym floor,' 'many state titles,' and 'parents are involved in many events and PTOs/Boosters.'
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent an: This bucket groups concrete safety incidents and ineffective handling reported in square reviews—guns/drug use on campus, daily fights, racialized bullying, tolerated harassment, Title IX/harassment complaints with no follow‑up, and inadequate adult intervention—e.g., 'guns on campus today,' 'drug deals in hallways,' 'horrendous job protecting my child from constant racialized bullying,' and 'No updates, no discipline from the offender.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete admi: This bucket covers recurring operational problems that reviewers tie to administration or governance: chaotic scheduling/enrollment management, counselor/scheduling breakdowns, ignorance of Ed Code, unresponsive offices, punitive attendance/tardy enforcement, intrusive search/discipline policies, and board/leadership indifference—examples include 'scheduling at the start of the year was awful,' 'administration isn't even aware of Ed Code,' 'attendance is unreasonable…or we don't get paid,' and 'the Board of Education does their best to ignore the myriad of serious issues.'
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: This bucket groups material differences about in‑class execution and student supports: square reviews repeatedly document uneven teacher quality, frequent substitutes/absences, inconsistent grading/grade posting, extensive before/after/Saturday tutoring, contested IEP/SpEd administration, and counseling breakdowns—evidenced by 'teacher quality varies widely,' 'many teachers think grading work and entering on Ed-line is optional,' 'teachers available most days before and after-school to offer tutoring,' and 'district Sped administrators are non compassionate and aggressively confrontational to parents.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute safety: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents (frequent fights, drug use, sexual assaults, thefts, bullying that produced PTSD) alongside heavy policing or punitive campus control (K‑9 searches, police presence, steel gates, benching/ISS for trivial infractions); circle reviews rarely mention safety incidents or securitization and instead omit law‑enforcement practices. Examples: “two fights a day,” “They treat kids like criminals and have dogs and police,” and “turned the school into a prison” versus Circle’s lack of comparable safety/security claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: Many square reviews list AP/honors/IB offerings, dual‑credit, STEM and career‑technical pathways, scholarship programs and concrete outcome metrics (ACT/SAT, National Merit, college matriculations), whereas circle reviews largely lack comparable evidence of organized advanced programs or measurable high‑level outcomes. Examples: “wide variety of AP courses,” “Dollars for Scholars… Many seniors receive 1k,” “college credit with UI or MCC,” and “Students are testing very high on ACT,” contrasted with Circle’s limited or inconsistent AP credit and no comparable outcome data.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews frequently allege unresponsive administrators, nepotism, district profit‑driven choices, manipulated metrics, school‑board capture, and policy failures (e.g., not returning parent calls, superintendent letters about transfers, hiring the superintendent’s daughter, spending on fields instead of books), while circle reviews seldom raise these systemic governance and fiscal misconduct claims. Examples: “I just got a letter from the superintendent… eligible to attend another district,” “the district… is far more concerned with the $$'s,” and “the school board does whatever the superintendent decides.”
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical pla: Square reviewers document concrete facility and resource deficits—dirty bathrooms, mold/rodent sightings, asbestos, no air conditioning, outdated desks/textbooks, portables, and overcrowded classes with too few books—whereas circle reviews rarely describe such severe sanitation, health or material shortages. Examples: “you can’t go one day without smelling mold or seeing a roach,” “books are a good 10 years old,” and “classes contain no fewer than 28 students,” versus Circle’s lack of facility/pest/shortage allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: Square reviews repeatedly enumerate rich extracurricular offerings, nationally ranked music/arts, competitive clubs/teams, booster/foundation support, and active alumni traditions or parental involvement, while circle reviews usually mention fewer or no comparable extracurricular breadth or organized community funding. Examples: “choir and band rank at the very top nationally,” “Booster Club and Niwot Foundation fund the school well,” “drama sold out more than a week straight,” and strong alumni ‘brotherhood’ and volunteer coaching references.
candidate_defs.Square entries report broader, more form: This bucket captures claims that square schools list concrete advanced-course and pathway infrastructure (AP/IB, dual‑enrollment, Early College, magnet/STEM/engineering tracks, multiple diploma levels, Project Lead the Way, Cisco, career centers) together with documented college outcomes (dozens of college credits earned, Ivy/MIT/Caltech/Duke admits, >90% college attendance). Examples: '25 AP/Dual Credit classes,' 'one child left with 33 college credits,' 'access to Advance Placement and challenging course material,' and 'Accelerated/dual‑enrollment models'—all present in square reviews but absent or far less detailed in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.Square entries report a wider and deeper: This groups concrete programmatic offerings outside core classes—robust athletics (stadiums, varsity programs, dedicated coaches), large band/music programs, theater, ROTC/JROTC, culinary, agriculture, robotics, FFA, clubs and extensive volunteer parent support—plus claims of high student participation (e.g., '1/3 involved in music, 1/2 in sports'). Examples: 'mighty band, culinary arts, agriculture program,' 'largest marching band…800 members,' and 'a stadium of a staggering $60 million' appear in square reviews but not in circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: This bucket covers concrete safety incidents and climate problems (daily lockdowns, gang fights, physical assaults, weapons on campus, drug use, sexual harassment) and failures to address them (bullying unhandled, staff complicity, ineffective RTC discipline). Representative items: 'lock‑down almost every day,' 'I was shoved into lockers,' 'students who have weapons on campus,' and 'actual bullying is not handled well at all'—all prominent in square entries and largely missing or reported as isolated in circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups leadership and governance problems: frequent principal turnover and purges, nepotism/'good‑old‑boy' cliques, silencing or retaliating against complainants, transfer denials tied to district funding, arbitrary enforcement of rules, and record‑keeping or scheduling failures. Examples: '4 different principals in 6 years,' 'they replaced people who disagreed,' 'denying parents transfers because they need the money,' and 'they almost cost my child his diploma by not giving him English 12'—all described more often in square reviews.
candidate_defs.Square entries report greater instructio: This bucket captures classroom‑level delivery and support failures: inconsistent teacher competence (some teachers 'should not teach,' absenteeism, busywork), poor or inconsistent implementation of IEP/504 accommodations, counselor nonresponsiveness or counseling errors, and ad hoc remediation (paid private tutoring, underused online classes). Examples: 'the counselors do not return phone calls,' 'All the books were crumbling,' 'The only grades were busy‑work,' and 'getting support for them is tough…you must advocate'—all appearing predominantly in square entries relative to circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and higher: These reviews describe concrete curricular breadth and rigor (IB, many AP/honors, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit, vocational pathways like engineering/culinary/AG, and 1:1 laptop/online course access) and cite measurable outcomes (scholarships, college matriculation, AP/IB exam scores) that circle reviews do not; examples include explicit IB/AP/dual‑enrollment listings, named college‑credit programs, AP exam averages, and claims of Ivy/huge scholarship totals.
candidate_defs.square entries report more diverse and h: Square reviews list many named clubs, high‑performing arts ensembles, and sustained championship athletics (track, softball, band/drill, Esprit de Corps) and emphasize wide opportunity and community integration around extracurriculars, whereas circle lacks comparable program detail; examples include long‑running state championships, award‑winning newspaper/band, and many named clubs and teams.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive bul: Square texts contain repeated allegations of student‑on‑student bullying, staff‑on‑student bullying, drug/gang activity, shooting/gun threats, sexual harassment, broken surveillance (cameras), and accounts of victims punished or ignored—often paired with claims that the school failed to secure or adequately respond to threats—whereas circle contains few or no parallel safety/harassment incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews document concrete leader/staff behaviors and system failures—frequent leadership turnover, promotion decisions harming programs, favoritism (athletes or principal's child), punitive responses to parents/teachers, altered votes/cover‑ups, credit‑tracking and notification failures, and persistent unresponsiveness—that degrade trust and operations; examples include parents told to drop complaints then being retaliated against, altered donation votes, erased credits before graduation, and district‑level manipulation claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pronounced fa: Square reviews repeatedly call out concrete resource and operational conditions—either positive (state‑of‑the‑art rebuilds, 1:1 laptops, strong dual‑enrollment labs) or negative (overcrowding, outdated buildings, disgusting restrooms, cafeteria shortages, unequal funding favoring sports, broken cameras, patchy special‑education transitions, weak/absent counseling)—whereas circle rarely details these physical/resource features; examples range from newly rebuilt campuses and laptop programs to rotten interiors, crowded classes, missing bathroom locks, and cut alt‑ed programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more safety incide: These reviews describe concrete safety problems (frequent fights, death threats, searches, pervasive drug/alcohol use ‘even in class’, racial assaults, and rampant bullying) and often link them to weak enforcement or transfers out (e.g., “fights everyday,” “drugs are everywhere, even in class,” “racially harassed … then brutally assaulted”). Circle reviews lack comparable reports of recurring violence, drug problems, or high‑frequency bullying, so this bucket captures campus safety and student‑misconduct incidents that are materially higher in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader academic: Square reviews enumerate concrete program offerings and facilities—many AP/IB/dual‑enrollment options, 10+–12+ languages, career/CTE classes, marching band, state‑level sports, new stadiums/pools, and wide elective choices (e.g., “offers over 10 languages,” “dual enrollment,” “new stadium and Olympic sized pool”). Circle reviews do not list comparable breadth of formal programs or major campus facilities, so this bucket groups claims about the presence and variety of curricular and extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete inst: Square reviews frequently name classroom practices and measurable results—tutorials and Task blocks, one‑on‑one teacher help, alternative pedagogies, AP pass rates, SOL/AP/SAT gains, and concrete college acceptances (e.g., “they offer tutorials,” “AP pass rates are unbelievably low,” “numerous kids assisted to the IVY leagues”). Circle reviews generally lack the same level of operational detail about instruction, assessment results, or program‑level learning supports, so this bucket groups evidence about how teaching is delivered and what measurable academic outcomes follow.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews describe leadership and policy problems—administrative unavailability, obsession with metrics, cronyism/favoritism in hiring and athletics, punitive disciplinary policies that sometimes punish victims, and procedural irritants (e.g., in‑person sign‑out, short sick‑room rules) with direct complaints such as “administration lacks integrity,” “good‑ol‑boys club,” or calls for charter conversion. Circle reviews do not present the same consistent pattern of systemic governance failures, so this bucket captures school‑level leadership, governance, and policy dysfunction.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit, con: Square reviews frequently describe counseling and support services in operational detail—both positive (after‑school ACT courses, responsive IEP implementation, proactive counselors) and negative (missed scholarship deadlines, ignored IEPs/504s, fights to obtain accommodations), e.g. “I fought with the district on getting him his 504 plan” and “a counselor has blown deadlines for scholarships.” Circle reviews rarely provide comparable, programmatic evidence about special‑education compliance, college‑counseling operations, or concrete accommodation outcomes, so this bucket groups documented support‑service practices and compliance issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive, fo: This bucket groups reviews where square schools list concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes (AP, IB, Engineering/STEM academies, dual‑enrollment/college credits, quantified ACT/college placements, National Merit/Ivy admits) that circle reviews do not; examples include mentions of an Engineering Academy with certifications and college credit, IB prominence, AP/dual‑enrollment portfolios, and named elite college matriculations.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, higher‑p: Includes reports where square schools emphasize flagship extracurriculars and campus facilities (award‑winning band/choir/theater, state/national championships, football stadium/pool/fitness center, robust club ecosystems) that circle entries lack; examples: ‘band is awesome…state champions,’ ‘high‑tech theater production resources,’ and named athletic facilities and booster fundraisers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: This groups texts describing pervasive safety/climate failures—high rates of bullying, substance use, fights, rapes/sexual assaults, suicides/overdoses—and reviewers’ accounts that staff or administration ignore, minimize, or even protect perpetrators; examples: reports of laced gummy bears sending kids to hospital, students stabbed with pencils, repeated bullying left unaddressed, and claims that administration ‘supports the bullies.’
candidate_defs.square entries report more visible, proa: Captures reviews emphasizing active, positive people‑centered practices—teachers easy to reach, tech systems to keep parents informed, principals greeting students, scheduled tutor time, superintendent responsiveness, and hands‑on counselor scholarship navigation—that circle reviews do not document; examples: ‘teachers volunteer before/after school,’ ‘they excel at utilizing technology to keep kids and parents informed,’ and ‘I spoke to the superintendent, he was great and very responsive.’
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational,: Groups concrete logistical and resource issues distinct from program breadth or teaching quality—outdated/run‑down buildings, pest infestations, food/cafeteria complaints, power outages, no nurse, oversized classes, budget cuts or prioritizing sports/tech over textbooks, transcript/counseling errors, restrictive internet filters, and harmful schedule changes; examples include ‘textbooks from 1989 vs 2016,’ ‘power goes out during the school day,’ ‘transcript never sent due to admin error,’ and ‘money for sports/tech but not basic instructional materials.’
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility and: This bucket groups reports about the physical plant and space constraints: square reviews repeatedly document broken/contaminated bathrooms, rodents/roaches, leaking roofs, insufficient desks/lockers, dangerous undersized halls and chronic overcrowding, and missing amenities/shade at lunch (e.g., “bathrooms are a wreck…smell like vape,” “packed into classes like sardines,” “leaks everywhere”), while circle reviews lack comparable facility/capacity failure evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries document more frequent an: This bucket captures concrete safety/behavior problems: square reviews describe recurring mass fights, in-school drug dealers and vaping, gang activity, bomb/weapon incidents, sexual harassment/coercion after school, and sustained bullying with poor follow-up (e.g., “drugs run rampant,” “fights almost every week,” an AR-15 incident, coerced 'favors' for rides), whereas circle reviews do not present these high-frequency, severe safety claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater availabili: This bucket groups concrete program and outcome evidence: square reviews enumerate large AP and STEM offerings, IB pockets, vocational/CTE and JROTC programs, extensive sports/music/performing-arts teams, and named college acceptances and scholarships (e.g., “State AP Honors school, offering 25 AP courses,” “many students went on to MIT/UCLA,” “JROTC award recognition”), while circle reviews rarely document comparable program breadth or measurable postsecondary placements.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures governance and operational failures: square reviews allege frequent principal turnover, nepotism/politics, boards retaining ineffective teachers, dishonest or punitive administrators, and failure to follow up on incidents (e.g., “3 principals in four years,” “principal lied to me,” “board keeps unworthy teachers,” “principal said he would talk to him but never did”), examples that circle reviews do not present to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit greater polarizat: This bucket groups classroom- and staff-level variability: square reviews show a strong split — pockets of highly effective, caring teachers, excellent counselors, and successful IEP outcomes alongside reports of teacher absenteeism/passive instruction, teacher belittlement, exclusionary denial of honors for students with disabilities, and staff harassment (e.g., “great teachers… and also teachers play videos and are often absent,” “we were not allowed in honor classes because I am visually disabled”), whereas circle reviews present fewer such extremes and more internally consistent teacher descriptions.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more extensive f: These reviews name concrete curricula and pathways (IB, many APs, early‑college/concurrent enrollment, medical/STEAM magnets, CTE/vo‑tech, academy/career tracks) and cite metrics or alumni outcomes (ACT/AP readiness, scholarships, selective college placements) that Circle reviews do not; examples include multiple claims of an entire IB Programme, ‘I took 9 AP classes,’ concurrent enrollment/UC/college credit, and full‑ride scholarships.
candidate_defs.Square entries report greater instructio: Many Square reviews describe a polarized instructional experience — honors/AP tracks and some named teachers provide rigorous instruction, after‑school help, and mentoring, while regular‑track classes, counseling, and IEP/504 adherence are uneven or failing; illustrative lines include 'honors/AP teachers care… regular teachers do the bare minimum,' 'teachers stay after school to help,' and 'teachers don't follow the 504 plan.'
candidate_defs.Square entries document broader, higher‑: Square reviewers repeatedly list and praise concrete outside‑class programs (award‑winning band/choir, AFJROTC, drama, DECA, strong sports with state titles, many clubs) and parent booster involvement, whereas Circle seldom enumerates comparable programs; examples: 'music program is spectacular,' 'won 3 State Wrestling tournaments,' 'lots of parent involvement especially in Boosters.'
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: Multiple Square reviews allege gangs, stabbings, guns, drug use/overdoses, daily bullying, assaults leading to hospitalization, and suicide/self‑harm consequences, often tied to inadequate response, a pattern not found in Circle; quoted evidence includes 'Extremely high gang activity,' 'trash can fire, a stabbing, and a gun problem,' 'teen suicides,' and 'Bullying is a huge problem… faculty fail to address it.'
candidate_defs.Square entries indicate more administrat: Square reviews contain numerous concrete managerial and operational complaints (administration ignores conflicts or parents, fake social‑media monitoring, grade interference for athletes, lost AP paperwork, chaotic registration, overcrowded buildings, pests, outdated tech and food‑service problems) whereas Circle rarely documents this cluster; examples include 'administrators do not like to deal with conflicts,' 'nepotism issues,' 'registration has been a nightmare,' 'roaches and bad food,' and 'overcrowding is horrible.'
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit stronger, more nu: This bucket captures concrete curricular depth and outcomes: square reviews repeatedly name AP/Pre‑AP breadth, IB/GT/dual‑enrollment and career‑academy offerings, high AP scores/National Merit counts, college credits/exemptions and Ivy/admissions outcomes (e.g., “most AP classes in town,” “almost the entire class scored 5’s,” dual‑enrollment/college credit exemptions), while circle reviews lack comparable program breadth or measurable college‑prep outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report a broader, higher‑: Square reviews list specific, high‑quality extracurricular infrastructure and successes—large auditoriums and performing‑arts centers, named arts/music programs (LISA, multiple orchestras/bands), extensive sports fields and championship teams, many clubs and niche programs (NJROTC, culinary restaurant)—whereas circle reviews do not provide the same level of program/facility detail or successes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more incidents of: This groups concrete safety and student‑behavior problems that square reviewers describe: frequent fights, vape/drug problems in bathrooms, ganglike activity, student assaults and even a bullying‑related suicide protest, plus complaints that staff fail to control or supervise students—issues that are largely absent from circle’s accounts.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers give specific examples of poor administration and processes—misfiled IEPs, scheduling and course‑placement errors, billing/treasurer mistakes, ignored emails/calls, victim‑blaming, refusal to provide accommodations and alleged malpractice to avoid reporting—while circle reviews contain far fewer concrete operational/recordkeeping complaints and more reports of responsive administrators.
candidate_defs.square entries report more resource and: Square texts frequently attribute service gaps to structural limits: very large class sizes and overcrowded campuses, insufficient counselors and teacher shortages, elective and program cuts, and pay‑to‑play or expensive extracurricular fees—practical resource/staffing problems that circle reviews do not document to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete safety failures (daily fights, bomb threats, sexual assaults, stabbings, assault with broken bones, pervasive drug use, vandalism, security-staff misconduct) and explicit official non‑response (on‑site deputy failed to file a report; administrators dismissing complaints). Example evidence: “Students deal with bullying and...sexual assault...nearly daily,” “many bomb threats,” and “On site Sheriff Deputy failed to file a report when my son was assaulted.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe a broader, highe: This captures reviews listing concrete program breadth and facility strengths — many clubs, award‑winning band/TV/academies, CTE/vocational shops, JROTC/law‑enforcement academies, 1:1 laptop programs, college partnerships and recent capital improvements — that circle reviews do not enumerate. Example evidence: “plenty of sports...AP courses...mock trial...band...won state/national awards,” “TV Production...won Telly Award,” and “collaboration with a science institute and art academy.”
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize an athletics‑fi: This bucket groups reviews that report football/athletics dominance, recruitment for athletes, differential funding and disciplinary leniency for athletes, and coach‑driven politics — distinct from just having many extracurriculars. Example evidence: “This school is very focused to sports, football in particular,” “thousands of dollars were given out for top athletic scholarships while art got $200,” and “unless you are a star athlete, everything gets swept under the rug.”
candidate_defs.square entries document greater administ: This groups complaints about governance and policy: strict/punitive rule enforcement and fees, opaque or politicized district decisions (rezoning, grading scales, tax/budget mismanagement), frequent leadership turnover, and administrators ignoring teacher/student feedback. Example evidence: “The administration ignores feedback...uses cookie cutter ideas,” “the 12 point scale is garbage,” “many principals over the last 4 years,” and fines for missing IDs or summer‑school fees tied to absences.
candidate_defs.square entries report weaker student‑fac: This bucket covers concrete operational failures in supports: special education enrollment barriers, 504/IEP noncompliance, understaffed or unresponsive counselors, mental‑health neglect, language/access barriers, and failures to protect or accommodate vulnerable students. Example evidence: “504 Education plans are not consistently followed,” “The counseling department is severely understaffed,” “this school is not equipped to deal with children who have special needs,” and “half the school speaks Spanish...language barrier.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe safety: This bucket groups items where square reviews describe concrete safety and discipline breakdowns (frequent fights, gang violence, drugs/alcohol, bomb threats, sexual‑misconduct accusations) and heavy or invasive responses (K9 searches, barb‑wire gates, security ‘thugs’), whereas circle reviews do not report those problems and often describe strict discipline or little trouble (examples: “fend for themselves against the gang violence,” “bomb threats and multiple drug arrests,” “lined kids on the wall for k9 units to sniff us” vs. circle: “there is no tolerance for bad behavior”).
candidate_defs.square entries document broader and high: This bucket captures square reviews that enumerate many clubs/teams and report competitive success or high‑level arts achievements (state championships, nationally‑recognized band, successful music/theater tours, Cybersecurity team, Project Rise after‑school), while circle reviews generally omit or understate such breadth and high achievement (examples: “clinched five sports titles,” “chorus went to Austria,” “Cybersecurity team top 5%” vs. circle’s lack of comparable extracurricular detail).
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extensive a: This groups items where square entries list formal programs and measurable outcomes (AP/IB/AVID, dual‑enrollment, Cambridge/early‑college, large AP credit accumulation, elite college admits, scholarship/college‑readiness evidence), whereas circle reviews lack such program detail or report weaker college prep (examples: “offers more than a dozen AP courses,” “ended up with 30+ hours of credit from AP,” “IB Program… AVID prepares you for college” vs. circle: ‘does NOT prepare your child for college’ or no AP/dual‑enrollment specifics).
candidate_defs.square entries evidence greater administ: This bucket contains claims that square schools tolerate poor hiring/credentialing, chronic staff absenteeism, public shaming by teachers, administrative nepotism/favoritism, ethical misconduct, ignored complaints, and retaliatory behavior, while circle reviews generally praise staff and do not make those systemic accusations (examples: “they accepted me without asking about my credentials,” “good ol boys network,” “principals were not very nice,” “administrator told me I should have lied about the reason my child was absent” vs. circle’s largely positive staff descriptions).
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete oper: This bucket covers square reviews that describe specific operational breakdowns and resource constraints—overcrowded lunch/classrooms or underpopulation, misallocated capital, mandatory participation fees, terrible Wi‑Fi/blocked apps, scheduling/assignment overload, guidance/counseling mistakes, absent ACT administration, no after‑school buses—while circle entries either praise resources or omit these operational failures (examples: “all 4 grades have to share the lunchroom,” “THE WIFI IS TERRIBLE,” “they didn’t even offer up to take the ACT,” “small tax base and the lack of funds” vs. circle’s references to ‘HUGE funding!!’).
candidate_defs.Square entries describe substantially br: These reviews repeatedly name concrete program breadth (many AP/honors/dual‑enrollment courses, magnet programs, large band/orchestra/theatre offerings, niche sports and arts, dozens of clubs) that Circle reviews do not; examples include claims of '17 different AP courses', 'Global Business magnet', 'amazing Chamber music program', and extensive athletics and club lists that Circle omits or portrays as limited.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent safe: Multiple Square reviews describe on‑campus drug use, frequent hallway fights, police/SRO presence, bullying ignored by staff, suicides, and out‑of‑pocket therapy costs—e.g. 'Bad lots of known drugs at school,' 'There were fights constantly in the halls,' and 'There have been 2 suicides'—problems Circle reviews do not raise or explicitly deny.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more inconsisten: Square reviewers give concrete examples of leadership dishonesty/absence, uneven enforcement, nepotism or pay‑to‑play favoritism, and discipline bias (e.g., 'assistant principal said "we don't really do that" about detention policy,' 'if you cannot afford to line the coaches pockets... you do not play,' and 'handbook isn't worth the paper it’s printed on'), complaints that Circle does not mirror.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more variable and: Square contains specific classroom failures and supports gaps (teachers 'rarely teach', empty classrooms, poor AP/test prep, inadequate remediation for learning difficulties, and guidance offices that 'do nothing' for college/scholarship help) alongside counterexamples of strong teachers; these program‑and‑delivery level instructional details and uneven counseling outcomes are largely absent or more positive in Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more detailed faci: Reviewers in Square supply concrete facility and operational evidence (large enrollment counts and overcrowding/portables, outdated vs. newly renovated buildings, food/cafeteria complaints, bus accident with unpaid bills, security cameras, 1:1 device rollouts and classroom AV) whereas Circle reviews rarely give comparable facility/resource detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher‑ac: These reviews emphasize concrete program breadth and high‑level achievements (advanced/AP/IB/dual‑credit courses, CTE/aviation/RT0C, award‑winning band/theater, extensive clubs and athletics) plus named post‑secondary outcomes (Yale, Presidential Scholars, high ACT/college credits). Examples: multiple state championships and national festival band performances, dual‑enrollment credits that cover a college freshman year, ROTC/CTE success stories and repeated college acceptances, which Circle reviews lack or contradict.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: These reviews describe ongoing violent or criminal student behavior (daily fights, recorded brawls, arson/vandalism), pervasive drug dealing/use in halls and community, and failures or delays in security response (late guards, ignored incidents, bomb‑squad/drug‑dog operations). Examples: parents saying students left the school because of threats, reports of drug dealing in hallways, and multiple bomb‑squad searches — phenomena not reported in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries report more explicit, org: Many Square reviews list concrete, active supports — functioning IEP/504 meetings, daily math tutoring, scheduled morning help periods (e.g., Cavalier morning), accessible counselors, online grade/assignment systems, College Access Centers and structured transition planning — while Circle reviews do not provide comparable, programmatic support details.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These entries call out leadership instability and governance problems (frequent principals, unresponsive/hostile office staff, cover‑ups), punitive or inconsiderate policies (overstrict dress/code enforcement, suspension practices, use of police in parent disputes), and contested decision‑making about programs. Examples include '3 principals in a year,' administrators known for calling police during parent meetings, threatened suspensions over vehicle flags or facial hair, and ignored petitions about curriculum or testing.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: Square reviewers frequently identify physical and operational constraints (overcrowded classes, 1:30+ ratios, aging buildings with pests/no AC, parking scarcity, poor food/bus logistics, cancelled classes) and disputes over funding priorities (athletics prioritized over arts, underfunded resource teachers), whereas Circle contains few comparable facility/resource complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries report richer, named adva: These reviews repeatedly list concrete programs and quantified outcomes (IB diploma, many AP offerings, dual‑enrollment/CCP, Advanced Learning/Advanced Standing, explicit SAT/PSAT prep programs and multi‑million dollar scholarship totals) and claim stronger college readiness/elite matriculation; Circle reviews offer few or no named advanced pathways or measurable college‑outcome claims. Examples: square contains IB/AP/CCP/dual‑enroll named pathways, explicit AP pass‑rate and scholarship dollar figures, and alumni reporting preparation for graduate school, whereas Circle lacks these specific program/outcome inventories.
candidate_defs.square entries document a broader, highe: Square reviews enumerate and celebrate specific, high‑performing extracurriculars (’best band’, marching band/pep/jazz, award‑winning theatre, NJROTC in decline/otherwise named, UIL/Science Olympiad/Knowledge Bowl successes, varsity→college athlete pathways) and note high participation; Circle reviews rarely list multiple named programs or competitive records, usually offering only generic praise. Examples: square names marching band, orchestra, debate/forensics, theatre, robotics and varsity/state competition results; Circle offers only general statements about extracurriculars or a single program mention.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more acute stude: Many square reviews recount concrete safety incidents (daily fights, gang problems, on‑campus drug buying/selling, sexual harassment, students attacked/knife incidents), routine substance use, invasive search/ drug‑testing procedures, and claims that discipline both fails and sometimes becomes over‑punitive; Circle reviews mostly omit such chronic safety or substance reports. Examples: square reports ‘drug use and drinking are rampant,’ students ‘bullied, attacked and seriously injured,’ bomb threats, searches, and claims admin often fails to protect victims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff‑level m: Square reviews frequently allege unprofessional teacher conduct (favoritism, public grade disclosure, political/sexual discussions in class), counselors/principals enabling diploma inflation or grade manipulation, nepotism/faculty favoritism, board resistance to reform, budget mismanagement, and hostile or rude administrative behavior—concrete governance and personnel failures distinct from student behavior. Examples: square cites teachers ‘give poor grades if they don’t like them,’ counselors used as schedulers, ‘tenured teachers making 150K+ should step down,’ alleged manipulation of graduation rates, and calls for outside audits.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray more cohesive, sm: Circle reviews more often describe small size, close teacher‑student connections, devoted/dedicated teachers and counselors, long family enrollment/retention, visible leadership and safe campuses, and fewer named programmatic claims; these are concrete accounts of community cohesion, staff engagement, and facility pride rather than program inventories. Examples: Circle notes ‘small community…connect better with your teachers,’ ‘teachers work very hard,’ families raising children through senior year, and statements like ‘the campus is beautiful/well kept’ or praise for safety and welcoming staff.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe frequent, severe safety incidents (multiple fights per week/day, gang activity, on‑campus drug use, sexual assaults, suicides/threats) plus staff/administration failing to stop or consistently remediate them ("security needs to keep an eye on Bullies," "they let it go"). Circle entries, by contrast, rarely name such repeated violence/drug/sexual‑assault episodes and more often describe a safer or improving campus. Examples: Square: "I hear about a fight probably two time a week... sexual assault happens... A LOT OF GANG affiliation" vs Circle: "my daughter feels safe" and emphasis on present improvements.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews contain concrete allegations about leadership problems (hiring unqualified leaders, auditing irregularities, billing errors), uneven or punitive discipline (zero‑tolerance abuses, grade/attendance penalties, athletic favoritism), and favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families; many cite inconsistent enforcement and apparent corruption. Circle reviews seldom describe scandals or such persistent administrative mismanagement, instead focusing on programmatic issues or one-off leadership complaints. Examples: Square: "they hire the most unqualified candidates... auditing irregularities... the administration does not care unless they have money" vs Circle: no comparable corruption/favoritism allegations.
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive a: Many square reviews enumerate AP/IB/magnet/early‑college/dual‑enrollment offerings, honors tracks, high AP/SAT results and documented college matriculation/scholarships, portraying clear college‑prep pathways. Circle reviews more often lack specific advanced-course evidence and emphasize general programming or local fit rather than named AP/dual‑credit outcomes. Examples: Square: "Very solid AP programs... one of the few schools to offer AP to freshmen... both sons graduated with full scholarships" vs Circle: "There is no gifted program, no AP classes" or only generic college-readiness claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader, higher-pr: Square reviews routinely list wide catalogs of clubs, competitive athletics, award-winning marching bands, vocational programs (culinary, auto‑body), and competitive arts achievements; they also cite community/pride tied to these programs. Circle reviews mention some arts or sports but rarely the same breadth, awards, or specialized CTE offerings. Examples: Square: "marching band won first place... Culinary and Auto‑Body programs are really good... Mock Trial, Scholastic Bowl" vs Circle: limited program mentions and few named awards.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater staffing ins: These reviews include high teacher turnover, frequent comments that teachers are 'hit or miss', reports of teacher bullying or absenteeism, inconsistent guidance counseling (both strong saving‑teacher anecdotes and repeated counseling failures), and variable after‑school support. Circle reviews portray more stable, committed staff and fewer accounts of chronic turnover or counselor dysfunction. Examples: Square: "teachers leaving often... 2 or 3 good teachers and about 3 bad teachers... The guidance office… They were horrible" versus Circle: frequent praise for long‑term committed staff and no parallel turnover narrative.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: This bucket captures concrete accounts of fights, gang activity, routine bullying, vaping/smoking/drug use, and physical assaults that reviewers place squarely inside the school (e.g., “quarterly fights,” “La Ganga Crips... Golpiaron a mi hija,” “vaping/smoking on school grounds,” and “I was bullied constantly. No one even tried to stop the bullying”), whereas circle reviews lack comparable reports of pervasive violence or on‑campus substance use.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: Includes reports that leadership and office staff favor athletes/wealthy families, publicly bully or ignore complainants, apply blanket or arbitrary punishments, or prioritize image over student care (e.g., “principal openly favors...,” “entire student population has to face punishment,” “dont even bother going to the principal”), while circle reviews generally do not document this pattern of systemic favoritism or punitive, nonresponsive governance.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader programm: Groups concrete program and outcome evidence—IB/AP/AVID/STEM/CTE pathways, early-college/dual-credit options, strong music/arts and competitive sports, alumni recognition and college placements (e.g., “full IB diploma,” “one of the best music programs,” “AP and College in High School,” National Merit and Ivy‑League admissions”), whereas circle entries rarely list comparable named programs, recognitions, or measurable college/test outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher insta: Covers operational instructional delivery problems and staffing patterns such as high teacher turnover, chronic use of poor-quality substitutes, limited tutoring/teacher availability, and failing IEP/504 support (e.g., “High turnover of teachers,” “No tutors available on campus,” “substitutes that paint their nails... babysitting,” and “They do not do what they say they will do in class for IEP or 504”), while circle reviews provide fewer such operational failures and more accounts of stable, caring staff.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pronounced: This bucket groups physical‑plant and operational facility facts: overcrowding and enrollment pressures, major renovations or newly built campuses, cleanliness/maintenance contrasts, and concrete security measures or failings (e.g., “crowded... 3100 kids,” “newly renovated... state-of-the-art pool,” “All classroom doors are locked,” “about 20 security guards,” and complaints of cockroaches/restroom sanitation), whereas circle reviews include few analogous descriptions of large-scale facility or secured‑access changes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: This bucket groups reviews where square schools list specific programmatic offerings and quantified outcomes (IB/AICE/AP, Honors, dual enrollment, engineering/biomed pathways, US News/state rankings, AP pass counts, state test pass rates) while circle reviews omit or lack those specifics — e.g., square mentions “IB, AICE, AP, band…2013 US News High School State/National Ranking,” “87% passed WA state Math test,” and “many honors and AP offerings” that circle does not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures accounts of routine, severe student-misconduct and safety failures at square schools — frequent fights, daily bullying, widespread drug use and even drug‑related deaths, sexualized behavior, and claims of staff inaction — for example: “fights EVERY day,” “This is a heavy duty drug school, my kids have 9 dead friends,” “bully RUN this place,” and “staff complacent about bullying,” contrasted with circle entries that do not describe this scale of safety breakdown.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews alleging management failures at square schools: hiding problems or refusing parent cooperation, nepotistic/alumni hiring, arbitrary or unequal discipline, scheduling and registrar errors, unresponsive counselors, and cover‑ups — examples include “Admin here hides all problems,” “Love to hire alumni,” “removed him from his IEP without my permission,” and “I have been trying to get an appointment… for WEEKS,” which circle reviews generally do not allege.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: This bucket groups concrete infrastructure and resourcing complaints in square reviews: trailers and overcrowded halls, no AC, closed libraries and cancelled tutoring from budget cuts, poor food and pest problems, and claims that money is funneled to athletic projects rather than textbooks or classrooms (e.g. “$80,000 on the baseball field but can’t get new textbooks,” “there are trailers everywhere,” “library no longer open afterschool”), contrasts absent in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete stud: This bucket captures square reviews that describe formal supports and community offerings — strong special‑education/IEP collaboration, social workers/psychologists, ROTC, internships/partnerships, large marching band/performing arts, robust clubs/travel opportunities, proactive teacher availability and parent‑teacher engagement, and alumni college matriculation anecdotes (e.g. “The 'I' in IEP is really emphasized here,” “Great support system of social workers and psychologists,” “the biggest marching band…214 members,” “partnered with Skills USA… internships at local hospitals,” “both graduated and went on to universities”) — features circle reviews typically don’t document.
candidate_defs.square entries report far more frequent,: This bucket covers concrete safety problems described as common in square reviews — e.g., repeated fights (‘fights every day’, ‘fights weekly’), gang/drug activity, arrests, alleged sexual assault and suicide attempts, and claims that administration denies or fails to address them (‘administration insists [bullying] does not exist’, ‘school has a r*pist’). It groups items about incident frequency/severity plus immediate enforcement breakdowns (parents not notified, security/police present but ineffective).
candidate_defs.square entries describe a wider, deeper: This groups programmatic offerings and formal pathways: square reviewers repeatedly list AP/IB/dual-enrollment, many electives, career academies (medical, engineering, culinary, law enforcement, etc.), dozens of clubs, JROTC/ROTC, strong arts/music/theater, and college-course access — concrete program availability and partnerships that circle reviews largely do not mention (circle instead notes a medical magnet in one instance).
candidate_defs.square entries report worse physical pla: This bucket captures durable facility and operational constraints reported more in square texts: overcrowded classes and cafeterias (e.g., 36:1 classes, students standing), aging and unsanitary facilities (leaks, vandalized restrooms, asbestos/mold allegations), limited parking/traffic bottlenecks and multi-building walking burdens, closed/locked bathrooms and broken equipment, and transportation failures (late/double-loaded buses).
candidate_defs.square entries allege more entrenched st: Includes governance and personnel issues: nepotism and favoritism (toward staff/athlete/wealthy kids), corruption/bribery claims, board/district mismanagement, high leadership turnover or calls to ‘completely restaff the administration’, administrators or teachers acting unprofessionally or rudely, and poor two‑way communication with parents — i.e., systemic governance and conduct failures distinct from single safety incidents or individual instructional quality.
candidate_defs.square entries show greater variability: Covers classroom and student‑support practices and outcomes: wide teacher-quality variation (excellent to 'worst' teachers), honors/AP students receiving much better attention than general or special‑needs students, delays or failures in 504/IEP implementation, inconsistent counseling (from discouraging college to providing full scholarships), delayed remediation (help not given until 11th grade), promotion despite failing, and mixed measurable postsecondary outcomes — concrete differences in how instruction, special supports, and college-prep are delivered and who benefits.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced: These entries describe concrete, organized college-prep curricula (many AP/IB/honors courses, entrance exams, Dual‑Credit), explicit selection/retention rules (quarterly cut scores, entrance exams), and measurable outcomes (students matriculating to Harvard, UNC, Bowdoin, West Point; AP scores, 25 AP credits, high graduation/test scores). Examples: claims of “many AP and Honors courses,” “IB workload and transfer hardships,” and specific college admissions and AP/dual-credit success that Circle reviews do not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: These entries document frequent safety incidents (drugs/vaping/smoking, repeated fights, physical assaults requiring surgery, threats, suicides), school security escalations (K9 searches, police arrests, removed bathrooms) and repeated reviewer claims that administration failed to stop or adequately respond. Examples: “drugs are a HUGE problem,” “2 suicides in past couple of years,” police called to break up fights, and administrators saying ‘nothing can be done,’ which Circle reviews generally do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational i: These entries describe day‑to‑day management failures (constant schedule/event cancellations, program eliminations, ran out of supplies, transportation breakdowns, overcrowding), plus unresponsive or absent staff (counselors who stand people up, principals not visible, lost records, no returned phone calls) forcing parents to advocate. Examples: “constantly schedule and cancel events,” “ran out of paper,” “counselors are generally unresponsive,” and ‘Remain involved… you are the only advocate,’ contrasts with Circle’s more specific administrative/program details or responsive examples.
candidate_defs.square entries report more institutional: These entries allege systematic inequities—athletes and donors/alumni or IB/elite-track students receive preferential treatment, paid extracurricular fees create access barriers, and social cliques/nepotism shape opportunities—often at the expense of average, low‑income, or non-favored students. Examples: “They care more about their athletes,” “If you’re wealthy then it’s a great school,” “It’s who you know,” and “IB kids and regular kids are segregated,” claims not present in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader, better‑: These entries list extensive, well-supported non-academic opportunities (award‑winning marching band, orchestra/chorus, theater, JROTC, many clubs, robust CTE/trade programs, competitive sports and academic teams) and concrete competitive successes and long‑running leadership in extracurriculars. Examples: “well over 30 clubs,” “award winning marching band,” “CTE with building trades and automotive,” and many district titles—offering program breadth and competitive outcomes that Circle entries rarely enumerate.
candidate_defs.square entries describe far broader and: These reviews repeatedly list concrete programs and outcomes—AP/IB/honors tracks, dual‑enrollment/transcripted college credit (RIT, community college), magnet/vocational tracks, championship band/arts, JROTC, many sports and clubs—and cite college placements and graduation rates as evidence; Circle reviews lack comparable named programs, dual‑credit claims, or alumni/college‑placement metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, sev: Multiple Square reviews name specific security events (bomb threats, soft lockdowns), weekly fights, drug incidents, racially driven violence, heavy police presence and chronic bullying; Circle reviews do not document comparable violent/drug/security incidents and instead offer milder behavior or isolated discipline concerns.
candidate_defs.square entries document more inconsisten: Square reviewers allege widespread instructional failures (teachers who 'do not teach,' overreliance on worksheets, poorly taught APs), teacher burnout and unprofessional conduct (playing games, offensive language), and teacher‑level favoritism ('teacher's pets,' legacy bias), whereas Circle reviews more often emphasize caring, competent staff and lack these instruction‑level accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse administrati: Square critiques include unresponsive administrators and counselors, late/lost grades, pandemic mismanagement, opaque or punitive policies (harsh absence‑to‑credit rules, Saturday school), poor outreach about graduation/FAFSA, and hostile front‑office behavior; Circle reviews seldom allege these operational failures and sometimes describe more organized leadership.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight greater systemi: Square reviews document IEP failures, GED‑only/self‑contained placements, delayed disability identification, racial slurs and majority‑hostile cultures, lack of LGBTQ supports (no GSA), and barriers to low‑income students accessing extracurriculars—issues Circle reviews do not raise or raise far less often.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms where reviewers describe concrete, repeated safety failures inside the building and campus — gangs, daily fights and assaults, drug/paraphernalia problems, rampant vaping, sexual activity/teen‑pregnancy concerns, students afraid to use restrooms, police interviews, and organized avoidance (walking out or seeking suspension). Examples: 'gang violence...a lot of bullying and a lot of fights,' 'Many many bad things like assaults and fights occur here on a daily basis,' 'Vaping is rampant in school,' and 'suspended...subjected...to the police.'
candidate_defs.square entries document more administrat: This bucket captures concrete governance and operations problems reviewers attribute to school/district leadership: lost/incorrect enrollment paperwork, nepotism and ‘positions for friends,’ principal misconduct or threats, uneven/resident‑fraud enforcement tied to athletics, botched device or schedule distribution, bus/transportation failures, and refusal to respond to parent complaints. Examples: 'They lost the school they were transferring in from paperwork,' 'rules don’t apply to them or their relatives,' 'Left 2 time message, no one call back,' and 'the principal does not care… he picks on the kids.'
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more n: This bucket groups concrete curricular offerings and outcome evidence: Pre‑AP/AP/Honors breadth, dual‑enrollment and formal college-credit partnerships, high SAT/AP metrics, associate‑degree graduation pathways, and named alumni college placements or raised graduation rates.
