candidate_defs.square entries report more specific indi: This bucket covers explicit, actionable student supports and accommodations mentioned in reviews: daily/after‑school tutoring, individualized teacher interventions and one‑on‑one remediation, formal IEP/special‑education provision (and sometimes failures to follow them), alternative/recovery programs, and counseling/mental‑health services (both praised and criticized). Examples: 'Grant offers tutoring daily before and after school,' 'Our daughter is on an IEP and has been supported,' 'teacher met with him after and before school,' and 'the OFL alternative program...to get recovery and graduate faster.'
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize a broader, more: This bucket groups reviewer claims about the extracurricular landscape and how resources/priorities are allocated — many clubs, competitive teams and state championships, outstanding music/theatre/arts programs, booster funding dynamics, athletics‑dominated culture/athlete privilege, specialized academies (ski, law, STEM), and scheduling/booster conflicts that shape participation. Examples: 'almost 100 different clubs... Homecoming... Battle of the Classes,' 'The music program is excellent,' 'We spend SO much money on athletics... NO opportunities other than sports,' 'Very active booster club,' and 'The Ski Academy continues to attract top athletes.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute student: These items describe concrete safety problems inside and around the school—frequent fights, gang presence, pervasive drug and vaping use, weapons/metal‑detector incidents, student assaults, and police involvement—paired with reports of ineffective on‑the‑ground control (e.g., 'Gang members are walking the halls,' 'There are fights almost every day,' 'High drug use... including drug use during gym classes,' 'Gun issues has also occurred'). Circle entries contain few or no comparable reports of organized violence, gangs, weapons, or schoolwide drug epidemics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and broader n: Many square reviews enumerate concrete program offerings and results—IB and AP counts, dual enrollment/PSEO, career academies, internships, free college trips, and specific high ACT/college acceptances (e.g., 'An IB World School offering 24 college credits,' 'Consistently places in the top 5% for AP/IB participation,' 'My oldest two children scored 34 and 36 on their ACTs')—whereas circle reviews largely lack comparable lists of formal advanced-credit programs or measurable college-placement claims.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: Square reviews contain numerous concrete facility and operations complaints—overcrowded classes and traffic ('many classes have over 30 students', 'Traffic is Terrible'), deteriorating buildings and sanitation ('cockroaches', 'mold in the food', 'the school is huge, falling apart'), bus safety/driver issues, missing books/materials, and awkward campus logistics (parking, stairs, lockers)—issues that Circle reviews rarely raise.
candidate_defs.square entries report more problematic g: Square reviewers repeatedly accuse leadership and governance of systemic faults—nepotism in hiring and extracurricular placement, administrators viewed as self‑serving or dishonest, district lawsuits/cover‑ups, and teacher morale/turnover tied to leadership (e.g., 'Nepotism galore... We keep hiring the wrong people,' 'Why has the District been sued 6-7 times?', 'teachers who used to be there who have left because of how bad the administration has become'), claims that are far more frequent than in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more uneven social: This cluster covers peer and staff practices that sort or marginalize students—pronounced cliques and social segregation, targeted bullying of newcomers, racism and mascot controversies, preferential treatment of affluent or top‑rank/athlete students, and cases where victims are sanctioned while perpetrators are not (e.g., 'they cater to upper class smart kids... dismiss the other half', 'there is a lot of cliques', 'She was bullied for her race', 'bullied... then suspended 3 days for fighting'), patterns largely absent or less prevalent in Circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report substantially broa: This bucket groups raw terms where square reviews list concrete program breadth (many AP courses, IB, dual‑enrollment, academies, award‑winning robotics, JROTC, strong CTE, internships, large fine‑arts/music programs) and cite measurable alumni outcomes (MIT/Harvard admits, full‑ride scholarships, college credits at graduation) that circle reviews do not. Examples: 'choice of over 20 AP classes', 'dual enrollment... 3 semesters of college already completed', '#1 robotics program', and multiple named elite college admits are direct evidence of this pattern.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent, con: This bucket captures reports of on‑campus safety incidents and substance/behavior problems reported more in square reviews — drug scenes, repeated K‑9 locker searches and busted users, e‑cigarette use, daily fights, multiple lockdowns (including a gun incident), high teen‑pregnancy claims, vandalism — plus claims that these problems are tolerated or ineffectively enforced. Examples: 'k-9 teams... they do bust a few people each time', 'fight happening every day', 'multiple lockdowns... kid bringing a gun', and 'High drug problems and admins just look away.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups items where square reviewers describe governance failures — rapid leadership turnover, the 'blame game', administrators who play favorites (often athletes), protection of ineffective/tenured teachers, mishandled racial incidents, named counselor misconduct, and parents pushed into legal escalation to get refunds or actions. Illustrative phrases: 'The blame game is a tradition among the administration', 'teachers stay because of tenure', 'VP and the principal don’t do their job', and 'the administration has practically endorsed it by punishing my kid's negative reaction to racial slurs.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups square statements about physical space and operational constraints: overcrowded classes (25–40 students), limited daily schedules (only six classes per day), long commutes/extended school days, chronic maintenance problems (mold, sewage, unclean bathrooms), contested budget choices (tech purchases over teacher pay or teaching materials), and active construction/renovation updates. Examples: 'classes are so over full', 'took 3 months for my refund after a reduced trip', 'bought IPADS for the administration... docked the teachers pay', and 'outdated and nasty... classrooms without air conditioning.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistently: This bucket includes circle claims that teachers/staff are uniformly supportive, administration is reachable, and the school feels tight‑knit and family‑friendly — endorsements of prompt communication, counselors/principals who respond, and community warmth — features that many square reviews either omit or explicitly counter. Representative evidence: 'teachers and staff truly do care', 'Friendly atmosphere, strong respect between students, staff and administration', 'I have always found it easy to get in touch with teachers and the administration', and explicit references to close community and valued extracurriculars like ROTC.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more concrete adva: These reviews name specific programmatic offerings and outcomes (IB, AP/ honors, dual‑enrollment, Business/Finance academies, CTE/LCTC pathways, modern trades/CAD, JROTC) and cite measurable college success (Ivy/West Point placements, high matriculation rates, national merit, published test rankings). Examples: multiple Square reviews list IB/Business Academy, ‘over 63% take an IB class’, dual‑enrollment credits, West Point and Ivy attendance, Carnegie Hall music tours — program detail and outcome evidence that Circle reviews largely omit.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent and: Square texts repeatedly describe campus safety crises and ongoing behavior problems — weekly fights, drug/alcohol sales/use, guns found and game‑day shootings, repeated code‑red lockdowns, pervasive bullying and social-media harassment — whereas Circle reviews rarely report weapons, lockdowns, or persistent violence. Examples: Square mentions guns in backpacks, code red lockdowns, 'a fight every week', and '98% of the highschool's population drinks,' contrasts absent from Circle.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive, hi: Square reviewers enumerate a wide menu of clubs/teams and name high-achieving programs (state championships, Speech & Debate with trophy walls, world‑class music programs, award‑winning choir, strong band and robotics) and strong booster/PTSA involvement; Circle reviews seldom list comparable breadth or high‑level achievements. Examples: Square cites Carnegie Hall performances, state titles in Track/Cross Country, 'over 80 activities', active PTSA/boosters and large alumni networks, while Circle focuses on a few local extracurriculars or is silent.
candidate_defs.Square entries document more administrat: Square reviews contain concrete governance claims — favoritism (athletes/wealthy students protected), cover‑ups around bullying/health complaints, poor or dishonest communication, IEP/ special‑education misconduct, misallocation of funds, protection of underperforming teachers, and threats or pursuit of legal/media action — while Circle reviews contain fewer such systemic governance accusations. Examples: Square complaints include 'they go to great lengths to cover up', 'one school psychologist runs IEPs for three campuses', 'administration turned a deaf ear to toxic mold', and alleged grade‑manipulation to protect state ratings.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe more consistent,: Circle reviews frequently praise accessible, motivating teachers, engaged guidance counselors, and stable teacher support; by contrast many Square reviews document understaffing, heavy substitute use, slow grading/feedback, uneven teacher quality (passive/video instruction, teachers who don’t teach certain subjects), and chaotic placement practices that harm student outcomes. Examples: Circle: 'teachers, office staff, athletic staff have all been so wonderful'; Square: 'very understaffed', 'math teachers gone replaced by substitutes', 'teachers just sit in front of a video.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete course/program offerings and measurable postsecondary outcomes (AP breadth, IB program/diplomas, dual‑credit, National Merit/Ivy acceptances) and/or emphasize a rigorous curriculum that prepares students for selective colleges (examples: “full IB program,” “many AP classes,” “National Merit semi‑finalist,” “Ivy League acceptances,” and claims that the curriculum ‘prepared me for college’). These items contrast with circle entries that omit or do not document similarly named advanced programs or college‑placement evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more and better‑do: This bucket captures descriptions of broad co‑curricular opportunity and high achievement (award‑winning band/performing arts, state championships, many clubs and varsity sports, new athletic facilities), e.g. “incredible performing arts programs,” “award‑winning Titan Marching Band,” “STATE CHAMPS,” and ‘around 30 clubs and 15 sports.’ Circle entries lack comparable inventories or documented high‑level extracurricular outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete, pro: This bucket covers reviews that name operational supports that actively help students—hands‑on counselors who coordinate with parents, teacher‑run after‑school tutoring, credit‑recovery pathways, autism/gifted programs, 1:1 device rollouts and STEM supports—examples include “counselors... make sure that each student has his or her schedule completed,” “great tutoring program run by the teachers,” and “Excellent teachers & paraprofessionals working in the Autism program.” Circle entries generally do not document this same set of organized, individualized support structures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and/: This bucket groups reviews documenting concrete safety and climate incidents (regular fights, stabbings/shootings, pervasive drug/vaping use, gang activity, sexual misconduct, sustained bullying, racism/homophobia and staff complicity or ineffective responses), e.g. “kids constantly doing drugs in the bathroom,” “Kids have been stabbed during fights,” “Racism is rampant…homophobia,” and staff who ‘laugh along.’ Circle entries rarely describe this level or frequency of safety/violence/hostility incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more active and co: This bucket captures named governance and policy actions and community responses—an engaged/visible board or PTSA, parental fundraising and open‑enrollment transfers, explicit administrative decisions that cut traditions or reallocate resources, allegations of favoritism/retaliation, and operational policy outcomes (meal‑account denials, budget‑driven program cuts, HVAC or facility investment choices), e.g. “The board of education is very active,” “parents open enrolled their kids,” “the principal dismantled famed traditions,” “they have denied children food if their account is low,” and “budget cuts make it far worse.” Circle entries do not similarly document this clustered set of governance/policy/community actions.
candidate_defs.square entries show stronger/ broader ad: These reviews name concrete program offerings (AP, IB, dual‑enrollment/Running Start, CTE/engineering/medical tracks, honors, magnet programs, SAT/AP supports) and cite measurable outcomes (AP scores, scholarships, selective‑college placements), whereas circle reviews rarely list such specific college‑prep offerings or outcomes (examples: 'AP, IB, dual enrollment, Running Start, AP Diplomas, full‑ride scholarships' vs. circle's absence of detailed AP/IB/dual‑enrollment evidence).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent stud: Many square reviews document fights, lockdowns, on‑campus drug use and vaping, arrests, pervasive bullying, racial harassment, and teachers/administrators failing to stop or appropriately discipline perpetrators; circle reviews lack this pattern or describe stronger safety/staff follow‑through (examples: 'weekly fights / lockdowns', 'drugs in bathrooms', 'bullying goes unchecked', 'students responsible still attending' vs. circle's silence on such schoolwide safety crises).
candidate_defs.square entries describe more operational: Square reviewers repeatedly report concrete bureaucratic breakdowns — long residency/enrollment lines, weeks to change schedules, missing transcripts/credit‑transfer problems, ineffective guidance counselors, poor college advising, and hard‑to‑find district contacts — while circle reviews rarely raise these systemic operational or counseling failures (examples: 'took a week to get my son's schedule changed', 'two hours of standing in line proving residency', 'office forgot to send my transcript', 'ineffective guidance counselors').
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, cap: Square reviews document overheating/AC failures causing heat‑illness, pest infestations, aging or underfunded buildings, severe overcrowding/hall congestion, and lengthy family travel/transport burdens, whereas circle reviews rarely present this cluster of physical infrastructure and capacity breakdowns (examples: '112 degrees… got heat stroke', 'rats and roaches', 'shoulder to shoulder in the hallway', '22 mile round trip pick‑ups').
candidate_defs.square entries describe broader and high: Square reviewers list award‑winning bands, ROTC, state‑championship athletics, many clubs, and inclusive activity pathways alongside claims that athletes/donors get preferential treatment and that non‑athletes can be marginalized; circle reviews generally report fewer or less prominent extracurriculars and less of the athletics‑driven social favoritism (examples: 'award winning ROTC, state champions, many clubs' paired with 'if you're not a jock… you're nothing' vs. circle's sparse extracurricular mentions).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket lumps reports of on-campus physical danger and substance problems: multiple reviewers describe daily fights, weapons/assaults in classrooms, gang activity, on-site police calls and visible ankle monitors, and in‑school drug sales (e.g., “weapons and violent fights in classrooms,” “half of the school vapes… juniors sell juuls,” “ask the school how often the police are called,” “girls doing coke in the bathroom”). Circle entries lack comparable concrete safety/violence evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more punitive, i: This bucket captures reviewer claims about leadership behavior and disciplinary practice: changing grades, suspending students for minor tardiness or off-campus incidents, administrators mischaracterizing victims or withholding video, coordinated staff-posting of positive reviews, and favoritism toward wealthy families/athletes (e.g., “It even went as far as changing teacher grades for the student,” “suspended for 5 days because I used the vending machine,” “they wrote up their reports with the bully as the victim,” “caters to the wealthy families…”). Circle reviews do not present this pattern of administrative misconduct or opaque discipline.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger and more: This bucket groups concrete program- and outcome-level academic strengths: presence of IB, many AP/Pre‑AP classes, AVID demonstration status, dual‑credit and career/technical offerings, documented National Merit and scholarship totals, and explicit college‑prep outcomes (e.g., “The school offers IB, AVID, AP and dual‑credit,” “8 National Merit winners… $16 MILLION in scholarships,” “tons of dual credit classes… Career and Technical department”). Circle entries generally do not list these formal program credentials or quantified outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize a wider, named: This bucket groups concrete commentary about extracurricular breadth plus physical resources and funding priorities: many named clubs, award-winning bands/orchestras, well‑funded athletics or, conversely, underfunded arts and football-prioritization, plus specific facility conditions and capital changes (e.g., “marching band won state,” “sports are funded very well,” “Drama and dance programs are limited with little budget,” “recent remodel/new track,” “building is very old… bathrooms unsanitary,” “pay to play for sports and marching band”). Circle reviews rarely enumerate this level of program/facility/funding detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket groups evidence about student supports: reviewers recount denied or uneven IEP/504 implementation, counselors who are overwhelmed or unhelpful, mental‑health accommodations that don’t qualify for SpEd, but also occasional praise for strong special‑ed teams—overall showing mixed/unreliable supports (e.g., “doesn't make your child eligible for Special Ed if your child is intelligent,” “the counselor there is in over her head… waited over two hours,” “good special education teams to work on IEP and get state funding,” “new special education teacher is wonderful!”). Circle reviews do not provide comparable, detailed accounts of special‑education or counseling capacity.
candidate_defs.square entries report more advanced/AP/I: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete, school-level college-prep offerings and outcomes (AP, IB, Pre‑AP, dual‑credit, early‑college pathways, honors curricula, and named elite college matriculations) that appear in square but not in circle; examples include claims of AP/IB/dual‑credit classes, a 100% graduation rate, Early College/CAS classes, and alumni attending selective colleges. Falling here means the review documents explicit advanced-course availability or documented postsecondary success (not just praise of teachers).
candidate_defs.square entries report more career, techn: This bucket captures explicit mentions of hands‑on and CTE programming that square reviewers list (welding certs, automotive/diesel repair, cosmetology, culinary, nursing, NJROTC, SolidWorks/engineering courses, certificate-earning CTE electives) whereas circle reviews lack comparable vocational program detail. Content fits when the review names specific trade/technical courses, certifications, or structured career pathways available on campus.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: This groups reports of concrete safety incidents and patterns—fights, gang activity, weapons/lockdowns, drug/alcohol use, sexual harassment, filmed racial assaults, repeated bullying—and reviewers' accounts that administrators either ignored, punished complainants, or mishandled reports (e.g., confidentiality breaches, brushing incidents under the rug, ineffective responses). A review belongs here when it documents repeated or severe safety/bullying/substance events plus failures or counterproductive administrative responses.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers allegations that school/district leadership apply rules unequally (athlete/insider favoritism, 'good old boys' clubs, nepotism), enact punitive or exclusionary policies (strict tardy rules, residency expulsions, public shaming), or make contested budget choices (centralized printing fees, cutting staff/cafeterias, perceived misuse/overpaid administrators, prioritizing athletics/security over academics). Reviews are placed here when they describe governance, policy enforcement, or budget decisions that advantage insiders or punish others rather than neutral operational facts.
candidate_defs.square entries report more inconsistent: This bucket groups concrete operational problems around instruction and supports: high teacher turnover and long substitute coverage, wide variation in teacher quality, inconsistent grading/grade‑manipulation claims, scheduler/counselor unresponsiveness, IEP noncompliance or poor special‑education implementation, and inadequate mental‑health supports. A review falls here when it documents procedural/operational failures in teaching, counseling, or special‑education services that materially affect student learning and wellbeing.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete adva: These reviews name formal offerings and results (IB Diploma, AP/Honors, dual-enrollment, Engineering/IT/Health academies, Governor’s School links, certifications, college acceptances and scholarship wins), presenting program availability and quantifiable postsecondary outcomes that Circle reviews do not (e.g., 'IB program,' 'dual enrollment opportunities,' 'helped get my kids into top universities').
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: Square reviewers document repeated physical incidents (stabbings, fights, gang presence), visible drug use, pervasive bullying, and complaints that security or staff enforce rules unevenly or ignore problems (e.g., 'fight every other week', 'students high in a classroom', 'security guards singling out specific people'), a pattern absent or unreported in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger athletics: Square contains repeated claims that sports (especially football) receive disproportionate funding, influence, and preferential treatment (coach nepotism, pay-to-play, new multi-million football fields) while arts are sidelined or cut (e.g., 'sports budget rises while arts programs are cut', 'Football is king'), critiques not found in Circle texts.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater variabilit: These reviews describe teacher-by-teacher divergence (some exemplary, many mediocre), extreme nightly homework and student exhaustion, pervasive class disruption interfering with learning, and allegations of grade curving or pressure to inflate scores (e.g., 'mass amount of homework… staying up until 1:00am', 'many teachers end up curving tests', 'unless you have a great teacher... you will be missing out'), whereas Circle does not report the same mix of execution failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviewers recount high leadership turnover, ignored parent complaints, punitive or invasive discipline, district budget mistrust and calls to oppose levies, and explicit accusations of administrators manipulating test scores or protecting insiders (e.g., 'assistant principals have come and gone every year', 'my letters are completely ignored', 'heard many stories of corruption… raising test scores'), a cluster of governance/operational failures not present in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures concrete safety and climate failures (frequent bullying, fights, stabbings, gang/drug use, sexual harassment, bathroom sex/drug incidents, arson/threats) plus repeated reports that staff/administration failed to stop or remediate them (e.g., “extreme bullying…not dealt with,” “a student was stabbed,” “people doing drugs in the bathroom”), all of which appear throughout square but are almost absent from Circle’s reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries exhibit more administrati: Includes explicit claims about leadership behavior and district governance — coverups, nepotism, protecting connected families, rude/uncaring office staff, misallocation of funds, intimidation of parents, and failure to respond to complaints (e.g., “Principal and Assistant Principal cover up complaints,” “misspending of appropriated funds,” “they will go after vocal parents”); Circle’s reviews lack these kinds of district‑level accusations and often praise administration instead.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, named: Groups concrete programmatic evidence (AP/IB/ROP/dual‑enrollment partnerships like SLU 1818, college credit transfers, above‑state test scores, specific college acceptances, formal academies) that square reviewers repeatedly cite as present and producing outcomes (e.g., ‘many honors and AP courses,’ ‘IB credits transferred,’ ‘OGT results top of district’), whereas Circle’s reviews rarely list such formal accelerated programs or district‑level metrics.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize larger, better‑: This bucket groups concrete extracurricular/facility facts: detailed athletic success and big facilities (stadiums, turf, weight rooms), broad lists of clubs/arts/ROTC, capital improvement projects, and also family fees and unequal funding across programs (pay‑to‑play costs, favored programs vs. underfunded academies); Circle instead highlights band/pep/performing‑arts spirit but provides far fewer examples of large capital athletic investment or the same scope of program fee complaints.
candidate_defs.square entries show internal polarity (c: Many square reviews simultaneously report top‑tier accomplishments (state championships, national arts awards, rigorous honors/AP/IB programs) and severe operational problems (ineffective counseling, inconsistent teachers, facility decay, overcrowding, discrimination), producing a highly heterogeneous portrait (“one of the best… ” vs “the WORST school”); Circle’s reviews by contrast tend to deliver a consistent, singular portrayal (uniformly positive program experience or a consistent list of operational complaints) rather than these stark contradictions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that document repeated student-on-student harm (daily fights, cyberbullying, multiple suicides/attempts, on-campus drug use, gang targeting, a 2021 riot) and say the school’s disciplinary system fails to stop it (bullies not punished, only stern talks or detentions, law-enforcement constantly needed). Example evidence: 'fights every single day', 'They mocked me on Facebook', '3 suicides in 3 yrs', 'students often chose not to wear masks...and most people didn't do anything about it', and 'two full time sheriffs on duty to break up weekly fights.' Circle entries by contrast explicitly describe feeling safe or do not report these systemic safety incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries document broader and more: This bucket groups reviews that list concrete programs and pathways (extensive AP/IB offerings, dual-enrollment/College Credit, career & technical education including associate-degree tracks, accredited academies, JROTC) and tie them to college matriculation and scholarships (Ivy admits, National Merit, large scholarship awards). Example evidence: 'over 20 APs offered', 'graduate with their Associates Degree in cyber technology', 'IB diploma', 'students accepted to Harvard, MIT, Ivies', and 'College Credit Plus/PLTW/NAF-certified academies.' Circle reviews lack this same breadth of named advanced/CTE programs or documented high-tier postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete admi: This bucket covers errors and bureaucratic failures that harm students’ records, schedules, or postsecondary opportunities—wrong addresses/parents called, missing yearbook entries, transcripts not sent causing application rejections, counselors unreachable or formulaic, administrators changing grades, and forced laptop/technology fees. Example evidence: 'called the wrong parent', 'they refused to send transcripts... application was not reviewed', 'teacher posted my grades to quite a few students', and 'we still have to pay for mandatory laptops.' Circle reviews do not contain the same volume of these operational failure anecdotes.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more extreme or: This bucket groups concrete, often-contrasting facility and capacity claims: many square reviews complain of severe overcrowding, 100+ portables, worn/dilapidated interiors and short lunches, while other square reviews emphasize new buildings, exceptional athletic fields, amphitheaters, and well‑equipped labs—showing pronounced variation in physical conditions and capacity issues not reflected in circle. Example evidence: 'primarily portables (102 to be exact)', 'building is extremely dirty', and elsewhere 'stunning, brand new school... athletic facilities are the envy' or 'outdoor amphitheater that seats a whole school.' Circle entries typically call their school small and do not report the same extremes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff miscond: This bucket captures reviews alleging staff participation in or tolerance of exclusionary conduct and systemic bias—teachers/coaches bullying students, staff enabling harassment toward Black/LGBTQ/low‑income students, shaming of underperforming pupils, grade/discipline favoritism for athletes or legacies, and shipping struggling students to alternative programs. Example evidence: 'Administrators and students are bullying black, gays, and Mexican's students', 'coaches bully non-athletic students', 'they give As to athletes', and 'students who are not "perfect" get shipped off to alternative schools.' Circle reviews do not document this same pattern of staff-enabled discrimination or systematic push-out practices.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader and more s: These reviews name concrete programmatic breadth (AP/IB/honors, dual‑credit, CTE/vocational classes, arts/award‑winning music, AFJROTC, robotics, theater, marching band, varsity sports, and many clubs) and specific outcomes (college matriculation, AP participation, music tours) that Circle reviews do not; examples include “30+ AP courses,” “IB programme,” “award‑winning music department,” and extensive CTE/dual‑credit offerings versus Circle’s explicit lack of AP/advanced placement and few electives.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Many Square reviews recount concrete safety incidents (daily fights, lockdowns, documented physical assaults, sexual incidents, theft, vaping/drug epidemics) and describe weak or punitive responses (restorative circles that fail, alleged non‑reporting to protect ratings, officer violence), whereas Circle reviews lack these severe safety allegations; representative lines include “my friend got bullied to death,” “on lock down many times,” “vaping epidemic,” and “they did not report bloody fights to the state.”
candidate_defs.square entries document more concrete ad: Square reviews repeatedly allege systemic governance problems—grade‑changing scandals, nepotism/favoritism (athletes, staff children, wealthy families), board/superintendent scandals, deliberate underreporting of incidents, and principal unresponsiveness or public rudeness—claims that Circle reviews do not make; examples: “very public grade changing trial,” “principal favors specific people,” “School board keeps hiring cronies,” and “students involved in bloody fights do not get reported to the state.”
candidate_defs.square entries provide richer, more spec: Square reviewers describe both concrete capital investments and clear shortages—new STEM/media renovations and award recognition alongside leaking roofs, moldy food, crowding, chronic scheduling failures, budget crises, program cuts, teacher strikes, technology rollouts (tablets/chromebooks) and staffing shortages/turnover—whereas Circle rarely supplies this operational detail; illustrative snippets include “media center renovated,” “roof leaked every time it rained,” “perennial scheduling problems,” and “teachers are on strike.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe more explicit, c: Reviews in Square routinely name both structured supports (math labs, college advisors, formal college counseling) and serious failings—IEP/504 noncompliance and OCR complaints, ADA ignorance, lack of special‑education individualization, overloaded counselors, large variability in teacher quality and tenure‑protected poor performers, and inconsistent differentiation for high‑achievers—while Circle provides little on these contested support practices; examples include “OCR has been contacted,” “the counselors are overloaded,” “teachers that cannot teach,” and “great college counselor who brings recruiters.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more student-safet: This bucket captures concrete accounts of safety and peer-harm problems: physical fights and bomb scares, pervasive drug use, gang-related violence, sexual assault/mishandling of victims, homophobic and racial harassment, and hate graffiti (e.g. “too many fights and 'bomb scares'”, “there is many gangs and gang related fights”, “S/A cases? Yeah they don’t do ANYTHING about that... This school punishes the victims”, “This school is littered with Nazi graffiti”, “The school is full of drugs…”). It groups items that describe unsafe student behavior and administrators’ ineffective or absent remediation of those incidents — a substantially different operational reality than the circle reviews describe.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility, inf: This bucket groups concrete, physical-plant and logistics failures: broken/locked/overcrowded bathrooms, mold/sewage smell, poor custodial upkeep, overcrowded lunches and passing times, unsafe/awkward building layouts, unreliable buses and unstable wifi, and chronic budget-driven cutbacks to services (e.g. “only one bathroom open for girls…500 female students”, “it smells really bad because of the mold and mildew”, “The wifi is extremely unreliable”, “The virtual option was a disaster… child is over a year behind”, “Lunch prices… $30 parking pass”, “sewer treatment plant is located in back of the school”). These are concrete, operational resource problems rather than general opinion or tone.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more explicit ad: This bucket groups factual program availability and outcomes: named magnet/AP/IB/AICE/STEM/dual-enrollment programs, high AP pass rates or AP credit, college-acceptance evidence and specific postsecondary placement anecdotes (e.g. “IB program”, “I left with enough AP credit to fill a full year of college”, “top students accepted to competitive colleges… UC Berkeley, Cornell, Brown and Stanford”, “she earned a 4/5 on the AP exam”, “AICE program and teachers are wonderful”). It captures concrete curricular pathways and measurable college-readiness outcomes described in square reviews but absent or far less documented in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff/adminis: This bucket covers concrete personnel and governance dysfunction: administrators and teachers who ignore emails or reports, teacher-on-student bullying or humiliating practices, punitive attendance/discipline or removal from classes, favoritism for athletes (grade and resource biases), misallocation of funds and school-board unresponsiveness, and bungled transcripts/credits (e.g. “When you email them, they never reply…”, “Teachers bully students and nothing is ever done about it”, “They will favor the athletes and give them higher grades”, “School board does not listen to the community”, “they didn't calculate credits correctly… gave F's for the quarter”). It separates human/governance breakdowns from physical-resource or curricular descriptions.
candidate_defs.square entries report broader extracurri: This bucket groups concrete extra-curricular ecosystem and community supports: extensive club lists, award-winning band and theater, marching band/chorus/drama, vocational/shop/engineering labs, ROTC, booster-funded sports/music support, active PTOs and organized parent events or scholarships (e.g. “over 200 clubs… over 20 sports”, “Marching Band, Chorus, Drama and art”, “a great community willing to provide scholarships… provide a laptop for all students!”, “Great PTO and engaged parents”, “Marine magnet program… state of the art new pool”). It captures the presence, scale and organization of non-classroom opportunities and parent/community mobilization that square reviewers cite more often than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more student safet: This bucket groups raw terms describing concrete student-safety problems that appear far more in square reviews — e.g., fights ‘almost daily,’ pervasive bullying, on-campus drug use and trafficking, gang activity, teen pregnancy, police/home armed responses, and multiple allegations of staff or student sexual misconduct that reviewers say went unaddressed. Items assigned here are about actual safety/behavior incidents and failures to remediate them (not about leadership style or programs).
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures or m: This cluster captures claims about programmatic and legal support for students with disabilities and mental‑health needs that are prominent in square reviews — examples include IEP/504 noncompliance, warnings that the SPED system is 'terrible,' 'atrocious' counseling departments, no social worker or insufficient counselors, and parents advised to constantly monitor accommodations. These items are specifically about specialized supports and their implementation (not general teacher quality or admin discipline).
candidate_defs.square entries document more extensive a: Raw terms here point to concrete academic-program breadth and outcome evidence emphasized by square reviewers — e.g., IB programs and international travel, many AP/honors courses, Running Start/dual‑enrollment, specialized STEM/creative academies, high scholarship totals and lists of selective college acceptances, and AP exam success. This bucket is about availability and measurable results of advanced/rigorous academic pathways (separate from how well everyday classes are taught).
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: This group contains items describing school governance and policy problems prominent in square reviews — strict or nit‑picky dress codes, inconsistent enforcement and favoritism (e.g., athlete/band bias), retaliation or unapproachable administrators, board‑level hostility/chaotic meetings, district leadership controversy, and allegations of administrative misconduct. These records are about policy, enforcement style, governance and complaint‑handling rather than student behavior per se.
candidate_defs.square entries report more extensive ext: This bucket groups concrete claims about out‑of‑class offerings and physical/operational resources that square reviews repeatedly cite — e.g., championship athletics, standout band/theatre/robotics teams, aviation hangars, internship/STEM partnerships, lists of clubs, plus facility notes ranging from brand‑new campuses and 1:1 device rollouts to extreme overcrowding, long lunch lines, and outdated buildings. It captures program/facility/resource presence and capacity (distinct from classroom instruction or admin policy).
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms where square reviews allege active on‑campus fights, gang/drug presence, police/staff misconduct, recurring shelter‑in‑place events, sexual harassment or severe injuries and unsafe emergency infrastructure (examples: “constant fights,” “huge drug problem,” “Police liason officer beats up handicapped kid,” recurring non‑drill shelter‑in‑place events, and claims that administration/police turn a blind eye). Circle entries lack these recurring, acute safety/crime claims and instead focus on disciplinary or climate concerns without the same severity or evidence of on‑campus criminal activity.
candidate_defs.square entries report a richer, more for: This bucket captures many square reports of concrete program offerings and outcomes—IB and AP availability, honors/dual‑enrollment, named academies, extensive AP counts and dual‑credit pathways, strong music/theatre/JROTC/athletics, and explicit college placements or scholarships (examples: “IB programming,” “15 AP classes,” “Dual enrollment,” “award winning music education,” and full‑tuition scholarships). Circle reviews do not enumerate comparable formal programs or measurable matriculation evidence and instead emphasize classroom-level concerns or a smaller set of opportunities.
candidate_defs.square entries report more concrete staf: This bucket groups raw terms that accuse staff or leaders of explicit misconduct, opaque favoritism, punitive discipline, naming of specific personnel, lost transcripts, and governance/turnover problems (examples: named teacher allegations like ‘Marchaun McCready,’ claims of rigged student elections and administrative favoritism, ‘lost transcripts… eventually found,’ and high coach/teacher turnover tied to administration). Circle entries rarely supply the same level of named incidents or systemic governance accusations and instead focus on different operational or curricular gripes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more facility and: Raw terms in this bucket describe tangible campus and operational failures—building deterioration, pests and sanitation, non‑working intercoms, lack of A/C, overcrowded classrooms/portables, scheduling/stacked schedules, busing/transport problems, and supply/arts‑funding shortages (examples: “building may be falling apart,” “45‑minute vomit cleanup,” “no A/C throughout the whole school,” “AP Calculus AB had 45 students stuffed into a portable,” and problematic bus schedules). Circle entries do not raise this broad set of physical or systemic capacity failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more failures in s: This bucket groups complaints about mismanaged special‑education/IEP/504 provision, ineffective or hostile counseling and college advising, lack of mental‑health and LGBTQ supports, and graduation/placement errors (examples: “They are not reading IEPs,” “If your child is on a 504 plan expect that to be completely ignored,” “counselors are ineffective… tell parents they do not need to go to college,” and mis‑scheduled students losing college opportunities). Circle entries rarely report these systemic support‑service failures and often describe better individualized support or at least do not raise these programmatic breakdowns.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more acute safety: This bucket captures reviewer accounts of concrete on‑campus safety crises in Square schools (daily drug deals/overdoses, lockdowns, frequent fights, physical assaults, sexual‑assault mishandling, severe bullying, and targeted harassment of queer/POC/disabled students) that Circle reviews do not describe — e.g., 'kids overdosing and going to clinics,' 'we had to go into a lockdown once,' 'there are drug users in every bathroom,' 'a young man severely beaten in a classroom,' and 'the bullying is OBSCENE.'
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive adv: This bucket groups concrete programmatic and outcome evidence in Square reviews — listings of AP/honors/IB/magnet/dual enrollment, AP pass‑rates, external rankings, and alumni college matriculation/scholarships — that Circle lacks; examples include 'gifted program,' 'AP classes,' 'Dual College program with Bunker Hill,' 'ranked the 3rd best high school in Georgia,' and 'many students go on to college with an academic scholarship.'
candidate_defs.Square entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers governance and procedural complaints unique to Square reviews — unanswered superintendent/office calls, alleged hiring/favoritism tied to donors or athletes, stingy or misdirected budgeting (e.g., turf over curriculum), held transcripts/fees, and destroyed or mishandled records — illustrated by quotes like 'We went to the Superintendent who did nothing so left the district,' 'it all depends on who you are, how much money you have,' 'they will hold your transcripts... send you to collections,' and 'my daughter's education file was destroyed.'
candidate_defs.Square entries report more inconsistent,: This bucket captures reviewer descriptions of how discipline and day‑to‑day rules are applied unevenly in Square schools — delayed punishments, tolerated chronic disruptors, preferential treatment for athletes/affluent students, inconsistent dress‑code enforcement, and arbitrary grading/timetable enforcement — e.g. 'punishment is meted out days or weeks after the behavior,' 'If you are an athlete with talent, you will get away with whatever you want,' 'teachers wait until the last day of the grading period to put in their grades,' and 'the dress code... seems to only affect women.'
candidate_defs.Square entries report more Special Educa: This bucket groups explicit, actionable special‑needs and welfare failures reported more in Square reviews — IEP/504 noncompliance, punitive misplacement of struggling students, denial of standard diplomas, poor coordination between SPED and general ed, understaffed/ineffective counseling, and suicide‑related crises — illustrated by: 'didn't follow our daughter's IEP accommodations (by law they have to),' 'the ones with disabilities do not graduate with a high school diploma... they receive a certificate of completion,' 'High School could have had better communication in the Special Education with regular Ed teachers,' and 'Lake Orion has the highest suicide rate in the area.'

candidate_defs.square entries describe broader, higher‑: Square reviews repeatedly name robust arts/STEM/athletics programs and achievements (award‑winning band, Carnegie Hall invitations, national robotics, five‑time golf state champs, multiple magnets) and also call out resource/funding bias toward male athletics or coach favoritism; this bucket groups items where a school is characterized by extensive extracurricular opportunities and/or explicit athletic prioritization that circle reviews lack.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent/seve: Square contains concrete incidents and trends—multiple suicides, pervasive bullying, racial/LGBTQ harassment, vaping/drug use on campus, fights and students withdrawn by families—and describes slow or ineffective responses from staff/leadership, whereas circle reviews emphasize a caring community and do not report these crises; items in this bucket document safety/mental‑health incidents and response breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries document stricter/inflexi: Square reviews cite rigid rules and enforcement (phone bans, closed‑campus lunch, restroom closures, confiscating phones), arbitrary or punitive discipline, nonresponsive or unethical administrators, transfer/enrollment barriers, and broken commitments from front office/district leaders; this bucket captures school‑level policy, enforcement style, and governance/communication dysfunction contrasted with circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report consistently carin: Circle reviews repeatedly describe dependable, professional teachers, available counselors and a supportive climate; square reviews instead document large within‑school variation—teachers who are outstanding alongside teachers who are unresponsive, unprofessional, spend class time on personal matters, teach with outdated materials, or provide inconsistent special‑education/ELL accommodations—so this bucket groups contrasts in day‑to‑day instructional competence and support availability.
